# Chapter 1: Machine learning cloud regression and optimization

## The Swiss army knife of optimization

## Abstract

This chapter is not about regression performed in the cloud. It is about considering your data set as a cloud of points or observations, where the concepts of dependent and independent variables (the response and the features) are blurred. It is a very general type of regression, offering backward-compatibility with existing methods. Treating a variable as the response amounts to setting a constraint on the multivariate parameter, and results in an optimization algorithm with Lagrange multipliers. The originality comes from unifying and bringing under the same umbrella a number of disparate methods, each solving a part of the general problem and originating from various fields. I also propose a novel approach to logistic regression, and a generalized R-squared adapted to shape fitting, model fitting, feature selection, and dimensionality reduction. In one example, I show how the technique can perform unsupervised clustering, with confidence regions for the cluster centers obtained via parametric bootstrap.

Besides ellipse fitting and its importance in **computer vision**, an interesting application is a nonperiodic sum of periodic time series. While rarely discussed in machine learning circles, such models explain many phenomena, for instance, ocean tides. It is particular useful in time-continuous situations where the error is not a white noise, but instead smooth and continuous everywhere, for instance, granular temperature forecast. Another curious application is modeling meteorite shapes. Finally, my methodology is model free and data driven, with a focus on numerical stability. Prediction intervals and confidence regions are obtained via bootstrapping. I provide Python code and synthetic data generators for replication purposes.

### Keywords

curve fitting; unsupervised regression; logistic regression; constrained optimization; time series; clustering

## 1.1 Introduction: circle fitting

The goal is to unify all regression techniques and present a simple, generic framework to solve most problems dealing with fitting an equation to a data set. Currently, there are dozens of types of regressions, each with its own methodology and algorithm. Here I propose a single methodology and a single algorithm to solve all these problems.

The originality of my technique resides in my approach and methodology, rather than in the type of math or algorithm being used. Like all generic methods, it is rather abstract and one would think more difficult to learn and describe. To the contrary, I believe it is actually more intuitive and easier to grasp. First, the dependent variable and independent features are interchangeable: the concept of dependent variables is even absent in my methodology. Thus I call it “cloud regression”, as the data set is viewed as a cloud of points, with no particular axis or dimension being privileged unless explicitly required. Then the technique is model-free: it uses resampling and bootstrap to build prediction intervals, or confidence intervals for the regression coefficients.

A judicious choice of notations makes my methodology backward-compatible with all existing techniques. The concept of R-squared is slightly modified to offer extra possibilities: measuring the quality of the fit for the full model versus a submodel of your choice. In standard regression, the submodel is a constant and referred to as the base model. Here the submodel could be fitting a circle if the full model is about ellipses, or fitting a plane versus an hyperplane in standard linear regression.

All regression books and chapters for beginners start with fitting a line. Here the easiest example – the first one to be taught – is fitting a circle centered at the origin. Think about it for a moment: intuitively, the estimated radius is the average radius computed on the data points. Indeed, this is the solution produced by my technique. The second easiest case is then fitting a line involving a slope and an intercept. Both examples are a particular case of fitting a quadratic form (ellipsoid).

This presentation is intended to beginners. There are examples, just as in standard regression, where the solution is not unique. In my opinion, nonuniqueness should be embraced rather than avoided: in real life one would expect that multiple, different shapes can fit to a particular data set. Finding several of them provides more insights about your data. However, conditions needed for uniqueness are not discussed here: this is the topic of a more advanced presentation.

In many cases, thanks to an appropriate reparameterization, the solution is obtained using simple constrained optimization and Lagrange multipliers. It has more to do with elementary calculus than advanced matrix algebra. In particular, there is no explicit mention of **eigenvalues** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eigenvalues_and_eigenvectors)\] or **singular value decomposition** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singular_value_decomposition)\]. Also, the shape does not need to have derivatives, though if it does, a faster implementation is possible, with a Newton-like algorithm. Indeed, the shape may be differentiable nowhere: think about fitting a Brownian motion to a set of observations.

I provide examples using synthetic data \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synthetic_data)\] and Python code. One of them involves time series forecasting with two periods *p*, *q*![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si1.png) where *p*/*q*![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si2.png) is not a rational number. Since *p* and *q* are among the parameters to be estimated, this is a true nonlinear problem that cannot be transformed into something linear via a link function \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generalized_linear_model#Link_function)\], unlike (say) logistic regression. A real-life application, to benchmark the performance of the method, is predicting ocean tides: large, granular geospatial data sets are available to test the prediction algorithm in this nonlinear context.

Finally, “cloud regression” encompasses the **general linear model** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_linear_model)\], the **generalized linear model** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generalized_linear_model)\] (and thus logistic regression), as well as **weighted least squares** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generalized_least_squares#Weighted_least_squares)\] (and thus Bayesian regression). Via the mapping *z* ↦ *w*![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si3.png) discussed in Section [1.1.1](#Chp001_1-34_B9780443218576000059.xhtml#s0015), it can accommodate splines as in **adaptive regression splines** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multivariate_adaptive_regression_spline)\]. Both cloud regression and the **total least squares** method \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Total_least_squares)\] minimize the sum of the squared distances between the data points and the shape, though my method does not give the response (called the dependent variable by statisticians) a particular status: in other words, it also works in the standard situation where there is no response, but just a cloud of points instead. In addition, my technique handles truly nonlinear situations, unlike the generalized linear model. For that reason, I call it the mother of all regressions.

This is not the first time a regression technique does not discriminate between dependent and independent variables: **partial least squares** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partial_least_squares_regression)\] also allows for that. See also [\[5\]](#Chp001_1-34_B9780443218576000059.xhtml#br0025).

### 1.1.1 Previous versions of my method

The current version is much more general, simpler, and radically different from the first implementation. However, it may help to provide some historical context. Initially, the goal was to compute the sum of the squared distances between a set of points (the observations, or the “cloud”), and a prespecified shape *Γ*[*θ*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si4.png) (a line, plane, or circle) belonging to a parametric family driven by a multidimensional parameter *θ*.

The idea was as follows. Let *P*[∞]![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si5.png) be a fixed point located extremely far away from the shape, and *P* be a point of the training set. Draw the line *L*[*P*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si6.png) that goes through *P* and *P*[∞]![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si5.png), and find the intersection *Γ*[*θ*] ∩ *L*[*P*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si7.png) closest to *P*, between the shape and the line. Let *Q*[*θ*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si8.png) be this point. The point in question may not be unique or may not exist (depending on *θ*), but the distance *Δ*[*θ*](*P*) = ||*P* − *Q*[*θ*]||![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si9.png) is, assuming there is an intersection. Then find *θ*^(\*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si10.png) that minimizes the sum of *Δ*[*θ*](*P*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si11.png) computed over all training set points *P*. This *θ*^(\*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si10.png), if unique, determines the shape that best fits the data. Traditional projection-based techniques compute the exact distance between a point and a shape, and therefore require the shape to be differentiable. The method based on *P*[∞]![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si5.png) works with shapes that are not differentiable. Some particular cases in the new implementation produce similar or identical results to those obtained with the *P*[∞]![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si5.png) method.

If the shape in question is a hyperplane and the context is traditional multivariate linear regression, then the shape is defined by *g*(*w*, *θ*) = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si12.png) where *w* = (*y*, *x*[1], …, *x*[*m*])![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si13.png) and *g*(*w*, *θ*) = *θ*[0]*y* + (*θ*[1]*x*[1] + ⋯ + *θ*[*m*]*x*[*m*])![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si14.png). Here *y* corresponds to the dependent variable, *x*[1], …, *x*[*m*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si15.png) to the features, and *θ*[0], *θ*[1], …, *θ*[*m*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si16.png) are the regression coefficients, with the constraint *θ*[0] =  − 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si17.png). In the new methodology, the constraint *θ*[0] =  − 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si17.png) is handled using a Lagrange multiplier, but other than that it leads to the same traditional solution. If there is an intercept, then *x*[1] = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si18.png). In the end, the goal is to propose a technique that is both general and intuitive, following the modern trend of explainable AI \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Explainable_artificial_intelligence)\].

In a second version of my methodology (not the current version), I introduced a mapping system, which essentially is a change of coordinates associated to a link function. The goal was to transform the data so that after the mapping, it is more amenable to a simple solution. Also, it is an attempt at obtaining a scale-independent solution: whether your unit is a mile or a kilometer should have no impact on the solution. In its most general form, the observations and parameters are denoted as *z* and *φ*. The shape satisfies the equation *h*(*z*, *φ*) = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si19.png). The mapping is defined as *g*(*w*, *θ*) = *ξ*(*h*(*z*, *φ*))![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si20.png) where *ξ* : ℝ → ℝ![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si21.png) is a strictly monotonic function, with *w* = *ν*(*z*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si22.png) and *θ* = *ϕ*(*φ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si23.png), for some multivariate one-to-one mappings *ν* and *ϕ*. All the computations are done in the (*w*, *θ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si24.png)\-space, thought it is possible to revert back to the original (*z*, *φ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si25.png) when computations are done, if ever needed.

I eventually dropped both *ξ* and simply ignored *φ* and *ϕ*, leading to a less abstract model, yet covering all practical cases. Thus in the current version, *h*(*z*, *φ*) = *g*(*w*, *θ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si26.png), and we do not care about *φ*. We may as well use *φ* = *θ*![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si27.png). The mapping *ν* gives rise to spline regression in the new method. However, when splines are used, they are prespecified rather than estimated, to avoid overfitting. Typically, they are chosen to simplify the computations.

Finally, I was interested in some original dimension-reduction technique. Not a true data-reduction technique, but it allows you to reduce the number of parameters by a factor of 2: consider *w* and *θ* to be complex, rather than real numbers, for instance, via a mapping *z* ↦ *w*![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si3.png) from ℝ²![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si28.png) to ℂ![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si29.png), with *w* = *ν*(*z*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si22.png). A benefit is the possibility to use a **conformal map** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conformal_map)\] for *ν*, thus preserving angles. Such an example is the **log-polar map** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Log-polar_coordinates)\] *z* = exp (*w*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si30.png) with *g*(*w*, *θ*) = *z*^(*θ*) = exp (*θ**w*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si31.png), which corresponds to using the polar coordinate system with *θ*, *z*, *w* ∈ ℂ![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si32.png): it makes things easier when dealing with circular data. The next step was to look at quaternions to reduce the number of parameters by a factor of 4, but there are a number of challenges. Anyway, I promised to keep things simple in this introductory presentation, so I will not discuss complex or quaternion mappings here. This is the topic of future research.

It is interesting to note that the problem of circle fitting has been quite extensively studied, see [\[6\]](#Chp001_1-34_B9780443218576000059.xhtml#br0030). Essentially, these methods solve the problem using *φ* and they are not trivial. The solution based on my method involves working with *θ* and leads to a very classic algorithm with a simple solution. The price to pay is that the *θ* parameters are less obvious to interpret: they are the coefficients of a quadratic form. To the contrary, the direct solution involves *φ* parameters that have obvious meaning: the radius of the circle, its center, and (in case of an ellipse) the rotation angle. However, my approach makes it a lot easier to generalize to ellipses and even far more complicated shapes, or hyperplanes for that matter, while at the same time having a solution that is even simpler than those discussed in [\[6\]](#Chp001_1-34_B9780443218576000059.xhtml#br0030) and applicable to the circle only. Of course, in this case there is a one-to-one mapping between *φ* and *θ*, see [here](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/1810677/center-and-axis-of-quadratic-surface). So you can always retrieve *φ* from *θ*.

## 1.2 Methodology, implementation details, and caveats

I encourage you to first read Section [1.1.1](#Chp001_1-34_B9780443218576000059.xhtml#s0015), as it provides a good amount of context. This section describes the details of the methodology. For simplicity, I do not describe the most general case, but a case that is general enough to cover all practical applications. I start by introducing the concept of data (called point cloud), parameter, and shape.

The **data** set is denoted as *W*, and consists of *m* + 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si33.png) variables and *n* observations. Thus *W* is an *n* × (*m* + 1)![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si34.png) matrix as usual. The *k*th row corresponds to the *k*th observation *W*[*k*] = (*W*[*k*, 0], *W*[*k*, 1], …, *W*[*k*, *m* + 1])![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si35.png). For backward compatibility with traditional models, I use the notation *W*[*k*, 0] = *Y*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si36.png) for the dependent variable or response (if there is one), and (*X*[*k*, 1], …, *X*[*k*, *m*]) = (*W*[*k*, 1], …, *W*[*k*, *m* + 1])![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si37.png) for the independent variables of features. The column vector corresponding to the response is denoted as *Y*, and the *n* × *m*![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si38.png) matrix representing the independent variables is denoted as *X*. The whole data set *W* is referred to as the point cloud.

The **parameter** is a multivariate column vector denoted as *θ* = (*θ*[0], *θ*[1], …, *θ*[*d*])![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si39.png), with *d* + 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si40.png) components. Typically, *d* = *m*![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si41.png) and *θ* satisfies some constraint, specified by *η*(*θ*) = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si42.png) for some function *η*. The most common functions are *η*(*θ*) = *θ*^(*T*)*θ* − 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si43.png), *η*(*θ*) = *θ*[0] + 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si44.png), and *η*(*θ*) = (*θ*[0] + ⋯ + *θ*[*d*]) − 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si45.png). Here ^(*T*) denotes the matrix/vector transposition operator.

The purpose is to fit a **shape** to the point cloud. The most typical shapes, after proper mapping, are hyperplanes or quadratic forms (ellipsoids). The former is a particular case of the latter. The shape belongs to a parametric family of equations driven by the multivariate parameter *θ*. The equation of the shape is *g*(*w*, *θ*) = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si12.png), for some function *g*. Typical examples include *g*(*w*, *θ*) = *w**θ*![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si46.png) and *g*(*w*, *θ*) = *w**θ* − 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si47.png), with *d* = *m*![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si41.png). The former usually involves an intercept: *X*[*k*, 1] = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si48.png) for all *k* = 1, …, *n*![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si49.png). Keep in mind that *w* and *θ* are vectors, but *g*(*w*, *θ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si50.png) is a real number, not a vector. Thus *wθ* represents a **dot product** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dot_product)\].

### 1.2.1 Solution, R-squared, and backward compatibility

The shape that best fits the data corresponds to *θ* = *θ*^(\*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si51.png), obtained by minimizing the squares:

$\\theta^{\\ast} = \\underset{\\theta}{\\arg⁡\\min}\\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{n}g^{2}(W\_{k},\\theta).$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si52.png)(1.1) 

The solution may not be unique. Uniqueness and numerical stability will be addressed in a future article, but the basics are covered in this book. The constraint *η*(*θ*) = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si42.png) guarantees that the solution requires solving a (sometimes nonlinear) system of *d* + 2![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si53.png) equations with *d* + 2![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si53.png) unknowns. In some cases, *d* ≤ *m*![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si54.png) to avoid **model identifiability** issues \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Identifiability)\]. Also, a large *d* may result in overfitting \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overfitting)\]. Then, you want *n* > *d*![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si55.png) otherwise the solution may not be unique unless you add more constraints on *θ*. The solution *θ*^(\*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si10.png) is obtained by solving the system

$\\left\\{ \\begin{aligned} {\\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{n}\\nabla\_{\\theta}\\lbrack g^{2}(W\_{k},\\theta)\\rbrack} & {= \\lambda\\nabla\_{\\theta}\\lbrack\\eta(\\theta)\\rbrack,} \\\\ {\\eta(\\theta)} & {= 0,} \\\\ \\end{aligned} \\right.$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si56.png)(1.2) 

where ∇[*θ*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si57.png) is the gradient operator with respect to *θ* \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gradient)\], and *λ* is called the **Lagrange multiplier** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagrange_multiplier)\]. This is a classic constrained convex optimization problem. The top part of [(1.2)](#Chp001_1-34_B9780443218576000059.xhtml#deq2) consists of a system of *d* + 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si40.png) equations with *d* + 2![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si53.png) unknowns *θ*[0], …, *θ*[*d*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si58.png), and *λ*. The bottom part is a single equation with *d* + 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si40.png) unknowns *θ*[0], …, *θ*[*d*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si58.png). Combined together, it constitutes a system of *d* + 2![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si53.png) equations with *d* + 2![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si53.png) unknowns. Note the analogy with **Lasso regression** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lasso_\(statistics\))\] when *η*(*θ*) = *θ*^(*T*)*θ* − 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si43.png), that is, when *θ*^(*T*)*θ* = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si59.png).

The **mean squared error** (MSE) relative to a particular *θ* is defined as

$\\text{MSE}(\\theta) = \\frac{1}{n}\\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{n}g^{2}(W\_{k},\\theta) \\geqslant \\text{MSE}(\\theta^{\\ast}).$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si60.png)(1.3) 

The inequality in [(1.3)](#Chp001_1-34_B9780443218576000059.xhtml#deq3) is an immediate consequence of [(1.1)](#Chp001_1-34_B9780443218576000059.xhtml#deq1). Now define the R-squared with respect to *θ* as

$R^{2}(\\theta) = 1 - \\frac{\\text{MSE}(\\theta^{\\ast})}{\\text{MSE}(\\theta)}.$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si61.png)(1.4) 

It follows immediately that 0 ≤ *R*²(*θ*) ≤ 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si62.png). A perfect fit corresponds to MSE(*θ*^(\*)) = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si63.png) (the whole cloud residing on the shape). In that case, if *θ* ≠ *θ*^(\*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si64.png) and the optimum *θ*^(\*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si10.png) is unique, then *R*²(*θ*) = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si65.png).

In traditional linear regression, the R-squared is defined as *R*²(*θ*[\*])![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si66.png) where *θ*[\*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si67.png) is the optimum *θ* for the base model. The base model corresponds to all the coefficients *θ*[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si68.png) attached to the independent variables set to zero, except the one attached to the intercept. In other words, in the base model, the predicted *Y* is constant, equal to the empirical mean of *Y*. As a result, MSE(*θ*[\*]) = Var\[*Y*\]![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si69.png), the empirical variance of *Y*. A consequence is that *R*²(*θ*[\*])![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si66.png) is the square of the correlation between the observed response *Y*, and the predicted response of the full model.

Backward compatibility with traditional linear regression works as follows. The standard univariate regression corresponds to *g*(*w*, *θ*) = *w**θ* = *θ*[0]*y* + *θ*[1]*x* + *θ*[2]![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si70.png), with the constraint *θ*[0] =  − 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si17.png). Thus *g*(*w*, *θ*) = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si12.png) if and only if *y* = *θ*[1]*x* + *θ*[2]![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si71.png). This generalizes to multivariate regression as well. A more elegant formulation in the new methodology is to replace the constraint *θ*[0] =  − 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si17.png) by the symmetric constraint *θ*[0]² + *θ*[1]² + *θ*[2]² = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si72.png). Note that *w* is a row vector and *θ* is a column vector.

### 1.2.2 Upgrades to the model

By a model, I mean the general setting of the method: there is no probabilistic model involved in this discussion. **Prediction intervals** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prediction_interval)\] for the individual error *g*(*W*[*k*], *θ*^(\*))![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si73.png) at each data point *W*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si74.png) (or for the estimated response attached to *Y*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si75.png), if there is an independent variable) and confidence regions \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confidence_region)\] for *θ*^(\*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si10.png) can be obtained via resampling and bootstrapping \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bootstrapping_\(statistics\))\]. This is also true for points outside the training set.

Also, the squares can be replaced by absolute values, as in **quantile regression** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantile_regression)\], to minimize the impact of outliers and for scale preservation: if a variable is measured in years, then squares are expressed in squared years, a metric that is meaningless. This leads to a modified, better metric to assess the quality of the fit, replacing the R-squared. See Section [7.4](#Chp007_113-129_B9780443218576000114.xhtml) about “performance assessment” in Chapter [7](#Chp007_113-129_B9780443218576000114.xhtml), for alternatives to the R-squared. The goodness-of-fit (say, the R-squared) should be measured on the validation set \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Training,_validation,_and_test_data_sets)\] even though *θ*^(\*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si10.png) is computed on a subset of the training set: this is a standard practice, called cross-validation \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross-validation_\(statistics\))\], illustrated on synthetic data in Chapter [8](#Chp008_131-145_B9780443218576000126.xhtml) about fuzzy regression.

Now, let us get back to the R-squared. In standard linear regression, the R-squared is defined as *R*²(*θ*[\*])![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si66.png) via formula [(1.4)](#Chp001_1-34_B9780443218576000059.xhtml#deq4), where *θ*[\*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si67.png) is the optimum *θ* for the base model (the predicted response is constant, equal the mean of *Y* for the base model). In the new methodology, there may be no response. Still, the definition of *R*²![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si76.png) extends to that situation, and is compatible with the traditional version. What is more, it leads to many possible *R*²![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si76.png), one for each submodel (not just the base model), and this is true too for the standard regression. A submodel corresponds to adding constraints on the parameter vector *θ* or, in other words, working with a subset of the parameter space. Let *θ*[\*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si67.png) be the optimum for a specific submodel, while *θ*^(\*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si10.png) is the optimum for the full model. Then the definition of *R*²![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si76.png), depending on *θ*[\*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si67.png), is unchanged. It could not be any simpler!

Now you can use *R*²![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si76.png) for model comparison purposes and even for feature selection \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feature_selection)\]. You can test the improvement obtained by using the full model over a submodel, with the metric *S*(*θ*[\*]) = *R*²(*θ*^(\*)) − *R*²(*θ*[\*])![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si77.png). Here *θ*[\*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si67.png) is the optimum *θ* attached to the submodel. Obviously, 0 ≤ *S*(*θ*[\*]) ≤ 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si78.png). The larger *S*(*θ*[\*])![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si79.png), the bigger the improvement. Conversely, the smaller, the better the performance of the submodel. Examples include fitting an ellipse (full model) versus fitting a circle (submodel) or using all the features (full model) versus using a subset (submodel). You can compare submodels and rank them according to *S*(*θ*[\*])![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si79.png). This allows you to identify the smallest set of features that achieve a good enough *S*(*θ*[\*])![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si79.png), for dimensionality reduction purposes \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimensionality_reduction)\].

Finally, another update consists of using positive weights *ψ*[*k*](*θ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si80.png) in formula [(1.1)](#Chp001_1-34_B9780443218576000059.xhtml#deq1). This amounts to performing **weighted regression** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generalized_least_squares#Weighted_least_squares)\]. For instance, data points far away from the optimum shape, that is, observations with a large *g*²(*W*[*k*], *θ*^(\*))![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si81.png), may be discarded to reduce the impact of outliers. Or the weights can be used to balance the coefficients *θ*[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si68.png), in an effort to achieve scale-invariance in the expression *wθ*. Then the top system in [(1.2)](#Chp001_1-34_B9780443218576000059.xhtml#deq2) becomes

$\\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{n}\\psi\_{k}(\\theta)\\nabla\_{\\theta}\\lbrack g^{2}(W\_{k},\\theta)\\rbrack + \\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{n}g^{2}(W\_{k},\\theta)\\nabla\_{\\theta}\\lbrack\\psi\_{k}(\\theta)\\rbrack = \\lambda\\nabla\_{\\theta}\\lbrack\\eta(\\theta)\\rbrack.$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si82.png)(1.5) 

## 1.3 Case studies

In Section [1.3.1](#Chp001_1-34_B9780443218576000059.xhtml#s0040), I show how to solve the logistic regression. The first version is standard least squares, to further illustrate backward compatibility with the traditional method. The second illustrates how it could be done if you want to follow the spirit of the new methodology. Then I discuss two fundamental examples based on synthetic data.

### 1.3.1 Logistic regression, two ways

In the traditional setting, *w* = (*y*, *x*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si83.png) where *y* is the response and *x* the features. For the logistic regression \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logistic_regression)\], we have

*g*(*w*, *θ*) = *g*(*y*, *x*) = *y* − *F*(*x**θ*), with   *x**θ* = *θ*[1]*x*[1] + ⋯ + *θ*[*m*]*x*[*m*].

![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si84.png)

Here *x*[1] = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si18.png) corresponds to the intercept, thus we have *m* − 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si85.png) actual features *x*[2], *x*[3], …, *x*[*m*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si86.png). There is no constraint on the parameter *θ*, thus there is no function *η*(*θ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si87.png). In formula [(1.2)](#Chp001_1-34_B9780443218576000059.xhtml#deq2), *η*(*θ*) = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si42.png) should be ignored, and *λ* = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si88.png). The function *F* is a cumulative distribution function with a symmetric density around the origin. In this case, *F*(*x**θ*) = 1/(1 + exp \[ − *x**θ*\])![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si89.png) is the standard **logistic distribution** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logistic_distribution)\].

In the new methodology, one would proceed as follows. First, the original data is denoted as *z* = (*v*, *u*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si90.png). The logistic regression applies to the original data. Here *v* is the response, and *u* the feature vector. The parameter *θ* is unchanged (not subject to a mapping), and still denoted as *θ*. This regression can be stated as

*g*(*z*, *θ*) = *g*(*v*, *u*) = *v* − *F*(*u**θ*), with   *u**θ* = *θ*[1]*u*[1] + … + *θ*[*m*]*u*[*m*].

![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si91.png)

The first step is to map *z* = (*v*, *u*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si90.png) onto *w* = (*y*, *x*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si83.png), with the hope of simplifying the problem, as discussed in Section [1.1.1](#Chp001_1-34_B9780443218576000059.xhtml#s0015). This is done via the link function *y* = *F*^( − 1)(*v*) = log \[*v*/(1 − *v*)\]![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si92.png) and *u* = *x*![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si93.png). Now we are back to

*g*(*z*, *θ*) = *g*(*w*, *θ*) = *g*(*y*, *x*; *θ*) = *y* − *x**θ*, with   *x**θ* = *θ*[1]*x*[1] + … + *θ*[*m*]*x*[*m*].

![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si94.png)

This is how standard linear regression is expressed in the new framework. But it is still the traditional linear regression, with nothing new. The final step consists in extending *θ*, adding one component *θ*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si95.png) to *θ*[1], …, *θ*[*m*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si96.png). With the new *θ* (still denoted as *θ*) we have *g*(*w*, *θ*) = *w**θ* = *θ*[0]*w*[0] + ⋯ + *θ*[*m*]*w*[*m*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si97.png). You need to add one constraint on *θ*. The constraint *θ*[0] =  − 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si17.png), that is, *η*(*θ*) = *θ*[0] + 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si44.png), yields the exact same solution as traditional linear regression. But *θ*^(*T*)*θ* = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si59.png), that is, *η*(*θ*) = *θ*^(*T*)*θ* − 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si43.png), makes the problem somehow symmetric, and more elegant.

However, in many applications, the response *v* in the original space is either 0 or 1, such as cancer versus noncancer, or fraud versus nonfraud. In this case, the link function is undefined. The mapping with the link function works if the response is a proportion, strictly between zero and one. Otherwise, the standard logistic regression is the best approach. A possible workaround is to use for *F* a distribution with a finite support, such as uniform on \[*a*, *b*\]![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si98.png). After all, the observed values (the features) are always bounded anyway. Then, intuitively, given *θ*, estimates of *a* and *b* are proportional respectively to the minimum and maximum of *U*[*k*]*θ*![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si99.png), over *k* = 1, …, *n*![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si49.png).

This suggests a new approach to logistic regression. First, use the model *v* = *F*[*θ*](*u**θ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si100.png) in the (*v*, *u*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si101.png)\-space, where 0 ≤ *v* ≤ 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si102.png) and *F*[*θ*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si103.png) is the empirical distribution \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empirical_distribution_function)\] of *uθ* given *θ*. Then choose *θ*^(\*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si10.png) that minimizes the sum of squared residuals:

$\\theta^{\\ast} = \\underset{\\theta}{\\arg⁡\\min}\\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{n}g^{2}(V\_{k},U\_{k};\\theta) = \\underset{\\theta}{\\arg⁡\\min}\\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{n}{(V\_{k} - F\_{\\theta}(U\_{k}\\theta))}^{2}.$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si104.png)

Remember, *U*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si105.png) is a row vector, and *θ* is a column vector; the dot product *U*[*k*]*θ*![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si99.png) is a real number. Also, *V*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si106.png) is the binary response attached to the *k*th observation, while *U*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si105.png) is the corresponding *m*\-dimensional feature vector, both in the original (*v*, *u*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si101.png)\-space. The empirical distribution *F*[*θ*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si103.png) is computed as follows: *F*[*θ*](*t*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si107.png) is the proportion of observed feature vectors, among *U*[1], …, *U*[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si108.png), satisfying *U*[*k*]*θ* ≤ *t*![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si109.png). Such a method could be called **CDF regression**. You can use the methodology presented here to solve it, but it would be very computer-intensive, because *F*[*θ*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si103.png) depends on *θ* in a nonobvious way. The predicted value for *V*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si106.png), is *F*[*θ*^(\*)](*U*[*k*]*θ*^(\*))![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si110.png) in this case.

### 1.3.2 Ellipsoid and hyperplane fitting

This is a fundamental example, with hyperplanes being a particular case of ellipsoids. I illustrate the methodology with an example based on synthetic data, in a small dimension. The idea is to represent the shape with a quadratic form. In two dimensions, the equations is

*θ*[0]*x*² + *θ*[1]*x**y* + *θ*[2]*y*² + *θ*[3]*x* + *θ*[4]*y* + *θ*[5] = 0.

![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si111.png)

The trick is to rewrite it with artificial variables *w*[0] = *x*²![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si112.png), *w*[1] = *x**y*![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si113.png), *w*[2] = *y*²![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si114.png), *w*[3] = *x*![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si115.png), *w*[4] = *y*![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si116.png), *w*[5] = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si117.png), so that we can use the general framework with *g*(*w*, *θ*) = *w**θ*![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si46.png). Again, *wθ* is the dot product. To avoid the trivial solution *θ*^(\*) = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si118.png), let us add the constraint *θ*^(*T*)*θ* = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si59.png), that is, *η*(*θ*) = *θ*^(*T*)*θ* − 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si43.png). Then, *θ*^(\*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si10.png) is solution of the system

$\\left\\{ \\begin{aligned} {(W^{T}W - \\lambda I)\\theta} & {= 0,} \\\\ {\\theta^{T}\\theta} & {= 1.} \\\\ \\end{aligned} \\right.$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si119.png)(1.6) 

The above solution is correct in any dimension. It is a direct application of [(1.2)](#Chp001_1-34_B9780443218576000059.xhtml#deq2). Here *W* is the *n* × 6![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si120.png) matrix containing the *n* observations. Thus, *W*[*k*0] = *X*[*k*]²![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si121.png), *W*[*k*1] = *X*[*k*]*Y*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si122.png), *W*[*k*2] = *Y*[*k*]²![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si123.png), *W*[*k*3] = *X*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si124.png), *W*[*k*4] = *Y*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si125.png), *W*[*k*5] = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si126.png). The Python code and additional details, for a slightly different version with a slightly different *η*(*θ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si87.png), can be found [here](https://scipython.com/blog/direct-linear-least-squares-fitting-of-an-ellipse/). I use it in my own code, available on my GitHub repository, [here](https://github.com/VincentGranville/Machine-Learning/blob/main/Source%20Code/fittingEllipse.py), under the name fittingEllipse.py. It is based on Halir's article about fitting ellipses [\[2\]](#Chp001_1-34_B9780443218576000059.xhtml#br0010).

The Python code checks if the fitted shape is actually an ellipse. However, in the spirit of my methodology, it does not matter if it is an ellipse, a parabola, a hyperbola, or even a line. The uniqueness of the solution is unimportant: indeed, if two very different solutions (say, an ellipse and a parabola) yield the same minimum mean squared error and are thus both optimal, it says something about the data set, something interesting to know. However, it would be interesting to compute *R*²(*θ*[\*])![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si66.png) using formula [(1.4)](#Chp001_1-34_B9780443218576000059.xhtml#deq4), where *θ*[\*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si67.png) corresponds to a circle. It would tell whether the full model (ellipse) over a significant improvement over the circle submodel.

Ellipsoid fitting shares some similarities with multivariate polynomial regression [\[7\]](#Chp001_1-34_B9780443218576000059.xhtml#br0035). The differences are:

*   •  Ellipse fitting is a “full” model; in the polynomial regression *y* = *θ*[1] + *θ*[2]*x* + *θ*[3]*x*²![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si127.png), the terms *y*²![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si128.png) and *xy* are always missing.
*   •  Polynomial regression fits a curve that is unbounded, such as *y* = *x*²![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si129.png), resulting in poor fitting; to the contrary, in ellipse fitting (if the solution is actually an ellipse) the solution is bounded.
*   •  To get as many terms in polynomial regression as in ellipse fitting, the only way is to increase the degree of the polynomial, which further increases the instability of the solution.

Finally, Umbach [\[6\]](#Chp001_1-34_B9780443218576000059.xhtml#br0030) proposes a different approach to ellipse fitting. It is significantly more complicated, and indeed, they stopped at the circle. In short, their method directly estimates the center, semiaxis lengths, and rotation angle via least squares, as opposed to estimating the coefficients in the quadratic form that represents the ellipse. More on parametric curves can be found in Chapter [6](#Chp006_103-111_B9780443218576000102.xhtml) on shape recognition.

#### 1.3.2.1 Curve fitting: 250 examples in one video

Ellipse fitting is performed by setting mode='CurveFitting' in the Python code. The program automatically creates a number of ellipses, specified by their parameters (center, lengths of semiaxes, and rotation angle), then generates a different training set for each ellipse, and outputs the result of the fitting procedure as an image. The images are then bundled together to produce a video, and an animated gif. Each image features a particular ellipse and training set, as well as the fitted ellipse based on the training set. The ellipse parameters are set by the variable params in the code: it is an array with five components. The number of ellipses is set by the parameter nframes, which also determines the number of frames in the output video.

Actually, the program does a little more: it works with ellipse arcs. Using the centroid of the training set to estimate the center of the ellipse does not work in this case. So the program retrieves the original, unknown ellipse even if the training set consists of points randomly distributed around a portion of that ellipse. The arc in question is determined by a lower and upper angle in polar coordinates, denoted respectively as tmin and tmax in the code, with tmin=0 and tmax=2*π* corresponding to the full ellipse.

The training set consists of *n* observations generated as follows. First sample *n* points on the ellipse (or the arc you are interested in). Then perturb these points by adding some noise. You have two options: noise\_CDF='Uniform' and noise\_CDF='Normal'. The amount of noise is specified by the parameter noise in the code. For the uniform distribution on the square \[ − *a*, *a*\] × \[ − *a*, *a*\]![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si130.png), noise represents *a*. For the bivariate normal distribution with covariance matrix *σ*²*I*![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si131.png) where *I* is the identity matrix, it represents *σ*²![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si132.png). There are various ways of sampling points on an ellipse. Three options are offered here, set by the parameter sampling. They are described in Section [1.3.2.3](#Chp001_1-34_B9780443218576000059.xhtml#s0060), in the paragraph “Sampling points on an ellipse arc”. The option 'Enhanced' is the only one performing stochastic sampling (points randomly picked up on the ellipse), and used in [Fig. 1.2](#Chp001_1-34_B9780443218576000059.xhtml#f0015).

In [Fig. 1.2](#Chp001_1-34_B9780443218576000059.xhtml#f0015), the size of the training set is *n* = 30![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si133.png) while in [Fig. 1.1](#Chp001_1-34_B9780443218576000059.xhtml#f0010), *n* = 250![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si134.png). In the code, *n* is represented by the variable npts. The training set is colored in red (light gray in print version), the fitted ellipse in blue (dark gray in print version), and if present on the image as in [Fig. 1.2](#Chp001_1-34_B9780443218576000059.xhtml#f0015), the true ellipse is in black. The latter appears as a polygon rather than an ellipse because the sampled points on the true ellipse are joined by segments, and *n* is small. Typically, the true and fitted ellipses are very close to each other, although there is a systematic bias too small to be noticed to the naked eye unless the ellipse eccentricity is high. More on this soon.

![Figure 1.1 Fitted ellipse (blue; dark gray in print version), given the training set (red; light gray in print version) distributed around a partial arc.](images/B9780443218576000059/gr001.jpg)

[Figure 1.1](#Chp001_1-34_B9780443218576000059.xhtml#cf0140) Fitted ellipse (blue; dark gray in print version), given the training set (red; light gray in print version) distributed around a partial arc.

![Figure 1.2 Confidence region in blue (dark gray in print version), n = 30 training set points; 50 training sets (left) vs 150 (right).](images/B9780443218576000059/gr002.jpg)

Figure 1.2 Confidence region in blue (dark gray in print version), *n* = 30 training set points; 50 training sets (left) vs 150 (right).

[Table 1.1](#Chp001_1-34_B9780443218576000059.xhtml#t0010) compares the exact parameter values (set by the user) of the true ellipse in [Fig. 1.2](#Chp001_1-34_B9780443218576000059.xhtml#f0015), to a few sets of estimated values obtained by least squares. Each set of estimates is computed using a different training set. All training sets are produced with same amount and type of noise, to give an idea of the variance of the parameter estimates at a specific level of noise. The five parameters are the ellipse center (*x*[0], *y*[0])![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si135.png), the lengths of the semiaxes (*a*[*p*], *b*[*p*])![Image](images/B9780443218576000059/si136.png), and the ellipse orientation (the rotation angle *ϕ*).
