Nodes with fewer than 10 articles are classified using the regression method via the LINEST Excel function, rather than the mini decision trees. Instead of standard regression, you can use a simplified logistic regression, as described in Section [1.3.1](#Chp001_1-34_B9780443218576000059.xhtml). There are ![Image](images/B9780443218576000060/fx006.jpg)observations (articles) and 74 nodes in the training set. By grouping all nodes with less than 10 observations into one node, we get down to 24 nodes. Correlations between individual features and the response *p* (logarithm of pageviews, denoted as pv in [Table 2.2](#Chp002_35-47_B9780443218576000060.xhtml#t0015)) is very low. Thus individual features have no predictive power. They must be combined together to gain predictive power. The full HDT method is superior to either the mini decision trees, or the regression model taken separately.

The index in [Table 2.2](#Chp002_35-47_B9780443218576000060.xhtml#t0015) is the pv of the node in question, divided by the average pv across all nodes. It measures the performance of the node. Finally, an article is classified as good or bad depending on whether its index is significantly larger or lower than one. The thresholds are user-defined. (See [Fig. 2.1](#Chp002_35-47_B9780443218576000060.xhtml#f0020).)

![Figure 2.1 Output from the Excel version of HDT.](images/B9780443218576000060/gr001.jpg)

[Figure 2.1](#Chp002_35-47_B9780443218576000060.xhtml#cf0070) Output from the Excel version of HDT.

### 2.3.3 Python code and dataset

The input dataset HDTdata4.txt is on my GitHub repository, [here](https://github.com/VincentGranville/Machine-Learning/blob/main/Source%20Code/HDTdata4.txt). The Python program HDT.py is listed below and can also be found on my GitHub repository, [here](https://github.com/VincentGranville/Machine-Learning/blob/main/Source%20Code/HDT.py). The output file hdt-out2.txt contains the usable key–value pairs (nodes) corresponding to popular articles, and the list of article IDs for each of these nodes. Finally, the variable pv represents *p*, the logarithm of the pageview count. The bivariate combinations (title keyword, article category) constitute the keys of the hash table list\_pv, while the pv are the hash table values. Keywords are either one- or two-token. For one-token keywords, the second token is marked as N/A. In short, keyword is a bivariate entity.

As for the error rate, since the focus is on producing good articles, I am interested only in minimizing the number of bad articles flagged as good: the false positives. To reduce error rates or the proportion of unclassified nodes, use more features (for instance, more of those listed in [Table 2.1](#Chp002_35-47_B9780443218576000060.xhtml#t0010)), three-token keywords, a larger training set, a better keyword cleaning mechanism, and fine-tune the parameters.

Of course, if you choose the option mode='perfect\_fit' in the program, your false positive rate drops to 0% on the training set, but doing may lower the performance on the validation set, and may leave many nodes unclassified. On the plus side, you have much fewer parameters to fine-tune: pv\_threshold\_good, pv\_threshold\_bad, and the minimum size of a usable node (the variable n in the code). The first two can be set respectively to 5% above and 10% below the global average pv. The minimum node size should be set above 2, and ideally above 5, though a large value results in more unclassified nodes. For mode='robust method', the parameters in the conditional statements defining good\_node and bad\_node were set manually based on an average pv of 6.83. These choices can be automated.

In the end, unclassified nodes are classified via regression in the spreadsheet (see Section [2.3.2](#Chp002_35-47_B9780443218576000060.xhtml#s0055)), but this has not yet been implemented in the Python code. But for my purpose (identifying what makes an article good), I did not need to add the regression part, as the mini decision trees alone (the nodes) provide enough valuable insights.

![](images/B9780443218576000060/gr002.jpg)

## 2.4 Model-free confidence intervals and perfect nodes

Node N-100-000000 in the spreadsheet has an average pv of 5.85. It consists of 10 articles with the following pv: 5.10, 5.10, 5.56, 5.56, 5.66, 5.69, 6.01, 6.19, 6.80, 6.80![Image](images/B9780443218576000060/si8.png). The 15th and 85th percentiles are 5.26 and 6.68, respectively, when computed with the Percentile function in Excel. Thus, \[5.26, 6.68\]![Image](images/B9780443218576000060/si9.png) is a 70% **confidence interval** (CI) for pv, for the node in question.

The whole CI including its upper bound is below the average pv of 6.83. In fact this node corresponds to articles posted after 2014, not a blog or forum question (it could be a video or event announcement), and with a title containing none of the keyword features in the spreadsheet (columns K:P in the data tab). This node has a maximum predictive power, in the sense that 100% of the articles that it contains are bad, and 0% are good. This would also be true if it was the other way around, with Good swapped with Bad. Such a node is called a **perfect node**. When selecting the option mode='Perfect fit' in the Python code, the method looks at perfect nodes only. The concept of **predictive power** is further discussed in Section [18.4.2](#Chp018_361-386_B9780443218576000229.xhtml).

### 2.4.1 Interesting asymptotic properties of confidence intervals

I focus here on traditional model-free confidence intervals, as computed in the above paragraphs. The reader should be aware that there are other ways to define them, for instance, **credible intervals** in the context of **Bayesian inference** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayesian_inference)\], or Bayesian-like **dual confidence intervals** as in Section [18.3](#Chp018_361-386_B9780443218576000229.xhtml).

In almost all cases, as the number *n* of observations becomes large within a node, the length of the confidence interval, in this case for the expected pv, is asymptotically *L*[*n*] ∼ *α**n*^(*β*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000060/si13.png). I discuss in an upcoming paper how to estimate *α* and *β*. The order of magnitude of the range *R*[*n*] = max (`pv`) − min (`pv`)![Image](images/B9780443218576000060/si14.png) computed on a node with *n* observations, depends on the distribution of pv, and more specifically, on the type of this distribution. The result is summarized in [Table 2.3](#Chp002_35-47_B9780443218576000060.xhtml#t0020), and discussed in the same upcoming article. In practice, pv may have a **mixture distribution**.

[Table 2.3](#Chp002_35-47_B9780443218576000060.xhtml#cf0085)

Order of magnitude for the expectation and standard deviation of the range *R*[*n*].

 
| pv distribution || Type || E\[*R*[*n*]\] || Stdev\[*R*[*n*]\] |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Uniform || short tail || 1 || 1/*n* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Gaussian || medium tail || $\\sqrt{\\log n}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000060/si10.png) || $1/\\sqrt{n}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000060/si11.png) |
| Exponential || fat tail || log *n*![Image](images/B9780443218576000060/si12.png) || 1 |

![Image](images/B9780443218576000060/t0020.png)

# Chapter 3: Gentle introduction to linear algebra – synthetic time series

## Abstract

This simple introduction to matrix theory offers a refreshing perspective on the subject. Using a basic concept that leads to a simple formula for the power of a matrix, I show how it can solve time series, Markov chains, linear regression, linear recurrence equations, pseudoinverse and square root of a matrix, data compression, principal components analysis (PCA) or dimension reduction, and other machine learning problems. These problems are usually solved with more advanced matrix algebra, including eigenvalues, diagonalization, generalized inverse matrices, and other types of matrix normalization. My approach is more intuitive and thus appealing to professionals who do not have a strong mathematical background, or who have forgotten what they learned in math textbooks. It will also appeal to physicists and engineers, and to professionals more familiar or interested in calculus, than in matrix algebra. Finally, it leads to simple algorithms, for instance, for matrix inversion. The classical statistician or data scientist will find my approach somewhat intriguing. The core of the methodology is the characteristic polynomial of a matrix, and in particular, the roots with lowest or largest moduli. It leads to a numerically stable method to solve Vandermonde systems, and thus, many linear algebra problems. Simulations include a curious fractal time series that looks incredibly smooth.

### Keywords

autoregressive models; time series; Vandermonde matrix; Weibull distribution; linear regression

This simple introduction to matrix theory offers a refreshing perspective on the subject. Using a basic concept that leads to a simple formula for the power of a matrix, I show how it can solve time series, Markov chains, linear regression, linear recurrence equations, pseudoinverse and square root of a matrix, data compression, principal components analysis (PCA) or dimension reduction, and other machine learning problems. These problems are usually solved with more advanced matrix algebra, including eigenvalues, diagonalization, generalized inverse matrices, and other types of matrix normalization. My approach is more intuitive and thus appealing to professionals who do not have a strong mathematical background, or who have forgotten what they learned in math textbooks. It will also appeal to physicists and engineers, and to professionals more familiar or interested in calculus, than in matrix algebra. Finally, it leads to simple algorithms, for instance, for matrix inversion. The classical statistician or data scientist will find my approach somewhat intriguing. The core of the methodology is the characteristic polynomial of a matrix, and in particular, the roots with lowest or largest moduli. It leads to a numerically stable method to solve Vandermonde systems, and thus, many linear algebra problems. Simulations include a curious fractal time series that looks incredibly smooth.

## 3.1 Power of a matrix

This is not a traditional tutorial on linear algebra. The material presented here, in a compact style, is rarely taught in college classes. It covers a wide range of topics, while avoiding excessive use of jargon or advanced math. The fundamental tool is the power of a matrix, and its byproduct, the characteristic polynomial. It can solve countless problems, as discussed later in this chapter, with illustrations. It has more to do with calculus, than matrix algebra.

For simplicity, in this section, I illustrate the methodology for a 2 × 2![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si1.png) matrix denoted as *A*. The generalization is straightforward. I provide a simple formula for the *n*th power of *A*, where *n* is a positive integer. I then extend the formula to *n* =  − 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si2.png) (the most useful case) and to noninteger values of *n*. Using the notation

$A = \\begin{pmatrix} a & b \\\\ c & d \\\\ \\end{pmatrix},\\quad\\text{~with~}A^{n} = \\begin{pmatrix} a\_{n} & b\_{n} \\\\ c\_{n} & d\_{n} \\\\ \\end{pmatrix} = \\begin{pmatrix} a & b \\\\ c & d \\\\ \\end{pmatrix} \\cdot \\begin{pmatrix} a\_{n - 1} & b\_{n - 1} \\\\ c\_{n - 1} & d\_{n - 1} \\\\ \\end{pmatrix},$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si3.png)

we obtain

$\\left\\{ \\begin{aligned} a\_{n} & {= a \\cdot a\_{n - 1} + b \\cdot c\_{n - 1},} \\\\ b\_{n} & {= a \\cdot b\_{n - 1} + b \\cdot d\_{n - 1},} \\\\ c\_{n} & {= c \\cdot a\_{n - 1} + d \\cdot c\_{n - 1},} \\\\ d\_{n} & {= c \\cdot b\_{n - 1} + d \\cdot d\_{n - 1}.} \\\\ \\end{aligned} \\right.$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si4.png)

Using elementary substitutions, this leads to the following system:

$\\left\\{ \\begin{aligned} a\_{n} & {= (a + d) \\cdot a\_{n - 1} - (ad - bc) \\cdot a\_{n - 2},} \\\\ b\_{n} & {= (a + d) \\cdot b\_{n - 1} - (ad - bc) \\cdot b\_{n - 2},} \\\\ c\_{n} & {= (a + d) \\cdot c\_{n - 1} - (ad - bc) \\cdot c\_{n - 2},} \\\\ d\_{n} & {= (a + d) \\cdot d\_{n - 1} - (ad - bc) \\cdot d\_{n - 2}.} \\\\ \\end{aligned} \\right.$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si5.png)

We are dealing with identical linear homogeneous recurrence relations. Only the initial conditions corresponding to *n* = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si6.png) and *n* = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si7.png) are different for these four equations. The solution to such equations is obtained as follows \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_recurrence_with_constant_coefficients)\]. First, solve the quadratic equation

*x*² − (*a* + *d*)*x* + (*a**d* − *b**c*) = 0.

![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si8.png)(3.1) 

The two solutions *r*[1], *r*[2]![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si9.png) are

$r\_{1} = \\frac{1}{2}\\left\\lbrack a + d + \\sqrt{{(a + d)}^{2} - 4(ad - bc)} \\right\\rbrack,r\_{2} = \\frac{1}{2}\\left\\lbrack a + d - \\sqrt{{(a + d)}^{2} - 4(ad - bc)} \\right\\rbrack.$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si10.png)

If the quantity under the square root is negative, then the roots are complex numbers. The final solution depends on whether the roots are distinct or not:

$A^{n} = \\left\\{ \\begin{array}{rlr} & {r\_{1}^{n}Q\_{1} + r\_{2}^{n}Q\_{2}} & {\\quad\\quad\\text{~if~}r\_{1} \\neq r\_{2},} \\\\ & {r\_{1}^{n}Q\_{1} + nr\_{1}^{n - 1}Q\_{2}} & {\\quad\\quad\\text{~if~}r\_{1} = r\_{2},} \\\\ \\end{array} \\right.$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si11.png)(3.2) 

with

$\\left\\{ \\begin{array}{rlr} & {Q\_{1} = (A - r\_{2}I)/(r\_{1} - r\_{2})} & {\\quad\\quad\\text{~if~}r\_{1} \\neq r\_{2},} \\\\ & {Q\_{2} = (A - r\_{1}I)/(r\_{2} - r\_{1})} & {\\quad\\quad\\text{~if~}r\_{1} \\neq r\_{2},} \\\\ & {Q\_{1} = I} & {\\quad\\quad\\text{~if~}r\_{1} = r\_{2},} \\\\ & {Q\_{2} = A - r\_{1}I} & {\\quad\\quad\\text{~if~}r\_{1} = r\_{2}.} \\\\ \\end{array} \\right.$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si12.png)(3.3) 

Here the symbol *I* represents the 2 × 2![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si1.png) identity matrix. The last four relationships were obtained by applying formula [(3.2)](#Chp003_49-60_B9780443218576000072.xhtml#deq6) to *A*^(*n*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si13.png), with *n* = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si6.png) and *n* = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si7.png). It is easy to prove (by recursion on *n*) that [(3.2)](#Chp003_49-60_B9780443218576000072.xhtml#deq6), together with [(3.3)](#Chp003_49-60_B9780443218576000072.xhtml#deq7), is the correct solution. If none of the roots is zero, then the formula is still valid for *n* =  − 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si2.png), and thus it can be used to compute the inverse of *A*.

## 3.2 Examples, generalization, and matrix inversion

For a *p* × *p*![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si14.png) matrix, the methodology generalizes as follows. The quadratic polynomial becomes a polynomial of degree *p*, known as the **characteristic polynomial**, and linked to the **Cayley–Hamilton theorem** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cayley%E2%80%93Hamilton_theorem)\]. If its roots are distinct, we have

$A^{n} = \\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{p}r\_{k}^{n}Q\_{k},\\quad\\text{with~}\\left( \\begin{array}{r} Q\_{1} \\\\ Q\_{2} \\\\ \\vdots \\\\ Q\_{p} \\\\ \\end{array} \\right) = V^{- 1}\\begin{pmatrix} I \\\\ A \\\\ \\vdots \\\\ A^{p - 1} \\\\ \\end{pmatrix} = \\begin{pmatrix} {1\\quad} & {1\\quad} & {\\ldots\\quad} & 1 \\\\ {r\_{1}\\quad} & {r\_{2}\\quad} & {\\ldots\\quad} & r\_{p} \\\\ {\\vdots \\quad} & {\\vdots \\quad} & {\\ddots \\quad} & \\vdots \\\\ {r\_{1}^{p - 1}\\quad} & {r\_{2}^{p - 1}\\quad} & {\\ldots\\quad} & r\_{p}^{p - 1} \\\\ \\end{pmatrix}^{- 1}\\begin{pmatrix} I \\\\ A \\\\ \\vdots \\\\ A^{p - 1} \\\\ \\end{pmatrix}$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si15.png)(3.4) 

The matrix *V* is a **Vandermonde matrix** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vandermonde_matrix)\], so there is an explicit formula to compute its inverse, see \[[Wiki](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Inverse_of_Vandermonde_Matrix)\]. For a fast algorithm for the computation of its inverse, see [\[9\]](#Chp003_49-60_B9780443218576000072.xhtml#br0045). However, inverting *V* should be avoided as it is a **numerically unstable** procedure. Instead, approximations methods based on selected roots of the characteristic polynomial – those with highest or lowest moduli – are preferred. They are discussed in Section [3.4.2](#Chp003_49-60_B9780443218576000072.xhtml#s0075).

The determinants of *A* and *V* are respectively equal to

$|A| = {( - 1)}^{p}r\_{1}r\_{2}\\cdots r\_{p},|V| = \\prod\\limits\_{1 \\leqslant k < l \\leqslant p}(r\_{k} - r\_{l}).$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si16.png)

Note that the roots can be real or complex numbers, simple or multiple, or equal to zero. Usually, the roots are ordered by decreasing modulus, that is,

|*r*[1]| ≥ |*r*[2]| ≥ |*r*[3]| ≥ ⋯ ≥ |*r*[*p*]|.

![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si17.png)

That way, a good approximation for *A*^(*n*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si13.png) is obtained by using the first three or four roots if *n* > 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si18.png), and the last three or four roots if *n* < 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si19.png). In the context of linear regression, one of the main problems consists of inverting a matrix, that is, using *n* =  − 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si2.png) in formula [(3.4)](#Chp003_49-60_B9780443218576000072.xhtml#deq8). Working with the first three roots only is equivalent to performing a **principal component analysis** (PCA) \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principal_component_analysis)\] as well as PCA-induced dimension reduction. This technique can be used for data compression.

If some roots have a multiplicity higher than one, the formulas must be adjusted. The solution can be found by looking at how to solve an homogeneous linear recurrence equation. See Theorem 4 in Section 8.2 of “Math 55 Lecture Notes” [\[3\]](#Chp003_49-60_B9780443218576000072.xhtml#br0015), taught at Berkeley University.

### 3.2.1 Example with a noninvertible matrix

Even if *A* is noninvertible, some useful quantities can still be computed when *n* =  − 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si2.png), not unlike using a **pseudoinverse matrix** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moore%E2%80%93Penrose_inverse)\] in the **generalized linear model** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generalized_linear_model)\] in regression analysis. Let us look at the following example, using the methodology previously discussed:

$A = \\begin{pmatrix} {1\\quad} & 2 \\\\ {2\\quad} & 4 \\\\ \\end{pmatrix}\\Longrightarrow A^{n} = 5^{n} \\cdot \\frac{1}{5}\\begin{pmatrix} {1\\quad} & 2 \\\\ {2\\quad} & 4 \\\\ \\end{pmatrix} + 0^{n} \\cdot \\frac{1}{5}\\left( \\begin{array}{rr} {4\\quad} & {- 2} \\\\ {- 2\\quad} & 1 \\\\ \\end{array} \\right).$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si20.png)

Note that 0^(*n*) = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si21.png) if *n* = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si6.png). The rightmost matrix attached to the second root 0 is of particular interest, and plays the role of a pseudoinverse matrix for *A*. If that second root was very close to zero rather than exactly zero, then the term involving the rightmost matrix would largely dominate in the expression of *A*^(*n*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si13.png), when *n* =  − 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si2.png). At the limit, some ratios involving the (nonexistent!) inverse of *A* still make sense. For instance,

*   •  The sum of the elements of the inverse of *A*, divided by its trace, is (4 − 2 − 2 + 1)/(4 + 1) = 1/5![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si22.png).
*   •  The arithmetic mean divided by the geometric mean of its elements, is 1/2.

### 3.2.2 Fast computations

If *n* is large, one way to efficiently compute *A*^(*n*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si13.png) is as follows. Let us say that *n* = 100![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si23.png). Do the following computations:

*A*² = *A* ⋅ *A*, *A*⁴ = *A*² ⋅ *A*², *A*⁸ = *A*⁴ ⋅ *A*⁴, *A*^(16) = *A*⁸ ⋅ *A*⁸, *A*^(32) = *A*^(16) ⋅ *A*^(16), *A*^(64) = *A*^(32) ⋅ *A*^(32), *A*^(100) = *A*^(64) ⋅ *A*^(32) ⋅ *A*⁴.

![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si24.png)

This can be useful to quickly get an approximation of the largest root of the characteristic polynomial, by eliminating all but the first (largest) root *r*[1]![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si25.png) in formula [(3.4)](#Chp003_49-60_B9780443218576000072.xhtml#deq8), and using *n* = 100![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si23.png). Once the first root has been found, it is easy to also get an approximation for the second, and then for the third. If, instead, you are interested in approximating the smallest roots, you can proceed the other way around, by using the formula for *A*^(*n*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si13.png), with *n* =  − 100![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si26.png) this time. Note that *A*^( − 100) = (*A*^( − 1))^(100)![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si27.png).

### 3.2.3 Square root of a matrix

Formula [(3.4)](#Chp003_49-60_B9780443218576000072.xhtml#deq8) works not only for integer values of *n*, but can be extended to fractional arguments, such as *n* = 1/2![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si28.png). Here, I illustrate how it works on an example. Thus, I show how to compute the **square root of a matrix** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Square_root_of_a_matrix)\], using the methodology developed so far. This problem has many applications, especially when the matrix *A* is symmetric **positive semidefinite** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Definite_matrix)\]: then it has only one symmetric positive semidefinite square root, denoted as *A*^(1/2)![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si29.png). See, for instance, Chapter [7](#Chp007_113-129_B9780443218576000114.xhtml) on linear regression and synthetic data, especially Section [7.2.1](#Chp007_113-129_B9780443218576000114.xhtml) entitled “correlation structure”. The square root is needed to generate synthetic data with a prespecified correlation matrix.

Now, using formula [(3.4)](#Chp003_49-60_B9780443218576000072.xhtml#deq8) with *n* = 1/2![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si28.png), let us compute the square root of the 2 × 2![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si1.png) matrix *A* defined as

$A = \\left( \\begin{array}{rr} {3\\quad} & 1 \\\\ {1\\quad} & 1 \\\\ \\end{array} \\right).$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si30.png)

Its characteristic polynomial, according to formula [(3.1)](#Chp003_49-60_B9780443218576000072.xhtml#deq4), is *x*² − 4*x* + 2![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si31.png). The roots are $r\_{1} = 1 + \\sqrt{2}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si32.png) and $r\_{2} = 1 - \\sqrt{2}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si33.png), and are both real and positive. According to formula [(3.2)](#Chp003_49-60_B9780443218576000072.xhtml#deq6), the matrices *Q*[1], *Q*[2]![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si34.png) are respectively equal to

$Q\_{1} = \\frac{A - r\_{2}I}{r\_{1} - r\_{2}} = \\frac{1}{4} \\cdot \\begin{pmatrix} {2 + \\sqrt{2}\\quad} & \\sqrt{2} \\\\ {\\sqrt{2}\\quad} & {2 - \\sqrt{2}} \\\\ \\end{pmatrix},\\quad Q\_{2} = \\frac{A - r\_{1}I}{r\_{2} - r\_{1}} = \\frac{1}{4} \\cdot \\begin{pmatrix} {2 - \\sqrt{2}\\quad} & {- \\sqrt{2}} \\\\ {- \\sqrt{2}\\quad} & {2 + \\sqrt{2}} \\\\ \\end{pmatrix}.$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si35.png)

The matrix *A* has one positive definite square root, namely

$A^{1/2} = \\sqrt{r\_{1}} \\cdot Q\_{1} + \\sqrt{r\_{2}} \\cdot Q\_{2} = \\frac{1}{2}\\begin{pmatrix} {\\sqrt{10 + \\sqrt{2}}\\quad} & \\sqrt{2 - \\sqrt{2}} \\\\ {\\sqrt{2 - \\sqrt{2}}\\quad} & \\sqrt{2 + \\sqrt{2}} \\\\ \\end{pmatrix}.$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si36.png)

It is easy to show that *A*^(1/2) ⋅ *A*^(1/2) = *A*![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si37.png). In higher dimensions, the Vandermonde system [(3.4)](#Chp003_49-60_B9780443218576000072.xhtml#deq8) is solved using the method described in Section [3.4.2](#Chp003_49-60_B9780443218576000072.xhtml#s0075).

## 3.3 Application to machine learning problems

I discussed principal component analysis (PCA), data compression via PCA, and pseudoinverse matrices in Section [3.2](#Chp003_49-60_B9780443218576000072.xhtml#s0015). Here I focus on applications to time series, Markov chains, and linear regression.

### 3.3.1 Markov chains

A **Markov chain** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markov_chain)\] is a particular type of time series or stochastic process. At iteration or time *n*, a system is in a particular state *i* with probability *P*[*n*](*i*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si38.png). The probability to move from state *i* at time *n* to state *j* at time *n* + 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si39.png) is called a transition probability and denoted as *p*[*i**j*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si40.png). It does not depend on *n*, but only on *i* and *j*. The Markov chain is governed by its initial conditions *P*[0](*i*), 1 ≤ *i* ≤ *p*![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si41.png), and the transition probability matrix denoted as *A*, containing the elements *p*[*i**j*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si40.png). The size of the transition matrix is *p* × *p*![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si14.png), where *p* is the number of potential states in the system. Thus 1 ≤ *i*, *j* ≤ *p*![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si42.png). As *n* tends to infinity, *A*^(*n*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si13.png) and the whole system reaches an equilibrium distribution. This is because

*   •  The **characteristic polynomial** attached to *A* has a root equal to 1.
*   •  The absolute value of any root is less than or equal to 1.

### 3.3.2 Time series: autoregressive processes

Autoregressive processes (AR) \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autoregressive_model)\] represent another basic type of time series. Unlike Markov chains, the number of potential states is infinite, and a state can any real value, not just an integer. Yet the time is still discrete. Time-continuous AR processes such as **Gaussian processes** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaussian_process)\] are not included in this discussion. An AR(*p*) process is defined as follows:

*X*[*n*] = *a*[1]*X*[*n* − 1] + ⋯ + *a*[*p*]*X*[*n* − *p*] + *e*[*n*].

![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si43.png)

Its **characteristic polynomial** is

*x*^(*p*) = *a*[1]*x*^(*p* − 1) + *a*[2]*x*^(*p* − 2) + ⋯ + *a*[*p* − 1]*x* + *a*[*p*].

![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si44.png)(3.5) 

Here {*e*[*n*]}![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si45.png) is a **white noise** process (typically uncorrelated Gaussian variables with same variance) \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_noise)\]. We assume that all expectations are zero. We are dealing here with a nonhomogeneous linear (stochastic) recurrence relation. The most interesting case is when all the roots of the characteristic polynomial have absolute value less than 1. Processes satisfying this condition are called **stationary**. In that case, the **autocorrelations** are decaying exponentially fast.

The lag-*k* covariances satisfy the relation

$\\gamma\_{k} = {Cov}\\lbrack X\_{n},X\_{n - k}\\rbrack = \\begin{cases} {a\_{1}\\gamma(k - 1) + \\cdots + a\_{p}\\gamma(k - p)\\quad} & {\\text{if~}k \\neq 0,} \\\\ {a\_{1}\\gamma(k - 1) + \\cdots + a\_{p}\\gamma(k - p) + \\sigma^{2}\\quad} & {\\text{if~}k = 0,} \\\\ \\end{cases}$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si46.png)

with

*σ*² = *V**a**r*\[*e*[*n*]\], *V**a**r*\[*X*[*n*]\] = *γ*(0), *ρ*(*k*) = *C**o**r**r*\[*X*[*n*], *X*[*n* − *k*]\] = *γ*(*k*)/*γ*(0).

![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si47.png)

Thus the autocorrelations can be explicitly computed, and are also related to the characteristic polynomial. This fact can be used for model fitting, as the autocorrelation structure uniquely characterizes the (stationary) time series. Note that if the white noise is Gaussian, then the *X*[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si48.png)'s are also Gaussian.

More about the autocorrelation structure can be found in lecture notes from Marc-Andreas Muendler [\[7\]](#Chp003_49-60_B9780443218576000072.xhtml#br0035), who teaches economics at UCSD. His material is very similar to what I discuss here, but more comprehensive. See also Barbara Bogacka's lecture notes on time series [\[1\]](#Chp003_49-60_B9780443218576000072.xhtml#br0005), especially Chapter 6. Finally, Section [3.4](#Chp003_49-60_B9780443218576000072.xhtml#s0055) in this chapter explores the mathematical aspects in more details.

### 3.3.3 Linear regression

Linear regression problems can be solved using the **ordinary least squares** (OLS) method \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordinary_least_squares)\]. The framework involves a response *y*, a data set *X* consisting of *p* features or variables and *m* observations, and *p* regression coefficients (to be determined) stored in a vector *b*. In matrix notation, the problem consists of finding *b* that minimizes the distance ||*y* − *X**b*||![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si49.png) between *y* and *Xb*. Here *X* is an *m* × *p*![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si50.png) matrix, and *y*, *b*![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si51.png) are column vectors. The solution is

*b* = *A*^( − 1)*X*^(*T*)*y*, with *A* = *X*^(*T*)*X*.

![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si52.png)

The techniques discussed in Section [3.4.2](#Chp003_49-60_B9780443218576000072.xhtml#s0075) can be used to compute the inverse of *A* using formula [(3.4)](#Chp003_49-60_B9780443218576000072.xhtml#deq8) with *n* =  − 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si2.png), either exactly using all the roots of its **characteristic polynomial**, or approximately using the 2–3 roots with the lowest moduli. You need to use the recursion [(3.8)](#Chp003_49-60_B9780443218576000072.xhtml#deq29) backward when implementing the methodology in Section [3.4.2](#Chp003_49-60_B9780443218576000072.xhtml#s0075), that is, for *n* =  − 1,  − 2![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si53.png), and so on, rather than for *n* = 1, 2![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si54.png), and so on.

If *A* is not invertible, the methodology described in Section [3.2.1](#Chp003_49-60_B9780443218576000072.xhtml#s0020) can be useful: it amounts to working with a pseudoinverse of *A*. Note that *A* is a *p* × *p*![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si14.png) matrix as in Section [3.2](#Chp003_49-60_B9780443218576000072.xhtml#s0015). Questions regarding confidence intervals can be addressed using model-free techniques as discussed in Chapter [8](#Chp008_131-145_B9780443218576000126.xhtml).

## 3.4 Mathematics of autoregressive time series

Here I connect the dots between the autoregressive **time series** described in Section [3.3.2](#Chp003_49-60_B9780443218576000072.xhtml#s0045), and the material in Section [3.2](#Chp003_49-60_B9780443218576000072.xhtml#deq6). For the AR(*p*) process in Section [3.3.2](#Chp003_49-60_B9780443218576000072.xhtml#s0045), we have

$X\_{n} = g(e\_{p},e\_{p + 1},\\ldots,e\_{n}) + \\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{p}r\_{k}^{n}q\_{k},\\quad\\text{with~}\\begin{pmatrix} q\_{1} \\\\ q\_{2} \\\\ \\vdots \\\\ q\_{p} \\\\ \\end{pmatrix} = V^{- 1}\\begin{pmatrix} X\_{0} \\\\ X\_{1} \\\\ \\vdots \\\\ X\_{p - 1} \\\\ \\end{pmatrix},$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si55.png)

where *V* is the same matrix as in formula [(3.4)](#Chp003_49-60_B9780443218576000072.xhtml#deq8), the *r*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si56.png)'s are the roots (assumed distinct here) of the **characteristic polynomial** defined by [(3.5)](#Chp003_49-60_B9780443218576000072.xhtml#deq17), and *g* is a linear function of *e*[*p*], *e*[*p* + 1], …, *e*[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si57.png). For instance, if *p* = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si58.png), we have

$g(e\_{p},e\_{p + 1},\\ldots,e\_{n}) = \\sum\\limits\_{k = 0}^{n - p}a\_{1}^{k}e\_{n - k}.$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si59.png)

This allows you to compute *V**a**r*\[*X*[*n*]\]![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si60.png) and *C**o**v*\[*X*[*n*], *X*[*n* − *k*]\]![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si61.png), conditionally to *X*[0], …, *X*[*p* − 1]![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si62.png). The limit, when *n* tends to infinity, allows you to compute the unconditional variance and autocorrelations attached to the process, in the stationary case. For instance, if *p* = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si58.png), we have

${Var}\\lbrack X\_{\\infty}\\rbrack = \\lim\\limits\_{n\\rightarrow\\infty}\\sum\\limits\_{k = 0}^{n - p}a\_{1}^{2k}{Var}\\lbrack e\_{n - k}\\rbrack = \\sigma^{2}\\sum\\limits\_{k = 0}^{\\infty}a\_{1}^{2k} = \\frac{\\sigma^{2}}{1 - a\_{1}^{2}},$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si63.png)

where *σ*² = *V**a**r*\[*e*[0]\]![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si64.png) is the variance of the white noise {*e*[*n*]}![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si45.png), and |*a*[1]| < 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si65.png) because we assumed stationarity. For the general case (any *p*), the formula, if *n* is larger than or equal to *p*, is

$g(e\_{p},e\_{p + 1},\\ldots,e\_{n}) = \\sum\\limits\_{k = 0}^{n - p}\\alpha\_{k}e\_{n - k},\\text{~~}\\text{with~}\\alpha\_{0} = 1,\\text{~~}\\alpha\_{k} = \\sum\\limits\_{t = 1}^{p}a\_{t}\\alpha\_{k - t}\\text{~~}\\text{if~}k > 0,\\text{~~}\\alpha\_{k} = 0\\text{~~}\\text{if~}k < 0.$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si66.png)

In this case, we have

${Var}\\lbrack X\_{\\infty}\\rbrack = \\sigma^{2}\\sum\\limits\_{k = 0}^{\\infty}\\alpha\_{k}^{2}.$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si67.png)

The initial conditions for the coefficients *α*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si68.png) correspond to *k* = 0,  − 1,  − 2, …,  − (*p* − 1)![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si69.png). Thus *α*[0] = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si70.png), and the remaining *α*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si68.png)'s (*k* < 0)![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si71.png) are zero. Thus, the recurrence relation for *α*[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si72.png) can be solved using the same roots *r*[1], …, *r*[*p*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si73.png) solution of Eq. [(3.5)](#Chp003_49-60_B9780443218576000072.xhtml#deq17). Assuming the roots are distinct, we have

$\\alpha\_{n} = \\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{p}r\_{k}^{n}q\_{k}^{\\prime},\\quad\\text{with~}\\begin{pmatrix} q\_{1}^{\\prime} \\\\ q\_{2}^{\\prime} \\\\ \\vdots \\\\ q\_{p}^{\\prime} \\\\ \\end{pmatrix} = W^{- 1}\\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\\\ 0 \\\\ \\vdots \\\\ 0 \\\\ \\end{pmatrix},\\quad\\text{and~}W = \\begin{pmatrix} {1\\quad} & {1\\quad} & {\\cdots\\quad} & 1 \\\\ {r\_{1}^{- 1}\\quad} & {r\_{2}^{- 1}\\quad} & {\\ldots\\quad} & r\_{p}^{- 1} \\\\ {\\vdots \\quad} & {\\vdots \\quad} & {\\ddots \\quad} & \\vdots \\\\ {r\_{1}^{- (p - 1)}\\quad} & {r\_{2}^{- (p - 1)}\\quad} & {\\ldots\\quad} & r\_{p}^{- (p - 1)} \\\\ \\end{pmatrix}.$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si74.png)(3.6) 

Again, a direct computation of *W*^( − 1)![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si75.png) is numerically unstable, except in some special cases. Typically, a few of the *r*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si56.png)'s are dominant. The others can be ignored, leading to approximations and increased stability. Finally, if two time series models, say an ARMA and an AR models, have the same variance and covariance structure, they are actually identical.

### 3.4.1 Simulations: curious fractal time series

To simulate the **autoregressive** time series described in Section [3.3.2](#Chp003_49-60_B9780443218576000072.xhtml#s0045), I proceed backwards: first, pick up the roots *r*[1], …, *r*[*p*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si73.png) of the **characteristic polynomial**, then compute the coefficients *a*[1], …, *a*[*p*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si76.png). This leads to interesting discoveries. I want at least one of the roots to have its modulus equal to one. The other roots must have a modulus strictly smaller than one. Roots can have a multiplicity greater than one. Depending on the roots, whether they are all real, whether some are complex, or whether some have a multiplicity greater than one, the pattern is very different. It falls into three categories:

*   •  Type 1: A very smooth time series if the root(s) with largest modulus has a multiplicity greater than one.
*   •  Type 2: A Brownian-like appearance if all the roots are real and distinct.
*   •  Type 3: An highly oscillating time series that fills a dense area when complex roots with modulus equal to one, are present.

In [Fig. 3.1](#Chp003_49-60_B9780443218576000072.xhtml#f0010), I have rescaled the horizontal and vertical axes so that the time series look time-continuous. With this transformation, Type 2 actually corresponds to a 1D **Brownian motion** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brownian_motion)\]. Type 3 has a curve that exhibits a **fractal dimension** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fractal_dimension)\] strictly between 1 and 2. Type 1 looks very smooth. It seems like it has derivatives of any order, everywhere. Thus it cannot be a Brownian motion. Yet if you zoom in or out, the same statistical properties (smoothness, expected numbers of bumps, and so on) repeat themselves. This means that we are dealing with a strange mathematical function: one that cannot be approximated by a Taylor series, yet very smooth and chaotic with self-replicating features at the same time. Also, we need to keep in mind that it is a **stochastic function**.

![Figure 3.1 AR models, classified based on the types of roots of the characteristic polynomial.](images/B9780443218576000072/gr001.jpg)

Figure 3.1 AR models, classified based on the types of roots of the characteristic polynomial.

The smoothness of a time series is typically measured using its **Hurst exponent** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurst_exponent)\]. The extreme, most chaotic case is a white noise, and the “middle case” is a Brownian motion. Here Type 3 seems more extreme than a white noise, and Type 1 is unusually smooth. Except for Type 3, the discrete version of these time series all have long-range autocorrelations.

#### 3.4.1.1 White noise: Fréchet, Weibull, and exponential cases

I use one of the simplest distributions to sample from, to generate the white noise {*e*[*n*]}![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si45.png). Using independent uniform deviates *U*[1], *U*[2], …![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si77.png) on \[0, 1\]![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si78.png), I first generate the deviates

*v*[*n*] = *τ*(−log(1−*U*[*n*]))^(*γ*), *n* = 1, 2, …

![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si79.png)(3.7) 

Then the noise *e*[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si80.png) is produced using

*e*[*n*] = *v*[*n*] − E\[*v*[*n*]\], with E\[*v*[*n*]\] = *τ**Γ*(1 + *γ*) and *V**a**r*\[*e*[*n*]\] = *V**a**r*\[*v*[*n*]\] = *τ*²\[*Γ*(1+2*γ*)−*Γ*²(1+*γ*)\].

![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si81.png)

Here *τ*, *γ*![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si82.png) are parameters, with $\\gamma > - \\frac{1}{2}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si83.png), and Γ is the **Gamma function** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamma_function)\]. We have the following cases:

*   •  If *γ* = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si84.png), then *v*[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si85.png) has an exponential distribution.
*   •  If  − 1 < *γ* < 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si86.png), then *v*[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si85.png) has a **Fréchet distribution**. If in addition, $\\gamma > - \\frac{1}{2}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si83.png), then its variance is finite.
*   •  If *γ* > 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si87.png), then *v*[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si85.png) has a **Weibull distribution**, with finite variance.

It is surprising that this distribution has different names, depending on whether *γ* < 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si88.png) or *γ* > 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si87.png). This distribution is discussed in my book on stochastic processes [\[5, pages 41–42\]](#Chp003_49-60_B9780443218576000072.xhtml#br0025).

#### 3.4.1.2 Illustration

The simulation results shown in [Fig. 3.1](#Chp003_49-60_B9780443218576000072.xhtml#f0010) come from my spreadsheet linear2-small.xlsx, available on my GitHub repository, [here](https://github.com/VincentGranville/Machine-Learning/blob/main/Spreadsheets/README.md). The cells highlighted in light yellow correspond to the model parameters, such as *τ*, *γ*, *a*[1], …, *a*[4]![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si102.png): you can modify them, and it will automatically update the picture. A much larger spreadsheet linear2.xlsx (about 30 MB), containing many interesting simulations, each with 50,000 observations, is available [here](https://ln5.sync.com/dl/4c157bf10/5be4uhcd-w6g99e8h-96ndb9t4-jshr672n).

The simulations use *τ* = *γ* = 0.5![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si103.png), and the characteristic polynomials *x*⁴ − (*a*[1]*x*³ + *a*[2]*x*² + *a*[3]*x* + *a*[4])![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si104.png) listed in [Table 3.1](#Chp003_49-60_B9780443218576000072.xhtml#t0010). The “Type 2” plot is a classic, while “Type 3 (a)” looks like an ordinary audio signal. In Types 3(a) and 3(b), the frequency of oscillations is extremely high: this explains while the curve seems to completely fill an area. The “Type 3(b)” time series is rather original. Its characteristic polynomial has two distinct real roots, each with multiplicity 2. Thus, you are unlikely to encounter it in college classes or textbooks.

[Table 3.1](#Chp003_49-60_B9780443218576000072.xhtml#cf0180)

Characteristic polynomials used in the simulations.

 
| Category || *a*[1] || *a*[2] || *a*[3] || *a*[4] || Factored version |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Type 1(a) || $\\frac{11}{4}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si89.png) || $- \\frac{21}{8}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si90.png) || 1 || $- \\frac{1}{8}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si91.png) || ${(x - 1)}^{2}(x - \\frac{1}{2})(x - \\frac{1}{4})$![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si92.png) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Type 1(b) || 2 || −2 || 2 || −1 || (*x*−1)²(*x*² + 1) |
| Type 2 || $\\frac{15}{8}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si93.png) || $- \\frac{35}{32}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si94.png) || $\\frac{15}{64}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si95.png) || $- \\frac{1}{64}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si96.png) || $(x - 1)(x - \\frac{1}{2})(x - \\frac{1}{4})(x - \\frac{1}{8})$![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si97.png) |
| Type 3(a) || 0 || $- \\frac{1}{2}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si98.png) || 0 || $\\frac{1}{2}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si99.png) || $(x^{2} + 1)(x^{2} - \\frac{1}{2})$![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si100.png) |
| Type 3(b) || 0 || 2 || 0 || −1 || ${(x - 1)}^{2}{(x - \\frac{1}{2})}^{2}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si101.png) |

![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/t0010.png)

But the truly spectacular plot, surprisingly, is “Type 1”. These curves are very smooth, but no matter how much you zoom in, it never becomes a flat line, unlike polynomials or well-behaved math functions. The “Type 1” curves in [Fig. 3.1](#Chp003_49-60_B9780443218576000072.xhtml#f0010) have this property: when differentiated, they become a “Type 2” curve. In short, these curves are the integral of Brownian motions, and called **Itô integrals** \[[Wiki](https://www.robots.ox.ac.uk/~lsgs/posts/2018-09-30-ito-strat.xhtml)\]. The “Type 2” curves are continuous, and their derivatives are white noises. If the multiplicity of the root with largest modulus is 3, then the corresponding curve is even smoother and can be differentiated three times. Its first derivative is a “Type 1” curve, and its second derivative is a “Type 2” curve.

Other unusual Brownian motions, this time in two dimensions, are discussed in Section [12.2.1](#Chp012_229-241_B9780443218576000163.xhtml). They include a family of Brownian motions, exhibiting an extraordinary strong clustering structure, depending on model parameters. Some Gaussian processes can have a behavior similar to “Type 1” depending on parameters, see [here](https://www.r-bloggers.com/2019/07/sampling-paths-from-a-gaussian-process/). For Gaussian processes, see also [\[8\]](#Chp003_49-60_B9780443218576000072.xhtml#br0040), especially Chapter 4. Finally, the top parameter values (root modulus, multiplicity, and so on) can be grouped into clusters. Each cluster leads to a specific type of time series. It makes our time series simulator – called a generative model – useful to produce synthetic data with parameter values matching those estimated on real-life time series. See also Section [1.4](#Chp001_1-34_B9780443218576000059.xhtml) on how to accomplish this in a different context.

### 3.4.2 Solving Vandermonde systems: a numerically stable method

**Vandermonde systems** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vandermonde_matrix)\] are notoriously **ill-conditioned** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Condition_number)\]. This explains why nobody really solves them, and instead, uses other techniques. Yet they could potentially be used to solve many problems, including linear regression and **eigenvalues** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eigenvalues_and_eigenvectors)\] via the characteristic polynomial, **Lagrange interpolation** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Runge%27s_phenomenon)\], Markov chains (computation of the **stationary distribution**), linear recurrence equations, principal component analysis (PCA), autoregressive time series, square root of a matrix, and more.

Using the methodology presented in this chapter, I propose a numerically stable algorithm to solve such systems, in a very indirect way. I illustrate my method on a particular example. Let us consider the autoregressive process

$X\_{n} = \\frac{3}{4}X\_{n - 1} + \\frac{7}{8}X\_{n - 2} - \\frac{3}{4}X\_{n - 3} + \\frac{1}{8}X\_{n - 4},$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si105.png)(3.8) 

with no white noise. In other words, let *τ* = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si106.png) in formula [(3.7)](#Chp003_49-60_B9780443218576000072.xhtml#deq27). The characteristic polynomial has roots $r\_{1} = 1,r\_{2} = - 1,r\_{3} = \\frac{1}{2},r\_{4} = \\frac{1}{4}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si107.png). Let the initial conditions be *X*[0] = 1, *X*[ − 1] = 0, *X*[ − 2] = 0, *X*[ − 3] = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si108.png) as in formula [(3.6)](#Chp003_49-60_B9780443218576000072.xhtml#deq26). Thus, I will be solving the Vandermonde system

$\\left( \\begin{array}{rrrr} {1\\quad} & {1\\quad} & {1\\quad} & 1 \\\\ {1\\quad} & {- 1\\quad} & {2\\quad} & 4 \\\\ {1\\quad} & {1\\quad} & {4\\quad} & 16 \\\\ {1\\quad} & {- 1\\quad} & {8\\quad} & 64 \\\\ \\end{array} \\right)\\begin{pmatrix} q\_{1}^{\\prime} \\\\ q\_{2}^{\\prime} \\\\ q\_{3}^{\\prime} \\\\ q\_{4}^{\\prime} \\\\ \\end{pmatrix} = \\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\\\ 0 \\\\ 0 \\\\ 0 \\\\ \\end{pmatrix}.$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si109.png)(3.9) 

We know that

*X*[*n*] = *r*[1]^(*n*)*q*[1]^′ + *r*[2]^(*n*)*q*[2]^′ + *r*[3]^(*n*)*q*[3]^′ + *r*[4]^(*n*)*q*[4]^′.

![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si110.png)(3.10) 

Computing *X*[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si48.png) iteratively using formula [(3.8)](#Chp003_49-60_B9780443218576000072.xhtml#deq29), we find that *X*[30] ≈ 1.6000![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si111.png) and *X*[31] ≈ 1.0667![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si112.png). The influence of *r*[3], *r*[4]![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si113.png) is negligible in formula [(3.10)](#Chp003_49-60_B9780443218576000072.xhtml#deq31), and we can reasonably ignore these two roots if *n* is large enough. Thus, if *n* = 30![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si114.png) we have 1.6000 ≈ *q*[1]^′ + *q*[2]^′![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si115.png), according to [(3.10)](#Chp003_49-60_B9780443218576000072.xhtml#deq31). And *n* = 31![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si116.png) yields 1.0667 ≈ *q*[1]^′ − *q*[2]^′![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si117.png). These two equations allow us to get a very good approximation both for *q*[1]^′![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si118.png) and *q*[2]^′![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si119.png). We do not care about *q*[3]^′![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si120.png) and *q*[4]^′![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si121.png) as the associated roots *r*[3], *r*[4]![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si113.png) have almost no impact on *X*[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si48.png) when *n* is large.

However, we can still compute them if we want to. Consider the subrecursion {*Y*[*n*]}![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si122.png) with characteristic polynomial (*x* − *r*[3])(*x* − *r*[4])![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si123.png), that is, $Y\_{n} = \\frac{3}{4}Y\_{n - 1} - \\frac{1}{8}Y\_{n - 2}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si124.png). Let the initial conditions be

*Y*[*n*] = *X*[*n*] − (*r*[1]^(*n*)*q*[1]^′ + *r*[2]^(*n*)*q*[2]^′), for *n* = 0,  − 1.

![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si125.png)(3.11) 

Use the approximated values *q*[1]^′ = 1.333![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si126.png) and *q*[2]^′ = 0.2667![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si127.png) computed in the previous step. Clearly, by design,

*Y*[*n*] = *r*[3]^(*n*)*q*[3]^′ + *r*[4]^(*n*)*q*[4]^′,

![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si128.png)(3.12) 

with $r\_{3} = \\frac{1}{2},r\_{4} = \\frac{1}{4}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si129.png). Also, since *r*[3]![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si130.png) dominates over *r*[4]![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si131.png), for *n* large enough, we have *Y*[*n*] ≈ *r*[3]^(*n*)*q*^′3![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si132.png), that is, *q*[3]^′ ≈ *r*[3]^( − *n*)*Y*[*n*] ≈ 2^(*n*)*Y*[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si133.png). Using formulas [(3.11)](#Chp003_49-60_B9780443218576000072.xhtml#deq32) and [(3.12)](#Chp003_49-60_B9780443218576000072.xhtml#deq33) combined with the approximated values of *q*[1]^′, *q*[2]^′![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si134.png) and *n* = 15![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si135.png), one eventually obtains *q*[3]^′ ≈ 2^(15)*Y*[15] ≈  − 0.6667![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si136.png). Now we are left with finding the last coefficient *q*[4]^′![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si121.png). It can be done using the linear recurrence with characteristic polynomial *x* − *r*[4]![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si138.png). The details are left as an exercise. The exact values are

$q\_{1}^{\\prime} = \\frac{4}{3} = 1.3333\\ldots,\\quad q\_{2}^{\\prime} = \\frac{4}{15} = 0.2666\\ldots,\\quad q\_{3}^{\\prime} = - \\frac{2}{3} = - 0.6666\\ldots,\\quad q\_{4}^{\\prime} = \\frac{1}{15} = 0.0666\\ldots$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si139.png)

If we have more than *p* = 4![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si140.png) unknowns, we can proceed iteratively in the same manner, obtaining approximate values successively for *q*[1]^′, *q*[2]^′![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si134.png), and so on, assuming the roots are ordered by modulus, with *r*[1]![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si25.png) having the largest modulus. We accumulate inaccuracies at each new iteration, but the loss of accuracy is controlled: the biggest losses are on the coefficients with the lowest impact. Roots with same moduli must be treated jointly, as I did here for *r*[1]![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si25.png) and *r*[2]![Image](images/B9780443218576000072/si141.png). If some roots have a multiplicity greater than 1, formula [(3.10)](#Chp003_49-60_B9780443218576000072.xhtml#deq31) must be adapted; see [\[3\]](#Chp003_49-60_B9780443218576000072.xhtml#br0015).

## 3.5 Math for machine learning: must-read books

In general, my methods are not traditional. I try to offer original content to the reader, presenting innovative methods explained in simple English, in a style that is pleasant to read. If you are looking for standard textbooks to learn the math of machine learning, I recommend “Mathematics for Machine Learning” [\[2\]](#Chp003_49-60_B9780443218576000072.xhtml#br0010) and “Introduction to Mathematical Statistics” [\[6\]](#Chp003_49-60_B9780443218576000072.xhtml#br0030). The book “Deep Learning” [\[4\]](#Chp003_49-60_B9780443218576000072.xhtml#br0020) also covers the math of matrix algebra. Lectures notes from Zico Kolter at Stanford University (2015), covering linear algebra, are available [here](https://cs229.stanford.edu/section/cs229-linalg.pdf). The book “Linear Algebra for Data Science” by Shaina Bennett (2021) is available online [here](https://shainarace.github.io/LinearAlgebra/), and features examples in R. See also “Introduction to Probability for Data Science” by Stanley Chan (2021) available [here](https://probability4datascience.com/), with Matlab® and Python code, especially the last chapter on random processes.

For hands-on references with Python code, [StatsModels.org](https://www.statsmodels.org/stable/user-guide.xhtml) is a vast GitHub repository covering a lot of linear algebra and time series. Another one is Statistics and Machine Learning in Python, [here](https://duchesnay.github.io/pystatsml/). See also the Python [Scikit-learn.org](https://scikit-learn.org/0.15/modules/linear_model.xhtml) guide about linear models, and [Interpretable Machine Learning](https://christophm.github.io/interpretable-ml-book/limo.xhtml). You will not find the math or type of examples discussed here, in any of these books. However, they are useful, classic, yet modern references.
