# Chapter 6: Shape classification and synthetization via explainable AI

## Abstract

Here I define the mathematical concept of shape and shape signature in two dimensions, using parametric polar equations. The signature uniquely characterizes the shape, up to a translation or scale factor. In practical applications, the data set consists of points or pixels located on the shape, rather than the curve itself. If these points are not properly sampled – if they are not uniformly distributed on the curve – they need to be reweighted to compute a meaningful centroid of the shape, and to perform shape comparisons. I discuss the weights, and then introduce metrics to compare shapes (observed as sets of points or pixels in an image). These metrics are related to the Hausdorff distance. I also introduce a correlation distance between two shapes. Equipped with these metrics, one can perform shape recognition or classification using training sets of arbitrary sizes. I use synthetic data in the applications. It allows you to see how the classifier performs, to discriminate between two very similar shapes, or in the presence of noise. Rotation-invariant metrics are also discussed.

### Keywords

Hausdorff distance; shape signature; shape classification; synthetic shapes; explainable AI

Here I define the mathematical concept of shape and shape signature in two dimensions, using parametric polar equations. The signature uniquely characterizes the shape, up to a translation or scale factor. In practical applications, the data set consists of points or pixels located on the shape, rather than the curve itself. If these points are not properly sampled – if they are not uniformly distributed on the curve – they need to be reweighted to compute a meaningful centroid of the shape, and to perform shape comparisons. I discuss the weights, and then introduce metrics to compare shapes (observed as sets of points or pixels in an image). These metrics are related to the Hausdorff distance. I also introduce a correlation distance between two shapes. Equipped with these metrics, one can perform shape recognition or classification using training sets of arbitrary sizes. I use synthetic data in the applications. It allows you to see how the classifier performs, to discriminate between two very similar shapes, or in the presence of noise. Rotation-invariant metrics are also discussed.

## 6.1 Introduction

A central problem in **computer vision** is to compare shapes and assess how similar they are. This is used, for instance, in text recognition. Modern techniques involve neural networks. Here, I revisit a methodology developed before computer even existed. With modern technology, it leads to an efficient, automated AI algorithm. The benefit is that the decision process made by this black-box system can be easily explained, and thus easily controlled.

To the contrary, neural networks use millions of weights that are impossible to interpret, potentially leading to overfitting. Why they work very well on some data and no so well on other data is a mystery. My “old-fashioned” classifier, adapted to modern data and computer architectures, leads to full control of the parameters. In other words, you know beforehand how fine-tuning the parameters will impact the output. Thus the word explainable AI \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Explainable_artificial_intelligence)\].

In an ideal world, one would want to blend both methods, to benefit from their respective strengths, and minimize their respective drawbacks. Such a blending is referred to as ensemble methods \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ensemble_learning)\]. Also, since we are dealing with sampled points located on a curve (the “shape”), the same methodology also applies to sound recognition.

## 6.2 Mathematical foundations

In this section, we are concerned with the mathematical concept of shape. Later on, I apply the methodology to shapes represented by sets of points or pixels, observed through a rectangular window – a digital image. The center of the window is the origin of the coordinate system. Shapes can be anything: they may represent a letter, an hieroglyph, or a combination of symbols. They may consist of multiple, nonconnected curves. We are only interested in the contour that defines the shape. It may or may not correspond to the boundary of a domain; the contour may not be closed and could consist of disconnected segments.

Furthermore, there is no color or gray scale involved. The mathematical shape model can be viewed as black on a white background, with no thickness. In practical applications, the rectangular image is centered around the shape, and the noise has been filtered out. See example in [Fig. 6.1](#Chp006_103-111_B9780443218576000102.xhtml#f0010), comparing two shapes.

![Figure 6.1 Comparing two shapes.](images/B9780443218576000102/gr001.jpg)

Figure 6.1 Comparing two shapes.

It is convenient, for illustrations purposes, to define a 2D mathematical shape using a parametric polar equation, as follows:

*r*[*t*] = *g*(*t*), *θ*[*t*] = *h*(*t*), with *t* ∈ *T*, *r*[*t*] ≥ 0, 0 ≤ *θ*[*t*] ≤ 2*π*.

![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si1.png)

Here *g*, *h*![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si2.png) are real-valued functions, and *T* is the index domain. An example with *n* = 20![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si3.png) points is as follows:

*θ*[*t*] = (*t* + *η*) *m**o**d* 2*π*, *r*[*t*] = *c* + *d*sin (*a**t*)sin (2*π**b* − *b**t*), *t* = 2*π**k*/*n* with *k* = 0, …, *n* − 1.

![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si4.png)(6.1) 

This example is pictured in [Fig. 6.1](#Chp006_103-111_B9780443218576000102.xhtml#f0010). The parameter *η* controls the rotation angle or orientation of the shape. By definition, *α* *m**o**d* *β* = *α* − *β*⌊*α*/*β*⌋![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si5.png) where the brackets represent the integer part function. A more simple example, corresponding to an elliptic arc, is

$r\_{t} = \\frac{p}{1 - \\epsilon\\cos t},\\quad\\theta\_{t} = t,\\quad 0 \\leqslant t \\leqslant t\_{0},$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si6.png)

where 0 < *ϵ* < 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si7.png), *p* > 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si8.png), and 0 < *t*[0] < 2*π*![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si9.png) are the parameters. The parameter *ϵ* is the eccentricity. Since the functions *g*(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si10.png) and *f*(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si11.png) are arbitrary, can be discontinuous, and may contain infinitely many parameters (for instance, the coefficient of a Taylor or Fourier series), it covers all the possible shapes that exist in the universe.

## 6.3 Shape signature

The concept of shape signature is not new, see [\[1](#Chp006_103-111_B9780443218576000102.xhtml#br0005),[3\]](#Chp006_103-111_B9780443218576000102.xhtml#br0015). Each shape (or set of points) is uniquely described by a normalized set called **signature**. In our context, this set can be a curve, a set of points, multiple broken curves, or a combination of these elements. The signature does not depend on the location or center of gravity of the shape. It depends on the orientation, though it is easy to generalize the definition to make it rotation-invariant, or to handle 3D shapes. The first step is to use the center of gravity (centroid) for the origin, and then rescale the shape by standardizing the variance of the radius *r*[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si12.png).

The centroid is the weighted average of the points located on the shape. Typically, the weight is constant. However, if the points are not uniformly distributed on the shape, you may use appropriate weights to correct for this artifact. This is illustrated in [Fig. 6.2](#Chp006_103-111_B9780443218576000102.xhtml#f0015). I now dive into the details of the reweighting procedure.

![Figure 6.2 Weighted centroid, shape signature.](images/B9780443218576000102/gr002.jpg)

Figure 6.2 Weighted centroid, shape signature.

### 6.3.1 Weighted centroid

Let (*x*[*t*], *y*[*t*])![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si13.png) be the standard coordinates of the observed points on the shape. In other words, *x*[*t*] = *r*[*t*]cos *θ*[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si14.png) and *y*[*t*] = *r*[*t*]sin *θ*[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si15.png). The centroid is defined as (*G*[*x*], *G*[*y*])![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si16.png) with

$G\_{x} = \\frac{1}{\\mu}\\int\_{T}w\_{t}x\_{t}dt,\\quad G\_{y} = \\frac{1}{\\mu}\\int\_{T}w\_{t}y\_{t}dt,\\quad\\text{with~}\\mu = \\int\_{T}w\_{t}dt.$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si17.png)(6.2) 

Here *w*[*t*] > 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si18.png) is the weight function, with *t* ∈ *T*![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si19.png). If *t* is discrete (for instance, the shape consists of observed data points), then the integrals are replaced by sums.

In most cases, the points are not evenly distributed on the curve. On a real data set, it translates by a curve that appears darker or thicker in locations with high point density; see [Fig. 6.2](#Chp006_103-111_B9780443218576000102.xhtml#f0015). If this is not a desirable feature, it can be eliminated by proper reweighting. To get the points evenly distributed on the curve, when computing the centroid, proceed as follows. Using notations from infinitesimal calculus, you want *Δ**s*[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si20.png), the length of an infinitesimal curve segment encompassing (*x*[*t*], *y*[*t*])![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si13.png), to be proportional to *w*[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si21.png). Since the proportion factor does not matter, we must have

$\\Delta s\_{t} = \\sqrt{{(\\Delta x\_{t})}^{2} + {(\\Delta y\_{t})}^{2}} = w\_{t}\\Delta t.$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si22.png)

This leads to

$w\_{t} = \\sqrt{\\left( \\frac{dx\_{t}}{dt} \\right)^{2} + \\left( \\frac{dy\_{t}}{dt} \\right)^{2}}.$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si23.png)

It can be rewritten using polar coordinates as

$w\_{t} = \\sqrt{\\left( \\frac{dr\_{t}}{dt} \\right)^{2} + r\_{t}^{2}\\left( \\frac{d\\theta\_{t}}{dt} \\right)^{2}}.$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si24.png)

The formula assumes differentiability of the functions involved. In many cases, there are points (values of *t*) where the functions are either left- or right-differentiable \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semi-differentiability)\], but not both. Use the left or right derivative for these points.

### 6.3.2 Computing the signature

We want a mathematical object, easy to compute, that uniquely characterizes a shape, up to a translation vector and scaling factor. The set of all polar coordinates (*r*[*t*], *θ*[*t*])![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si25.png), with *t* ∈ *T*![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si19.png), uniquely characterizes the shape. But it is not scale- or translation-invariant. To fix this problem, you first need to change the coordinate system to make the centroid (*G*[*x*], *G*[*y*])![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si16.png) defined by formula [(6.2)](#Chp006_103-111_B9780443218576000102.xhtml#deq4), the origin. You may use the weight function *w*[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si21.png) discussed in Section [6.3.1](#Chp006_103-111_B9780443218576000102.xhtml#s0025). Then, you need to rescale by a factor *σ*. Eventually, the new coordinates are

*u*[*t*] = *σ*^( − 1) ⋅ (*x*[*t*] − *G*[*x*]) = *ρ*[*t*]cos *φ*[*t*], *v*[*t*] = *σ*^( − 1) ⋅ (*y*[*y*] − *G*[*y*]) = *ρ*[*t*]sin *φ*[*t*].

![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si26.png)

Here *u*[*t*], *v*[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si27.png) are the new Cartesian coordinates replacing *x*[*t*], *y*[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si28.png), and *ρ*[*t*], *φ*[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si29.png) the new polar coordinates replacing *r*[*t*], *θ*[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si30.png). For reasons that will become obvious when comparing two shapes in Section [6.4](#Chp006_103-111_B9780443218576000102.xhtml#s0040), the scaling factor is chosen as follows:

$\\sigma = \\sqrt{\\int\_{T}{(x\_{t} - G\_{x})}^{2} + {(y\_{t} - G\_{y})}^{2}dt}.$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si31.png)

It follows immediately that

$\\rho\_{t} = \\sigma^{- 1} \\cdot \\sqrt{{(x\_{t} - G\_{x})}^{2} + {(y\_{t} - G\_{y})}^{2}},\\quad\\text{and~}\\int\_{T}\\rho\_{t}^{2}dt = 1.$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si32.png)(6.3) 

Now the signature is defined as the set of all (*ρ*[*t*], *φ*[*t*])![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si33.png) with *t* ∈ *T*![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si19.png). By construction, 0 ≤ *φ*[*t*] ≤ 2*π*![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si34.png). When plotting the signature, to keep it bounded on \[0, 2*π*\] × \[0, 1\]![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si35.png) regardless of the shape, one can use *ρ*[*t*]/(1 + *ρ*[*t*])![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si36.png) instead of *ρ*[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si37.png) on the vertical axis. An example of signature is shown in [Fig. 6.2](#Chp006_103-111_B9780443218576000102.xhtml#f0015) (right plot).

### 6.3.3 Example

The shape illustrated in Figs. [6.2](#Chp006_103-111_B9780443218576000102.xhtml#f0015) and [6.3](#Chp006_103-111_B9780443218576000102.xhtml#f0020) is different from that defined by [(6.1)](#Chp006_103-111_B9780443218576000102.xhtml#deq2). This time, it is defined by the parametric polar equation

*θ*[*t*] = (2*π* + 2*π*sin (*c**t*) + *η*) *m**o**d* 2*π*, *r*[*t*] = *t*^(*a*)(1 − *t*)^(*b*), *t* ∈ *T* = \[0, 1\].

![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si38.png)(6.4) 

Again, *η* is the angle determining the orientation of the shape. The point density, visible to the naked eye, is much higher on the right side of the shape on the left plot in [Fig. 6.2](#Chp006_103-111_B9780443218576000102.xhtml#f0015). This is even more pronounced on the lower part. As a result, the centroid (orange dot; dark gray in print version) attracted to the dense area of the curve. Once this effect is corrected by the weight function, the new centroid (gray dot) now appears well “centered”. Note that the weight function *w*[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si21.png), pictured in [Fig. 6.3](#Chp006_103-111_B9780443218576000102.xhtml#f0020), is bimodal. It was chosen to integrate to one, thus it represents a probability distribution on *T* = \[0, 1\]![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si39.png).

![Figure 6.3 Weight function used in Fig. 6.2.](images/B9780443218576000102/gr003.jpg)

Figure 6.3 Weight function used in [Fig. 6.2](#Chp006_103-111_B9780443218576000102.xhtml#f0015).

## 6.4 Shape comparison

I start with a correlation metric based on the mathematical theory developed so far. I then discuss its strengths and weaknesses, and how to improve it. A full implementation on a real data set is investigated in Section [6.5](#Chp006_103-111_B9780443218576000102.xhtml#s0050). I use the notation *ρ*[*t*], *φ*[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si29.png) for the first shape, and *ρ*[*t*]^′, *φ*[*t*]^′![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si40.png) for the second. Assuming the parametric polar equations are such that (possibly after an appropriate transformation) *φ*[*t*] = *φ*[*t*]^′![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si41.png) for *t* ∈ *T*![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si19.png), then define

*γ* = ∫[*T*](*ρ*[*t*] − *ρ*[*t*]^′)²*d**t* = ∫[*T*]*ρ*[*t*]²*d**t* + ∫*ρ*[*t*]^′²*d**t* − 2∫[*T*]*ρ*[*t*]*ρ*[*t*]^′*d**t* = 2 − 2*λ*,

![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si42.png)

where

*λ* = ∫[*T*]*ρ*[*t*]*ρ*[*t*]^′*d**t*.

![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si43.png)

It follows from [(6.3)](#Chp006_103-111_B9780443218576000102.xhtml#deq10) that 0 ≤ *λ* ≤ 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si44.png). Furthermore, the two shapes are identical (up to a scaling factor and translation vector) if and only if *λ* = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si45.png). The correlation *λ* measures how close the two shapes are from each other. It relies on the fact that *φ*[*t*] = *φ*[*t*]^′![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si41.png). It this assumption is mildly violated, the classifier may still work on simple data sets, for instance, to recognize the letters of the alphabet. But it may fail is the discrepancy between *φ*[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si46.png) and *φ*[*t*]^′![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si47.png) is significant.

It is not always possible to satisfy *φ*[*t*] = *φ*[*t*]^′![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si41.png) for complicated shapes consisting of multiple arcs. But it can always be done for closed, convex shapes. Also, if the shapes are identical but rotated, usually *λ* ≠ 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si48.png). The coefficient *λ* depends on the orientation angles *η*, *η*^′![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si49.png) of each shape, illustrated in formula [(6.1)](#Chp006_103-111_B9780443218576000102.xhtml#deq2). For this reason, *λ* is also denoted as *λ*(*η*, *η*^′)![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si50.png).

To circumvent this problem, one can use

$\\lambda^{\\ast} = \\min\\limits\_{\\eta,\\eta^{\\prime}}\\lambda(\\eta,\\eta^{\\prime}).$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si51.png)

Then the two shapes are identical, up to the scaling factors, translation vectors, and orientations, if and only if *λ*^(\*) = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si52.png). Due to symmetry, one can set *η* = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si53.png). In practice, the metric  − log (1 − *λ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si54.png) or  − log (1 − *λ*^(\*))![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si55.png) is used instead. See [\[4\]](#Chp006_103-111_B9780443218576000102.xhtml#br0020) for a general reference on shape correlation.

Of course, it is always possible to compare two shapes by comparing their signatures, see [\[2\]](#Chp006_103-111_B9780443218576000102.xhtml#br0010). One way to do it is as follows. For each point *P*[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si56.png) on the first shape signature, find its closest neighbor *Q*[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si57.png) on the second shape signature, and compute the distance *D*[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si58.png) between these two points. Then compute

*D* = ∫[*T*]*D*[*t*]*d**t*.

![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si59.png)

Repeat the operation by swapping the roles of the first and second shape: for each point *Q*[*t*]^′![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si60.png) on the second shape signature, find its closest neighbor *P*[*t*]^′![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si61.png) on the first shape signature, and compute the distance *D*[*t*]^′![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si62.png) between these two points. Then compute

*D*^′ = ∫[*T*]*D*[*t*]^′*d**t*.

![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si63.png)

If *D* = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si64.png), the first shape is a subset of the second shape. If *D*^′ = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si65.png), the second shape is a subset of the first shape. If *D* = *D*^′ = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si66.png), the shapes are identical. Thus *δ* = min (*D*, *D*^′)![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si67.png) is a metric measuring shape similarity. It is closely related to the **Hausdorff distance** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hausdorff_distance)\], albeit less sensitive to outliers.

### 6.4.1 Shape classification

Now that we have a metric to compare two shapes, we can use it as a similarity measure to perform shape classification. If shapes *S*[1]![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si68.png) and *S*[2]![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si69.png) have  − log (1 − *λ*) > *α*![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si70.png), we may write *S*[1] ∼ *S*[2]![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si71.png) to mean that they are equivalent (very similar). In this case, *α* = 8![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si72.png) is a good threshold. In character recognition, if you have a training set with thousands of hieroglyphs, you can use this technique to classify any new hieroglyph as equivalent to one or more in your training set, or as yet uncategorized (a brand new one, or one so poorly written that it is not recognizable).

## 6.5 Application

In all the cases investigated, including the mathematical ones, the computations were performed using sample points on the shape, corresponding to evenly spaced values of *t*. I used sums rather than integrals, and derivatives such as *d**x*[*t*]/*d**t*![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si73.png) were replaced by differences between successive values of *x*[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si74.png). You can find the computations in my spreadsheet Shapes4.xlsx, located on my GitHub repository, [here](https://github.com/VincentGranville/Machine-Learning/blob/main/Spreadsheets/README.md).

**Spreadsheet and data**

The two main examples are:

*   •  20 points for the case pictured in [Fig. 6.1](#Chp006_103-111_B9780443218576000102.xhtml#f0010). Here I tested 8 pairs of shapes; you can find the summary in the animated Gif, posted [here](https://mltechniques.com/2022/04/20/computer-vision-shape-classification-via-explainable-ai/). In addition, I introduced various levels of noise to test the discriminating power of the classifier. The amount of noise is controlled by the parameter Precision.
*   •  1000 points for the case pictured in [Fig. 6.2](#Chp006_103-111_B9780443218576000102.xhtml#f0015). Details are in the Shape\_Signature tab in the spreadsheet. In the same tab, you will find the computation of the weight function, the weighted centroid, and the computations related to the new coordinate system *ρ*[*t*], *φ*[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si29.png). 

My simulations rely on synthetic data \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synthetic_data)\]. In other words, I use mathematically-generated shapes. The benefit is that you can generate a large class of shapes (actually, infinitely many), mimicking any existing shape, and compare the performance of various shape classifiers. In particular, you can assess how well a specific metric can detect different, yet very similar shapes, or how it performs when various levels of noise are introduced. Modern methods combine real observations with synthetic data to further enrich training sets. This is known as **augmented data** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_augmentation)\].

Several other machine learning techniques, tested on synthetic data and accompanied by professional summary spreadsheets, are available (along with the data sets and source code), in my book “Stochastic Processes and Simulations: A Machine Learning Perspective”. Many are described in Chapter [16](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml).

## 6.6 Exercises

The first exercise has an elegant solution. The second is an application of the principles discussed.

Exercise 6.1

Find the weight function satisfying *Δ*(*w*[*t*]*x*[*t*]) = *Δ*(*w*[*t*]*y*[*t*])![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si75.png). This is related to the material presented in Section [6.3.1](#Chp006_103-111_B9780443218576000102.xhtml#s0025). It uses the same notations.

**Solution**

You need to find *w*[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si21.png) satisfying *x*[*t*]*Δ**w*[*t*] + *w*[*t*]*Δ**x*[*t*] = *y*[*t*]*Δ**w*[*t*] + *w*[*t*]*Δ**y*[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si76.png). Dividing by Δ*t*, and letting *Δ**t* → 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si77.png), we get

$x\_{t}\\frac{dw\_{t}}{dt} + w\_{t}\\frac{dx\_{t}}{dt} = y\_{t}\\frac{dw\_{t}}{dt} + w\_{t}\\frac{dy\_{t}}{dt},$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si78.png)

that is,

$(x\_{t} - y\_{t})\\frac{dw\_{t}}{dt} = \\left( \\frac{dy\_{t}}{dt} - \\frac{dx\_{t}}{dt} \\right)w\_{t}.$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si79.png)

This is successively equivalent to

$\\frac{d}{dt}(\\log w\_{t}) = \\frac{1}{w\_{t}}\\frac{dw\_{t}}{dt} = \\frac{1}{x\_{t} - y\_{t}}\\left( \\frac{dy\_{t}}{dt} - \\frac{dx\_{t}}{dt} \\right),\\log w\_{t} = \\int\\frac{1}{x\_{t} - y\_{t}}\\left( \\frac{dy\_{t}}{dt} - \\frac{dx\_{t}}{dt} \\right)dt + C,w\_{t} = C^{\\prime}\\exp\\left\\lbrack - \\int\_{0}^{t}\\frac{1}{y\_{\\tau} - x\_{\\tau}}\\left( \\frac{dy\_{\\tau}}{d\\tau} - \\frac{dx\_{\\tau}}{d\\tau} \\right)d\\tau \\right\\rbrack,$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si80.png)

where *C*, *C*^′![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si81.png) are constants, with *C*^′ > 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si82.png). The value of *C*^′![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si83.png) is unimportant when using formula [(6.2)](#Chp006_103-111_B9780443218576000102.xhtml#deq4). However, you can choose it so that the weight function integrates to one. Or you can use *C*^′ = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si84.png). I assumed, without loss of generality, that the integration domain *T* is an interval containing the origin *τ* = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si85.png).

You can test this formula on a line segment, defined by *x*[*t*] = *t*![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si86.png), *y*[*t*] = *a* + *b**t*![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si87.png), with *t* ∈ \[0, 1\]![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si88.png). This is the most basic shape other than a finite set of points! A slightly more difficult exercise is to find the weight function satisfying |*Δ*(*w*[*t*]*x*[*t*])| = |*Δ*(*w*[*t*]*y*[*t*])|![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si89.png). [Exercise 6.1](#Chp006_103-111_B9780443218576000102.xhtml#enun0010) is a starting point to solve this problem. 

Exercise 6.2

Compare the shape in [Fig. 6.2](#Chp006_103-111_B9780443218576000102.xhtml#f0015) with that of [Fig. 6.4](#Chp006_103-111_B9780443218576000102.xhtml#f0025), using the metrics presented in this chapter (*D* and *λ*). These shapes correspond to Eq. [(6.4)](#Chp006_103-111_B9780443218576000102.xhtml#deq11). The first has parameters *a* = 7![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si90.png), *b* = 6![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si91.png), *c* = 8![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si92.png). The second has parameters *a* = *b* = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si93.png), *c* = 2*π*![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si94.png). In both cases, *η* = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si53.png). Use 1000 sample points on each shape for comparison purposes. Order the points according to *t*, then according to *φ*[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si46.png), to see the impact on *λ*. Set *η* = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si53.png), and choose *η*^′![Image](images/B9780443218576000102/si95.png) (the orientation of the second shape) to maximize the similarity between the two shapes.

![Figure 6.4 Another interesting shape.](images/B9780443218576000102/gr004.jpg)

[Figure 6.4](#Chp006_103-111_B9780443218576000102.xhtml#cf0125) Another interesting shape.

**Solution**

A starting point is my spreadsheet Shapes4.xlsx, available on my GitHub repository, [here](https://github.com/VincentGranville/Machine-Learning/blob/main/Spreadsheets/README.md). This type of shape is analyzed in the Shape\_Signature tab.

# Chapter 7: Synthetic data, interpretable regression, and submodels

## Little known secrets about linear regression

## Abstract

The technique discussed here handles a large class of problems. In this article, I focus on a simple one, namely linear regression. I solve it with an iterative algorithm (fixed point) that shares some resemblance to gradient boosting, using machine learning methods and explainable AI, as opposed to traditional statistics. In particular, the algorithm does not use matrix inversion. It is easy to implement in Excel (I provide my spreadsheet) or to automate as a black-box system. Also, it is numerically stable, can generalize to nonlinear problems. Unlike the traditional statistical solution leading to meaningless regression coefficients, here the output coefficients are easier to understand, leading to better interpretation. I tested it on a rich collection of synthetic data sets: it performs just as well as the standard technique, even after adding noise to the data. I then show how to measure the impact of individual features, or groups of features (and feature interaction), on the solution. A model with *m* features has 2^(*m*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si1.png) submodels. I show how to draw more insights by analyzing the performance of each submodel. Finally, I introduce a new metric called *score* to measure model performance. Based on comparison with the base model, it is more meaningful than R-squared or mean squared error.

### Keywords

tabular data; linear regression; synthetic data; step-wise regression; explainable AI; feature selection

The technique discussed here handles a large class of problems. In this article, I focus on a simple one, namely linear regression. I solve it with an iterative algorithm (fixed point) that shares some resemblance to gradient boosting, using machine learning methods and explainable AI, as opposed to traditional statistics. In particular, the algorithm does not use matrix inversion. It is easy to implement in Excel (I provide my spreadsheet) or to automate as a black-box system. Also, it is numerically stable, can generalize to nonlinear problems. Unlike the traditional statistical solution leading to meaningless regression coefficients, here the output coefficients are easier to understand, leading to better interpretation. I tested it on a rich collection of synthetic data sets: it performs just as well as the standard technique, even after adding noise to the data. I then show how to measure the impact of individual features, or groups of features (and feature interaction), on the solution. A model with *m* features has 2^(*m*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si1.png) submodels. I show how to draw more insights by analyzing the performance of each submodel. Finally, I introduce a new metric called *score* to measure model performance. Based on comparison with the base model, it is more meaningful than R-squared or mean squared error.

## 7.1 Introduction

Here, *X* denotes the input. It is represented as a matrix with *n* rows and *m* columns; *n* is the number of observations, and *m* the number of features, also called dependent variables. The response (also called independent variable or output) is a column vector with *n* entries, and denoted as *Y*. The *m* regression coefficients (unknown, to be estimated) are stored in a column vector denoted as *β*. Thus we have

*Y* = *X**β* + *ϵ*,

![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si2.png)(7.1) 

where *ϵ* – also a column vector with *n* entries – is the error. The problem consists of finding a suitable *β* that, in some way, minimizes the error. If there was no error term, Eq. [(7.1)](#Chp007_113-129_B9780443218576000114.xhtml#deq1) could be rewritten as *X*^(*T*)*Y* = *X*^(*T*)*X**β* + *Λ**β* − *Λ**β*![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si3.png), that is,

*β* = *Λ*^( − 1)*X*^(*T*)*Y* + (*I* − *Λ*^( − 1)*X*^(*T*)*X*)*β*.

![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si4.png)

Here Λ is any nonsingular (invertible) *m* × *m*![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si5.png) matrix, and ^(*T*) denotes the matrix or vector transposition operator \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transpose)\]. This gives rise to the following iterative algorithm:

*β*[*k* + 1] = *Λ*^( − 1)*X*^(*T*)*Y* + (*I* − *Λ*^( − 1)*X*^(*T*)*X*)*β*[*k*],

![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si6.png)(7.2) 

starting with some initial configuration *β*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si7.png) for the parameter vector (the regression coefficients). I use a diagonal matrix for Λ, so the methodology does not involve complicated matrix inversions.

I also use the following notations: *M* = *X*^(*T*)*X*![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si8.png) and *S* = *I* − *Λ*^( − 1)*M*![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si9.png). The convergence of this iterative algorithm, and how fast it converges, is entirely governed by how fast *S*^(*k*) → 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si10.png) as *k* → ∞![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si11.png). It requires a careful choice of Λ. I discuss later how to update Λ at each iteration *k*: in an adaptive version of this algorithm, Λ is replaced by *Λ*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si12.png) in [(7.2)](#Chp007_113-129_B9780443218576000114.xhtml#deq3), with the hope that it boosts convergence. The general term for this type of iteration, which also encompasses Newton optimization and gradient descent, is a **fixed point algorithm** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fixed-point_iteration)\].

The remaining of this discussion focuses on the choice of Λ and *β*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si7.png), with convergence implications and computational complexity, tested on **synthetic data** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synthetic_data)\]. I show that with very few iterations, one generally gets a very good predictor, even though the estimated parameter vector is quite different from the target one used in the simulations. In short, the R-squared arising from rough approximations, based on a few iterations of the fixed point algorithm, is very similar to that obtained using the full standard statistical apparatus. Despite the nonstatistical perspective and the absence of statistical model, I explain how to compute confidence intervals for the estimated regression coefficients and for the predicted values. The whole framework is designed to facilitate interpretation, and thus it falls in the category of explainable AI \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Explainable_artificial_intelligence)\].

Finally, I want to offer a simple version of this method, simple enough to easily be implemented in Excel. The choice *β*[0] = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si13.png) and Λ minimizing the **Frobenius norm** of *S* \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matrix_norm)\] (see also [\[2\]](#Chp007_113-129_B9780443218576000114.xhtml#br0010)) not only works well but also leads to simple formulas, and an interesting connection to **eigenvalues** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eigenvalues_and_eigenvectors)\] (see also [here](https://mathoverflow.net/questions/421309/power-of-a-matrix-largest-eigenvalue-in-absolute-value-and-convergence-acceler)). The last part of this chapter focuses on assessing the influence of each feature, and the impact of feature interaction. The synthetic training set data discussed in Section [7.2](#Chp007_113-129_B9780443218576000114.xhtml#s0015) allows you to simulate and test a large number of varied situations. Eventually, model performance is measured on a validation set, not on a training set.

## 7.2 Synthetic data sets and the spreadsheet

Rather than testing the methodology on a few real-life data sets, I tested it on a large number of very different synthetic data sets, each with its unique correlation structure. These data sets are generated via simulations, as follows. First, generate *m* column vectors *Z*[1], …, *Z*[*m*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si14.png), with *Z*[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si15.png) consisting of *n* deviates *Z*[*i**j*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si16.png) (1 ≤ *i* ≤ *m*![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si17.png), 1 ≤ *j* ≤ *n*![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si18.png)). One of the simplest distributions to sample from is the **generalized logistic**. See examples in Chapter [16](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml), to simulate cluster processes. In this case I used

$Z\_{ij} = - \\log\\frac{U\_{ij}^{\\gamma}}{1 - U\_{ij}^{\\gamma}},$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si19.png)

where *γ* > 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si20.png) is a parameter, and *U*[*i**j*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si21.png)'s are independently and identically distributed uniform deviates on \[0, 1\]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si22.png). Then, I generated *m* column vectors *X*[1], …, *X*[*m*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si23.png) as random linear combinations of the *Z*[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si15.png)'s:

$X\_{i} = \\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{m}w\_{ij}Z\_{i},\\quad i = 1,\\ldots,m.$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si24.png)(7.3) 

The *m* × *m*![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si5.png) matrix *W* = (*w*[*i**j*])![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si25.png) is called the weight matrix. Here again, the *w*[*i**j*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si26.png)'s are deviates from the same family of generalized logistic distributions. Finally, the simulated response is

$Y = \\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{m}\\alpha\_{i}X\_{i} + \\tau\\epsilon,\\quad i = 1,\\ldots,m,$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si27.png)

where *ϵ* (a column vector with *n* independent entries) is an artificially generated white noise, and *τ* ≥ 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si28.png) controls the amount of noise. The *α*[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si29.png)'s can be prespecified or randomly generated. In any case, the exact, prespecified set of regression coefficients is the column vector *α* = (*α*[1], …, *α*[*m*])^(*T*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si30.png). The estimated coefficients, at the *k*th iteration of the fixed point algorithm, using formula [(7.2)](#Chp007_113-129_B9780443218576000114.xhtml#deq3), comprise the column vector *β*[*k*] = (*β*[*k*1], …, *β*[*k**m*])^(*T*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si31.png). Thus in this setting, we are able to measure how close the estimate *β*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si32.png) is to the exact value *α*. In real-life applications, the exact value is never known. If it was, there would be no need to perform statistical inference.

### 7.2.1 Correlation structure

Let *Ω*[*X*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si33.png) (respectively *Ω*[*Z*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si34.png)) be the *m* × *m*![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si5.png) **covariance matrix** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Covariance_matrix)\] attached to *X*[1], …, *X*[*m*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si23.png) (respectively to *Z*[1], …, *Z*[*m*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si14.png)). Likewise, define the correlation matrices as *R*[*X*], *R*[*Z*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si35.png), with

*R*[*X*] = \[*D*(*Ω*[*X*])\]^( − 1/2)*Ω*[*X*]\[*D*(*Ω*[*X*])\]^( − 1/2) and *R*[*Z*] = \[*D*(*Ω*[*Z*])\]^( − 1/2)*Ω*[*Z*]\[*D*(*Ω*[*Z*])\]^( − 1/2).

![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si36.png)

Here *D*(*A*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si37.png) is the matrix consisting of the diagonal elements of the matrix *A*. We have

*Ω*[*X*] = *W**Ω*[*Z*]*W*^(*T*) = (*W**Ω*[*X*]^(1/2))(*W**Ω*[*X*]^(1/2))^(*T*), thus *W* = *Ω*[*X*]^(1/2)*Ω*[*Z*]^( − 1/2).

![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si38.png)

These formulas allow you to easily compute *R*[*X*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si39.png) based on the weight matrix *W* and *Ω*[*W*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si40.png). Though more difficult, it is possible to solve the inverse problem: prespecify the correlation structure *R*[*X*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si39.png) of the data set, and then find *W* that yields the desired, target *R*[*X*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si39.png). This is best accomplished using an iterative algorithm similar to the fixed point discussed in Section [7.1](#Chp007_113-129_B9780443218576000114.xhtml#s0010), using the above formulas.

The formulas to solve the inverse problem involve the **square root** of **positive semidefinite matrices** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Square_root_of_a_matrix)\]. The solution is not unique. See how it is done, in Chapter [3](#Chp003_49-60_B9780443218576000072.xhtml) entitled “Gentle Introduction to Linear Algebra”. Without loss of generality, a simplification consists of simulating standardized *Z*[1], …, *Z*[*m*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si14.png) (from a distribution with zero mean and unit variance) so that *R*[*Z*] = *Ω*[*Z*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si41.png) is the identity matrix. If, in addition, the observed *X*[1], …, *X*[*m*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si23.png) are also standardized, then *R*[*X*] = *Ω*[*X*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si42.png), and thus, *W* = *R*[*X*]^(1/2)![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si43.png). Multiple square roots exist, in the same way that 2 and −2 are two “square roots” of 4.

### 7.2.2 Standardized regression

Under stable conditions, the predicted values for *Y* are very close to those obtained via standard statistical regression, even though the estimated regression coefficients may be quite different. The accompanying spreadsheet and computations are now stable. However, in previous tests, with a different damping schedule (the matrix Λ), sometimes the *β*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si32.png) diverged as *k* → ∞![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si11.png). Yet after normalizing *β*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si32.png), the instability was essentially removed and, again, the predicted *Y* was sound. I provide here the normalizing formula, to guarantee that the standard deviation of the response *Y*, denoted as *σ*[*Y*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si44.png), is identical to that measured on the predicted *Y*. The new *β*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si32.png), denoted as *β*[*k*]^(\*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si45.png), is computed as follows:

$\\beta\_{k}^{\\ast} = \\frac{\\sigma\_{Y}}{\\sqrt{\\beta\_{k}^{T}\\Omega\_{X}\\beta\_{k}}} \\cdot \\Omega\_{W}\\beta\_{k}.$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si46.png)

This may be useful if you modify Λ when doing some research, as a technique to stabilize the predictions. I also included the computation of *β*[*k*]^(\*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si45.png) in the spreadsheet. However, it is best to avoid standardizing the regression coefficients when the algorithm is numerically stable. It results in more realistic variance in the predicted values as the uncorrected regression acts as a smoother, but it also comes with a price – a larger mean squared error.

To the contrary, shifting the predicted values so that their mean matches that of the observed values on the training set, is always useful. It is included in my computations (and in the spreadsheet) as a final, postprocessing step. It does not impact the R-squared. Also, it allows you to ignore the intercept parameter in the regression model. Indeed, this is an easy workaround to using an actual intercept parameter.

### 7.2.3 Initial conditions

The neutral choice *β*[0] = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si13.png) as the starting vector of regression coefficients, for the iterative fixed point algorithm, works well. Another option consists of choosing regression coefficients that preserve the correlation sign between the response *Y*, and each feature *X*[1], …, *X*[*m*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si23.png). Here, *X*[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si48.png) is the *i*th column of the matrix *X*. Let

$c\_{i} = \\frac{{Cov}\\lbrack Y,X\_{i}\\rbrack}{{Var}\\lbrack X\_{i}\\rbrack},\\quad c = {(c\_{1},\\ldots,c\_{m})}^{T},\\quad Q = \\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{m}c\_{i}X\_{i} = Xc,$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si49.png)

with *ω* a real number chosen to minimize the error *ϵ*^(*T*)*ϵ* = (*Y* − *ω**Q*)^(*T*)(*Y* − *ω**Q*) = *Y*^(*T*)*Y* − 2*Q*^(*T*)*Y**ω* + *Q*^(*T*)*Q**ω*²![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si50.png). We have

$w = \\frac{Y^{T}Q}{Q^{T}Q} = \\frac{Y^{T}Xc}{c^{T}X^{T}Xc}\\quad\\text{and}\\quad{Var}\\lbrack c\_{i}X\_{i}\\rbrack = {Var}\\lbrack Y\\rbrack \\cdot \\rho^{2}\\lbrack X\_{i},Y\\rbrack = \\sigma\_{Y}^{2} \\cdot \\rho^{2}\\lbrack X\_{i},Y\\rbrack,$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si51.png)

where *ρ* denotes the correlation function. Now, *β*[0] = *ω**c*![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si52.png) is a starting point that makes sense, easy to interpret, and better then *β*[0] = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si13.png). It significantly reduces the residual error, over the base model *β* = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si53.png). In many cases, it yields a residual error almost comparable to that of the best predictors.

As an illustration, let us say that *X*[2] = *X*[3]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si54.png). You should avoid highly correlated features in your data set, but in some cases the interdependencies among several features are strong but much harder to detect, and result in the same problem. In my example, assuming both *X*[2]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si55.png) and *X*[3]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si56.png) are positively correlated to the response *Y*, a model with +4 and −2 for the regression coefficients attached to *X*[2]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si55.png) and *X*[3]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si56.png), performs just as well as −2, +4 or +1, +1. The *β*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si7.png) proposed here addresses this issue: it guarantees that the regression coefficients attached to *X*[2]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si55.png) and *X*[3]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si56.png) are both positive in this example, and identical if *X*[2] = *X*[3]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si54.png). It makes the regression coefficients much easier to interpret. In addition, this technique is numerically stable and more robust.

### 7.2.4 Simulations and Excel spreadsheet

Formulas and computations described in Section [7.2](#Chp007_113-129_B9780443218576000114.xhtml#s0015) are implemented in my spreadsheet Regression5.xlsx, available [here](https://github.com/VincentGranville/Machine-Learning/blob/main/Spreadsheets/README.md) on my GitHub repository. This material covers a large chunk of the spreadsheet, with the remaining explained in the next sections.

The Test and Results tabs in the spreadsheet contain the following:

*   •  The random deviates *Z*[1], …, *Z*[*m*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si14.png) are in the Test tab in columns A:F. The zero-mean noise is in column H. The amount of noise in the response *Y* is controlled by the parameter Noise in cell E:5 in the Results tab. As a general rule, cells highlighted in light yellow in the Results tab correspond to parameters or hyperparameters that you can modify. The parameter *γ* just above in cell E:4 is the core parameter of the generalized logistic distribution used to simulate the column vectors *Z*[1], …, *Z*[*m*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si14.png).
*   •  The flag in cell E:7 in the Results tab allows you to choose either *β*[0] = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si13.png), or the special *β*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si7.png) discussed in Section [7.2.3](#Chp007_113-129_B9780443218576000114.xhtml#s0030).
*   •  By default, the regression uses the traditional *β*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si32.png). If you want to use the normalized *β*[*k*]^(\*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si45.png) instead, they are iteratively computed in cells AX2:ES7 in the Test tab. For instance, cells BL2:BL7 represent *β*[15]^(\*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si57.png), that is, the 15th iterate (*k* = 15![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si58.png)) in the fixed point algorithm, stored as a column vector. The standard *β*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si32.png) are computed in cells AX20:ES25 in the same tab.
*   •  Column I in the Test tab is the response *Y*. The features *X*[1], …, *X*[*m*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si23.png), also called independent variables, are in columns J:O in the same tab. They are generated as linear combinations of the random vectors *Z*[1], …, *Z*[*m*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si14.png). More precisely, *X* = *W**Z*![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si59.png) as per Eq. [(7.3)](#Chp007_113-129_B9780443218576000114.xhtml#deq5), where *W* is the *m* × *m*![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si5.png) weight matrix. The random weight matrix *W* is stored in cells B15:G20 in the Results tab. The actual, true (random) regression parameters are just above in the same tab, in cells B12:G12.
*   •  Intermediary computations are in the Test tab. For instance, the *m* × *m*![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si5.png) matrix *X*^(*T*)*X*![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si60.png) is stored in cells AP2:AU7, the vector *X*^(*T*)*Y*![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si61.png) in cells AN2:AN7, the correlation matrix *R*[*X*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si39.png) in cells AE3:AJ8, and the covariance matrix *Ω*[*X*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si33.png) in cells AE12:AJ17.

The interactive spreadsheet extensively uses the SumProduct and Transpose Excel functions, to easily multiply a row vector by a column vector with just one simple operation. It also makes matrix multiplications easier.

## 7.3 Damping schedule and convergence acceleration

The *m* × *m*![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si5.png) diagonal matrix *Λ*^( − 1)![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si62.png) in Eq. [(7.2)](#Chp007_113-129_B9780443218576000114.xhtml#deq3) is called the damping parameter, or **preconditioner** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Preconditioner)\] of the fixed point iteration. It governs the rate of convergence. The fixed point algorithm converges if |*φ*| < 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si63.png), where *φ* = *φ*(*S*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si64.png) is the largest eigenvalue of *S* = *I* − *Λ*^( − 1)*X*^(*T*)*X*![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si65.png), in absolute value. The smaller the |*φ*|![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si66.png), the faster the convergence. The convergence speed is eventually determined by how fast *S*^(*k*) → 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si10.png) as *k* → ∞![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si11.png), itself being a function of |*φ*|![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si66.png). Thus, it makes sense to choose Λ so that *S* is close to zero. One way to do it is to choose Λ that minimizes the Frobenius norm of *S* or, in other words, Λ that minimizes the sum of the square of the coefficients of *S*. This leads to

$\\lambda\_{i}^{- 1} = \\frac{1}{m\_{ii}}\\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{m}m\_{ij}^{2},\\quad i = 1,\\ldots,m,$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si67.png)(7.4) 

where *λ*[1], …, *λ*[*m*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si68.png) are the diagonal elements of the diagonal matrix Λ, and *m*[*i**j*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si69.png) is the *j*th element in column *i*, of the matrix *M* = *X*^(*T*)*X*![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si8.png). In practice, with this choice of Λ, assuming *M* is not singular, the fixed point iteration always converges, and *m*[*i**i*] > 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si70.png). See discussion on this topic, [here](https://mathoverflow.net/questions/421309/power-of-a-matrix-largest-eigenvalue-in-absolute-value-and-convergence-acceler).

### 7.3.1 Spreadsheet implementation

The *λ*[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si71.png)'s are computed in cells AL2:AL7 in the Test tab. Also, |*φ*|![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si66.png) is iteratively computed in cells AY59:ES59 in the same tab. The method used in the spreadsheet to compute |*φ*|![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si66.png) is known as **power iteration** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_iteration)\]. See also [here](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/2554808/finding-approximation-of-largest-eigenvalue).

Now we have everything in place to compute the regression coefficients. They are found in cells K5:P5 (computation based on *k* = 15![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si58.png) iterations) and K6:P6 (based on *k* = 100![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si72.png) iterations) in the Results tab. The final value of |*φ*|![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si66.png) is in cell K21, also in the Results tab. Note that values of |*φ*|![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si66.png) above 0.95 means that the system is **ill-conditioned** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Condition_number)\]. For instance, some features are almost linear combinations of other features. It typically results in poor performance. In this case, using a few iterations (*k* = 15![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si58.png)), together with the initial *β*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si7.png) suggested in Section [7.2.3](#Chp007_113-129_B9780443218576000114.xhtml#s0030), works best. It also avoids overfitting issues.

The predicted values of *Y*, obtained after *k* = 15![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si58.png) and *k* = 100![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si72.png) iterations, are in columns P and Q, respectively, in the Test tab. The predicted values obtained with *β*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si7.png) alone (as computed in Section [7.2.3](#Chp007_113-129_B9780443218576000114.xhtml#s0030)) are in column S, while those obtained with traditional regression are in column U and produced with the Linest Excel function. The filtered response, obtained by removing the artificial noise introduced in the observed (synthetic) data, is in column R. The computational complexity of the fixed point regression is the same as multiplying two *m* × *m*![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si5.png) matrices, multiplied by the number of iterations in the fixed point algorithm.

### 7.3.2 Interpretable regression with no overfitting

The regression coefficient vector *β*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si7.png) introduced in Section [7.2.3](#Chp007_113-129_B9780443218576000114.xhtml#s0030) is intuitive, robust, and preserves the correlation signs: by design, a feature positively correlated with the response *Y* gets assigned a positive correlation coefficient, as previously discussed. In addition, its performance is nearly as good as optimum regression coefficients, in many situations. It definitely performs well above the base model, unless the amount of noise is substantial. But in that case, all models perform badly, unable to improve over the base model. See Section [7.4.1](#Chp007_113-129_B9780443218576000114.xhtml#s0065) for performance comparison. If your problem is ill-conditioned (for instance, some features are nearly identical or linear combinations of other features), traditional techniques will lead to meaningless regression coefficients, or fail entirely. To the contrary, the *β*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si7.png) in question handles this situation very well.

All of this makes the *β*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si7.png) in question a good starting point for the fixed point iteration, if the goal is to obtain a robust solution, easy to interpret, and not prone to overfitting. It can be improved by using a few iterations of the fixed point algorithm. The more iterations, the closer you get to the standard “exact” solution, but you eventually lose interpretability. With fewer iterations, you may still get a good performance, yet avoid many of the aforementioned problems. One way to decide when to stop is to run many iterations, and compare your R-squared obtained after (say) 10 versus 100 iterations. If the difference is negligible, use the regression coefficients obtained at iteration *k* = 10![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si73.png). Instead of using R-squared, I suggest to use the metric *s* defined in Section [7.4](#Chp007_113-129_B9780443218576000114.xhtml#s0060).

### 7.3.3 Adaptive damping

A possible way to boost convergence is to use a matrix Λ that depends on *k*, and denoted as *Λ*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si12.png). The most simple example is when *Λ*[*k*] = *λ*(*k*) ⋅ *I*![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si74.png) where *λ*(*k*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si75.png) is a real number and *I* is the *m* × *m*![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si5.png) identity matrix. Then, choose *λ*(*k*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si75.png) that minimizes ||(*I* − *λ*^( − 1))*β*[*k*]||[2]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si76.png), that is,

$\\lambda(k) = \\underset{\\lambda}{\\arg⁡\\min}\\text{~~}||(I - \\lambda^{- 1})\\beta\_{k}||\_{2} = \\underset{\\lambda}{\\arg⁡\\min}\\text{~~}{\\lbrack(I - \\lambda^{- 1}M)\\beta\_{k}\\rbrack}^{T}(I - \\lambda^{- 1}M)\\beta\_{k} = \\underset{\\lambda}{\\arg⁡\\min}\\text{~~}\\beta\_{k}^{T}\\beta\_{k} - 2\\lambda^{- 1}\\beta\_{k}^{T}M\\beta\_{k} + \\lambda^{- 2}{(M\\beta\_{k})}^{T}M\\beta\_{k} = \\frac{{(M\\beta\_{k})}^{T}M\\beta\_{k}}{\\beta\_{k}^{T}M\\beta\_{k}}.$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si77.png)

Again, *M* = *X*^(*T*)*X*![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si8.png). Preliminary tests did not show large improvements over using a fixed Λ. Indeed, about 20% of the time, instead of converging, the successive iterates of the regression coefficients oscillate. Yet this issue is easy to address, and adaptive damping – where Λ depends on *k* – has potential to handle data sets with a larger *m* (the number of features). The worst case, by far in my 100 tests or so, is pictured in [Fig. 7.1](#Chp007_113-129_B9780443218576000114.xhtml#f0010). The drawback, compared to using preconditioning only (a fixed Λ), is that it requires more computations. For a recent machine learning application of preconditioners in a similar context, see [\[1\]](#Chp007_113-129_B9780443218576000114.xhtml#br0005).

![Figure 7.1 Regression coefficients oscillating when using adaptive damping.](images/B9780443218576000114/gr001.jpg)

Figure 7.1 Regression coefficients oscillating when using adaptive damping.

## 7.4 Performance assessment on synthetic data

I use three metrics to measure the goodness-of-fit between the observed (synthetic) response *Y* and the predicted response denoted here as *P*. These metrics are computed on a validation set, not on the training set: this is a standard cross-validation procedure to avoid overfitting and performance inflation. Thus, what I call R-squared is actually closer, but not identical, to “predictive R-squared” and PRESS statistics \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PRESS_statistic)\]. The same applies to MSE. The synthetic control set is in the Control tab in the spreadsheet.

The three metrics are:

*   •  The R-squared *r*, with 0 ≤ *r* ≤ 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si78.png), is the square of the correlation between *Y* and *P*. It is also equal to \[*σ*[*Y*]² − (*Y* − *P*)^(*T*)(*Y* − *P*)\]/*σ*[*Y*]²![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si79.png).
*   •  The root mean squared error or RMSE \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Root-mean-square_deviation)\], defined as $e = \\sqrt{{(Y - P)}^{T}(Y - P)}/n$![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si80.png), where *n* is the number of observations. It is a much better measure of the actual error, compared to the mean squared error (MSE). In particular, if *Y* is measured in (say) miles, then RMSE is measured in miles, while MSE is measured in square miles. Likewise, if *Y* is measured in years, RMSE is measured in years while MSE is measured in square years – a meaningless metric.
*   •  The score *s*, with 0 ≤ *s* ≤ 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si81.png), defined as *s* = 1 − *e*(*P*)/*e*(*P*[0])![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si82.png). Here, *P*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si83.png) is the base model, corresponding to *β* = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si53.png) (thus, the predicted value is constant after adjustment, equal to the mean value of *Y* computed on the training set). In particular, *s* measures the improvement over the base model, using RMSE ratios, while *r* does the same using MSE ratios instead. In my opinion, *s* is more intuitive and more realistic than *r*. It is related to *r* via the formula *r* = 2*s* − *s*²![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si84.png), or equivalently, $s = 1 - \\sqrt{1 - r}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si85.png). We always have *r* ≥ *s*![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si86.png), so *r* is an inflated measure of goodness-of-fit.

Since the model is trained on the test data set, but model performance is measured on the validation set, the above performance metrics are hybrid. In particular, as a result, the relationship *r* = 2*s* − *s*²![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si84.png) is almost satisfied, but not exactly. Also, on rare occasions (with very noisy data), *r* can be slightly negative. The performance results are shown in the Results tab, in cells J13:R19. I also included the performance metrics for the simple model consisting in using the regression coefficient vector *β* = *β*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si87.png) defined in Section [7.2.3](#Chp007_113-129_B9780443218576000114.xhtml#s0030). In the spreadsheet, this model is referred to as “Predicted *P*[*b*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si88.png)”.

In addition, the spreadsheet allows you to choose which features to include or not in the model, in the fixed point iteration. The feature selection flags are stored in cells B4:B9 in the Results tab. The default value is 1, corresponding to inclusion. This is particularly useful to test how much model improvement is gained by using all features, versus a subset of them. On real data, some features are usually missing because the model developer was not aware of them, and they are not captured in the data set: in other words, they are unobserved. The feature selection flags allow you to compare the performance on observed data, versus the performance obtained with a dream data set that would include all the relevant features.

Finally, the use of synthetic data offers a big benefit: you can test and benchmark algorithms on millions of very different data sets, all at once. This assume that the synthetic data is properly generated. It is both an art and a science to design such data sets. It typically involves a decent amount of mathematics, sometimes quite advanced. It is my hope that this article will help the reader build good quality, rich synthetic data that covers a large spectrum of potential real life situations. Other synthetic data sets are found in Chapter [5](#Chp005_83-102_B9780443218576000096.xhtml) featuring synthetic clusters, and in Chapter [6](#Chp006_103-111_B9780443218576000102.xhtml) entitled “Computer Vision: Shape Classification via Explainable AI”, featuring synthetic shapes.

### 7.4.1 Results

I tested the methodology on a synthetic data set with *n* = 1000![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si89.png) observations and *m* = 6![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si90.png) features. The validation set also has 1000 observations. Because the data is artificially generated, the exact regression coefficients are known. They are listed in the row labeled “Exact” in [Table 7.1](#Chp007_113-129_B9780443218576000114.xhtml#t0010). The observed data *Y* is a mixture of the exact data and artificial noise. The amount of noise is controlled by the parameter Noise in the spreadsheet. The exact data is the vector *Xβ*, with *β* being the true, prespecified regression coefficients (also artificially generated). Note that *X* is also artificially generated, using the method described in Section [7.2.4](#Chp007_113-129_B9780443218576000114.xhtml#s0035).

The orange dots form the scatterplot of *Y* versus the exact (unobserved) data.

[Fig. 7.2](#Chp007_113-129_B9780443218576000114.xhtml#f0015) (left plot) shows how the six regression coefficients converge in the fixed point iterations, starting with the vector *β*[0] = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si13.png). The same matrix Λ is used at all times, unlike in [Fig. 7.1](#Chp007_113-129_B9780443218576000114.xhtml#f0010). The right plot in [Fig. 7.2](#Chp007_113-129_B9780443218576000114.xhtml#f0015) is a scatterplot of *Y* versus the residual error *ϵ* = *Y* − *X**β*![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si92.png), using *β* = *β*[15]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si93.png) measured on the training set. In idealized statistical models, *ϵ* is assumed to be a white noise. Clearly, this is not the case here, with larger observed values (on the horizontal axis) having a tendency to have a larger error. However, this data is very useful to simulate *ϵ*, to use in model-free confidence and prediction intervals, as discussed in Section [7.4.2](#Chp007_113-129_B9780443218576000114.xhtml#s0070).

In particular, I increased the amount of noise in the validation set, compared to the training set. I did it to better emulate real data, where performance is usually lower outside the training set. It explains why the R-squared is sensibly better when measured on the training set, as opposed to the validation set.

However, *β*[100]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si95.png) and Excel provide good approximations.

### 7.4.2 Distribution-free confidence intervals

This will be the topic of a future article. Here I provide a quick overview, using **resampling** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resampling_\(statistics\))\] and related data-driven techniques. Let *Y* = *P* + *ϵ*![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si100.png), *P* = *X**β*![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si101.png) be the regression model, with *Y* the observed (synthetic) response, *P* the predicted values, *X* the *n* × *m*![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si102.png) matrix representing the features (with values synthetically generated; *n* is the sample size), *β* the regression coefficient vector, and *ϵ* the residual error vector. In other words, *β* is the vector minimizing (*Y* − *X**β*)^(*T*)(*Y* − *X**β*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si103.png), or its approximation using the fixed point algorithm.

The starting point is to randomly shuffle the *n* entries of *ϵ*, to create a new error vector *ϵ*^′![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si104.png). Let *Y*^′ = *Y* − *ϵ* + *ϵ*^′![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si105.png), that is, *Y*^′ = *X**β* + *ϵ*^′![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si106.png). Now find *β*^′![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si107.png) that minimizes (*Y*^′ − *X**β*^′)^(*T*)(*Y*^′ − *X**β*^′)![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si108.png). Now you get a new set of regression coefficients, *β*^′![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si107.png). Repeat this operation 100 times, and you get 100 sets of regression coefficients: *β*, *β*^′, *β*^″![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si109.png), and so on.

This model-free procedure immediately provides confidence intervals for the regression coefficients, by looking at the empirical distribution \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empirical_distribution_function)\] of each regression coefficient across the 100 data sets. Now for a particular feature vector (*x*[1], …, *x*[*m*])![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si110.png) – whether part of the training set or not – the predicted value can be obtained in 100 different ways: *p* = *x**β*![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si111.png), *p*^′ = *x**β*^′![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si112.png), *p*^″ = *x**β*^″![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si113.png), and so on. The empirical distribution of *p*, *p*^′, *p*^″![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si114.png), and so on, provides a **prediction interval** for the predicted value of the response, at the arbitrary location *x* in the feature space. Another way to do it to resample *ϵ* with replacements (rather than by random permutations). This is then a bootstrapping technique \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bootstrapping_\(statistics\))\].

This methodology assumes that the individual residual errors are independently and identically distributed. I discuss how to address this issue in Section [7.4.2.1](#Chp007_113-129_B9780443218576000114.xhtml#s0075). Also it assumes that the error is additive, not multiplicative. In the latter case, one might want to work with a transformed version of *Y* rather than *Y* itself. For an Excel implementation, see the Regression5\_Static spreadsheet on my GitHub repository, [here](https://github.com/VincentGranville/Machine-Learning/blob/main/Spreadsheets/README.md). In the Test tab, column AD corresponds to *ϵ*^′ = *ϵ*![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si115.png), and column AE to *ϵ*^″![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si116.png). Sort columns AE:AF by AF (uniform deviates) to reshuffle the residual error. Then *Y* is automatically replaced by *Y*^″![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si117.png) in column I, and the new regression coefficient vector *β*^″![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si118.png) is in cells K6:P6 in the Results tab.

#### 7.4.2.1 Parametric bootstrap

Another option is to use Gaussian deviates for *ϵ*^′, *ϵ*^″![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si119.png), and so on. They need to have the same variance as the one computed on the observed residual error *ϵ*. This approach is known as **parametric bootstrap**.

If *ϵ* is autocorrelated, for example, if you are dealing with time series and one of the features is the time, it is possible to use an autoregressive process that has the same autocorrelation structure as *ϵ*, to simulate *ϵ*^′, *ϵ*^″![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si119.png), and so on. Likewise, if *ϵ* is correlated to *Y*, this can be handled with some appropriate parametric model. Parametric bootstrap for linear regression is discussed in [\[4\]](#Chp007_113-129_B9780443218576000114.xhtml#br0020). Distribution-free predictive inference for regression is discussed in [\[5\]](#Chp007_113-129_B9780443218576000114.xhtml#br0025).

## 7.5 Feature selection

In Section [7.5.1](#Chp007_113-129_B9780443218576000114.xhtml#s0085), I compare the performance of the regression coefficients obtained for each of the potential feature combinations. The performance metric is a significantly improved version of the R-squared; also, it is applied to the validation set, not to the training set. Then, in Section [7.5.2](#Chp007_113-129_B9780443218576000114.xhtml#s0090), I discuss stepwise feature selection techniques (forward, backward), adding or removing one or two features at a time, based on the feature table built in Section [7.5.1](#Chp007_113-129_B9780443218576000114.xhtml#s0085). The comprehensive feature summary table allows you to quickly perform stepwise regression (which is more interpretable than a full fledged regression), and to assess whether or not this technique fails to catch good enough configurations, at least for the data set investigated here.

### 7.5.1 Combinatorial approach

Here I look at all the 2^(*m*) − 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si120.png) possible configurations of features *X*[1], …, *X*[*m*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si23.png), to asses the importance of individual features and feature interaction, in a way that is more insightful than looking at cross-correlations between features. For each configuration, I computed the regression coefficient vector using three methods: fixed point with 15 iterations, fixed point with 100 iterations (starting with *β*[0] = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si13.png) in both cases), and then the special *β*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si7.png) alone (no iteration) defined in Section [7.2.3](#Chp007_113-129_B9780443218576000114.xhtml#s0030). All rankings, unless otherwise specified, are based on 100 iterations of the fixed point algorithm.

I use the score metric *s* defined in Section [7.4](#Chp007_113-129_B9780443218576000114.xhtml#s0060) – a meaningful, monotonic function of the R-squared – to measure performance. If you use the R-squared instead, the rankings would still be the same. The full model has *m* = 6![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si90.png) features. All other models are submodels, referred to as configurations: they miss one or more features. The metric *s* is computed on the validation set, not the training set.

The summary table in the Regression5\_Static.xlsx spreadsheet, in the Results tab; see columns U:AS. The spreadsheet is available [here](https://github.com/VincentGranville/Machine-Learning/blob/main/Spreadsheets/README.md). It has the same structure as the spreadsheet described in Sections [7.2](#Chp007_113-129_B9780443218576000114.xhtml#s0015), [7.2.4](#Chp007_113-129_B9780443218576000114.xhtml#s0035), and [7.3.1](#Chp007_113-129_B9780443218576000114.xhtml#s0045). The difference is that the data set is static in this case, so you cannot generate different data sets. The methodology is inspired by the book “Interpretable Machine Learning” [\[6\]](#Chp007_113-129_B9780443218576000114.xhtml#br0030), particularly Chapter 7 focusing on permutation feature importance and feature interactions. The higher the *s*, the better the performance. Note that if the performance was computed on the training set rather than the validation set, then we would have 0 ≤ *s* ≤ 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si81.png).

[Table 7.3](#Chp007_113-129_B9780443218576000114.xhtml#t0020) shows the top achievable performance given *m* (the number of features used in the computation) on a same (synthetic) data set. The three performance columns correspond respectively to 15 iterations, 100 iterations, and the special *β*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si7.png). The table is also in the spreadsheet in cells AP12:AS19, where you can find the detailed computations. For the performance of each individual configuration, see Tables [7.4](#Chp007_113-129_B9780443218576000114.xhtml#t0025) and [7.5](#Chp007_113-129_B9780443218576000114.xhtml#t0030): a configuration denoted as 3, 4, 6![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si121.png) means that only *X*[3], *X*[4]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si122.png), and *X*[6]![Image](images/B9780443218576000114/si99.png) are used for the computation of the regression coefficients.
