# Chapter 11: High quality random numbers for data synthetization

## Abstract

High quality random numbers are critical in large-scale simulations such as data synthetization. I discuss a new test of randomness for pseudorandom number generators (PRNG), to detect subtle patterns in binary sequences. The test shows that congruential PRNGs, even the best ones, have flaws that can be exacerbated by the choice of the seed. This includes the Mersenne twister used in many programming languages including Python. I also show that the digits of some numbers such as $\\sqrt{2205}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si1.png), conjectured to be perfectly random, fail this new test, despite the fact that they pass all the standard tests. I propose a methodology to avoid these flaws, implemented in Python. The test is particularly useful when high quality randomness is needed. This includes cryptographic and military-grade security applications, as well as synthetic data generation and simulation-intensive **Markov chain Monte Carlo** methods. The origin of this test is in number theory and connected to the Riemann Hypothesis. In particular, it is based on Rademacher stochastic processes. These random multiplicative functions are a number-theoretic version of Bernoulli trials. This chapter features state-of-the-art research on this topic, as well as an original, simple, integer-based formula to compute square roots to generate random digits. It is offered with a Python implementation that handles integers with millions of digits.

### Keywords

law of the iterated logarithm; strongly random; pseudorandom numbers; test of randomness; quadratic irrational

High quality random numbers are critical in large-scale simulations such as data synthetization. I discuss a new test of randomness for pseudorandom number generators (PRNG), to detect subtle patterns in binary sequences. The test shows that congruential PRNGs, even the best ones, have flaws that can be exacerbated by the choice of the seed. This includes the Mersenne twister used in many programming languages including Python. I also show that the digits of some numbers such as $\\sqrt{2205}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si1.png), conjectured to be perfectly random, fail this new test, despite the fact that they pass all the standard tests. I propose a methodology to avoid these flaws, implemented in Python. The test is particularly useful when high quality randomness is needed. This includes cryptographic and military-grade security applications, as well as synthetic data generation and simulation-intensive **Markov chain Monte Carlo** methods. The origin of this test is in number theory and connected to the Riemann Hypothesis. In particular, it is based on Rademacher stochastic processes. These random multiplicative functions are a number-theoretic version of Bernoulli trials. This chapter features state-of-the-art research on this topic, as well as an original, simple, integer-based formula to compute square roots to generate random digits. It is offered with a Python implementation that handles integers with millions of digits.

## 11.1 Introduction

Let *χ*( ⋅ )![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si2.png) be a function defined for strictly positive integers, with *χ*(1) = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si3.png) and *χ*(*a**b*) = *χ*(*a*)*χ*(*b*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si4.png) for any integers *a*, *b* > 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si5.png). Such a function is said to be **completely multiplicative** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Completely_multiplicative_function)\]. Here we are interested in the case where *χ* takes on two possible values, +1 and −1. The core of my methodology is based on the following, well-known identity:

$\\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{\\infty}\\chi(k)k^{- z} = \\prod\\limits\_{p \\in P}\\frac{1}{1 - \\chi(p)p^{- z}}.$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si6.png)(11.1) 

The product is over all prime integers ordered by increasing values: *P* = {2, 3, 5, 7, 11, …}![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si7.png) is the set of all primes. Such a product is called an **Euler product** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euler_product)\]. The series on the left-hand side is called a **Dirichlet series** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet_series)\]. The argument *z* = *σ* + *i**t*![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si8.png) is a complex number. You do not need to know anything about complex numbers to understand this chapter. The only important fact is that the series or product converges only if *σ* – the real part of *z* – is large enough, typically larger than 0, $\\frac{1}{2}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si9.png), or 1, depending on *χ*. If *χ* is a constant function, thus equal to 1, then the product and series converge to the **Riemann zeta function** *ζ*(*z*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si10.png) \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_zeta_function)\] if *σ* > 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si11.png).

For primes *p*, let the *χ*(*p*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si12.png)'s be independent random variables, with $\\text{P}\\lbrack\\chi(p) = 1\\rbrack = \\text{P}\\lbrack\\chi(p) = - 1\\rbrack = \\frac{1}{2}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si13.png). The product, denoted as *L*[*P*](*z*, *χ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si14.png), is known as a **Rademacher random multiplicative function**, see [\[5\]](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml#br0025), [\[6\]](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml#br0030), and [\[9\]](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml#br0045). If *z* is a complex number, we are dealing with **complex random variables** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_random_variable)\]. From the product formula and the independence assumption, it is easy to obtain

$E\\lbrack L\_{P}(z,\\chi)\\rbrack = \\prod\\limits\_{p \\in P}E\\left\\lbrack \\frac{1}{1 - \\chi(p)p^{- z}} \\right\\rbrack = \\prod\\limits\_{p \\in P}\\frac{1}{1 - p^{- 2z}} = \\zeta(2z).$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si15.png)(11.2) 

Thus the expectation is finite if $\\sigma = \\Re(z) > \\frac{1}{2}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si16.png). A similar argument can be used for the variances.

Now let us replace the random variables *χ*(*p*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si12.png) by pseudorandom numbers, taking the values +1 or −1 with probability $\\frac{1}{2}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si9.png). If these generated numbers are “random enough”, free of dependencies, then one would expect them to satisfy the laws of Rademacher random multiplicative functions. The remaining of this chapter explores this idea in details, with a focus on applications.

## 11.2 Pseudorandom numbers

There is no formal definition of pseudorandom numbers. Intuitively, a good set of pseudorandom numbers is a deterministic binary sequence of digits that satisfies all statistical tests of randomness. Of course, it makes no sense to talk about randomness if the sequence contains very few digits, say one or two. So pseudorandom numbers (PRN) are associated with infinite sequences, even though in practice one only uses finite subsequences.

A rigorous definition of PRN sequences requires the convergence of the multivariate empirical distribution \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empirical_distribution_function)\] of any finite subsequence of *m* digits, to the known theoretical value under the assumption of full randomness. Let the PRN sequence be denoted as {*d*(*k*)}![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si17.png) with *k* = 1, 2![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si18.png), and so on. A subsequence of *m* digits is defined by its indices, denoted as *i*[1], *i*[2], …, *i*[*m*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si19.png). The convergence of the empirical distribution means that regardless of the indices 0 ≤ *i*[1] < *i*[2] < ⋯![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si20.png) we have

$\\lim\\limits\_{n\\rightarrow\\infty}\\frac{1}{n}\\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{n}I\\left\\lbrack d(k + i\_{1}) = k\_{1},d(k + i\_{2}) = k\_{2},\\ldots,d(k + i\_{m}) = k\_{m} \\right\\rbrack = 2^{- m}$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si21.png)(11.3) 

for any (*k*[1], *k*[2], …, *k*[*m*])![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si22.png) in { − 1,  + 1}^(*m*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si23.png). Here *I* is the indicator function: *I*\[*A*\] = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si24.png) if *A* is true, otherwise *I*\[*A*\] = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si25.png). The following number *λ* is of particular interest:

$\\lambda = \\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{\\infty}d^{\\prime}(k) \\cdot 2^{- k},\\quad\\text{with~}d^{\\prime}(k) = \\frac{1 + d(k)}{2} \\in \\{ 0,1\\}.$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si26.png)(11.4) 

Thus the *d*^′(*k*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si27.png)'s are the binary digits of the number *λ*, with 0 ≤ *λ* ≤ 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si28.png).

The connection between the multiplicative function *χ*( ⋅ )![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si2.png) in formula [(11.1)](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml#deq1) and the *d*(*k*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si29.png)'s is as follows. Denote the *k*th prime as *p*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si30.png), with *p*[1] = 2![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si31.png). Then *d*(*k*) = *χ*(*p*[*k*])![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si32.png). The traditional definition of PRNs is equivalent to requiring *λ* be a **normal number** in base 2 \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normal_number)\]. I introduce a stronger criterion of randomness in Section [11.2.1](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml#s0020).

### 11.2.1 Strong pseudorandom numbers

Convergence of the empirical joint distributions, as defined by formula [(11.3)](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml#deq3), has a few important implications. The **Kolmogorov–Smirnov test** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kolmogorov%E2%80%93Smirnov_test)\], the **Berry–Esseen inequality** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berry%E2%80%93Esseen_theorem)\] and the **law of the iterated logarithm** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_of_the_iterated_logarithm)\] can be applied to the PRN sequence {*d*(*k*)}![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si17.png). These three fundamental results provide strong limitations on the behavior of finite PRN sequences. If a sequence {*d*(*k*)}![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si17.png) or its representation by the number *λ* does no stay within these limits, then it does not emulate pure randomness. However, some quasirandom PRN sequences, with weak dependencies, meet these requirements, yet are not truly “random”. For instance, a number can be normal in base 2, yet have digits that exhibit some dependencies, see [here](https://mathoverflow.net/questions/426815/normal-numbers-and-law-of-the-iterated-logarithm). The purpose of this section is to introduce stronger requirements in order to catch some of these exceptions. This is where the multiplicative function *χ*( ⋅ )![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si2.png) comes into play.

The function *χ*( ⋅ )![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si2.png), initially defined for primes *p*, is extended to all strictly positives integers via *χ*(*a**b*) = *χ*(*a*)*χ*(*b*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si4.png). Because the *χ*(*p*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si12.png)'s are independent among prime numbers (by construction), the full sequence {*χ*(*k*)}![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si33.png) over all *k* must behave in a certain way. Obviously, if *k* is a square integer, *χ*(*k*) = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si34.png). But if *k* is not a square, we still have $P\\lbrack\\chi(k) = 1\\rbrack = P\\lbrack\\chi(k) = - 1\\rbrack = \\frac{1}{2}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si35.png). For instance, *χ*(4200) = *χ*(4)*χ*(25)*χ*(6)*χ*(7) = *χ*(6)*χ*(7)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si36.png). Since the product of two independent random variables with **Rademacher distribution** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rademacher_distribution)\] has a Rademacher distribution, it follows that *χ*(6) = *χ*(2)*χ*(3)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si37.png) has a Rademacher distribution, and thus *χ*(4200) = *χ*(6)*χ*(7)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si38.png) also has a Rademacher distribution. So, the *χ*(*k*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si39.png)'s are identically distributed with zero mean, unless *k* is a square integer. However, they are not independently distributed, even after removing square integers, or even if you only keep **square-free integers** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Square-free_integer)\].

I now define three fundamental functions, which are central to my new test of randomness. First, define the following sets:

*   •  *S*[1](*n*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si40.png) contains all prime integers ⩽*n*.
*   •  *S*[2](*n*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si41.png) contains all positive square-free integers ⩽*n*.
*   •  *S*[3](*n*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si42.png) contains all positive nonsquare integers ⩽*n*.

So each of these sets contains at most *n* elements. Then, define the three functions as

$L\_{1}(n) = \\sum\\limits\_{k \\in S\_{1}(n)}\\chi(k),\\quad L\_{2}(n) = \\sum\\limits\_{k \\in S\_{2}(n)}\\chi(k),\\quad L\_{3}(n) = \\sum\\limits\_{k \\in S\_{3}(n)}\\chi(k).$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si43.png)(11.5) 

Now, I can introduce my new test of randomness.

#### 11.2.1.1 New test of randomness for PRNGs

Let *d*(1), *d*(2), …![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si44.png) be a sequence of integer numbers, with *d*(*k*) ∈ { − 1, 1}![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si45.png) and *P* = {*p*[1], *p*[2], …}![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si46.png) be the set of prime numbers. The goal is to test how random the sequence {*d*(*k*)}![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si17.png) is, based on the first *n* elements *d*(1), …, *d*(*n*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si47.png). The algorithm is as follows:

*   •  Step 1. Set *χ*(*p*[*k*]) = *d*(*k*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si48.png), where *p*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si30.png) is the *k*th prime number (*p*[1] = 2![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si31.png)).
*   •  Step 2. For *k* ∉ *P*![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si49.png) with prime factorization *k* = *p*[1]^(*a*[1])*p*[2]^(*a*[2])⋯![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si50.png), set *χ*(*k*) = *χ*^(*a*[1])(*p*[1])*χ*^(*a*[2])(*p*[2])⋯![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si51.png), with *χ*(1) = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si3.png).
*   •  Step 3. Using formula [(11.5)](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml#deq5), compute $L\_{3}^{\\ast}(n) = |L\_{3}(n)|/\\sqrt{n\\log\\log n}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si52.png).
*   •  Step 4. If *L*[3]^(\*)(*n*) < 0.5![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si53.png) or *L*[3]^(\*)(*n*) > 1.5![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si54.png), the sequence {*d*(*k*)}![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si17.png) (the first *n* elements) lacks true randomness.

This test is referred to as the “**prime test**”. Let us illustrate Step 2 with *k* = 4200![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si55.png): since 4200 = 2³ ⋅ 3 ⋅ 5² ⋅ 7![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si56.png), we have *χ*(4200) = *χ*³(2)*χ*(3)*χ*²(5)*χ*(7) = *χ*(2)*χ*(3)*χ*(7)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si57.png).

Some nonrandom sequences may pass the prime test. So you should never use this test alone to decide whether a sequence is good enough. Also, the standardization of *L*[3](*n*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si58.png), using the $\\sqrt{n\\log\\log n}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si59.png) denominator, is not perfect, but good enough for all practical purposes, assuming 10⁴ < *n* < 10^(15)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si60.png). This test can detect departure from randomness that no other test is able to uncover. I discuss practical examples and a Python implementation later in this chapter.

A PRN sequence that satisfies [(11.3)](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml#deq3) and passes all the existing tests, including the prime test, is called **strongly pseudorandom**. The corresponding real number *λ* defined by formula [(11.4)](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml#deq4) is called **strongly normal**. It should not be difficult to prove that almost all numbers are strongly normal. Thus almost all PRN sequences are strongly pseudorandom. Yet creating one that can be proved to be strongly pseudorandom is as difficult as proving that a given number is normal (and a fortiori, strongly normal). Interestingly, none of the sequences produced by **congruential random number generators** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_congruential_generator)\] are strongly pseudorandom, for the same reason that no rational number is normal: in both cases, *d*(*k*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si29.png) is periodic.

Modern test batteries include the **Diehard tests** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diehard_tests)\] published in 1995, and the **TestU01** framework \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TestU01)\], introduced in 2007.

#### 11.2.1.2 Theoretical background: the law of the iterated logarithm

The prime test checks whether the multiplicative function *χ*(*k*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si39.png) derived from {*d*(*k*)}![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si17.png) satisfies a particular version of the **law of the iterated logarithm** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_of_the_iterated_logarithm)\]. Truly random sequences {*d*(*k*)}![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si17.png) satisfy that law. Since {*χ*(*k*)}![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si33.png) is multiplicative and thus nonrandom, the law of the iterative algorithm must be adapted to take care of the resulting dependencies. In particular, the $\\sqrt{n\\log\\log n}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si59.png) weight used to standardize *L*[3](*n*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si58.png) provides only an approximation, good enough for all practical purposes. The exact weight is discussed in [\[6\]](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml#br0030) and [\[9\]](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml#br0045).

Many sequences {*d*(*k*)}![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si17.png) satisfy the basic law of the iterated logarithm without the prime number / Euler product apparatus introduced in this chapter. This is the case for most of the sequences studied here. However, by looking at *χ*(*k*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si39.png) rather than the original *d*(*k*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si29.png), we are able to magnify flaws that are otherwise undetectable by standard means. An example is the Mersenne twister implemented in Python, passing the standard test, but failing the prime test when the seed is set to 200.

#### 11.2.1.3 Connection to the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis

The **Generalized Riemann Hypothesis** (GRH) \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generalized_Riemann_hypothesis)\] is one of the most famous unsolved problems in mathematics. It states that the function *L*(*z*, *χ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si61.png) defined by formula [(11.1)](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml#deq1) has no root if $\\frac{1}{2} < \\sigma = \\Re(z) < 1$![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si62.png). Here *z* = *σ* + *i**t*![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si8.png) is a complex number, and *σ* = ℜ(*z*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si63.png) is its real part. It applies to a particular class of functions *χ*( ⋅ )![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si2.png), those that are “well behaved”. Of course, without any restriction on *χ*( ⋅ )![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si2.png), there are **completely multiplicative functions** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Completely_multiplicative_function)\] known to satisfy GRH. For instance, the function defined by *χ*(*p*[2*k*]) =  − 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si64.png), *χ*(*p*[2*k* + 1]) = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si65.png) where *p*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si30.png) is the *k*th prime number. The corresponding *L*(*z*, *χ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si61.png) has no root if $\\sigma > \\frac{1}{2}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si66.png) because the product converges for *σ* > 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si67.png), and, of course, the product has no root. The sequence {*χ*(*p*[*k*])}![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si68.png) is obviously nonrandom as it perfectly alternates, and thus I labeled it CounterExample in [Table 11.1](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml#t0010).
