![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/t0010.png)

If the Euler product in formula [(11.1)](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml#deq1) converges for some *σ* > *σ*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si69.png), it is equal to its series expansion when *σ* > *σ*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si69.png), it converges for all *σ* > *σ*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si69.png), and *L*(*z*, *χ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si61.png) satisfies GRH when *σ* > *σ*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si69.png). When *σ* < 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si70.png), the convergence is **conditional** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conditional_convergence)\], making things more difficult. Another example that trivially satisfies GRH if $\\sigma > \\frac{1}{2}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si66.png) is when *χ*( ⋅ )![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si2.png) is a random variable with $P\\lbrack\\chi(p) = 1\\rbrack = P\\lbrack\\chi(p) = - 1\\rbrack = \\frac{1}{2}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si71.png) for primes *p*. In this case convergence means that *L*(*z*, *χ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si61.png) has finite expectation as proved by formula [(11.2)](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml#deq2), and finite variances. This function *χ*( ⋅ )![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si2.png) is called a **random Rademacher multiplicative function**, see [\[7\]](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml#br0035). Here the *χ*(*p*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si12.png)'s are identically and independently distributed over the set of all primes, and the definition is extended to all strictly positive integers with the formula *χ*(*a**b*) = *χ*(*a*)*χ*(*b*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si4.png).

So, if we were able to find a “nice enough” pseudorandom, yet deterministic function *χ*( ⋅ )![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si2.png) with convergence of the Euler product when *σ* > *σ*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si69.png) for some *σ*[0] < 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si72.png), a function *χ*( ⋅ )![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si2.png) that is random enough over the primes (like its sister, the truly stochastic version) to guarantee the convergence of the product, then it would be a major milestone towards proving GRH. Convergence of the product would imply that:

*   •  *L*(*z*, *χ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si61.png) is **analytic** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analytic_function)\], because the product is equal to its series expansion, which trivially satisfies the **Cauchy–Riemann equations** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cauchy%E2%80%93Riemann_equations)\],
*   •  *L*(*z*, *χ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si61.png) has no root if *σ* > *σ*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si69.png) since the product has no root.

As discussed, examples that are “not so nice” exist; “nice enough” means that *L*(*z*, *χ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si61.png) satisfies a **Dirichlet functional equation** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Functional_equation_\(L-function\))\]. Typically, “nice enough” means that *L*(*z*, *χ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si61.png) is a **Dirichlet-***L* **function** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet_L-function)\]. Besides the **Riemann zeta function** where *χ*(*p*) = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si73.png) is the trivial Dirichlet character, the most fundamental example is when *χ* = *χ*[4]![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si74.png) is the nontrivial **Dirichlet character modulo** 4 \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet_character)\]. This example is featured in [Fig. 11.1](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml#f0010) where $\\sigma = \\frac{1}{2}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si75.png) (left plot) and contrasted with a not so nice example on the right plot, corresponding to a pseudorandom sequence {*χ*(*p*[*k*])}![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si68.png). The *χ*[4]![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si76.png) example is referred to as Dirichlet4 in [Table 11.1](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml#t0010). Note that for $\\sigma = \\frac{1}{2}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si75.png), *L*(*z*, *χ*[4])![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si77.png) has infinitely many roots just like the Riemann zeta function, though its roots are different: this is evident when looking at the left plot in [Fig. 11.1](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml#f0010). The (conjectured) absence of root is when $\\frac{1}{2} < \\sigma < 1$![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si78.png).

![Figure 11.1 Orbit of L(z,χ) at \\sigma = \\frac{1}{2}Image, with 0 < t < 200 and χ = χ4 (left) versus pseudorandom χ (right).](images/B9780443218576000151/gr001.jpg)

Figure 11.1 Orbit of *L*(*z*,*χ*) at $\\sigma = \\frac{1}{2}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si75.png), with 0 < *t* < 200 and *χ* = *χ*[4] (left) versus pseudorandom *χ* (right).

I went as far as to compute the Euler product for *L*(*z*, *χ*[4])![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si77.png) when *z* = *σ* = 0.99![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si79.png). It nicely converges to the correct value, without the typical growing oscillations associated to lack of convergence, agreeing with the value computed using the series expansion in formula [(11.1)](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml#deq1). It means that the product converges at least for all *z* with *σ* = ℜ(*z*) ≥ 0.99![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si80.png). Thus there is no root for *L*(*z*, *χ*[4])![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si77.png) if *σ* ≥ 0.99![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si81.png). This would be an immense milestone compared to the best known result (no root if *σ* ≥ 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si82.png)) if it was theoretically possible to prove the convergence in question, supported only by empirical evidence. Convergence implies that the sequence {*χ*[4](*p*[*k*])}![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si83.png) is random enough over the primes *p*[1], *p*[2]![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si84.png), and so on. That is, the gap between +1 and −1 in the sequence never grows too large (that is, runs of same value can only grow so fast), and the proportion of +1 and −1 tends to $\\frac{1}{2}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si9.png) fast enough, despite the known **Chebyshev's bias** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chebyshev%27s_bias)\]. The fact that the proportion eventually converges to $\\frac{1}{2}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si9.png) when using more and more terms in the sequence, is a consequence of **Dirichlet's theorem** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet%27s_theorem_on_arithmetic_progressions)\]. This is how close we are – or you may say how far – to proving GRH.

There are other “nice functions” *χ*( ⋅ )![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si2.png) that fit within the GRH framework. For instance, with primes that are not integers, such as Beurling primes [\[8\]](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml#br0040) (discussed later in this chapter) or **Gaussian primes** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaussian_integer)\]. For a general family of such functions, see the **Dedekind zeta function** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedekind_zeta_function)\]. For a general introduction to the Riemann zeta function and related topics, see [\[2\]](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml#br0010) and [\[10\]](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml#br0050).

### 11.2.2 Testing well-known sequences

The binary sequences analyzed here are denoted as {*d*(*k*)}![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si17.png), with *d*(*k*) ∈ { − 1,  + 1}![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si85.png) and *k* = 1, 2![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si18.png), and so on. The tests, restricted to *d*(*k*) ≤ *n*![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si86.png), are based on $L\_{3}^{\\ast}(n) = L\_{3}(n)/\\sqrt{n\\log\\log n}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si87.png), with *L*[3](*n*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si58.png) defined by [(11.5)](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml#deq5). Again, *χ*(*p*[*k*]) = *d*(*k*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si48.png) for prime numbers, and *χ*( ⋅ )![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si2.png) is extended to nonprime positive integers via *χ*(*a**b*) = *χ*(*a*)*χ*(*b*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si4.png). Finally, *p*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si30.png) is the *k*th prime with *p*[1] = 2![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si31.png). In my examples, ![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/fx001.jpg)in [Table 11.1](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml#t0010), and ![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/fx002.jpg)in Figs. [11.2](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml#f0015) and [11.3](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml#f0020).

![Figure 11.2 L\_{3}^{\\ast}(n)Image test statistic for four sequences: Python\[200\] and SQRT\[90,91\] fail.](images/B9780443218576000151/gr002.jpg)

Figure 11.2 *L*[3]^(\*)(*n*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si126.png) test statistic for four sequences: Python\[200\] and SQRT\[90,91\] fail.

![Figure 11.3 |L3(n)| test statistic for four sequences: Python\[200\] and SQRT\[90,91\] fail.](images/B9780443218576000151/gr003.jpg)

Figure 11.3 |*L*[3](*n*)| test statistic for four sequences: Python\[200\] and SQRT\[90,91\] fail.

The fact that a sequence fails the test for a specific *n* does not mean it fails for all *n*. The success or failure also depends on the seed (the initial conditions). Some seeds require many iterations – that is, a rather large *n* – before randomness kicks in. The test should not be used for small *n*, say *n* < 1000![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si88.png). Finally, passing the test does not mean that the sequence is random enough. I provide examples of poor PRNGs that pass the test. Typically, to assess the randomness character of a sequence, one uses a battery of tests, not just one test. However, the prime test can detect patterns that no other one can. In some sense, it is a last resort test.

The sequences investigated here fall into four types:

*   •  Discrete chaotic **dynamical systems** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamical_system)\]. In one dimension, many of these systems are driven by a recursion *x*[*k* + 1] = *g*(*x*[*k*])![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si89.png), where *g* is a continuous mapping from \[0, 1\]![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si90.png) onto \[0, 1\]![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si90.png). The initial value *x*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si91.png) is called the seed. Typically, *d*(*k*) = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si92.png) if *x*[*k*] < 0.5![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si93.png), otherwise *d*(*k*) =  − 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si94.png). The **logistic map** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logistic_map)\], with *g*(*x*) = 4*x*(1 − *x*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si95.png), is labeled Logistic in [Table 11.1](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml#t0010) as well as in the Python code in Section [11.3.2](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml#s0065). The **shift map** in base *b*, defined by *g*(*x*) = *b**x* − ⌊*b**x*⌋![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si96.png) where the brackets represent the integer part function, here with *b* = 3![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si97.png), is labeled Base3. The case *b* = 2![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si98.png) is known as the **dyadic map** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dyadic_transformation)\]. The number ⌊*b**x*[*k*]⌋![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si99.png) is the *k*\-digit of the seed *x*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si91.png), in base *b* > 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si100.png). In particular, if *x*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si91.png) is a rational number, then the sequence {*d*(*k*)}![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si17.png) is periodic, and thus nonrandom. Even in the best-case scenario (using a random seed), the sequence {*d*(*k*)}![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si17.png) is autocorrelated. These dynamical systems are studied in detail in my book on chaotic dynamical systems [\[4\]](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml#br0020).
*   •  **Mersenne twister** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mersenne_Twister)\] as implemented in the Python function random.random(). This congruential PRNG is also another type of dynamical system, though technically “nonchaotic” because the sequence {*x*[*k*]}![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si101.png) is periodic. It emulates randomness quite well as the period is very large. Likewise, the shift map with a large base *b* and a bad seed *x*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si91.png) (a rational number resulting in periodicity) will emulate randomness quite well if *x*[0] = *q*/*p*![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si102.png), where *p*, *q*![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si103.png) are integers and *p* is a very large prime. Both in the table and in the figures, I use the label Python for the Mersenne twister. It fails the prime test for various seeds, especially if the seed is set to 200. See also Section [11.3.1](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml#s0060).
*   •  Number-theoretic sequences related to the distribution of prime numbers or **Beurling primes**. Sequences of this type are labeled Dirichlet4. The main one, with the seed set to 3, corresponds to *χ*(*p*[*k*]) =  + 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si104.png) if *p*[*k*] ≡ 1 *m**o**d* 4![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si105.png) and *χ*(*p*[*k*]) =  − 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si106.png) if *p*[*k*] ≡ 3 *m**o**d* 4![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si107.png). Here *χ*(2) = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si108.png). This function, denoted as *χ*[4]![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si76.png), is the nontrivial **Dirichlet character modulo 4** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet_character)\]. The sequence barely fails the *L*[3]^(\*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si109.png) test; the full function *χ*[4]![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si76.png) defined over all positive integers (not just the nonsquare integers) is periodic. The sister sequence (with the seed set to 1) has *χ*(*p*) =  − *χ*[4](*p*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si110.png) if *p* is prime. Sequences based on Beurling primes (a generalization of prime numbers to nonintegers) are not included here, but discussed in Chapter [17](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml). The Python code in Section [11.3.2](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml#s0065) can easily be adapted to handle them. The DirichletL.py code posted [here](https://github.com/VincentGranville/Experimental-Math-Number-Theory/blob/main/Source-Code/dirichletL.py) on my GitHub repository, includes Beurling primes. These numbers are studied in Diamond [\[3\]](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml#br0015) and Hilberdink [\[8\]](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml#br0040).
*   •  Binary digits of **quadratic irrational** numbers. I use a simple, original recursion to compute these digits: see code description in Section [11.3.3](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml#s0070). The Python code painlessly handles the very large integers involved in these computations. Surprisingly, $\\sqrt{2}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si111.png) passes the prime test as expected, but $\\sqrt{2205}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si1.png) does not. Sequences based on these digits are labeled SQRT in this document.

The dyadic map is impossible to implement in Python due to the way computations are performed in the CPU: the iterates {*x*[*k*]}![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si101.png) are (erroneously) all equal to zero after about 45 iterations. This is why I chose the shift map with *b* = 3![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si97.png). In this case, the iterates are also all wrong after 45 iterations due to propagating errors caused by limited machine precision (limited to 32 bits). Even with 64 or any finite number of bits, the problem persists. However, with *b* = 3![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si97.png), the *x*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si112.png)'s keep oscillating properly and maintain their statistical properties forever (including randomness or lack of), due to the **ergodicity** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ergodicity)\] of the system. The result is identical to using a new seed every 45 iterations or so.

The dyadic map with *b* = 2![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si98.png), in principle, could be used to compute the binary digits of the seed $x\_{0} = \\sqrt{2}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si113.png), but because of the problem discussed, it does not work. Instead, I use a special recursion to compute these digits. If you replace *b* = 2![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si98.png) by *b* = 2 − 2^( − 31)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si114.png) (the closest you can get to avoid complete failure) the *x*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si112.png)'s produced by the Python code, even though also completely wrong after 45 iterations, behave as expected from a statistical point of view: this is a workaround to using *b* = 2![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si98.png). The same problem is present in other programming languages.

#### 11.2.2.1 Reverse-engineering a pseudorandom sequence

Many of the sequences defined by a recursion *x*[*k* + 1] = *g*(*x*[*k*])![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si89.png), where *x*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si91.png) is the seed, can be reverse-engineered, and are thus unsafe to use when security is critical. This includes sequences produced by congruential PRNGs. By reverse engineering, I mean that if you observe *m* consecutive digits, you can easily compute all the digits, and thus correctly “guess” the whole sequence. In the case of the Mersenne twister, *m* = 624![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si115.png) is conjectured to be the smallest possible value even though the period is ![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/fx003.jpg), see [here](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mersenne_Twister). For the shift map in base *b*, while *x*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si112.png) is asymptotically uniformly distributed on \[0, 1\]![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si90.png) if *x*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si91.png) is random, the vectors (*x*[*k*], *x*[*k* + 1])![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si116.png) lie in a very specific configuration: *x*[*k* + 1] − *x*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si117.png) is a small integer, making the sequence {*x*[*k*]}![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si101.png) anything but random. As a result, for any positive integer *q*, the empirical **autocorrelation** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autocorrelation)\] between (*x*[1], *x*[2], *x*[3], …)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si118.png) and (*x*[*q* + 1], *x*[*q* + 2], *x*[*q* + 3], …)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si119.png) computed on the infinite sequence, is equal to 1/*b*^(*q*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si120.png) if *b* is an integer ⩾2. A good sequence should have zero autocorrelations for all *q*.

It is possible to significantly improve the base sequence {*x*[*k*]}![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si101.png), to make it impossible to reverse-engineer. In the case of the shift map, using *d*(*k*) = ⌊*b**x*[*k*]⌋![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si121.png) instead of *x*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si112.png), results in zero autocorrelations and perfect randomness if the seed *x*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si91.png) is random. A seed such as $x\_{0} = \\sqrt{2}/2$![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si122.png) or *x*[0] = log 2![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si123.png) is conjectured to achieve this goal. The explanation is as follows: *d*(*k*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si29.png) is the *k*th digit of *x*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si91.png) in base *b*. Even if you were to observe ![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/fx004.jpg)consecutive digits of $\\sqrt{2}/2$![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si124.png), there is no way to predict what the next digit will be, if you do not know that $x\_{0} = \\sqrt{2}/2$![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si122.png). Actually, even if you have that information, it is still impossible to predict the next digit. Any sequence of *m* digits is conjectured to occur infinitely many times at arbitrary locations for a seed such as $\\sqrt{2}/2$![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si124.png). So given any such string of *m* digits (no matter how large *m* is), it is impossible to tell where it takes place in the infinite sequence of digits, and thus impossible to correctly predict all the subsequent digits.

However, because of machine precision (the problem discussed in Section [11.2.2](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml#s0040)), the *x*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si112.png)'s generated by a computer for the shift map (or any map for that matter) eventually become periodic. Thus {*d*(*k*)}![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si17.png) becomes periodic, too. A workaround is the use exact arithmetic to compute *d*(*k*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si29.png), as in my Python code in Section [11.3.3](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml#s0070). Another solution is to use **Bailey–Borwein–Plouffe formulas** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bailey%E2%80%93Borwein%E2%80%93Plouffe_formula)\] to compute the digits. There are many BBP formulas for various good **transcendental** seeds \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transcendental_number)\] such as $x\_{0} = \\frac{\\pi}{4}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si125.png), but as far as I know, none for the subset of **algebraic numbers** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_number)\] such as $x\_{0} = \\sqrt{2}/2$![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si122.png).

#### 11.2.2.2 Illustrations

Figs. [11.2](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml#f0015) and [11.3](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml#f0020) show the core statistics of the prime test, defined by formula [(11.5)](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml#deq5): *L*[3]^(\*)(*n*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si126.png) and |*L*[3](*n*)|![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si128.png), for *n* between ![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/fx005.jpg)and ![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/fx006.jpg). If *L*[3]^(\*)(*n*) < 0.5![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si53.png) or *L*[3]^(\*)(*n*) > 1.5![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si54.png), the sequence {*d*(*k*)}![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si17.png) (the first *n* elements) lacks true randomness; it is not **strongly pseudorandom**. [Table 11.1](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml#t0010) summarizes these findings for a larger collection of sequences, computed at ![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/fx001.jpg). The notation Python\[200\] corresponds to the Python implementation of the Mersenne twister, using the random.random() function and the seed 200, that is, random.seed(200). Similarly, SQRT\[90,91\] is for the binary digits of $\\sqrt{2205}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si1.png), obtained using the bivariate seed *y* = 90, *z* = 91![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si129.png) in the code in Section [11.3.3](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml#s0070). Not surprisingly, the sequence Base3\[0.72\] fails, as 0.72 = 18/25![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si130.png) is a rational number with a small denominator. Thus *d*(*k*) = *χ*(*p*[*k*])![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si32.png) is periodic with a rather small period. The column labeled Status in [Table 11.1](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml#t0010) indicates if the sequence in question fails or passes the prime test.

For convenience, I also included a type of sequences called CounterExample. For this type of sequences, *χ*(*p*[*k*])![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si131.png) perfectly alternates between −1 and +1. One of the two resulting sequences {*d*(*k*)}![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si17.png) barely passes the test, the other fails. Now, the Dirichlet4 sequence with seed set to 3, has perfectly alternating *d*(*k*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si29.png)'s and is thus nonrandom. It fails the prime test, but barely. This means that passing this test is not a guarantee of randomness. Only failing the test is a guarantee of nonrandomness.

The prime test can be extended using the option All in the Python code. To do so, define the *L*[4]![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si132.png) statistics as follows:

$L\_{4}(n) = \\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{n}\\chi(k),\\quad L\_{4}^{\\ast}(n) = \\frac{|L\_{4}(n)|}{\\sqrt{n\\log\\log n}}.$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si133.png)(11.6) 

Now with *L*[4]^(\*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si134.png) rather than *L*[3]^(\*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si109.png), the Dirichlet4 sequence with the seed set to 3 would dramatically fail the prime test, rather than just barely failing. It would reveal that despite the appearances, there is something definitely nonrandom about this sequence. Indeed, it satisfies *χ*(4*k* + 1) = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si135.png), *χ*(4*k* + 3) =  − 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si136.png), and *χ*(2*k*) = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si137.png). The details of the *L*[4]^(\*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si134.png) version of the prime test still need to be worked out, thus I did not include it in this chapter.

Finally, if you swap  − 1/ + 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si138.png) in the {*d*(*k*)}![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si17.png) sequence, the new sequence may pass the test even if the original fails (or the other way around). This is the case for the sequence SQRT\[90,91\]. Also, the *L*[3]^(\*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si109.png) scale should be interpreted as an earthquake scale: an increase from 0.35 to 0.45, or from 1.3 to 1.8, represents a massive difference. A sequence with a low *L*[3]^(\*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si109.png) alternates too frequently compared to a random sequence, resulting in a ratio +1 versus −1 too close to 50% among the *d*(*k*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si29.png)'s. The ratio in question corresponds to the column labeled *P*\[*d*(*k*) = 1\]![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si139.png) in [Table 11.1](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml#t0010).

Exercise 11.1

**– Pseudorandom sequence generated by rational numbers**. Let *q*[*k*] = 2^( − {*k*log[2]3})![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si140.png) be a rational number (*k* = 1, 2![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si18.png), and so on), where the brackets represent the **fractional part function** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fractional_part)\]. For instance, *q*[6] = 512/729![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si141.png). Let *M*[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si142.png) be the median of {*q*[1], …, *q*[*n*]}![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si143.png). Thus if *n* is odd, then *M*[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si142.png) is the middle term after rearranging the *q*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si144.png)'s in increasing order. Prove that (1) $M\_{n}\\rightarrow\\sqrt{2}/2$![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si145.png) as *n* → ∞![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si146.png), (2) the binary digit expansion of *q*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si144.png) has period 2 ⋅ 3^(*k* − 1)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si147.png), and (3) the proportion of 0 and 1 among these digits is exactly 50/50.

**Solution**

Solution to (2) and (3) is found [here](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/3310862/what-is-the-period-of-the-fraction-1-3k-in-base-2-for-k-1-2-dots); (3) follows from the **equidistribution modulo** 1 \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equidistribution_theorem)\] of the sequence {*k*log[2]3}![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si148.png). This implies that the *q*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si144.png)'s are distributed like 2^( − *U*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si149.png) where *U* is uniformly distributed on \[0, 1\]![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si90.png).

## 11.3 Python code

The code in Section [11.3.3](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml#s0070) focuses on big integers and computing the binary digits for a class of quadratic irrational numbers, using an original, not well-known recursion, possibly published here for the first time. This code is very short, and the description is accompanied by pretty cool math. I recommend that you start looking at it, before digging into the main program in Section [11.3.2](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml#s0065).

The main program deals with the prime test. Before that, Section [11.3.1](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml#s0060) discusses some generalities related to Python and other languages, pertaining to PRNG issues and fixes.

### 11.3.1 Fixes to the faulty random function in Python

The default Python function to generate pseudorandom numbers is random.random(), available in the random library. It is based on the **Mersenne twister** congruential generator \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mersenne_Twister)\], and documented [here](https://docs.python.org/3/library/random.xhtml). As discussed in Section [11.2.2](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml#s0040), it is not suitable for cryptographic and other applications where pure randomness is critical. Indeed, the documentation comes with the following warning: “The pseudorandom generators of this module should not be used for security purposes”.

One way to improve random.random() is to avoid particularly bad seeds, such as 200 or 4, in the random.seed() call. You may also use binary digits of some **quadratic irrational numbers** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_irrational_number)\], using the Python code in Section [11.3.2](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml#s0065). Again, it is a good idea to check, using the prime test proposed in this chapter, which irrational numbers to avoid. Also this method may be slow, as it involves working with very big integers. A workaround is to store large tables of precomputed digits in a secure location. The number of quadratic irrationals you can choose from is infinite. Also, your digit sequence should never start with the first binary digit of such numbers, but rather at a random position, to make hacking more difficult.

For instance, to generate your sequence {*d*(*k*)}![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si17.png), set *d*(3*k*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si150.png) to *δ*(*g*[1](*k*), *α*[1])![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si151.png), set *d*(3*k* + 1)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si152.png) to *δ*(*g*[2](*k*), *α*[2])![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si153.png), and set *d*(3*k* + 2)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si154.png) to *δ*(*g*[3](*k*), *α*[3])![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si155.png) where

*   •  The numbers *α*[1], *α*[1], *α*[3]![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si156.png) are three quadratic irrationals, say $\\sqrt{2},\\sqrt{10},\\sqrt{41}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si157.png),
*   •  The number (*δ*(*k*, *α*) + 1)/2![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si158.png) is the *k*th binary digit of the quadratic irrational *α*,
*   •  The functions *g*[1], *g*[2], *g*[3]![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si159.png) are used for scrambling: for instance, *g*[1](*k*) = 5 ⋅ 10⁵ + 2*k*![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si160.png), *g*[2](*k*) = 3 ⋅ 10⁵ + 3*k*![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si161.png), and *g*[3](*k*) = 7 ⋅ 10⁶ − *k*![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si162.png).

Another solution is to use for your sequence {*d*(*k*)}![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si17.png) a **bitwise XOR** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitwise_operation)\] on two pseudorandom sequences: the binary digits of (say) $\\sqrt{2}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si111.png) and $\\sqrt{41}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si163.png), starting at arbitrary positions.

There are also Python libraries that provide solutions suitable for cryptographic applications. For instance, os.urandom() uses the operating system to create random sequences that cannot be seeded, and are thus not replicable. See [here](https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.xhtml#os.urandom) and [here](https://docs.python.org/3/library/secrets.xhtml#module-secrets).

### 11.3.2 Prime test implementation to detect subtle flaws in PRNGs

The code presented here performs the prime test, computing *L*[3](*n*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si58.png). The variable nterms represents *n*, and it is set to ![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/fx007.jpg). Rather than directly computing *L*[3](*n*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si58.png), the code iteratively computes more granular statistics, namely minL and maxL; *L*[3](*n*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si58.png) is the maximum between \-minL and maxL, obtained at the last iteration.

The seeds and the sequences are initialized in the main part, at the bottom. The default category nonSquare is used for *L*[3]![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si164.png). The other categories, Prime and All, are respectively for *L*[1]![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si165.png) defined in formula [(11.5)](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml#deq5) and *L*[4]![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si132.png) defined in formula [(11.6)](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml#deq6). If you use the function createSignHash() rather than the default createSignHash2(), you can easily compute *L*[2]![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si166.png). The code is somewhat long only because it covers all the options discussed in Section [11.2.2](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml#s0040), and more. It heavily relies on hash tables (dictionaries in Python) rather than arrays, because the corresponding arrays would be rather sparse, consume a lot of memory, and slow down the computations. In addition, the code can easily handle Beurling primes (noninteger primes) thanks to the hash tables. A lengthier version named dirichletL.py, computing the orbit of *L*[*P*](*z*, *χ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si14.png) for *z* in the complex plane when $\\sigma = \\Re(z) \\geqslant \\frac{1}{2}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si167.png) is fixed, for any set of primes *P* (finite or infinite) including Beurling primes, is available on GitHub, [here](https://github.com/VincentGranville/Experimental-Math-Number-Theory/blob/main/Source-Code/dirichletL.py).

The Python code does not use any exotic library other than primePy. To install this library, type in the command pip install primePy on the Windows command prompt or its Unix equivalent, as you would to install any library. There is a possibility that some older versions of Python would require the BigNumber library. The code was tested under Python 3.10. The source code, featured below, is also on GitHub: look for [randomNumbersTesting.py](https://github.com/VincentGranville/Experimental-Math-Number-Theory/blob/main/Source-Code/randomNumbersTesting.py).

![](images/B9780443218576000151/gr004.jpg)

### 11.3.3 Special formula to compute 10 million digits of $\\sqrt{2}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si111.png)

The purpose of this code is twofold: to show you how to process integers with millions of digits in Python, and to offer a simple mechanism to compute the binary digits of some quadratic irrational numbers such as $\\sqrt{2}/2$![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si124.png). The first problem is solved transparently with no special code or library in Python 3.10. In short, this is a nonissue. With older versions of Python, you might have to install the BigNumber library. See documentation [here](https://pypi.org/project/BigNumber/). Nevertheless, it would be a good idea to track the size of the integers that you are working with (y and z in my code), as eventually their size will become the bottleneck, slowing down the computations.

As for the actual computation of the digits, it is limited here to ![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/fx007.jpg)digits, but I compare these digits with those obtained from an external source: Sagemath, see [here](https://mltblog.com/3uMZQ4s). It shows, as it should, that both methods produce the same digits, for the number $\\sqrt{2}/2$![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si124.png) in particular.

The special recursion used for the digit computation is as follows:

  **If** *z*[*k*] < 2*y*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si168.png) **then**

*y*[*k* + 1] = 4*y*[*k*] − 2*z*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si169.png)

*z*[*k* + 1] = 2*z*[*k*] + 3![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si170.png)

*d*(*k*) = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si92.png)

  **else**

*y*[*k* + 1] = 4*y*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si171.png)

*z*[*k* + 1] = 2*z*[*k*] − 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si172.png)

*d*(*k*) = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si173.png).

The bivariate seed (the initial condition) is determined by the values of *y*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si174.png) and *z*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si175.png). You need *z*[0] > *y*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si176.png) and *z*[0] ≠ 2*y*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si177.png). Then the binary digits *d*(*k*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si29.png) are those of the number

$x\_{0} = \\frac{- (z\_{0} - 1) + \\sqrt{{(z\_{0} - 1)}^{2} + 8y\_{0}}}{4},$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si178.png)

see [here](https://mltblog.com/3REtOB9). In particular, if *y*[0] = 2, *z*[0] = 5![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si179.png), then $x\_{0} = - 1 + \\sqrt{2}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si180.png). Using the change of variables *u*[*k*] = 2*y*[*k*] − *z*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si181.png) and *v*[*k*] = 2*z*[*k*] + 3![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si182.png), the recurrence can be rewritten as: 

  **If** *u*[*k*] > 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si183.png) **then**

*u*[*k* + 1] = 4*u*[*k*] − *v*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si184.png)

*v*[*k* + 1] = 2*v*[*k*] + 3![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si185.png)

*d*(*k*) = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si92.png)

  **else**

*u*[*k* + 1] = 4*u*[*k*] + *v*[*k*] − 2![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si186.png)

*v*[*k* + 1] = 2*v*[*k*] − 5![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si187.png)

*d*(*k*) = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si173.png).

Now *v*[*k*] − 5![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si188.png) is divisible by 8. Let *w*[*k*] = (*v*[*k*] − 5)/8![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si189.png). We have *d*(*k*) = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si92.png) if *w*[*k* + 1]![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si190.png) is odd, otherwise *d*(*k*) = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si173.png). We also have the following one-dimensional backward recursion, allowing you to compute the digits backward all the way down to the first digit:

  **If** *w*[*k* + 1]![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si190.png) is odd, **then**

*v*[*k*] = (*v*[*k* + 1] − 3)/2![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si192.png)

*d*(*k*) = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si92.png)

  **else**

*v*[*k*] = (*v*[*k* + 1] + 5)/2![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si193.png)

*d*(*k*) = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si173.png).

These recursions are reminiscent of the unsolved **Collatz conjecture** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collatz_conjecture)\]. Below is the source code, also available on GitHub: look for [randomNumbers-sqrt2.py](https://github.com/VincentGranville/Experimental-Math-Number-Theory/blob/main/Source-Code/randomNumbers-sqrt2.py).

![](images/B9780443218576000151/gr008.jpg)

## 11.4 Military-grade PRNG based on quadratic irrationals

If you produce simulations or create synthetic data that requires billions or trillions of random numbers (such as in Section [1.3.4.1](#Chp001_1-34_B9780443218576000059.xhtml)), you need a pseudorandom number generator (PRNG) that is not only fast, but in some cases truly emulates randomness. Usually you cannot have both. Congruential PRNGs are very fast and can be pretty good at emulating randomness. The Mersenne twister available in Python and in other languages has a very large period, more than enough for any practical need. Yet, depending on the seed, it has flaws caused by the lack of perfect randomness in the distribution of prime numbers. These were revealed by the **prime test** in Section [11.2.2](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml#s0040). To the contrary, PRNGs based on irrational numbers exhibit stronger randomness if you skip the first few digits and carefully choose your numbers. But they tend to be very slow.

In this section I propose a new approach to obtain billions of trillions of digits from combinations of **quadratic irrationals** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_irrational_number)\] such as $\\sqrt{2}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si111.png) or $\\sqrt{7583}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si194.png), based on the algorithm in Section [11.3.3](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml#s0070). The goal is to produce replicable random numbers. If you want to use them for strong encryption, you need to use a seed that is hardware-generated so that the same seed is never used more than once.

### 11.4.1 Fast algorithm rooted in advanced analytic number theory

The idea to get a fast algorithm is simple. Instead of producing *n* digits from a single number, I generate *r* digits from *m* different numbers, with *n* = *r**m*![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si195.png). While the Python code relies only on basic additions and very few operations, the computation of *n* binary digits of a single irrational number involves very large integers. The **computational complexity** is *O*(*n*²)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si196.png). If instead you generate *r* digits from *m* numbers, the computational complexity drops to *O*(*r**m*²)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si197.png). In the most extreme and very interesting case where *r* = *n*![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si198.png) and *m* = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si199.png), the computational complexity is *O*(*n*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si200.png), just as fast as the Mersenne twister. The method is based on two deep results in number theory:

*   •  The binary digits of a quadratic irrational behave as an infinite realization of independent Bernoulli trials with equal proportions of 0 and 1. This unproven conjecture is one of the most difficult unsolved problems in mathematics. Very strong empirical results involving trillions of digits, support this hypothesis.
*   •  Two sequences of digits from irrational numbers that are linearly independent over the set ℚ![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si201.png) of rational numbers have zero cross-correlation. The correlation is defined as the empirical correlation in this case.

The latter is a consequence of the following theorem: the correlation *ρ*(*p*, *q*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si202.png) between the sequences ({*p**b*^(*k*)*α*})![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si203.png) and ({*q**b*^(*k*)*α*})![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si204.png) indexed by *k* = 0, 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si205.png), and so on, where *p*, *q*![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si103.png) are positive integers with no common divisors, *b* > 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si100.png) is an integer, and *α* is a positive irrational, is equal to *ρ*(*p*, *q*) = (*p**q*)^( − 1)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si206.png). Here { ⋅ }![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si207.png) denotes the fractional part function.

A proof (by [William Huber](https://www.analysisandinference.com/team/william-a-huber-phd)) of this unpublished theorem can be found [here](https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/422354/correlations-between-two-sequences-of-irrational-numbers), with additional discussion on this topic, [here](https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/450922/cross-correlations-in-digit-distributions). Note that ⌊*b* ⋅ {*b*^(*k*)*α*}⌋![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si208.png) is the *k*th digit of *α* in base *b*. The brackets represent the integer part function. Thus, if *α*[1] = *p**α*![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si209.png) and *α*[2] = *q**α*![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si210.png), the correlation between the sequences ({*b*^(*k*)*α*[1]})![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si211.png) and ({*b*^(*k*)*α*[2]})![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si212.png) is *ρ*(*p*, *q*) = (*p**q*)^( − 1)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si206.png). If *α*[1], *α*[2]![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si213.png) are irrational and linearly independent over ℚ![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si201.png), then the only way you can write *α*[1] = *p**α*![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si209.png), *α*[2] = *q**α*![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si210.png) is by letting *p*, *q*![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si103.png) tend to infinity, thus the correlation vanishes. It implies that the correlation between the digit sequences of *α*[1]![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si214.png) and *α*[2]![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si215.png) is zero.

There is more number theory involved. In particular, the method uses the new algorithm described in Section [11.3.3](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml#s0070) to compute the binary digits of quadratic irrationals. It is also connected to **square-free integers**, and approximations of irrational by rational numbers which is linked to continued fractions. Square-free integers \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Square-free_integer)\] are also discussed in Sections [11.2.1](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml#s0020) and [17.2.2.2](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml). They represent 61% of all positive integers: the exact proportion is 6/*π*²![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si216.png).

### 11.4.2 Fast PRNG: explanations

Each positive integer *c* can be written as *c* = *a**b*![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si217.png), where *a* is a square, and *b* is square-free. For instance, if *c* = 3⁵ × 13⁶ × 19![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si218.png), then *a* = 3⁴ × 13⁶![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si219.png) and *b* = 3 × 19![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si220.png). If *c* is a square, then *c* = *a*![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si221.png) and *b* = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si222.png).

The quadratic irrationals used here are characterized by a bivariate **seed** (*y*[0], *z*[0])![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si223.png). Given a seed, the successive iterations produce the binary digits of the number

$x\_{0} = \\frac{- (z\_{0} - 1) + \\sqrt{{(z\_{0} - 1)}^{2} + 8y\_{0}}}{4}.$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si224.png)(11.7) 

The connection to square-free integers is as follows: *c* = (*z*[0] − 1)² + 8*y*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si225.png) cannot be a square. I use the notation *c* = *a**b*![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si217.png), where *a* is the square part of *c* and *b* is the square-free part. Thus, we must have *b* > 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si100.png). I use a large number of seeds to generate a large number of quadratic irrationals. The cross-correlation between the two digit sequences in any pair of quadratic irrationals must be zero. Based on the theory in Section [11.4.1](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml#s0080), it means that once a seed produces a specific *b*, any future seed with the same *b* must be rejected. This is accomplished using the variable accepted in the code, along with the **hash table** (dictionary in Python) squareFreeList. The key for this hash table is actually *b*.

The number of digits produced for each quadratic irrational is specified by the parameter size. The total number of quadratic irrationals is determined by Niter. Not all of them are used: a few are rejected for the reason just mentioned. All the binary digits of all the accepted quadratic irrationals are stored in the hash table digits. For instance, digits\[(b,k)\] is the *k*th digit of the quadratic irrational with square-free part *b*. The seed (*y*[0], *z*[0])![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si223.png) corresponding to this number is squareFreeList\[b\].

Due to the particular choice of seeds in the Python code (with *y*[0] = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si226.png)), many quadratic irrationals are close to zero. More specifically, formula [(11.7)](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml#deq8) yields the following approximation: *x*[0] ≈ *y*[0]/(*z*[0] − 1)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si227.png). So the first few digits are biased and should be skipped. This is accomplished via the parameter offset. There are other problematic quadratic irrationals such as those with *z*[0] − 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si228.png) being a power of 2. A future version of this algorithm can reject these quadratic irrationals, and also reject those that are too close to a number already in the hash table. However, increasing the parameter offset is the easiest option to eliminate these problems. The next step is to run a standard battery of tests such as the **Diehard tests**, and check whether this PRNG passes all of them depending on the parameters and configuration.

I have not tested yet the algorithm with size=1: this is the fastest way to generate many digits (assuming Niter is increased accordingly), and possibly the best choice assuming offset is large enough. In particular, if you extract just one digit of each quadratic irrational, there is a faster way to do it, see Section [11.4.4](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml#s0095).

### 11.4.3 Python code

Now that I explained all the details about the algorithm, here is the Python code. It is also available on GitHub, [here](https://github.com/VincentGranville/Experimental-Math-Number-Theory/blob/main/Source-Code/strongprng.py), under the name stronprng.py.

![](images/B9780443218576000151/gr012.jpg)

### 11.4.4 Computing a digit without generating the previous ones

If offset is large, you spend time computing digits (at the beginning of the binary expansion of each quadratic irrational) that you will use only to get the subsequent digits. There is a more efficient approach: use a different seed (*y*[0]^′, *z*[0]^′)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si229.png). The new seed has the benefit of keeping the square-free part *b* unchanged. To get the digit in position *k* in one shot (assuming the first position corresponds to *k* = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si230.png)), use the seed *y*[0]^′ = 2^(2*k*)*y*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si231.png), *z*[0]^′ = 2^(*k*)(*z*[0] − 1) + 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si232.png). Then *x*[0]^′ = 2^(*k*)*x*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si233.png), so your quadratic irrational is multiplied by 2^(*k*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si234.png). This is a direct consequence of formula [(11.7)](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml#deq8). However, this will not work if *y*[0]^′ ≥ *z*[0]^′![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si235.png), which is always the case when *k* is large enough. So you need to work with a different (*y*[0]^′, *z*[0]^′)![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si229.png), one that leads to *x*[0]^′ = ⌊2^(*k*)*x*[0]⌋![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/si237.png). I describe how to do it efficiently in Section 5.3.3 in my book on chaotic dynamical systems [\[4\]](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml#br0020).

Finally, by digits, I mean the binary digits on the right starting after the decimal point. The position *k* that you select for the starting digit may be randomized: it can depend on the quadratic irrational. This makes it very difficult to reverse-engineer your sequence of random digits.

### 11.4.5 Security and comparison with other PRNGs

The spreadsheet [strongprng.xlsx](https://github.com/VincentGranville/Experimental-Math-Number-Theory/blob/main/Source-Code/strongprng.xlsx) (on GitHub) compares the quadratic irrational PRNG with the Mersenne twister. The test involves ![Image](images/B9780443218576000151/fx008.jpg)quadratic irrationals, one per row. Based on the acceptation rule, only 4971 were used. For each of them, I computed 400 binary digits and skipped the first 100 as suggested in the methodology. So in total, there are 4971 blocks, each with 300 digits. The tab corresponding to the Mersenne twister has the same block structure with the same number of digits: it was produced using the option PRNG='Mersenne' in the Python code. The numbers in brackets in column D represent the block ID: the number *b* in the case of the quadratic irrational PRNG, and nothing in particular in the case of the Mersenne twister.

I computed some summary statistics: digit expectation and variance for each column and for each row, as well as cross-correlations between rows, and also between columns. The results are as expected and markedly similar when comparing the two PRNGs. You would expect any decent PRNG to pass these basic tests, so this is not a surprise. You need more sophisticated tests to detect hard-to-find departure from randomness; that was the purpose of Section [11.2.2](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml#s0040) with the prime test. [Fig. 11.4](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml#f0040) shows 5000 correlation values. They are not statistically different from zero, and independent despite the fact that they correspond to seeds produced in chronological order. Indeed, their joint distribution is identical to that produced with the Mersenne twister (not shown in the picture, but included in the spreadsheet).

![Figure 11.4 Correlations are computed on sequences consisting of 300 binary digits.](images/B9780443218576000151/gr015.jpg)

[Figure 11.4](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml#cf0300) Correlations are computed on sequences consisting of 300 binary digits.

Whether using the Mersenne twister or quadratic irrationals, the compression factor – based on the zip tool applied to the 1.5 million raw digits – is about the same and equal to almost 8. This is the worst achievable compression factor: each character (8 bits) representing a digit is turned into 1 bit of information. It means that the zip tool is unable to detect any pattern in the digits that would allow for any amount of real compression.

#### 11.4.5.1 Important comments

There are very few serious articles in the literature dealing with digits of irrational numbers to build PRNGs. It seems that this idea was abandoned long ago due to the computational complexity and the erroneous belief that it defeats the nondeterministic nature of randomness. It is my hope that my quadratic irrational PRNG debunks all these myths. Note that there has been attempts to use chaotic dynamical systems to build PRNGs. See, for instance, [\[11\]](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml#br0055) and [\[1\]](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml#br0005). My upcoming book on dynamical systems explores many new related methods in great details.

Also, my PRNGs, by combining thousands to billions of quadratic irrationals, present some similarity to **combined linear congruential generators** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combined_linear_congruential_generator)\]. They avoid the drawbacks that these generators are facing. In the context of congruential generators, combining is used to increase the period and randomness. In the case of quadratic irrational PRNGs, the period is always infinite, and the goal is to increase security, but not randomness which is already maximum with just one number. Also using many quadratic irrationals each with a few digits runs a lot faster than one number with many digits. In addition, using many quadratic irrationals leads to a very efficient implementation using a distributed architecture.

Finally, while it sounds like a cave-man idea to publish a table of random digits, it servers a very important purpose that has been forgotten in modern scientific research and benchmarking – replicability. You are free to reuse my Excel spreadsheet if you want your research to be replicable. Of course, you would get the same digits if you use the Python code with the same seeds. This is not true with the Mersenne twister: the digits may depend on which version of Python you use. Also, one advantage of the quadratic irrational PRNG is its portability, and the fact that you will get the same digits regardless of your programming language. Time permitting, I will publish a much larger table with at least a trillion digits. In the meanwhile, if you need such a table, feel free to email me at [vincentg@MLTechniques.com](mailto:vincentg@MLTechniques.com).

### 11.4.6 Curious application: a new type of lottery

The following application requires a very large number of pseudorandom numbers generated in real-time, as fast as possible. The digits must emulate randomness extremely well. It would benefit from using the quadratic irrational PRNG. The idea consists of creating a virtual, market-neutral stock market where people buy and sell stocks with tokens. In short, a synthetic stock market where you play with synthetic money (tokens). Another description is a lottery or number guessing game. You pay a fee per transaction (with real money), and each time you make a correct guess, you are paid a specific amount, also in real money. The participant can select different strategies ranging from conservative and limited to small gains and low volatility, to aggressive with a very small chance to win a lot of money.

The algorithm that computes the winning numbers is public; it requires some data input, also publicly published (the equivalent of a public key in cryptography). So you can use it to compute the next winning number and be certain to win each time, which would very quickly result in bankruptcy for the operator. However, the public algorithm necessitates billions of years of computing time to obtain any winning number with certainty. But you can guess the winning number: your odds of winning by pure chance (in a particular example) is 1/256.

The operator uses a private algorithm that very efficiently computes the next winning number. From the public algorithm, it is impossible to tell – even if you are the greatest computer scientist or mathematician in the world – that there is an alternative that could make the computations a lot faster: the private algorithm is the equivalent of a private key in cryptography. The public algorithm takes as much time as breaking an encryption key (comparable to factoring a product of two very large primes), while the private version is equivalent to decoding a message if you have the private key (comparable to finding the second factor in the number in question if you know one of the two factors – the private key).

Needless to say, any very slight deviation resulting from flaws in the PRNG will quickly lead to either the bankruptcy of the operator, or the operator enriching itself and being accused of lying about the neutrality of the simulated market. I made a presentation on this topic at the Operations Research Society conference (INFORMS) in 2019, in a session exploring biases in algorithms. See the abstract [here](https://www.abstractsonline.com/pp8/#!/6818/presentation/6842). The full paper will be included in my upcoming book “Experimental Math and Probabilistic Number Theory”.
