# Chapter 12: Some unusual random walks

## Testing and leveraging quasirandomness

## Abstract

This is a follow-up to Chapter [11](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml) about “Detecting Subtle Departures from Randomness”, where I introduced the prime test to identify very weak violations of various laws of large numbers. Pseudorandom sequences failing this test usually pass most test batteries, yet are unsuitable for a number of applications, such as security, strong cryptography, or intensive simulations. The purpose here is to build such sequences with very low, slow-building, long-range dependencies, but that otherwise appear as random as pure noise. They are useful not only for testing and benchmarking tests of randomness, but also in their own right to model almost random systems, such as stock market prices. I introduce new categories of random walks (or quasi-Brownian motions subject to constraints), and discuss the peculiarities of each category. For completeness, I included related stochastic processes discussed in some of my previous articles, for instance, integrated and 2D clustered Brownian motions. All the processes investigated here are drift-free and symmetric, yet not perfectly random. They all start at zero.

### Keywords

constrained random walk; Brownian motion; Lévy flight; autoregressive processes; entropy; integrated Brownian motion

This is a follow-up to Chapter [11](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml) about “Detecting Subtle Departures from Randomness”, where I introduced the prime test to identify very weak violations of various laws of large numbers. Pseudorandom sequences failing this test usually pass most test batteries, yet are unsuitable for a number of applications, such as security, strong cryptography, or intensive simulations. The purpose here is to build such sequences with very low, slow-building, long-range dependencies, but that otherwise appear as random as pure noise. They are useful not only for testing and benchmarking tests of randomness, but also in their own right to model almost random systems, such as stock market prices. I introduce new categories of random walks (or quasi-Brownian motions subject to constraints), and discuss the peculiarities of each category. For completeness, I included related stochastic processes discussed in some of my previous articles, for instance integrated and 2D clustered Brownian motions. All the processes investigated here are drift-free and symmetric, yet not perfectly random. They all start at zero.

## 12.1 Symmetric unbiased constrained random walks

The standard symmetric 1D **random walk** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Random_walk)\] fundamental to this chapter is a sequence {*S*[*n*]}![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si1.png) with *n* ≥ 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si2.png), starting at *S*[0] = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si3.png), and recursively defined by *S*[*n*] = *X*[*n*] + *S*[*n* − 1]![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si4.png), for *n* > 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si5.png). Here *X*[1], *X*[2]![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si6.png), and so on, are independent random variables with $P\\lbrack X\_{n} = 1\\rbrack = P\\lbrack X\_{n} = - 1\\rbrack = \\frac{1}{2}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si7.png). Thus {*S*[*n*]}![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si1.png) is a time-discrete stochastic process, and indeed the most basic one. In Sections [12.1.2](#Chp012_229-241_B9780443218576000163.xhtml#s0020) and [12.1.3](#Chp012_229-241_B9780443218576000163.xhtml#s0040), I drop the assumption of independence, leading to modified random walks such as those described in [\[6](#Chp012_229-241_B9780443218576000163.xhtml#br0030),[9\]](#Chp012_229-241_B9780443218576000163.xhtml#br0045). More general references include [\[1](#Chp012_229-241_B9780443218576000163.xhtml#br0005),[8\]](#Chp012_229-241_B9780443218576000163.xhtml#br0040).

With proper rescaling, a random walk becomes a time-continuous stochastic process *S*[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si8.png) called **Brownian motion** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brownian_motion)\], with *t* ∈ ℝ^+![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si9.png). See the time series in gray in [Fig. 12.1](#Chp012_229-241_B9780443218576000163.xhtml#f0010), displaying a particular instance: it shows the first ![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/fx001.jpg)values of *S*[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si10.png) in a short window, giving the appearance of a Brownian motion. By contrast, each of the orange, red, and gray time series represents one instance of a specific type of non-Brownian motion. Sections [12.1.2](#Chp012_229-241_B9780443218576000163.xhtml#s0020) and [12.1.3](#Chp012_229-241_B9780443218576000163.xhtml#s0040) focus on these three types of processes, which are quasi-, but not fully random.

![Figure 12.1 Typical path Sn with Image for four types of random walks.](images/B9780443218576000163/gr001.jpg)

Figure 12.1 Typical path *S*[*n*] with ![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/fx002.jpg)for four types of random walks.

### 12.1.1 Three fundamental properties of pure random walks

The standard random walk {*S*[*n*]}![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si1.png) (illustrated in gray in [Fig. 12.1](#Chp012_229-241_B9780443218576000163.xhtml#f0010)) is the base or reference process, used to build more sophisticated models. It has too many properties to list in this short chapter. However, the following are the most relevant to our discussion:

*   •  **Law of the iterated logarithm** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_of_the_iterated_logarithm)\]. In our context, it is stated as follows:

$\\lim\\sup\\frac{|S\_{n}|}{\\sqrt{2nv\\log\\log n}} = 1\\quad\\text{as~}n\\rightarrow\\infty.$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si11.png)(12.1) 

*   Here, as per **Hartman–Wintner theorem** \[[Wiki](https://encyclopediaofmath.org/wiki/Law_of_the_iterated_logarithm)\], *v* = *V**a**r*\[*X*[1]\] = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si12.png). See [\[8\]](#Chp012_229-241_B9780443218576000163.xhtml#br0040), pages 118–123, for a version adapted to Brownian motions.
*   •  Expected number of **zero crossings** in *S*[1], …, *S*[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si13.png), denoted as *N*[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si14.png). Here a zero-crossing is an index 0 < *k* ≤ *n*![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si15.png) such that *S*[*k*] = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si16.png). For *n* > 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si5.png), we have (see [here](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/1684576/expected-of-returns-in-a-symmetric-simple-random-walk))

$E\\lbrack N\_{2n}\\rbrack = - 1 + \\frac{2n + 1}{4^{n}}\\begin{pmatrix} {2n} \\\\ n \\\\ \\end{pmatrix} \\sim \\frac{2}{\\sqrt{\\pi}} \\cdot \\sqrt{n}\\quad\\text{as~}n\\rightarrow\\infty.$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si17.png)

*   
*   •  Distribution of **first hitting time** to zero \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First-hitting-time_model)\], or first zero crossing after *S*[0] = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si3.png), also called time of first return. The random variable in question is denoted as *T*. It is defined as follows: *T* = *n*![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si18.png) (with *n* > 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si5.png)) if and only if *S*[*n*] = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si19.png) and *S*[*k*] ≠ 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si20.png) if 0 < *k* < *n*![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si21.png). We have *P*\[*T* = *n*\] = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si22.png) if *n* is odd, and *E*\[*T*\] = *V**a**r*\[*T*\] = ∞![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si23.png). Yet, our random walks cross the X-axis infinitely many times. We also have the following **probability generating function** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probability-generating_function)\] (see [here](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/64919/biased-random-walk-and-pdf-of-time-of-first-return)):

$\\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{\\infty}{(2x)}^{2n}P\\lbrack T = 2n\\rbrack = 1 - \\sqrt{1 - 4x^{2}}\\quad\\text{if~}x \\leqslant \\frac{1}{4}.$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si24.png)

*   From this one can obtain

$P\\lbrack T = 2n\\rbrack = \\frac{1}{(2n - 1)4^{n}}\\begin{pmatrix} {2n} \\\\ n \\\\ \\end{pmatrix} \\sim \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{4\\pi}} \\cdot n^{- 3/2}\\quad\\text{as~}n\\rightarrow\\infty,E\\lbrack T^{- 1}\\rbrack = \\int\_{0}^{1/2}\\frac{1 - \\sqrt{1 - 4x^{2}}}{x}dx = 1 - \\log 2.$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si25.png)

*   

Note that *E*\[*T*^( − 1)\]![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si26.png) is finite, while *E*\[*T*\]![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si27.png) is infinite. The fact that *E*\[*T*\] = ∞![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si28.png) explains why the sequence *S*[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si10.png) can stay above or below the X-axis for incredibly long time periods, as shown in [Fig. 12.1](#Chp012_229-241_B9780443218576000163.xhtml#f0010) for the gray curve.

The above three statistics $|S\_{n}|/\\sqrt{2n\\log\\log n}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si29.png), *N*[2*n*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si30.png), and *T*^( − 1)![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si31.png) can be used to design tests of randomness for pseudorandom number generators. Indeed, the **prime test** in Chapter [11](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml) relies on a number-theoretic version of the law of the iterated logarithm (LIL). The purpose is to detect very weak departures from randomness, even in sequences that are random enough to pass the classic LIL test, yet not fully random. In this chapter, the goal is to simulate quasirandom sequences, rather than creating new tests of randomness.

I now describe special types of modified random walks that lack true independence in the sequence {*X*[*n*]}![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si32.png). In particular, I discuss why they are special and of great interest, with a focus on applications.

### 12.1.2 Random walks with more entropy than pure random signal

One way to introduce dependencies in the sequences is to increase the frequency of oscillations (and thus the entropy) in the gray curve in [Fig. 12.1](#Chp012_229-241_B9780443218576000163.xhtml#f0010). The gray curve represents a realization of a pure random walk. To achieve this goal, you may want the sequence to violate the law of the iterated logarithm: you want to build a sequence that would satisfy a modified law of the iterated logarithm with $\\sqrt{2n\\log\\log n}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si33.png) in formula [(12.1)](#Chp012_229-241_B9780443218576000163.xhtml#deq1) replaced by (say) *n*^(2/5)![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si34.png).

To accomplish this, you need to add constraints when simulating the sequence in question. Yet you want to preserve quasirandomness – the absence of drifts and autocorrelations in the sequence {*X*[*n*]}![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si32.png) – even though there is some modest lack of independence. So modest indeed that most statistical tests would fail to catch it, even though it can made highly visible to the naked eye: see the red, and especially the blue curve in [Fig. 12.1](#Chp012_229-241_B9780443218576000163.xhtml#f0010).

#### 12.1.2.1 Applications

Such sequences can be used to generate synthetic data (see Chapter [7](#Chp007_113-129_B9780443218576000114.xhtml)) or to model barely-constrained stochastic processes, such as stock price fluctuations in an almost perfect market. See also [\[4\]](#Chp012_229-241_B9780443218576000163.xhtml#br0020). Another application is to introduce an undetectable backdoor in some encryption systems without third parties (government or hackers) being able to notice it, depending on the strength of the dependencies. This type of backdoor can help the encryption company decrypt a message when requested by a legitimate user who lost his key, even though the encryption company has no standard mechanism to store or retrieve keys (precisely to avoid government interference).

This assumes that there is a mapping between the type of weak dependencies introduced in a specific sequence, and the type of algorithm (or the key) used to decrypt the sequence in question. The mapping can be made too loose for full decryption even by the parent company, but helpful to retrieve partial data, such as where the sequence originates from: in this case, the type of dependencies is a proxy for a signature. All that is needed is to add some extra bits so that the sequence has the desired statistical behavior.

Ironically, you need a very good, industrial-grade **pseudorandom number generator** (PRNG) to generate almost perfectly random sequences. PRNGs that are not good enough – such as the **Mersenne twister** – may introduce irregularities that can interfere with those you want to introduce. This is discussed in detail in Chapter [11](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml) on PRNGs.

#### 12.1.2.2 Algorithm to generate quasirandom sequences

One way to generate such sequences is as follows:

 *S* = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si35.png)

 **For** *n* = 1, 2, …![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si36.png)

  Generate random deviate *U* on \[0, 1\]![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si37.png)

  *M* = *g*(*n*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si38.png)

  **If** (*S* <  − *M*![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si39.png) and $U < \\frac{1}{2} - \\epsilon$![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si40.png)) or (*S* > *M*![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si41.png) and $U < \\frac{1}{2} + \\epsilon$![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si42.png)) or (|*S*| ≤ *M*![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si43.png) and $U < \\frac{1}{2}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si44.png))

  **Then**

*X*[*n*] =  − 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si45.png)

  **Else**

*X*[*n*] = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si46.png)

  *S* = *S* + *X*[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si47.png)

  *S*[*n*] = *S*![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si48.png)

Here $0 < \\epsilon < \\frac{1}{2}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si49.png) and *α* > 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si50.png). The function *g*(*n*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si51.png) is positive and growing more slowly than $\\sqrt{n}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si52.png). Typically, *g*(*n*) = *α**n*^(*β*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si53.png) with $0 \\leqslant \\beta \\leqslant \\frac{1}{2}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si54.png), or *g*(*n*) = *α*(log *n*)^(*β*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si55.png) with *β* ≥ 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si56.png). The Python code in Section [12.3.2](#Chp012_229-241_B9780443218576000163.xhtml#s0070) performs this simulation: choose the option deviations='Small'. You can customize the function *g*(*n*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si51.png), denoted as G in the code. The option mode='Power' corresponds to *g*(*n*) = *α**n*^(*β*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si53.png), while mode='Log' corresponds to *g*(*n*) = *α*(log *n*)^(*β*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si55.png).

Results are displayed in [Fig. 12.1](#Chp012_229-241_B9780443218576000163.xhtml#f0010). The color scheme is as follows:

*   •  Gray curve: *ϵ* = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si57.png), corresponding to a pure random walk.
*   •  Blue curve: *g*(*n*) = log *n*![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si58.png), *ϵ* = 0.05![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si59.png).
*   •  Red curve: *g*(*n*) = *n*^(*β*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si60.png) with *β* = 0.35![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si61.png), *ϵ* = 0.05![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si59.png).

The yellow curve represents a very different type of process, discussed in Section [12.1.3](#Chp012_229-241_B9780443218576000163.xhtml#s0040).

#### 12.1.2.3 Variance of the modified random walk

The symmetric nature of the modified random walk {*S*[*n*]}![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si1.png) defined in Section [12.1.2.2](#Chp012_229-241_B9780443218576000163.xhtml#s0030) results in several identities. Let *p*[*n*](*m*) = *P*(*S*[*n*] = *m*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si62.png), with  − *n* ≤ *m* ≤ *n*![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si63.png). Also, let *S*[0] = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si3.png) and *p*[0](0) = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si64.png). Then *p*[*n*](*m*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si65.png) can be recursively computed using some modified version of the Pascal triangle recursion:

$p\_{n + 1}(m) = \\left\\lbrack \\frac{1}{2} + \\epsilon \\cdot A\_{n}(m - 1) \\right\\rbrack p\_{n}(m - 1) + \\left\\lbrack \\frac{1}{2} - \\epsilon \\cdot A\_{n}(m + 1) \\right\\rbrack p\_{n}(m + 1),$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si66.png)(12.2) 

where *A*[*n*](*m*) = *χ*\[*m* <  − *g*(*n*)\] − *χ*\[*m* > *g*(*n*)\]![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si67.png). Here *χ* is the indicator function: *χ*(*ω*) = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si68.png) if *ω* is true, otherwise *χ*(*ω*) = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si69.png). Some of the identities in question include:

$\\sum\\limits\_{m = - n}^{n}m \\cdot p\_{n}(m) = E\\lbrack S\_{n}\\rbrack = 0,\\quad\\sum\\limits\_{m = - n}^{n}A\_{n}(m)p\_{n}(m) = 0,\\quad\\sum\\limits\_{m = - n}^{n}m^{2}A\_{n}(m)p\_{n}(m) = 0,\\sum\\limits\_{m = - n}^{n}m^{2}\\left\\lbrack A\_{n - 1}(m - 1)p\_{n - 1}(m - 1) + A\_{n - 1}(m + 1)p\_{n - 1}(m + 1) \\right\\rbrack = 0.$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si70.png)

From these identities, it is easy to establish a recursion for the variance:

${Var}\\lbrack S\_{n + 1}\\rbrack = {Var}\\lbrack S\_{n}\\rbrack + 1 - \\delta\_{n},\\quad\\text{with~}\\delta\_{n} = 8\\epsilon \\cdot \\sum\\limits\_{m > g(n)}m \\cdot p\_{n}(m).$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si71.png)(12.3) 

The sum for *δ*[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si72.png) is finite since *p*[*n*](*m*) = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si73.png) if *m* > *n*![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si74.png). Of course, *V**a**r*\[*S*[0]\] = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si75.png). Also, if *ϵ* = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si57.png), the sequence is perfectly random: *δ*[*n*] = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si76.png), *V**a**r*\[*S*[*n*]\] = *n*![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si77.png), and $S\_{n}/\\sqrt{n}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si78.png) converges to a normal distribution. In turn, the law of the iterated logarithm is satisfied. Conversely, this is violated if *ϵ* > 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si79.png). Formula [(12.3)](#Chp012_229-241_B9780443218576000163.xhtml#deq7), combined with **Hoeffding's inequality** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoeffding%27s_inequality)\], may provide some bounds for *V**a**r*\[*S*[*n*]\]![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si80.png).

[Fig. 12.3](#Chp012_229-241_B9780443218576000163.xhtml#f0020) shows *δ*[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si72.png) for four types of modified random walks, using the following color scheme:

*   •  Yellow: *g*(*n*) = 10![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si81.png), *ϵ* = 0.05![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si59.png)
*   •  Red: *g*(*n*) = *n*^(*β*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si60.png), *β* = 0.50![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si82.png), *ϵ* = 0.05![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si59.png)
*   •  Blue: *g*(*n*) = *n*^(*β*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si60.png), *β* = 0.45![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si83.png), *ϵ* = 0.05![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si59.png)
*   •  Purple: *g*(*n*) = *n*^(*β*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si60.png), *β* = 0.55![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si84.png), *ϵ* = 0.05![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si59.png)

The curve that coincides with the X-axis (*δ*[*n*] = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si76.png)) corresponds to *ϵ* = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si57.png), that is, to pure randomness regardless of *g*(*n*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si51.png). It is not colored in [Fig. 12.3](#Chp012_229-241_B9780443218576000163.xhtml#f0020). Finally, the Python code in Section [12.3.1](#Chp012_229-241_B9780443218576000163.xhtml#s0065) computes *V**a**r*\[*S*[*n*]\]![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si80.png) exactly (not via simulations) using two different methods, proving that formula [(12.3)](#Chp012_229-241_B9780443218576000163.xhtml#deq7) is correct.

### 12.1.3 Random walks with less entropy than pure random signal

In Section [12.1.2](#Chp012_229-241_B9780443218576000163.xhtml#s0020), I focused on creating sequences with higher oscillation rates than dictated by randomness, resulting in lower amplitudes. Doing the opposite – decreasing the oscillation rate – is more difficult. For instance, using *g*(*n*) = *n*^(*β*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si60.png) with $\\beta > \\frac{1}{2}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si85.png) will not work. You cannot do better than $\\sqrt{n}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si52.png) because of the law of the iterated logarithm: boosting *β* beyond the threshold $\\frac{1}{2}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si86.png) is useless.

A workaround is to use the following algorithm:

 *S* = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si35.png)

 **For** *n* = 1, 2, …![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si36.png)

  Generate random deviate *U* on \[0, 1\]![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si37.png)

  *M* = *g*(*n*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si38.png)

  **If** ( − *M* < *S* < 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si87.png) and $U < \\frac{1}{2} + \\epsilon$![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si42.png)) or (0 < *S* < *M*![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si88.png) and $U < \\frac{1}{2} - \\epsilon$![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si40.png)) or (*S* = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si35.png) and $U < \\frac{1}{2}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si44.png))

  **Then**

*X*[*n*] =  − 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si45.png)

  **Else**

*X*[*n*] = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si46.png)

  *S* = *S* + *X*[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si47.png)

  *S*[*n*] = *S*![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si48.png)

The Python code in Section [12.3.2](#Chp012_229-241_B9780443218576000163.xhtml#s0070), with the option deviations='Large', performs this simulation. The yellow time series in [Fig. 12.1](#Chp012_229-241_B9780443218576000163.xhtml#f0010) is a realization of such a modified random walk, in this case with *g*(*n*) = *α**n*^(*β*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si53.png), with *α* = 0.30![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si89.png), *β* = 0.54![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si90.png), and *ϵ* = 0.01![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si91.png). It is unclear if the yellow curve will ever cross again the horizontal axis after ![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/fx001.jpg)iterations, but it is expected to do so. To the contrary, the other three curves (gray, red, blue) are guaranteed to cross the horizontal axis infinitely many times, even though the random variable *T* measuring the spacing between two crossings (referred to as the **hitting time** in Section [12.1.1](#Chp012_229-241_B9780443218576000163.xhtml#s0015)) has infinite expectation.

For pure random walks (the gray curve in [Fig. 12.1](#Chp012_229-241_B9780443218576000163.xhtml#f0010)), the average number of times that *S*[*k*] = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si16.png) when 0 < *k* ≤ 2*n*![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si92.png) is asymptotically equal to $\\sqrt{4n/\\pi}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si93.png), as discussed in Section [12.1.1](#Chp012_229-241_B9780443218576000163.xhtml#s0015). One would expect this value to be about 178 when ![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/fx004.jpg). For the gray curve, the observed value is 243. Keep in mind that huge variations are expected between different realizations of the same random walk, due to the fact that *E*\[*T*\] = ∞![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si28.png). Indeed, averaged over three realizations, the value 243 was down to 185. Also, a faulty pseudorandom number generator could easily lead to results that are off, in this case.

One would expect much larger values for the “nonrandom” red and blue curves. The observed values are respectively 747 and 1783, based on a single realization in each case. Likewise, the yellow curve is expected to have a much smaller value: in [Fig. 12.1](#Chp012_229-241_B9780443218576000163.xhtml#f0010), that value is 105.

## 12.2 Related stochastic processes

There are countless types of random walks or quasi-Brownian motions that are – on purpose and by design – not perfectly random. One could write an encyclopedia on this topic. A good reference is the book by Mörters and Peres [\[8\]](#Chp012_229-241_B9780443218576000163.xhtml#br0040), published in 2010. My goal in this section is to present two examples (one in two dimensions) that are very recent, interesting, and related to the material discussed in Section [12.1](#Chp012_229-241_B9780443218576000163.xhtml#s0010). I built these stochastic processes in the last two years, to address modeling issues with fintech applications in mind.

### 12.2.1 From Brownian motions to clustered Lévy flights

Here I discuss a 2D Brownian motion generated using some specific probability distributions. Depending on the parameters, these distributions may or may not have an infinite expectation or variance. Things start to get interesting when the expectation becomes infinite (and the Brownian motion is no longer Brownian), resulting in a system exhibiting a strong clustering structure.

In some sense, it is similar to the examples studied earlier, where moving away from the law of the iterated logarithm resulted in unusual patterns: either very strong or very weak oscillations. Note that all the simulations performed here consist of discrete random walks rather than time-continuous Brownian motions. They approach Brownian motions very well, but since modern computers (at least to this date) are “digital” as opposed to “analog”, everything is broken down into bits, and is thus discrete, albeit with a huge granularity.

In one dimension, we start with *S*[0] = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si3.png) and *S*[*n*] = *S*[*n* − 1] + *R*[*n*]*θ*[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si94.png), for *n* = 1, 2![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si95.png), and so on. If the *R*[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si96.png)'s are independently and identically distributed (iid) with an exponential distribution of expectation 1/*λ*![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si97.png) and *θ*[*n*] = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si98.png), then the resulting process is a stationary **Poisson point process** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poisson_point_process)\] with intensity function *λ* on ℝ^+![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si99.png); the *R*[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si96.png)'s are the successive **interarrival times**. If the *θ*[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si100.png)'s are iid with $P(\\theta\_{n} = 1) = P(\\theta\_{n} = - 1) = \\frac{1}{2}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si101.png), and independent from the *R*[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si96.png)'s, then we get a totally different type of process, which, after proper rescaling, represents a time-continuous **Brownian motion** in one dimension. For general references, see [\[2](#Chp012_229-241_B9780443218576000163.xhtml#br0010),[3\]](#Chp012_229-241_B9780443218576000163.xhtml#br0015).

I generalize it to two dimensions, as follows. Start with (*S*[0], *S*[0]^′) = (0, 0)![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si102.png). Then generate the points (*S*[*n*], *S*[*n*]^′)![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si103.png), with *n* = 1, 2![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si95.png), and so on, using the recursion

*S*[*n*] = *S*[*n* − 1] + *R*[*n*]cos (2*π**θ*[*n*]),

![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si104.png)(12.4) 

*S*[*n*]^′ = *S*[*n* − 1]^′ + *R*[*n*]sin (2*π**θ*[*n*]),

![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si105.png)(12.5) 

where *θ*[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si100.png) is uniform on \[0, 1\]![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si37.png), and the radius *R*[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si96.png) is generated using the formula

$R\_{n} = \\frac{1}{\\lambda}\\left( - \\log(1 - U\_{n}) \\right)^{\\gamma},$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si106.png)(12.6) 

where *U*[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si107.png) is uniform on \[0, 1\]![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si37.png). Also, *λ* > 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si108.png), and the random variables *U*[*n*], *θ*[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si109.png) are all independently distributed. If *γ* >  − 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si110.png), then $E\\lbrack R\_{n}\\rbrack = \\frac{1}{\\lambda}\\Gamma(1 + \\gamma)$![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si111.png) where Γ is the **gamma function** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamma_function)\]. In order to standardize the process, I use *λ* = *Γ*(1 + *γ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si112.png). Thus, *E*\[*R*[*n*]\] = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si113.png) and if $\\gamma > - \\frac{1}{2}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si114.png),

${Var}\\lbrack R\_{n}\\rbrack = \\frac{\\Gamma(1 + 2\\gamma)}{\\Gamma^{2}(1 + \\gamma)} - 1.$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si115.png)

We have the following cases:

*   •  If *γ* = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si116.png), then *R*[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si96.png) has an exponential distribution.
*   •  If  − 1 < *γ* < 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si117.png), then *R*[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si96.png) has a **Fréchet distribution**. If in addition, $\\gamma > - \\frac{1}{2}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si114.png), then its variance is finite.
*   •  If *γ* > 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si118.png), then *R*[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si96.png) has a **Weibull distribution**, with finite variance.

Interestingly, the Fréchet and Weibull distributions are two of the three **attractor distributions** in **extreme value theory**.

The two-dimensional process consisting of the points (*S*[*n*], *S*[*n*]^′)![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si103.png) is a particular type of random walk. The random variables *R*[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si96.png) represent the (variable) lengths of the successive increments. Under proper rescaling, assuming the variance of *R*[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si96.png) is finite, it tends to a time-continuous two-dimensional Brownian motion. However, if *V**a**r*\[*R*[*n*]\] = ∞![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si119.png), it may not converge to a Brownian motion. Instead, it is very similar to a **Lévy flight** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%A9vy_flight)\], and produces a strong cluster structure, with well separated clusters. See [Fig. 12.4](#Chp012_229-241_B9780443218576000163.xhtml#f0025), based on $\\gamma = - \\frac{1}{2}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si120.png), *λ* = 8![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si121.png), and featuring the first ![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/fx005.jpg)points of the bivariate sequence {(*S*[*n*], *S*[*n*]^′)}![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si122.png).

The Lévy flight uses a **Lévy distribution** \[[Wiki](https://bit.ly/3rV7mrq)\] for *R*[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si96.png), which also has infinite expectation and variance. Along with the **Cauchy distribution** (also with infinite expectation and variance), it is one of the few **stable distributions** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stable_distribution)\]. Such distributions are attractors for an adapted version of the **Central Limit Theorem** (CLT), just like the Gaussian distribution is the attractor for the CLT. A well-written, seminal book on the topic is “Limit Distributions for Sums of Independent Random Variables”, by Gnedenko and Kolmogorov [\[5\]](#Chp012_229-241_B9780443218576000163.xhtml#br0025).

For a simple introduction to Brownian and related processes, see the website [RandomServices.org](https://www.randomservices.org/) by Kyle Siegrist, especially the chapter on standard Brownian motions, [here](https://www.randomservices.org/random/brown/Standard.xhtml). The processes discussed in Section [12.2.1](#Chp012_229-241_B9780443218576000163.xhtml#s0050) are further investigated in my book “Stochastic Processes and Simulations: A Machine Learning Perspective” [\[7\]](#Chp012_229-241_B9780443218576000163.xhtml#br0035).

### 12.2.2 Integrated Brownian motions and special autoregressive processes

The Brownian motions pictured in [Fig. 12.5](#Chp012_229-241_B9780443218576000163.xhtml#f0030) are generated by simple time-discrete **autoregressive time series** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autoregressive_model)\]. Thus, the base process is autocorrelated, but the limit (after rescaling) is still a standard Brownian motion and thus perfectly random, if the autocorrelation structure is weak enough.

This autoregressive (AR) model is driven initial conditions *S*[1], …, *S*[*p*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si123.png) and the recursion

*S*[*n*] = *a*[1]*S*[*n* − 1] + … + *a*[*p*]*S*[*n* − *p*] + *e*[*n*],

![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si124.png)

where *a*[1], …, *a*[*p*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si125.png) are real coefficients satisfying some conditions to guarantee **stationarity**. By choice, the sequence {*e*[*n*]}![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si126.png) is a **white noise**: *E*\[*e*[*n*]\] = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si127.png), *V**a**r*\[*e*[*n*]\] = *σ*²![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si128.png) is fixed (it does not depend on *n*), and the *e*[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si129.png)'s are independently and identically distributed.

The behavior of this process, and thus of the resulting Brownian motions pictured in [Fig. 12.5](#Chp012_229-241_B9780443218576000163.xhtml#f0030), is determined by the roots of its **characteristic polynomial** of degree *p*,

*x*^(*p*) = *a*[1]*x*^(*p* − 1) + *a*[2]*x*^(*p* − 2) + … + *a*[*p* − 1]*x* + *a*[*p*].

![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si130.png)

These roots can be real or complex, and simple or multiple. A borderline case, as far as stationarity is concerned, is when the root with highest modulus has a **modulus** equal to 1. If the modulus in question is above 1, the process is no longer stationary. The modulus of a real number *a* is its absolute value |*a*|![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si131.png), and for a complex number *a* + *b**i*![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si132.png), it is defined as $\\sqrt{a^{2} + b^{2}}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000163/si133.png). If in addition the root with largest modulus is multiple, then something unusual happens: the resulting Brownian motion is very smooth and is not a Brownian motion anymore. It becomes is an integrated Brownian motion; its derivative is a Brownian motion. See the top left plot in [Fig. 12.5](#Chp012_229-241_B9780443218576000163.xhtml#f0030). The other plots in the same figure correspond to other awkward situations, regarding the roots of the characteristic polynomials and the resulting behavior. This is discussed in detail in Chapter [3](#Chp003_49-60_B9780443218576000072.xhtml) on linear algebra.

# Chapter 13: Divergent optimization algorithm and synthetic functions

## When all else fails

## Abstract

In this chapter, I discuss an unusual optimization algorithm. Why would anyone be interested in an algorithm that never converges to the solution you are looking for? This version of the fixed-point iteration, when approaching a zero or an optimum, emits a strong signal and allows you to detect a small interval likely to contain the solution: the zero or global optimum in question. It may approach the optimum quite well, but subsequent iterations do not lead to convergence: the algorithm eventually moves away from the optimum, or oscillates around the optimum without ever reaching it.

The **fixed-point iteration** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fixed-point_iteration)\] is the mother of all optimization and root-finding algorithms. In particular, all **gradient-based** optimization techniques \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gradient_descent)\] are a particular version of this generic method. In this chapter, I use it in a very challenging setting. The target function may not be differentiable or may have a very large number of local minima and maxima. All the standard techniques fail to detect the global optima. In this case, even the fixed-point method diverges. However, somehow, it can tell you the location of a global optimum with a rather decent precision. Once an approximation is obtained, the method can be applied again, this time focusing around a narrow interval containing the solution to achieve higher precision. Also, this method is a lot faster than brute force such as **grid search**.

I first illustrate the method on a specific problem. Then, generating synthetic data that emulates and generalizes the setting of the initial problem, I illustrate how the method performs on different functions or data sets. The purpose is to show how synthetic data can be used to test and benchmark algorithms, or to understand when they work, and when they do not. This, combined with the intuitive aspects of my fixed-point iteration, illustrates a particular facet of explainable AI. Finally, I use a smoothing technique to visualize the highly chaotic functions involved here. It highlights the features of the functions that we are interested in, while removing the massive noise that makes these functions almost impossible to visualize in any meaningful way.

### Keywords

fixed-point algorithm; factorization; divergent algorithm; synthetic function; root finding; smoothing; discrete optimization

## 13.1 Introduction

While the technique discussed here is a last resort solution when all else fails, it is actually more powerful than it seems at first glance. First, it also works in standard cases with “nice” functions. However, there are better methods when the function behaves nicely, taking advantage of the differentiability of the function in question, such as the **Newton algorithm** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newton%27s_method)\] (itself a fixed-point iteration). It can be generalized to higher dimensions, though I focus on univariate functions here.

Perhaps the attractive features are the fact that it is simple and intuitive, and quickly leads to a solution despite the absence of convergence. However, it is an empirical method and may require working with different parameter sets to actually find a solution. Still, it can be turned into a black-box solution by automatically testing different parameter configurations. In that respect, I compare it to the empirical **elbow rule** to detect the number of clusters in unsupervised clustering problems. I discuss the elbow rule and its automation in Section [18.6](#Chp018_361-386_B9780443218576000229.xhtml). Another fixed-point algorithm leading to explainable AI in the context of linear regression is discussed in Section [7.1](#Chp007_113-129_B9780443218576000114.xhtml).

### 13.1.1 The problem, with illustration

The method can solve two types of problems: finding the zeros of a function, or its optima (maxima or minima). Optima correspond to a zero of the derivative, so finding them is a root-finding problem. In my example, the functions typically have multiple global minima that we want to detect. The initial problem is to find a factor *b* of a large integer number *a*. Here *a* is fixed, and the function is denoted as *f*(*b*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si1.png) with *f*(*b*) = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si2.png) if and only if *b* is such a factor (integer number) different from 1 and *a*. If *b* is not a factor, then *f*(*b*) > 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si3.png). Initially, the interest was to factor a number that is a product of two large primes, as this has implications in cryptography. However, the technique led to a much larger class of applications where it has much more value than for factoring integers.

The first step was to change the problem setting: extending the function *f*(*b*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si1.png) which accepts an integer argument *b*, into a continuous function where *b* is a real number. Here *f*(*b*) = *a* *m**o**d* *b*![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si4.png). So to get a continuous extension, one has to define the modulo operator for arguments *b* that are not integer numbers. Finally, it led to

$f(b) = a - \\lfloor b + \\epsilon\\rfloor\\left\\lfloor \\epsilon + \\frac{a}{\\lfloor b + \\epsilon\\rfloor} \\right\\rfloor,\\quad b > 0.$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si5.png)(13.1) 

The brackets represent the integer part function, and *ϵ* = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si6.png). However, in the code, *ϵ* = 10^( − 8)![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si7.png) to avoid problems caused by numerical precision. Formula [(13.1)](#Chp013_243-258_B9780443218576000175.xhtml#deq1) defines the base function, denoted as fmod in the Python code. It is a piecewise constant function, pictured in [Fig. 13.1](#Chp013_243-258_B9780443218576000175.xhtml#f0010) between *b* = 2900![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si8.png) and *b* = 3200![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si9.png), using *a* = 3083 × 7919![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si10.png). Thus the interval \[2900, 3200\]![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si11.png) contains the root *b* = 3083![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si12.png). There are no other roots besides 3083 and 7919 since these two integers are prime numbers. Also note that 0 ≤ *f*(*b*) < *b*![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si13.png). Optimization methods based on the gradient are guaranteed not to work here.

![Figure 13.1 Function f(b) as a better alternative to g(b) in Fig. 13.2. Root at b = 3083.](images/B9780443218576000175/gr001.jpg)

Figure 13.1 Function *f*(*b*) as a better alternative to *g*(*b*) in [Fig. 13.2](#Chp013_243-258_B9780443218576000175.xhtml#f0015). Root at *b* = 3083.

Note that instead of *f*(*b*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si1.png), I could have used *g*(*b*) = 2 − cos (2*π**b*) − cos (2*π**a*/*b*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si14.png). This function is also positive and equal to zero only if *b* is an integer number that divides the integer *a*. In addition, *g* is bounded with 0 ≤ *g*(*b*) ≤ 4![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si15.png), and infinitely differentiable. Yet it has a very large number of local minima and maxima: the frequency of oscillations is insanely high. For all purposes, *g* is just as chaotic of *f*, indeed worse than *f*, and no standard optimization algorithm could handle it. The function *g* is pictured in [Fig. 13.2](#Chp013_243-258_B9780443218576000175.xhtml#f0015).

![Figure 13.2 Function g(b) = 2 - \\cos(2\\pi b) - \\cos(2\\pi a/b)Image, with a = 3083 × 7919.](images/B9780443218576000175/gr002.jpg)

Figure 13.2 Function *g*(*b*) = 2 − cos (2*π**b*) − cos (2*π**a*/*b*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si14.png), with *a* = 3083 × 7919.

## 13.2 Nonconverging fixed-point algorithm

In this section, I start with the function *f*(*b*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si1.png) defined by formula [(13.1)](#Chp013_243-258_B9780443218576000175.xhtml#deq1). I investigate a larger class of functions in Section [13.3](#Chp013_243-258_B9780443218576000175.xhtml#s0040). The trick is to massively amplify the zero, creating ripple effects that the fixed point iteration can leverage to narrow down on the solution. In the end, instead of looking at convergence (absent here), you look at the strength of a signal *ρ*[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si16.png) at iterations *n* = 1, 2![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si17.png), and so on. The value of *ρ*[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si16.png) is typically close to 1, but high values (above 2) indicate that something unusual is happening. Typically, such high values are created when stepping over a root.

### 13.2.1 Trick leading to intuitive solution

Let us assume that *f* is positive and that its minimum value is zero. If *f* takes on negative values, replace *f*(*b*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si1.png) by the absolute value |*f*(*b*)|![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si18.png) or by the square *f*²(*b*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si19.png). This works both in root-finding and optimization problems. In optimization, *f* is the derivative of the target function. The base function *f* (or its absolute value or square) is denoted as *f*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si20.png).

The goal is to apply successive transformations to make the function *f*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si20.png) more amenable to root detection. The first transformation consists of taking the logarithm, thus creating a vertical bottomless abyss in the graph of the function, around any root. In practice, it is implemented as follows: the new function is simply

*f*[1](*b*) = max \[log(*f*[0](*b*)),*δ*\],

![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si21.png)

where *δ* is a negative number, large enough in absolute value. In the Python code, *δ* is represented by logeps, and set to −10. This parameter controls the depth of the abyss, that now has a bottom. It helps discriminate between a value very close to zero, and a value exactly equal to zero. For instance, if *f*[0](*b*) = 0.01![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si22.png), then *f*[1](*b*) =  − 4.61![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si23.png), while if *f*[0](*b*) = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si24.png), then *f*[1](*b*) =  − 10![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si25.png).

The second step consists in enlarging the abyss. Its walls will change from vertical to inclined. The width of the abyss, and the slope of its walls, is controlled by the parameter window in the Python code, and referred to here as *w*. In a nutshell, this transformation is a **moving average** applied to *f*[1]![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si26.png). The resulting function is

$f\_{2}(b) = \\frac{1}{2w + 1}\\sum\\limits\_{k = - w}^{w}f\_{1}(b + kh).$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si27.png)

The increment *h* is set to 1 as it makes sense in my particular problem. I did not test other values.

The third step is a linear transformation, turning *f*[2]![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si28.png) into *f*[3]![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si29.png), with *f*[3](*b*) = *p* + *q**f*[2](*b*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si30.png). The parameters *p* and *q* are respectively denoted as offset and slope in the Python code. The functions *f*[0], *f*[1]![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si31.png), and *f*[3]![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si29.png) are respectively denoted as fmod, fmod2, and fresidue in the Python code. The blue curve (dark gray in print version) in [Fig. 13.3](#Chp013_243-258_B9780443218576000175.xhtml#f0020) is the *f*[3]![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si29.png) transform associated to the *f*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si20.png) function pictured in [Fig. 13.1](#Chp013_243-258_B9780443218576000175.xhtml#f0010), with *p* =  − 100![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si32.png) and *q* = 20![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si33.png). Subsequent transformations discussed in Section [13.4](#Chp013_243-258_B9780443218576000175.xhtml#s0070) are done only for embellishment, and are irrelevant to the fixed point algorithm.

![Figure 13.3 Transformed function f3, amplifying the root at b = 3083.](images/B9780443218576000175/gr003.jpg)

Figure 13.3 Transformed function *f*[3], amplifying the root at *b* = 3083.

### 13.2.2 Root detection: method and parameters

The fixed-point algorithm starts with an initial value *b*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si34.png), and then proceeds iteratively as follows:

*b*[*n* + 1] = *b*[*n*] + *μ**f*(*b*[*n*]).

![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si35.png)(13.2) 

If the sequence (*b*[*n*])![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si36.png) converges, the function *f* is continuous and *μ* ≠ 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si37.png), then *b*[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si38.png) must converge to some *b*^(\*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si39.png) such that *f*(*b*^(\*)) = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si40.png), thus *b*[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si38.png) converges to a root of *f*. You can allow *μ* to depend on *n*, and in one example I successfully used $\\mu = 1/\\sqrt{b\_{n}}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si41.png). The function *f* used here is actually the function *f*[3]![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si29.png) defined in Section [13.2.1](#Chp013_243-258_B9780443218576000175.xhtml#s0025) and pictured in blue (dark gray in print version) in [Fig. 13.3](#Chp013_243-258_B9780443218576000175.xhtml#f0020). This function is not even continuous, and the fixed point iteration does not converge. Other functions are investigated in Section [13.3](#Chp013_243-258_B9780443218576000175.xhtml#s0040). Here, the purpose is to explain how the fixed point iteration can help find a root despite the lack of convergence.

Many of the parameters in the Python code are described in Section [13.2.1](#Chp013_243-258_B9780443218576000175.xhtml#s0025), including offset, slope, and logeps. The parameter eps corresponds to *ϵ* in Section [13.1.1](#Chp013_243-258_B9780443218576000175.xhtml#s0015). The main parameters driving the fixed-point iteration are:

*   •  mu, corresponding to *μ* in formula [(13.2)](#Chp013_243-258_B9780443218576000175.xhtml#deq4). A large value results in bigger jumps in the fixed point iteration, allowing you to find a root faster, but with an increased risk of missing all roots when *μ* becomes too large.
*   •  window, corresponding to *w* in Section [13.2.1](#Chp013_243-258_B9780443218576000175.xhtml#s0025). A large *w* increases your chances of finding a root. The price to pay is reduced precision. If *b*^(\*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si39.png) is a root and the fixed point iteration succeeds in locating it, it will not find *b*^(\*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si39.png), but instead, it will tell you that there might be a root in the interval \[*b*^(\*) − *w*, *b*^(\*) + *w*\]![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si42.png), without knowing what the actual *b*^(\*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si39.png) is. Thus a large *w* is useful to get a rough approximation of where a root is located.

I illustrate these features, as well as how fast this algorithm is compared to brute force, on a real example in Section [13.2.3](#Chp013_243-258_B9780443218576000175.xhtml#s0035). The algorithm does not converge with the type of functions discussed here: the successive iterates *b*[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si38.png) become larger and larger as *n* increases, or they may oscillate without ever converging. Of course, if the function is smooth enough and with the right parameters, it will converge. But we are not interested in that case.

Since there is no convergence in my examples, how can the algorithm detect a root? Now I explain how it works. First, define *Δ*[*n*] = *b*[*n*] − *b*[*n* − 1]![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si43.png). Then let *ρ*[*n*] = *Δ*[*n*]/*Δ*[*n* − 1]![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si44.png). The number *ρ*[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si16.png) is called the **signal** at iteration *n*. Usually, *ρ*[*n*] ≈ 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si45.png). If *ρ*[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si16.png) is unusually low or high, we say that the signal is strong. In my examples, a value *ρ*[*n*] > 2![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si46.png) usually means that there is a root close to *b*[*n* − 1]![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si47.png). Details are discussed in Section [13.2.3](#Chp013_243-258_B9780443218576000175.xhtml#s0035).

Finally, the functions investigated here have many values close to zero. The brute force method consisting of testing a very large number of values may not even work. In most cases, finding *b* such that *f*[0](*b*) = 0.001![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si48.png) does not mean that there is a *b*^(\*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si39.png) close to *b* such that *f*[0](*b*^(\*)) = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si49.png). For the same reason, the efficient but naive **bisection method** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bisection_method)\] will also fail. Note that my method is empirical: a strong signal does not always correspond to a root, and the absence of strong signal does not mean that there is no root. Testing with different parameter sets helps.

### 13.2.3 Case study: factoring a product of two large primes

The goal here is to find at least one of the two roots of the function *f*[0](*b*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si50.png) pictured in [Fig. 13.1](#Chp013_243-258_B9780443218576000175.xhtml#f0010), and defined by [(13.1)](#Chp013_243-258_B9780443218576000175.xhtml#deq1). Using the transformations described in Section [13.2.1](#Chp013_243-258_B9780443218576000175.xhtml#s0025), I will actually work with the third transform *f*[3](*b*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si51.png) in the fixed point iteration (formula [(13.2)](#Chp013_243-258_B9780443218576000175.xhtml#deq4)), starting with *b*[0] = 2000![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si52.png). The two roots are the two prime factors of *a* = 7919 × 3083![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si53.png), that is, *b*^(\*) = 3083![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si54.png) and *b*^(\*) = 7919![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si55.png). So finding one root makes it straightforward to find the other.

Finding the roots of *f*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si20.png) is the same as finding the roots of *g*(*b*) = 2 − cos (2*π**b*) − cos (2*π**a*/*b*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si14.png) pictured in [Fig. 13.2](#Chp013_243-258_B9780443218576000175.xhtml#f0015). The parameters values are those in the Python code in Section [13.3.3](#Chp013_243-258_B9780443218576000175.xhtml#s0065). The results are displayed in [Table 13.1](#Chp013_243-258_B9780443218576000175.xhtml#t0010), Fig. [13.4](#Chp013_243-258_B9780443218576000175.xhtml#f0025) and [13.5](#Chp013_243-258_B9780443218576000175.xhtml#f0030). The root *b*^(\*) = 3083![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si54.png) is detected at iteration *n* = 31![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si56.png). Since *ρ*[31] = 4.72![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si57.png) is exceptionally high, there is a strong possibility that the algorithm stepped over a root in the previous iteration (*n* = 30![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si58.png)). Indeed, *b*[30] = 3086.18![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si59.png) is close to the root *b*^(\*) = 3083![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si54.png). What the algorithm tells is that there is probably a root in the interval \[*b*[30] − *w*, *b*[30] + *w*\]![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si60.png) where *w* is the size of the window (the parameter window in the Python code) set to 5 here.

At this point, after testing *b* = 3081, 3082![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si61.png), and 3083 to find the root, one can stop the algorithm. It does not converge anyway: *b*[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si38.png) is getting bigger and bigger, faster and faster, as shown in [Table 13.1](#Chp013_243-258_B9780443218576000175.xhtml#t0010). The second root is simply *b*^(\*) = 7919 = *a*/3083![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si62.png). Surprisingly though, at iteration *n* = 127![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si63.png), there is another spike, namely *ρ*[127] = 2.00![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si64.png). Again, *b*[126] = 7915.67![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si65.png) is close to the second root *b*^(\*) = 7919![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si55.png). There is another, weaker spike at *n* = 71![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si66.png), with *ρ*[71] = 1.88![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si67.png). This one is a false positive.

## 13.3 Generalization with synthetic random functions

Perhaps the synthetic example most closely resembling *f*[0](*b*) = *a* *m**o**d* *b*![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si68.png) discussed in Section [13.2.2](#Chp013_243-258_B9780443218576000175.xhtml#s0030) is *f*[0](*b*) = ⌊*b**U*[*b*]⌋![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si69.png) where the *U*[*b*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si70.png)'s are independent random deviates on \[0, 1\]![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si71.png). The major difference is the independence assumption. For *a* *m**o**d* *b*![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si72.png), the residues somewhat behave as if they were independent (assuming the *b*'s are integers and *a* is fixed), but they are not really independent. To use *f*[0](*b*) = ⌊*b**U*[*b*]⌋![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si69.png), set mode='Random' in the Python code.

### 13.3.1 Example

Unlike in the example based on a product of two primes, now the **random function** *f*[0](*b*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si50.png) has infinitely many roots. They are more and more spaced out as *b* increases. In this example, with the seed of the random generator set to seed=105, the first few roots are

5646, 15156, 59004, 122345, 689987, 1021037, 1186047, 2829138.

![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si73.png)

The statistical distribution of the roots and the number of expected roots in any given interval is studied in Section [13.3.2](#Chp013_243-258_B9780443218576000175.xhtml#s0050). I used the same Python code with same parameters as in Section [13.2.3](#Chp013_243-258_B9780443218576000175.xhtml#s0035), also starting with *b*[0] = 2000![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si52.png). This time, at iteration *n* = 87![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si74.png), we have *ρ*[*n*] = 2.52![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si75.png) which is extremely high. Again, this points to a root at iteration *n* − 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si76.png), with *b*[86] = 5650.48![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si77.png). The actual root is *b*^(\*) = 5646![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si78.png). It could be anywhere between *b*[86] − *w*![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si79.png) and *b*[86] + *w*![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si80.png), with *w* set to 5 in this case, via window=5. So it suffices to test *b* = 5645![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si81.png) and *b* = 5646![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si82.png) to find the root. The values of *ρ*[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si16.png) for successive iterations of the fixed point algorithm, between *n* = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si83.png) and *n* = 130![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si84.png), are displayed in [Fig. 13.6](#Chp013_243-258_B9780443218576000175.xhtml#f0035).

![Figure 13.6 Signal strength ρn, first 130 fixed-point iterations; n = 87 leads to a root.](images/B9780443218576000175/gr006.jpg)

[Figure 13.6](#Chp013_243-258_B9780443218576000175.xhtml#cf0160) Signal strength *ρ*[*n*], first 130 fixed-point iterations; *n* = 87 leads to a root.

With the current parameters, the algorithm misses the next root *b*^(\*) = 15156![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si85.png). Decreasing *μ* or increasing *w* (or a combination of both that minimizes the number of required iterations) may lead to that root, most likely in more than 100 iterations. Note that high values of *ρ*[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si16.png) are also found at *n* = 11![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si86.png) and *n* = 14![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si87.png), respectively *ρ*[11] = 2.28![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si88.png) and *ρ*[14] = 1.90![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si89.png). These are false positives and can easily be ruled out. It is unusual to reach a root in as few as 20 iterations for this kind of problem, especially when starting far away from the root.

[Fig. 13.7](#Chp013_243-258_B9780443218576000175.xhtml#f0045) features the random function discussed in this section, with a visible absolute minimum around *b* = 5646![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si82.png) both for the blue (dark gray in print version) and orange (mid gray in print version) curves, but invisible (although present) for the initial function *f*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si20.png) in red (light gray in print version). Here *b* ∈ \[5500, 5800\]![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si90.png). The blue (dark gray in print version) curve is the transformed version of *f*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si20.png), referred to as *f*[3]![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si29.png), while the orange (mid gray in print version) curve is the result after additional smoothing discussed in Section [13.4](#Chp013_243-258_B9780443218576000175.xhtml#s0070). The vertical axis for the blue (dark gray in print version) and orange (mid gray in print version) curves is on the left. For the red (light gray in print version) curve, it is on the right.

![Figure 13.7 Random function from Section 13.3.1, with root at b = 5646.](images/B9780443218576000175/gr009.jpg)

Figure 13.7 Random function from Section [13.3.1](#Chp013_243-258_B9780443218576000175.xhtml#s0045), with root at *b* = 5646.

### 13.3.2 Connection to the Poisson–binomial distribution

Depending on the sequence of random deviates (*U*[*b*])![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si91.png), the new function *f*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si20.png) may have zero, one, or more than one integer root in any specific interval \[*s*, *t*\]![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si92.png). The expected number of integer roots is a random variable *N*(*s*, *t*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si93.png) with a **Poisson–binomial distribution** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poisson_binomial_distribution)\]. Assuming *s* and *t* are integers, the expectation, variance, and probability of no root are respectively

$E\\lbrack N(s,t)\\rbrack = \\sum\\limits\_{k = s}^{t}\\frac{1}{k},\\quad{Var}\\lbrack N(s,t)\\rbrack = \\sum\\limits\_{k = s}^{t}\\frac{1}{k}\\left( 1 - \\frac{1}{k} \\right),\\quad P\\lbrack N(s,t) = 0\\rbrack = \\prod\\limits\_{k = s}^{t}\\left( 1 - \\frac{1}{k} \\right).$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si94.png)

When *s*, *t*![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si95.png) are very large and *t*/*s* → *λ*![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si96.png), the Poisson–binomial distribution is well approximated by a Poisson distribution of expectation log *λ*![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si97.png). A proof of this advanced result (not even taught in graduate classes) can be found in my book on stochastic processes [\[1\]](#Chp013_243-258_B9780443218576000175.xhtml#br0005), in Section 2.3.1. This result generalizes the well-known convergence of Binomial to Poisson distribution under some assumptions. It is a particular case of **Le Cam's inequality** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le_Cam's_theorem)\]; see also [\[2\]](#Chp013_243-258_B9780443218576000175.xhtml#br0010).

Applied to the problem in Section [13.2.2](#Chp013_243-258_B9780443218576000175.xhtml#s0030) with *f*[0](*b*) = *a* *m**o**d* *b*![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si68.png), with *b* ∈ \[2900, 3200\]![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si98.png), the chance to find at least one root in that interval is approximately 1 − exp ( − log *λ*) = 1 − 1/*λ*![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si99.png). Since *λ* = *t*/*s*![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si100.png) with *s* = 2900![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si101.png), *t* = 3200![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si102.png), the chance in question is about 9.4%. Note that $t < \\sqrt{a}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si103.png). In general, this condition is required for the result to be valid. The absence of root in the interval $\\lbrack 2,\\sqrt{a}\\rbrack$![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si104.png) would mean that *a* is a prime number.

#### 13.3.2.1 Location of the next root: guesstimate

Let *T*[*s*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si105.png) be the location of the first root larger than *s*. I am interested in the ratio *R*[*s*] = *T*[*s*]/*s* > 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si106.png). From the previous discussion, the distribution of successive roots approximately follows a **nonhomogeneous Poisson process** when *s* is large. It is easy to prove that *R*[*s*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si107.png) has an infinite expectation. However, log *R*[*s*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si108.png) has a finite expectation. Let us compute it, using the Poisson approximation. We have

*P*(log *R*[*s*] > *τ*) = *P*\[*T*[*s*] > *s*exp (*τ*)\] = exp ( − *τ*).

![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si109.png)

Thus,

*E*\[log *R*[*s*]\] = ∫[0]^∞exp ( − *τ*)*d**τ* = 1.

![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si110.png)

So, given a root *b*^(\*) > 2000![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si111.png), one would expect the next one to be of the order *e* ⋅ *b*^(\*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si112.png), with *e* = 2.718…![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si113.png) This is consistent with the successive roots displayed at the beginning in Section [13.3.1](#Chp013_243-258_B9780443218576000175.xhtml#s0045).

#### 13.3.2.2 Integer sequences with high density of primes

The Poisson–binomial distribution, including its Poisson approximation, can also be used in this context. The purpose is to find fast-growing integer sequences with a very high density of primes, see [here](https://mathoverflow.net/questions/374305/sequences-with-high-densities-of-primes-how-to-boost-them-to-get-even-more-and).

The probability for a large integer *a* to be prime is about 1/log *a*![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si114.png), a consequence of the prime number theorem \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_number_theorem)\]. Let *a*[1], *a*[2], …![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si115.png) be a strictly increasing sequence of positive integers, and *N* denote the number of primes among *a*[*n*], *a*[*n* + 1], …, *a*[*n* + *m*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si116.png) for some large *n*. Assuming the sequence is independently and congruentially equidistributed, then *N* has a Poisson–binomial distribution of parameters *p*[*n*], …, *p*[*n* + *m*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si117.png), with *p*[*k*] = 1/log *a*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si118.png). It is unimportant to know the exact definition of congruential equidistribution. Roughly speaking, it means that the joint empirical distribution of residues across the *a*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si119.png)'s, is asymptotically indistinguishable from that of a sequence of random integers. Thus a sequence where 60% of the terms are odd integers does not qualify (that proportion should be 50%).

This result is used to assess whether a given sequence of integers is unusually rich, or poor, in primes. If it contains far more large primes than the expected value *p*[*n*] + … + *p*[*n* + *m*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si120.png), then we are dealing with a very interesting, hard-to-find sequence, useful both in cryptographic applications and for its own sake. One can build confidence intervals for the number of such primes, based on the Poisson–binomial distribution under the assumption of independence and congruential equidistribution. A famous example of such a sequence (rich in prime numbers) is *a*[*k*] = *k*² − *k* + 41![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si121.png) \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulam_spiral)\]. If *n*, *m* → ∞![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si122.png) and *p*[*n*]² + … + *p*[*n* + *m*]² → 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si123.png), then the distribution of *N* is well approximated by a Poisson distribution, thanks to Le Cam's theorem.

### 13.3.3 Python code: finding the optimum

This Python code performs the transformations from *f*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si20.png) to *f*[3]![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si29.png) as described in Section [13.2.1](#Chp013_243-258_B9780443218576000175.xhtml#s0025) and run the fixed point algorithm on *f*[3]![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si29.png) to find a minimum of *f*[3]![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si29.png), and thus a root of *f*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si20.png). The parameters are described in Section [13.2.2](#Chp013_243-258_B9780443218576000175.xhtml#s0030). The case mode='Prime' corresponds to the example discussed in Section [13.2.3](#Chp013_243-258_B9780443218576000175.xhtml#s0035), while the case mode='Random' corresponds to the random function studied in Section [13.3.1](#Chp013_243-258_B9780443218576000175.xhtml#s0045). The results are saved in a tab-separated text file rmodb.txt. The full version with curve smoothing, tabulation, and saving the values of the various transforms is in Section [13.4](#Chp013_243-258_B9780443218576000175.xhtml#s0070).

A potential improvement is to handle the situation when *b*[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si38.png) decreases to the point of becoming negative. Also, the values of *f*[0](*b*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si50.png) and *f*[3](*b*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si51.png) are not stored in some array or hash table, but instead computed on the fly. Some may be computed multiple times, and the code is not efficient in that regard. This is particularly true if the parameter window is large.

![](images/B9780443218576000175/gr007.jpg)

## 13.4 Smoothing highly chaotic curves

All the functions discussed so far are piecewise constant. The purpose here is to beautify these functions to make them look smooth and continuous, while preserving the key feature: the roots, corresponding to massive dips in the graph of these functions. This is best illustrated in [Fig. 13.7](#Chp013_243-258_B9780443218576000175.xhtml#f0045), where the original function *f*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si20.png) in red is impossible to interpret, while the blue (dark gray in print version) curve *f*[3]![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si29.png) clearly features the minimum. The orange (mid gray in print version) curve is the final result obtained after smoothing the blue (dark gray in print version) curve, using the three transformations fresidue2, fresidue3 and fresidue4 in the Python code in Section [13.4.1](#Chp013_243-258_B9780443218576000175.xhtml#s0075), in that order.

### 13.4.1 Python code: smoothing

The code is also available on my GitHub repository, [here](https://github.com/VincentGranville/Main/blob/main/realmod_full.py). In addition to smoothing, it also produces a tab-separated text file rmod.txt. This files contains the tabulated values of the function *f*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si20.png) and its successive transforms, for *b* in a range specified by the user.

![](images/B9780443218576000175/gr010.jpg)

## 13.5 Connection to synthetic data: random functions

First, there is a strong similarity between the various transforms used to magnify the roots and beautify the curves, and the concept of **transformers** in **Seq2seq neural networks** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seq2seq)\]. But the true connection to synthetic data is about how the simulations can be used to generate random functions mimicking the deterministic ones that we deal with in real life. This also applies to the random Rademacher functions discussed in Section [17.3.5](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml), mimicking deterministic multiplicative functions, also related to prime numbers as in this section.

The functions discussed here have a variable number of roots, a certain behavior (piecewise constant, roots are spaced out) and a certain potential range of values depending on the argument. These values, for a specific argument, are typically equally likely to show up. There is also some relative independence between (say) *f*(*b*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si1.png) and *f*(*b* + 1)![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si124.png). These are the parameters of the real-life functions *f*(*b*) = *a* *m**o**d* *b*![Image](images/B9780443218576000175/si4.png) where *a* is a large fixed integer number with few divisors. Remember that the initial goal was to factor a product a two very large primes – a very hard problem of considerable interest in cryptography. Here the product in question is the number *a*.

To study the divergent fixed-point algorithm, and to benchmark and improve it in this context, I used synthetic random functions that mimic the properties of the original functions. Each random function is uniquely determined by the seed parameter. Thus, we have access to an infinite collection of functions, both for the real (determined by *a*) and the random ones. Assessing whether the synthetic functions are a good fit or not, as a proxy to represent the real-life functions, is the central “synthetic data” problem. The functions can be categorized in different types, depending on the number of roots and other parameter values. The problem is to simulate functions that can be used as substitutes, in each category.

To achieve this goal, some random functions must be ruled out from some categories, as being too different from the target functions that they try to emulate. Comparing two functions (a random one with a set of real-life functions within a specific category) is done by comparing their core parameters (number of roots and so on). In particular, random functions with no root below some threshold, are rejected. The mechanism that produces the suitable random functions is called a generative model. It is discussed in its most general form in Section [1.4](#Chp001_1-34_B9780443218576000059.xhtml).

## References

*   [\[1\]](#Chp013_243-258_B9780443218576000175.xhtml#cf0175) V. Granville, *Stochastic Processes and Simulations: A Machine Learning Perspective*. MLTechniques.com; 2022. [\[Link\]](https://mltechniques.com/product/album/).

# Chapter 14: Synthetic terrain generation and AI-generated art

## Abstract

This chapter provides an introduction to **agent-based modeling** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agent-based_model)\] and computer vision techniques in Python, diving into the technical details of a specific class of problems. I show how to use generative models based on synthetic data, to simulate terrain evolution or other natural phenomena such as cloud formation or climate change. The material is accessible and targeted to software engineers interested in understanding and applying the machine learning and probabilistic background behind the scene, as well as to machine learning professionals interested in the programming aspects and scientific computing. The end-goal is to help the reader design and implement his own models and generate his own data sets, by showcasing an interesting application with all the details. My Python code can also be used as an end in itself. This type of application is referred to as **generative AI**.

From a machine learning perspective, the stochastic processes involved can be compared to spatial time series or time-continuous **chaotic dynamical systems**. There is a similarity with **constrained Brownian motions**, where at each time, rather than observing a typical observation (say a vector of stock prices), the observation consists of a particular configuration of the entire space (for instance, a moving storm system at a given time). In this chapter, the focus is on stationary-like processes. I briefly discuss the probabilistic models behind my algorithms, to explain when they work, and when they do not. However, I limit theoretical discussions to the essential, so that software engineers and other professionals lacking a strong mathematical background, can easily read and benefit from my presentation.

A possible use of my methodology is to automatically generate and label a large number of different landscapes (mountains, sea, land, combinations, and so on) to create a large training set. The training set can be used as **augmented data** for landscape classification, or to generate more landscape within a specific category to further enrich the classifier. The methodology can also be used to simulate transitions and reconstruct the hidden statistical behavior over short periods of time, when granular observations are not available. Finally, in addition to modeling and simulating uncontrolled evolutionary processes, the animated data visualizations also feature image morphing, both in the state space (coalescing physical shapes) and the spectral space (palette and color morphing).
