The data, computations and results are in the spreadsheet [PB\_independence.xlsx](https://github.com/VincentGranville/Point-Processes/tree/main/Spreadsheets), described later in this section.

The point counts attached to a realization *ω* of the point process, is denoted as *N*[*ω*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si55.png). The aggregated point count over the *m* realizations is denoted as *N*, and the set of *m* realizations is denoted as Ω. Now, for *i* = 1, 2, 3![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si56.png) and *j*[1], *j*[2], *j*[3] ∈ ℕ![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si57.png), I can define the following quantities:

$p\_{i}(j) = \\frac{1}{m}\\sum\\limits\_{\\omega \\in \\Omega}\\chi\\lbrack N\_{\\omega}(B\_{i}) = j\\rbrack,p(j\_{1},j\_{2},j\_{3}) = \\frac{1}{m}\\sum\\limits\_{\\omega \\in \\Omega}\\text{~~}\\prod\\limits\_{i = 1}^{3}\\chi\\lbrack N\_{\\omega}(B\_{i}) = j\_{i}\\rbrack,$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si58.png)(16.7) 

$p^{\\prime}(j\_{1},j\_{2},j\_{3}) = \\frac{1}{m^{3}}\\prod\\limits\_{i = 1}^{3}\\text{~~}\\sum\\limits\_{\\omega \\in \\Omega}\\chi\\lbrack N\_{\\omega}(B\_{i}) = j\_{i}\\rbrack,$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si59.png)(16.8) 

where *χ* is the indicator function \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indicator_function)\]. For instance, *p*[1](3) = 0.043![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si60.png) means that in 43 realizations out of ![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/fx001.jpg), the domain *B*[1]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si61.png) contained exactly 3 points. Also, *p*^′(*j*[1], *j*[2], *j*[3]) = *p*[1](*j*[1])*p*[2](*j*[2])*p*[3](*j*[3])![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si62.png). The three point counts *N*(*B*[1])![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si63.png), *N*(*B*[2])![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si64.png), *N*(*B*[3])![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si65.png) are independently distributed if and only if formulas [(16.7)](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#deq9) and [(16.8)](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#deq10) represent the same quantity when *m* = ∞![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si66.png). In other words, the three point counts are independently distributed if *p* → *p*^′![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si67.png) pointwise \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pointwise_convergence)\], as *m* → ∞![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si68.png).

To avoid future confusion, *p* and *p*^′![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si69.png) are denoted as *p*[*A*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si70.png) and *p*[*A*]^′![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si71.png) to emphasize the fact that they are attached to the process *M*[*A*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si48.png). To test for independence, I simulated *m* realizations of a sister point process *M*[*B*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si72.png): one with the same marginal distributions for the three point counts, using the estimates *p*[*i*](*j*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si73.png) obtained from *M*[*A*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si48.png), but this time with guaranteed independence of the point counts, by design. Likewise, I define the functions *p*[*B*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si74.png) and *p*[*B*]^′![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si75.png). Let *ρ*[*A*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si76.png) be the correlation between *p*[*A*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si70.png) and *p*[*A*]^′![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si71.png), computed across all triplets satisfying

min {*p*[*A*](*j*[1], *j*[2], *j*[3]), *p*[*A*]^′(*j*[1], *j*[2], *j*[3])} > *ϵ*.

![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si77.png)

I chose *ϵ* = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si78.png). In my example, there were fewer than 7 × 7 × 7 = 343![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si79.png) such triplets. Finally, the statistic of the test is *ρ*[*A*]²![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si80.png).

#### 16.1.3.1 Results and interpretation

In the spreadsheet [PB\_independence.xlsx](https://github.com/VincentGranville/Point-Processes/tree/main/Spreadsheets), the tab Dataset\_A corresponds to *M*[*A*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si48.png), and Dataset\_B corresponds to *M*[*B*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si72.png). The same computations are done in tab Dataset\_C for another point process *M*[*C*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si81.png), identical to *M*[*A*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si48.png) except that this time *s* = 4![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si82.png). With such a “large” *s*, *M*[*C*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si81.png) is not that different from a stationary Poisson point process: in particular, the point counts are almost independent (no statistical test could detect that they are not, unless using extremely large samples).

The main findings are displayed in [Fig. 16.2](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#f0015). Blue represents the *M*[*A*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si48.png) process, gray represents *M*[*B*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si72.png), and red represents *M*[*C*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si81.png). Each blue dot corresponds to a vector (*p*[*A*], *p*[*A*]^′)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si83.png) attached to a particular (*j*[1], *j*[2], *j*[3])![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si84.png). In case of perfect independence, all the dots should be on the main diagonal. Blue dots are two far away from the main diagonal, and thus the point counts in *M*[*A*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si48.png) are not independent. To the contrary, *M*[*B*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si72.png) (supposed to exhibit independence by construction) and *M*[*C*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si81.png) (known from theory to exhibit near-independence) are close enough to each other and to the main diagonal. If you repeat the experiment with *M*[*B*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si72.png) a hundred times, you will get a hundred gray regression lines, generating a confidence curve for the test. Note that the *R*²![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si85.png) displayed for the three regression lines in [Fig. 16.2](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#f0015), are identical to *ρ*[*A*]²![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si80.png), *ρ*[*B*]²![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si86.png), *ρ*[*C*]²![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si87.png), confirming the somewhat poor performance of *M*[*A*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si48.png). The slope of the regression line is also an indicator of lack of independence, if it is not close enough to one. Again, *M*[*B*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si72.png) is the loser here, when measured against the slope. The intercept of the regression line (when different enough from zero) further confirms this.

![Figure 16.2 A new test of independence (R-squared version).](images/B9780443218576000205/gr002.jpg)

Figure 16.2 A new test of independence (R-squared version).

A version of this test, available in the spreadsheet, relies on the Kolmogorov–Smirnov statistics instead of the R-squared. It works with aggregated rather than raw frequencies. In short, you replace the empirical probabilities *p*[*A*], *p*[*A*]^′![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si88.png) (the frequencies) by empirical aggregated probabilities *P*[*A*], *P*[*A*]^′![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si89.png), that is, the empirical distributions. The statistic of the test is the uniform norm \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uniform_norm)\] *δ*[*A*] = ||*P*[*A*] − *P*[*A*]^′||[∞]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si90.png). It leads to the same conclusion. Since the argument of the functions *p*[*A*], *p*[*A*]^′![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si88.png) are the triplets (*j*[1], *j*[2], *j*[3])![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si84.png) and are unordered, there are many different ways to build the empirical distribution. However, the differences among these constructions are minuscule. See also the section “Interactions in Point Pattern Analysis” in [\[22\]](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#br0110).

#### 16.1.3.2 About the spreadsheet

The interactive spreadsheet is on my GitHub repository; see [PB\_independence.xlsx](https://github.com/VincentGranville/Point-Processes/tree/main/Spreadsheets). The Summary tab controls the parameters *s*, *λ*, and the upper/lower bounds of the intervals *B*[1], *B*[2], *B*[3]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si91.png). It also contains the results: the R-squared's *ρ*[*A*]², *ρ*[*B*]², *ρ*[*C*]²![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si92.png) respectively in cells B11, C11, D11, and the Kolmogorov–Smirnov statistics *δ*[*A*], *δ*[*B*], *δ*[*C*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si93.png) respectively in cells B12, C12, D12. Columns J, K, L represent the triplets (*j*[1], *j*[2], *j*[3])![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si84.png), also available in concatenated format in column I. For the *M*[*A*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si48.png) process, the empirical probabilities *p*[*A*], *p*[*A*]^′![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si88.png) are in columns Q, R, and the empirical distributions *P*[*A*], *P*[*A*]^′![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si89.png) are in columns S, T. For *M*[*B*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si72.png) and *M*[*C*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si81.png), the corresponding values are in columns Z to AD and AI to AM, respectively.

In the Dataset\_A and Dataset\_C tabs, each row (except the first one) represents a realization of the underlying point process, respectively *M*[*A*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si48.png) and *M*[*C*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si81.png). The 41 points of each realization are in columns F to AT. The first row (same columns) stores the indices of the points in question. I used the logistic distribution for *F*.

The Dataset\_B tab corresponds to *M*[*B*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si72.png). It is organized differently. The actual points of each realization are not computed as they are not needed this time. Thus they are not in the spreadsheet. Instead, point counts summarizing each “unobserved” realization are in columns I, J, K, corresponding respectively to *B*[1], *B*[2], *B*[3]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si91.png). Columns Q and R, representing the values of *p*[*B*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si74.png) and *p*[*B*]^′![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si75.png) (with the argument in column F), are derived from these counts. Remember that *M*[*B*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si72.png) was designed so that (1) *p*[*B*]^′ = *p*[*A*]^′![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si94.png) and (2) the point counts *N*(*B*[1]), *N*(*B*[2]), *N*(*B*[3])![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si95.png) are independent.

## 16.2 Cluster processes and nearest neighbor graphs

Poisson–binomial processes and compound systems derived from these processes are used to model cluster structures. Here, I discuss radial **cluster processes** associated to perturbed lattices, and potential applications. The examples are produced as follows. First, I generate a 2D realization of a Poisson–binomial process, called the parent process. Then around each point (*X*[*h*], *Y*[*k*])![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si4.png) of the parent process, I generate a random number of points (up to 15 per location) radially distributed around the parent center (*X*[*h*], *Y*[*k*])![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si4.png). The collection of all the “child” points constitute the cluster process, as pictured in green in Figs. [16.3](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#f0020) and [16.4](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#f0025). The points of the parent process – the centers – are in blue.

![Figure 16.3 Radial cluster process (s = 0.2, λ = 1) with centers in blue; zoom in on the left.](images/B9780443218576000205/gr003.jpg)

Figure 16.3 Radial cluster process (*s* = 0.2, *λ* = 1) with centers in blue; zoom in on the left.

![Figure 16.4 Radial cluster process (s = 2, λ = 1) with centers in blue; zoom in on the left.](images/B9780443218576000205/gr004.jpg)

Figure 16.4 Radial cluster process (*s* = 2, *λ* = 1) with centers in blue; zoom in on the left.

### 16.2.1 Synthetic, semirigid cluster structures

To simulate radial distributions (also called radial intensities in this case), I use a **generalized logistic distribution** (see Section 2.1.1 in [\[20\]](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#br0100)) instead of the Gaussian one, for the child process. The generalized logistic distribution has nice features: easy to simulate, easy to compute the cumulative distribution function (CDF), and it has many parameters, offering a lot of flexibility for the shape of the density. The peculiarity of the Poisson–binomial process offers two options:

*   •  Classic option. Child processes are centered around the points of the parent process, with exactly one child process per point.
*   •  Ad-hoc option. Child processes are centered around the bivariate lattice locations (*h*/*λ*, *k*/*λ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si96.png), with exactly one child process per location, and *h*, *k* ∈ ℤ![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si5.png).

In the latter case, if *s* is small, the child process attached to the index (*h*, *k*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si3.png) has its points distributed around (*X*[*h*], *X*[*k*])![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si97.png) – a point of the parent process – thus it will be similar to the classic option. This is because if *s* is small, then (*h*/*λ*, *k*/*λ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si96.png) is close to (*X*[*h*], *X*[*k*])![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si97.png) on average. It becomes more interesting when *s* is neither too small nor too large.

Figs. [16.3](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#f0020) and [16.4](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#f0025) show two extreme cases. The parent process modeling the cluster centers, is Poisson–binomial. It is simulated with intensity function *λ* = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si49.png), using a uniform distribution for *F*. The **scaling factor** is *s* = 0.2![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si98.png) in [Fig. 16.3](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#f0020), and *s* = 2![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si99.png) in [Fig. 16.4](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#f0025). The left plot is a zoom-in. Around each center (marked with a blue cross in the picture), up to 15 points are radially distributed, creating the overall cluster structure. These points are the actual, observed points of the process, referred to as the child process. The distance between a point (*X*^′, *Y*^′)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si100.png) and its cluster center (*X*, *Y*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si101.png) has a **half-logistic distribution** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half-logistic_distribution)\]. The simulations shown here are performed using formulas [(16.9)](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#deq12) and [(16.10)](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#deq13):

$X^{\\prime} = X + \\log\\left( \\frac{U}{1 - U} \\right)\\cos(2\\pi V),$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si102.png)(16.9) 

$Y^{\\prime} = Y + \\log\\left( \\frac{U}{1 - U} \\right)\\sin(2\\pi V).$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si103.png)(16.10) 

Here *U* and *V* are independent uniform deviates on \[0, 1\]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si104.png). The **quantile function** $Q(U) = \\log\\frac{U}{1 - U}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si105.png) corresponds to a standard logistic distribution.

The contrast between Figs. [16.3](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#f0020) and [16.4](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#f0025) is due to the choice of the scaling factor *s*. The value *s* = 0.2![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si98.png), close to zero, strongly reveals the underlying lattice structure. Here this effect is strong because of the choice of *F* (it has a very thin tail), and the relatively small variance of the distance between a point and its associated cluster center. It produces repulsion among neighbor points: we are dealing with a **repulsive process**. When *s* = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si10.png), all the randomness is gone. Modeling applications include optimum distribution of sensors (for instance, cell towers), crystal structures, and bonding patterns of molecules in chemistry.

By contrast, *s* = 2![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si99.png) makes the cluster structure much more apparent. This time, there is **attraction** among neighbor points: we are dealing with an **attractive process**. It can model many types of structures, associated to human activities or natural phenomena, such as the distribution of galaxies in the universe. [Fig. 16.5](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#f0030) provides an example, related to the manufacture of kitchen countertops.

![Figure 16.5 Manufactured marble lacking true lattice randomness (left).](images/B9780443218576000205/gr005.jpg)

Figure 16.5 Manufactured marble lacking true lattice randomness (left).

[Fig. 16.5](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#f0030) shows luxury kitchen countertops called “Inverness bronze Cambria quartz”, on the left. While the quality (and price) is far superior to all other products from the same company, the rendering of marble veins is not done properly. It looks man-made: not the kind of patterns you would find in real stones. The pattern is too regular, as if produced using a very small value of the scaling factor *s*. An easy fix is to use patterns generated by the cluster processes described here. To increase randomness, increase *s*. The picture on the right shows a more realistic rendering of randomness.

### 16.2.2 Python code to generate cluster processes

The Python code for the simulations is also on my GitHub repository, [here](https://github.com/VincentGranville/Point-Processes/blob/main/Source%20Code/PB_radial.py).

![](images/B9780443218576000205/gr006.jpg)

### 16.2.3 References on cluster processes

Typical examples of cluster point processes include **Neyman–Scott** (see [here](https://hpaulkeeler.com/tag/neyman-scott-point-process/)) and **Matérn** (see [here](https://hpaulkeeler.com/simulating-a-thomas-cluster-point-process/)). Useful references include Baddeley's textbook “Spatial Point Processes and their Applications” [\[4\]](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#br0020), Sigman's course material (Columbia University) on one-dimensional **renewal processes** for beginners, entitled “Notes on the Poisson Process” [\[39\]](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#br0195), Last and Kenrose's book “Lectures on the Poisson Process” [\[27\]](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#br0135), and Cressie's comprehensive 900-page book “Statistics for Spatial Data” [\[11\]](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#br0055). Cluster point processes are part of a larger field known as **spatial statistics**, encompassing other techniques such as geostatistics, kriging, and tessellations. For lattice-based processes known as **perturbed-lattice point processes**, more closely related to the theme of this chapter (lattice processes), and also more recent with applications to cellular networks, see the following references:

*   •  “On Comparison of Clustering Properties of Point Processes” [\[9\]](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#br0045)
*   •  “Clustering and percolation of point processes” [\[8\]](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#br0040)
*   •  “Clustering comparison of point processes, applications to random geometric models” [\[10\]](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#br0050)
*   •  “Stochastic Geometry-Based Tools for Spatial Modeling and Planning of Future Cellular Networks” [\[26\]](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#br0130)
*   •  “Hyperuniform and rigid stable matchings” [\[28\]](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#br0140)
*   •  “Rigidity and tolerance for perturbed lattices” [\[38\]](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#br0190)
*   •  “Cluster analysis of spatial point patterns: posterior distribution of parents inferred from offspring” [\[37\]](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#br0185)
*   •  “Recovering the lattice from its random perturbations” [\[42\]](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#br0210)
*   •  “Geometry and Topology of the Boolean Model on a Stationary Point Processes” [\[44\]](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#br0220)
*   •  “On distances between point patterns and their applications” [\[29\]](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#br0145)

More general references include two comprehensive volumes on point process theory by Daley and Vere-Jones [\[12](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#br0060),[13\]](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#br0065), a chapter by Johnson [\[23\]](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#br0115), books by Møller and Waagepetersen, focusing on statistical inference for spatial processes [\[32](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#br0160),[33\]](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#br0165), and “Point Pattern Analysis: Nearest Neighbor Statistics” by Anselin [\[3\]](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#br0015) focusing on point inhibition/aggregation metrics. See also [\[31\]](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#br0155) by Møller, and “Limit Theorems for Network Dependent Random Variables” [\[24\]](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#br0120), available online [here](https://arxiv.org/abs/1903.01059).

There are different ways to simulate **radial processes**; the most popular method uses a bivariate Gaussian distribution for the child process. Poisson point processes with **nonhomogeneous** radial intensities are discussed in my article “Estimation of the Intensity of a Poisson Point Process by Means of Nearest Neighbor Distances” [\[19\]](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#br0095). The focus is on radial, and thus nonhomogeneous intensity functions: in this case *λ* depends on the location, as opposed to a stationary Poisson process where *λ* is constant. Estimating the **intensity function** of such a process is equivalent to a **density estimation** problem, using kernel density estimators \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kernel_density_estimation)\].

### 16.2.4 Superimposed perturbed lattices: an alternative to mixture models

When the points of *m* independent Poisson–binomial processes with same distribution *F* are bundled together, we say that the processes are **superimposed**. The result may no longer be Poisson–binomial, unlike the superimposition of standard Poisson processes (itself a special case of Poisson–binomial, with *s* = ∞![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si106.png)). Indeed, if the scaling factor *s* is small and *m* > 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si107.png) is not too small, the resulting process exhibits clustering around each lattice location. Also, the intensities or scaling factors of each individual point process may be different, and the resulting process may not be homogeneous. Superimposed point processes also called **interlaced** processes.

I first describe mixtures before moving to interlaced processes. The two models share many similarities, but also some differences. A **mixture** of *m* point processes, denoted as *M*, is defined as follows:

*   •  We have *m* independent point processes *M*[1], …, *M*[*m*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si108.png) with same distribution *F*.
*   •  The intensity and scaling factor attached to *M*[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si109.png) are denoted respectively as *λ*[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si110.png) and *s*[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si111.png) (*i* = 1, …, *m*![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si112.png)).
*   •  The points of *M*[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si109.png) (*i* = 1, …, *m*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si113.png) are denoted as (*X*[*i**h*], *Y*[*i**k*])![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si114.png).
*   •  The point (*X*[*h*], *Y*[*k*])![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si4.png) of the mixture process *M* is equal to (*X*[*i**h*], *Y*[*i**k*])![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si114.png) with probability *π*[*i*] > 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si115.png), *i* = 1, …, *m*![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si112.png).

The *π*[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si116.png)'s are the mixture proportions, and their sum is equal to one. While mixing or superimposing Poisson–binomial processes seem like the same operation, which is true for stationary Poisson processes, in the case of Poisson–binomial processes, these are distinct operations resulting in significant differences when the scaling factors are very small. The difference is most striking when *s* = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si10.png). In particular, superimposed processes are less random than mixtures. This is due to the discrete nature of the underlying lattice. However, with larger scaling factors, the behavior of mixed and superimposed processes tend to be similar.

[Fig. 16.6](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#f0040) represents a realization of *m* superimposed shifted stretched Poisson–binomial processes, called *m***\-interlacing**. For each individual process *M*[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si109.png), *i* = 1, …, *m*![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si112.png), the distribution attached to the point (*X*[*i**h*], *X*[*i**k*])![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si117.png) (with *h*, *k* ∈ ℤ![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si5.png)) is

$P(X\_{ih} < x,Y\_{ik} < y) = F\\left( \\frac{x - \\mu\_{i} - h/\\lambda}{s} \\right)F\\left( \\frac{y - \\mu\_{i}^{\\prime} - k/\\lambda^{\\prime}}{s} \\right),\\quad i = 1,\\ldots,m.$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si118.png)

This generalizes formula [(16.1)](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#deq1). The parameters used for the model pictured in [Fig. 16.6](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#f0040) are:

*   •  Number of superimposed processes: *m* = 4![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si119.png); each one displayed with a different color,
*   •  Color: red for *M*[1]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si120.png), blue for *M*[2]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si121.png), orange for *M*[3]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si122.png), black for *M*[4]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si123.png),
*   •  Scaling factor: *s* = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si10.png) (left plot) and *s* = 5![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si124.png) (right plot),
*   •  Intensity: *λ* = 1/3![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si125.png) (X-axis) and $\\lambda^{\\prime} = \\sqrt{3}/3$![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si126.png) (Y-axis),
*   •  Shift vector, X-coordinate: *μ*[1] = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si127.png), *μ*[2] = 1/2![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si128.png), *μ*[3] = 2![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si129.png), *μ*[4] = 3/2![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si130.png),
*   •  Shift vector, Y-coordinate: *μ*[1]^′ = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si131.png), $\\mu\_{2}^{\\prime} = \\sqrt{3}/2$![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si132.png), *μ*[3]^′ = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si133.png), $\\mu\_{4}^{\\prime} = \\sqrt{3}/2$![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si134.png),
*   •  *F* distribution: standard centered **logistic distribution** with zero mean and variance *π*²/3![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si135.png).

For simulation purposes, the points (*X*[*i**h*], *Y*[*i**k*])![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si114.png) of the *i*th process *M*[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si109.png) (*i* = 1, …, *m*![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si112.png)), are generated as follows: 

$X\_{ih} = \\mu\_{i} + \\frac{h}{\\lambda} + s \\cdot \\log\\left( \\frac{U\_{ih}}{1 - U\_{ih}} \\right),$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si136.png)(16.11) 

$Y\_{ik} = \\mu\_{i}^{\\prime} + \\frac{k}{\\lambda^{\\prime}} + s \\cdot \\log\\left( \\frac{U\_{ik}}{1 - U\_{ik}} \\right),$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si137.png)(16.12) 

where *U*[*i**j*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si138.png) are uniformly and independently distributed on \[0, 1\]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si104.png) and  − *n* ≤ *h*, *k* ≤ *n*![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si139.png). I chose *n* = 25![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si140.png) in the simulation – a window much larger than that of [Fig. 16.6](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#f0040) – to avoid **boundary effects** in the picture. The boundary effect is sometimes called **edge effect**. The unobserved data points outside the window of observations, are referred to as **censored data** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Censoring_\(statistics\))\]. Of course, in my simulations their locations and features (such as which process they belong to) are known by design. But in a real data set, they are truly missing or unobservable, and statistical inference must be adjusted accordingly [\[15\]](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#br0075).

![Figure 16.6 Four superimposed Poisson–binomial processes: s = 0 (left), s = 5 (right).](images/B9780443218576000205/gr008.jpg)

Figure 16.6 Four superimposed Poisson–binomial processes: *s* = 0 (left), *s* = 5 (right).

Formulas [(16.11)](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#deq15) and [(16.12)](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#deq16) are also used in Section [5.2.1](#Chp005_83-102_B9780443218576000096.xhtml) in the context of clustering and supervised classification. A simple introduction to mixtures of ordinary Poisson processes is found on the Memming blog, [here](https://memming.wordpress.com/2012/08/28/mixture-of-point-processes/). In Section [16.3.2](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#s0105), I discuss statistical inference: detecting whether a realization of a point process is Poisson or not, and detecting the number of superimposed processes (similar to estimating the number of clusters in a **cluster process**, or the number of components in a **mixture model**). In Section [16.3](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#s0080), I discuss a black-box version of the **elbow rule** to detect the number of clusters or mixture components, or the number of superimposed processes.

#### 16.2.4.1 Hexagonal lattice, nearest neighbors

The source code to produce [Fig. 16.6](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#f0040) is on my GitHub repository: [PB\_NN.py](https://github.com/VincentGranville/Point-Processes/blob/main/Source%20Code/PB_NN.py) for the nearest neighbor graph, and [av\_demo.r](https://github.com/VincentGranville/Point-Processes/blob/main/Videos/av_demo.r) for the visualizations.

Surprisingly, it is possible to produce a point process with a regular **hexagonal lattice** using simple operations on a small number (*m* = 4![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si119.png)) of square lattices: superimposition, stretching, and shifting. A **stretched lattice** is a square lattice turned into a rectangular lattice, by applying a multiplication factor to the X and/or Y coordinates. A **shifted lattice** is a lattice where the grid points have been shifted via a translation.

Each point of the process almost surely (with probability one) has exactly one nearest neighbor. However, when the scaling factor *s* is zero, this is no longer true. On the left plot in [Fig. 16.6](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#f0040), each point (also called **vertex** when *s* = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si10.png)) has exactly 3 nearest neighbors. This causes some challenges when plotting the case *s* = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si10.png). The case *s* > 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si141.png) is easier to plot, using arrows pointing from any point to its unique nearest neighbor. I produced the arrows in question with the arrow function in R \[[Wiki](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/graphics/html/arrows.xhtml)\]. A bidirectional arrow between points A and B means that B is a nearest neighbor of A, and A is a nearest neighbor of B. All arrows on the left plot in [Fig. 16.6](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#f0040) are bidirectional. Boundary effects are easily noticeable, as some arrows point to nearest neighbors outside the window. Four colors are used for the points, corresponding to the 4 shifted stretched Poisson–binomial processes used to generate the hexagon-based process. The color indicates which of these 4 process, a point is attached to.

The source code handles points with multiple nearest neighbors. It produces a list of all points with their nearest neighbors, using a **hash table**. A point with 3 nearest neighbors has 3 entries in that list: one for each nearest neighbor. A group of points that are all connected by arrows is called a **connected component** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Component_\(graph_theory\))\]. A path from a point of a connected component to another point of the same connected component, following arrows while ignoring their direction, is called a **path** in **graph theory**.

In my definition of connected component, the direction of the arrow does not matter: the underlying **graph** is considered **undirected** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_graph)\]. An interesting problem is to study the size distribution, that is, the number of points per connected component, especially for standard Poisson processes. See [Exercise 16.1](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#enun0010). In graph theory, a point is called a **vertex** or **node**, and an arrow is called an **edge**. More about nearest neighbors is discussed in Exercises 18 and 19 in [\[20\]](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#br0100).

Finally, if you look at [Fig. 16.6](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#f0040), the left plot seems to have more points than the right plot. But they actually have roughly the same number of points. The plot on the right seems to be more sparse, because there are large areas with no points. But to compensate, there are areas where several points are in close proximity.

#### 16.2.4.2 Exercises: nearest neighbor graphs, size of connected components

These exercises complement the material introduced in Section [16.2.4](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#s0060), offering a deeper dive in some aspects of graph theory. They are not designed to test your knowledge, but instead, to expand it. Rather than trying to solve them, read the solution. I also mention open (unsolved) questions linked to these problems, in particular regarding **random graphs**.

Exercise 16.1

Nearest neighbors and size distribution of connected components. Simulate 10 realizations of a stationary Poisson process of intensity *λ* = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si49.png), each with *n* = 10³![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si142.png) points distributed over a square window. Identify the **connected components** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Component_\(graph_theory\))\] and their size (the number of points in each connected component). The purpose of the exercise is to study the distribution of the size, denoted as *S*. In particular, what is the proportion of connected components with only 2 points (*P*\[*S* = 2\]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si143.png)), 3 points (*P*\[*S* = 3\]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si144.png)), and so on? For connected components, use the **undirected graph**, that is, points *V*[*i*], *V*[*j*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si145.png) (also called vertices) are connected if *V*[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si146.png) is nearest neighbor to *V*[*j*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si147.png), or the other way around. The questions are:

*   •  Estimate the probabilities in question via simulations. When computing the proportions using multiple realizations of the same process, do we get a similar empirical distribution for *S*, across all realizations? Does the empirical distribution seem to convergence, when increasing *n*, say from *n* = 10³![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si142.png) to *n* = 10⁴![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si148.png) or *n* = 10⁵![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si149.png)?
*   •  Do the same experiment with a Poisson–binomial process, with *λ* = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si49.png) and *s* = 0.15![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si150.png). Do we get the same distribution for *S*? What about *P*\[*S* = 2\]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si143.png)?
*   •  Generate a particular type of **random graph**, called **random NN graph**, as follows. Let *V*[1], …, *V*[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si151.png) be the *n* **vertices** of the graph (their locations do not matter). For the “nearest neighbor” to vertex *V*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si152.png) (*k* = 1, …, *n*![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si153.png)), randomly pick up one of the *n* vertices except *V*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si152.png) itself. Two points (vertices) can have the same nearest neighbor. Now study the distribution of *S* via simulations. Is it the same as for the graph generated by the nearest neighbors in a stationary Poisson point process?
*   •  This is the most difficult part. Let *P*(*S* = *k*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si154.png), *k* = 2, 3, …![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si155.png) be the size distribution for connected components of a stationary Poisson process; *S* is a random variable. Of course, it does not depend on *λ*. Does it uniquely characterize the Poisson process, in the same way that the exponential distribution for interarrival times uniquely characterizes the Poisson process in one dimension? Do we have $P(S = 2) = \\frac{1}{2}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si156.png), not only for Poisson processes, but also for a much larger class of point processes?

Useful references about random graphs \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Random_graph)\] include “The Probabilistic Method” by Alon and Spencer [\[1\]](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#br0005), and “Random Graphs and Complex Networks” by Hofstad [\[41\]](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#br0205). See also [here](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/3883829/distribution-of-size-of-connected-components-in-erdos-renyi-random-graphs-in-the).

**Hints**

Beware of the **boundary effect**; to minimize the impact, use a uniform distribution for *F* (the distribution attached to the points of the Poisson–binomial process) and *n* > 10³![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si157.png). When the scaling factor *s* is zero, there is only one connected component of infinite size (*P*\[*S* = ∞\] = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si158.png)): this is a singularity, as illustrated on the left plot in [Fig. 16.6](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#f0040). But as soon as *s* > 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si141.png), all the connected components are of finite size and rather small. The smallest ones have two points as each point has a nearest neighbor, thus *P*\[*S* < 2\] = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si159.png). When *s* = ∞![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si106.png), the process becomes a stationary Poisson process.

I conjecture that stationary Poisson processes and some other (if not all) Poisson–binomial processes share the exact same discrete probability distribution for the size of connected components defined by nearest neighbors, and abbreviated as CCS distribution. Thus, unlike the point count distribution or nearest neighbor distance distributions, the CCS distribution can not be used to characterize a Poisson process. For random graphs, the CCS distribution is different from that of a Poisson process. I used a **Kolmogorov–Smirnov test** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kolmogorov-Smirnov_test)\] (see also [\[17\]](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#br0085)) to compare the two empirical CCS distributions – the one attached to Poisson processes versus the one attached to random NN graphs – and concluded, based on my sample size (*n* = 10⁴![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si148.png) points or vertices), that they were statistically different.

To conclude, it appears that the CCS distribution cannot be arbitrary. Many point processes seem to have the same CCS distribution, called **attractor distribution**, and these processes constitute the **domain of attraction** of the attractor. The concepts of domain of attraction and attractor is used in other contexts such as **dynamical systems** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attractor)\] or extreme value theory \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generalized_extreme_value_distribution)\] (also, see [\[5\]](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#br0025), page 317). The most well known analogy is the **Central Limit Theorem**, where the Gaussian distribution is the main attractor, and the Cauchy distribution is another. In Chapter 11 of “The Probabilistic Method” [\[1\]](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#br0005), dealing with the size of connected components in random graphs, the author introduces a random variable *T*[*c*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si160.png), also counting a number of vertices (called **nodes** in the book). Its distribution has all the hallmarks of an attractor. See Theorem 11.4.2 (page 202) in the book in question.

To find the connected components, you can use the source code in Section [16.2.4.3](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#s0075). To simulate point processes, you can use the program [PB\_NN.py](https://github.com/VincentGranville/Point-Processes/blob/main/Source%20Code/PB_NN.py) available on GitHub and described in section 6.4 in [\[20\]](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#br0100): it produces an output file [PB\_NN\_dist\_full.txt](https://github.com/VincentGranville/Point-Processes/blob/main/Data/PB_NN_dist_full.txt) that can be used as input, without any change, to the connected components algorithm in section [16.2.4.3](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#s0075). [Exercise 16.2](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#enun0015) features a similar problem, dealing with cliques rather than connected components.

Exercise 16.2

Maximum clique problem. In **undirected graphs** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/?title=Undirected_graph)\], a **clique** is a set of vertices (also called nodes) all connected to each other. In **nearest neighbor** graphs, two points are connected if one of them is a closest neighbor to the other. How would you identify a clique of maximum size in such a graph? No need to design an algorithm from scratch; instead, search the literature. Finding the maximum clique \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clique_problem)\] is NP-hard \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NP-hardness)\], and the problem is related to the “P versus NP” conjecture \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P_versus_NP_problem)\]. The maximum clique problem has many applications, in particular in social networks. Probabilistic properties of cliques in **random graphs** are discussed in “Cliques in random graphs” [\[6\]](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#br0030) and “On the evolution of random graphs” [\[16\]](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#br0080). See also the **Erdős–Rényi model** \[[Wiki](https://bit.ly/3uzQzNF)\]. More recent articles include [\[18](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#br0090),[30\]](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#br0150).

**Solution**

In two dimensions, in an **undirected nearest neighbor graph**, the minimum size of a maximum clique is 2 (as each point has a nearest neighbor), and the maximum size is 3. A maximum clique must be a **connected component**. See definition of connected component in [Exercise 16.1](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#enun0010). If each point has exactly one nearest neighbor, then a connected component of size *n* > 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si161.png) has *n* or *n* − 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si162.png) edges (the arrows on the right plot in [Fig. 16.6](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#f0040)), while a clique of size *n* has exactly $\\frac{1}{2}n(n - 1)$![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si163.png) edges. This is why maximum cliques of size larger than 3 do not exist. But in *d* dimensions, a maximum clique can be of size *d* + 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si164.png). The maximum clique can be found using the **MaxCliqueDyn algorithm** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MaxCliqueDyn_maximum_clique_algorithm)\].

#### 16.2.4.3 Python code to compute connected components

The Python code [PB\_NN\_graph.py](https://github.com/VincentGranville/Point-Processes/blob/main/Source%20Code/PB_NN_graph.py) is also on GitHub. I also used it to produce the connected components in the problem described in Section [15.3](#Chp015_277-292_B9780443218576000199.xhtml). There are many implementations available online. The algorithm presented here does not use recursions unlike most others. Instead, it relies on a data structure called stack. It is just as fast as any efficient alternative, and was tested on nearest neighbor graphs. Two points are considered connected if one of the two points is the nearest neighbor to the other one. The first column of the input file represents the index idx of a point, and NNidx\[idx\] (in the second column) is the index of a point that has point idx as nearest neighbor.

The algorithm works as follows. Browse the list of points. If a point idx has not yet been assigned to a connected component, create a new connected component cliqueHash\[idx\] containing idx; find the points connected to idx, add them to the stack (stack). Find the points connected to the points connected to idx, and so on recursively, until no more points can be added. Each time a point is added to cliqueHash, decrease the stack size by one. It takes about 2*n* steps to find all the connected components, where *n* is the number of points. This algorithm does not use recursive functions; it uses a stack instead, which emulates recursivity.

The first part of the code creates the undirected graph hash, as follows: if a point with index k is nearest neighbor to a point with index idx, add point idx to hash\[k\], and add point k to hash\[idx\]. Thus hash\[idx\] contains all the points (their indices) directly connected to point idx; the points are separated by the tilde symbol.

![](images/B9780443218576000205/gr009.jpg)

## 16.3 Statistical inference for point processes

This section covers the following topics: estimation of the core parameters of Poisson–binomial processes (intensity and scaling factor), and the Rayleigh test to assess – based on the distribution of nearest neighbor distances – whether or not a spatial data set exhibits patterns not expected in a random distribution. Minimum contrast estimation, predicting extreme distances between neighboring points, and retrieving the underlying, hidden distribution *F* attached to a Poisson–binomial process are discussed in Section [16.4](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#s0130).Testing the independence of points counts is covered in Section [16.1.3](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#s0025). Detecting clusters and estimating their number in a cluster process similar to a mixture are discussed in Chapter [5](#Chp005_83-102_B9780443218576000096.xhtml).

### 16.3.1 Estimation of core parameters

It is assumed that the point process covers the entire space ℝ![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si165.png) or ℝ²![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si166.png) with infinitely many points, and that only a finite number of points are observed through a finite (typically rectangular) window or interval. Here I focus on the one-dimensional case. For processes in two dimensions, see Section [16.3.2.1](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#s0110).

In one dimension, the two most fundamental parameters are the intensity *λ* and the scaling factor *s*. The standard estimator of *λ* proposed here is asymptotically unbiased \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consistent_estimator)\]. For a more generic, model-free method yielding an unbiased estimator simultaneously for *s* and *λ*, along with confidence regions, see Section [18.3](#Chp018_361-386_B9780443218576000229.xhtml). The goal of this section is to offer efficient estimators, easy to compute, and taking advantage of the properties of the underlying model.

#### 16.3.1.1 Intensity

There are various ways to estimate the intensity *λ* (more specifically, *λ*^(*d*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si167.png) in *d* dimension) using **interarrival times** (one dimension), nearest neighbors distances (in two dimensions) or the point count distribution *N*(*B*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si19.png) computed on some interval *B*. A good estimator with small variance, assuming boundary effects are mitigated, is the total number of observed points divided by the area (or length, in one dimension) of the window of observations.

The expected value of the interarrival times is 1/*λ*![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si38.png). Thus, if you average all the interarrival times across all the observed points (called events in one dimension), you get an unbiased estimator of 1/*λ*![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si38.png). Its multiplicative inverse will be a slightly biased estimator of *λ*; if the number of points is large enough (say >50), the bias is negligible.

#### 16.3.1.2 Scaling factor

Once *λ* has been estimated, the scaling factor *s* can be estimated by leveraging the fact that *E*\[*T*^(*r*)(*λ*, *s*)\] = *E*\[*T*^(*r*)(1, *λ**s*)\]/*λ*^(*r*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si168.png) for any *r* > 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si169.png). Here *T*(*λ*, *s*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si170.png) is the interarrival time (a random variable) or, in other words, the distance between a point and its nearest neighbor to the right on the X axis, in one dimension. This result does not depend on the distribution *F*. For a proof, see Theorem 4.2 in my book “Stochastic Processes and Simulations: A Machine Learning Approach”.

With *r* = 2![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si171.png), let

*   •  *τ*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si172.png) be your estimate of *T*²(*λ*, *s*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si173.png) (the average value computed on your data set),
*   •  *τ*^′ = (*λ*[0])^(*r*) ⋅ *τ*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si174.png), where *λ*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si175.png) is your estimate of *λ* (see Section [16.3.1.1](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#s0090)),
*   •  *s*^′![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si176.png) be the solution to *E*\[*T*^(*r*)(1, *s*^′)\] = *τ*^′![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si177.png).

Then *s*[0] = *s*^′/*λ*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si178.png) is an estimate of *s*.

Example

Here *F* is the logistic distribution, and I chose *r* = 2![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si171.png). Any *r* > 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si169.png) except *r* = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si179.png) would work. If *λ*[0] = 1.45![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si180.png) and *τ*[0] = 0.77![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si181.png), then *τ*^′ = (*λ*[0])²*τ*[0] = 1.61![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si182.png). Looking at the *E*\[*T*²(1, *s*^′)\]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si183.png) table, to satisfy *E*\[*T*²(1, *s*^′)\] ≈ 1.61![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si184.png), you need *s*^′ = 0.65![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si185.png). Thus *s*[0] = *s*^′/*λ*[0] = 0.45![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si186.png). These numbers match those obtained by simulation. To view or download the table, look at the *E*\[*T*²\]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si187.png) tab in [PB\_inference.xlsx](https://github.com/VincentGranville/Point-Processes/tree/main/Spreadsheets).

The equation *E*\[*T*²(1, *s*^′)\] = *τ*^′![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si188.png), where *s*^′![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si176.png) is the unknown, can be solved using numerical methods. The easiest way is to build a granular table of *E*\[*T*²(1, *s*)\]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si189.png) for various values of *s*, by simulating Poisson–binomial processes of intensity *λ* = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si49.png) and scaling factor *s*. Then finding *s*^′![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si176.png) consists in browsing and interpolating the table in question the old fashioned way, to identify the value of *s* closest to satisfying *E*\[*T*²(1, *s*)\] = *τ*^′![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si190.png). This can, of course, be automated. There are two ways to perform the simulations in question:

*   •  Generating one realization of each process with a large number of points (that is, one realization for each 0 < *s* < 20![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si191.png) with *λ* = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si49.png) and *s* increments equal to 0.01),
*   •  Or generating many realizations of each process, each one with a rather small number of points. 

Either way, the results should be almost identical due to **ergodicity** if the same *F* is used in both cases. The simulations also allow you to compute the theoretical variance of the estimators in question (at least a very good approximation). This is useful when multiple estimators (based on different statistics) are available, to choose the best one: that with minimum variance. Simulations also allow you to compute **confidence intervals** for your estimators.

#### 16.3.1.3 Alternative estimation method

It is also possible to use the point count *N*(*B*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si19.png) to estimate *s*. The idea is to partition the state space (the real line in one dimension, where the points reside) into short intervals *B*[*k*] = \[*k*/*λ*, (*k* + 1)/*λ*\[![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si192.png), *k* = 0,  ± 1,  ± 2![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si193.png), and so on, covering the observed points; beware of the **boundary effect**. This assumes that *λ* is known or estimated. Let *N*[*k*] = *N*(*B*[*k*])![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si194.png) be the random variable counting the number of observed points in *B*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si195.png). We have *E*\[*N*[*k*]\] = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si196.png). Also *V**a**r*\[*N*[*k*]\] ≤ 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si197.png) does not depend on *k* thanks to the choice of *B*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si195.png) (see Section [16.1.2](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#s0020)). The variance is maximum and equal to 1 when *s* = ∞![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si106.png).

It is possible, for any value of *s* and *λ*, to compute the theoretical variance *v*(*λ*, *s*) = *V**a**r*\[*N*[*k*]\]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si198.png) using either simulations or formula [(16.4)](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#deq5) with *a* = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si199.png) and *b* = 1/*λ*![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si200.png). It slightly depends on *F*, but barely. Now compute the empirical variance of *N*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si201.png) as the average (*N*[*k*] − 1)²![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si202.png) across all the *B*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si195.png)'s, based on your observations, assuming *λ* is known or estimated. This empirical variance is denoted as *v*[0](*λ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si203.png). The estimated value of *s* is the one that makes the empirical and theoretical variances identical, that is, the *unique* value of *s* that solves the equation *v*(*λ*, *s*) = *v*[0](*λ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si204.png). This method easily generalizes to higher dimensions, see Section [16.3.2.1](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#s0110). The fact that *E*\[*N*[*k*]\] = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si196.png) is a direct consequence of Theorem 4.1 in the same book.

See the *N*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si201.png) tab in [PB\_inference.xlsx](https://github.com/VincentGranville/Point-Processes/tree/main/Spreadsheets) for a Poisson–binomial process simulation with a **generalized logistic** *F* and computation of *E*\[*N*[*k*]\]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si205.png) and *V**a**r*\[*N*[*k*]\]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si206.png) in Excel.

### 16.3.2 Spatial statistics, nearest neighbors, clustering

Here the focus is on 2D point processes. Section [16.3.2.3](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#s0120) features an original test to determine whether the point distribution – more precisely the nearest distances – in a particular data set is consistent with that of a Poisson process. In short, it tests whether you are dealing with a realization of a **Poisson process**, or a more complex process such as an *m*\-mixture: a superimposition of Poisson–binomial processes.

#### 16.3.2.1 Inference for two-dimensional processes

Let us assume for now that we are dealing with a single two-dimensional Poisson–binomial point process. Some of the methodology discussed in Section [16.3.1](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#s0085) for the one-dimensional case can be generalized to higher dimensions. The point count distribution in a square of side 1/*λ*![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si38.png) has expectation equal to 1. So, one way to estimate *λ* is to partition the window of observations *W* into small squares $B\_{h,k}(\\lambda) = \\left\\lbrack \\frac{h}{\\lambda},\\frac{h + 1}{\\lambda}\\left\\lbrack \\times \\left\\lbrack \\frac{k}{\\lambda},\\frac{k + 1}{\\lambda}\\lbrack \\right. \\right. \\right.$![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si207.png) for various values of the (unknown) *λ*, compute the number of points *N*[*h*, *k*](*λ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si208.png) (called **point count**) in each of these squares, and find *λ* that minimizes the empirical variance

$v(\\lambda) = \\sum\\limits\_{h,k}\\left( N\_{h,k}(\\lambda) - 1 \\right)^{2}$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si209.png)

computed on the observations. The sum is over *h*, *k* ∈ ℤ ∩ *W*^′![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si210.png), where *W* is the window of observation, and *W*^′![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si211.png) is slightly smaller than *W* to mitigate **boundary effects**. In short, your estimate of the **intensity** *λ* is defined as $\\lambda\_{0} = \\underset{\\lambda}{\\arg⁡\\min}\\text{~~}v(\\lambda)$![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si212.png).

The benefit of this approach is that it also allows you to easily estimate the **scaling factor** *s*. Since *v*(*λ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si213.png) also depends on the unknown *s*, let us denote it as *v*(*λ*, *s*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si214.png). Also, let *V*(*λ*, *s*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si215.png) be the theoretical variance of the point count *N*(*B*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si19.png) in $B = \\left\\lbrack 0,\\frac{1}{\\lambda}\\left\\lbrack \\times \\left\\lbrack 0,\\frac{1}{\\lambda}\\lbrack \\right. \\right. \\right.$![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si216.png), computed using simulations or via formula [(16.4)](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#deq5). The estimated value of *s*, assuming *λ*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si175.png) is the estimate of *λ*, is the solution to the equation *v*(*λ*[0], *s*) = *V*(*λ*[0], *s*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si217.png).

Another simple estimator, this time for *λ*^(*d*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si167.png), is the total number of observed points in the observation window *W*, divided by the area of *W*. Here *d* = 2![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si218.png) is the dimension. Estimators of *λ* and *s* may also be obtained using **nearest neighbor** distances, in a way similar to using interarrival times in one dimension as in Section [16.3.1.1](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#s0090). I have not checked if the random variable *S*, defined as the size of the **connected components** associated to the undirected **nearest neighbor graph** (see [Exercise 16.1](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#enun0010)), is of any use to estimate *s*. confidence regions for (*λ*, *s*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si219.png) can be built using the methodology in Section [16.4.1](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#s0135).

#### 16.3.2.2 Other possible tests

Besides estimating the core parameters, many other properties or features can be tested. They are too numerous to be treated in details here, so I only provide a quick summary.

*   •  **Anisotropy** – testing if the point distribution is statistically identical in all directions. This is the case for all the examples discussed in this chapter. Testing for anisotropy can be done using *ρ*(*z*, *r*) = *N*\[*B*(*z*, *r*)\]/(*π**r*²)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si220.png) where *B*(*z*, *r*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si221.png) is a circle of radius *r* centered at *z*, and *N* is the point count distribution. In case of anisotropy, and assuming *r* is not too small so that each circle has at least 20 points, there should be only little variations among the *ρ*(*z*, *r*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si222.png)'s computed at different (*z*, *r*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si223.png). Simulate a truly anisotropic process (stationary Poisson) with the same number of points in the window of observations, to find exactly what “only little variations” means.
*   •  **Stationarity** – testing whether *N*\[*B*(*z*, *r* + *t*)\] − *N*\[*B*(*z*, *r*)\]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si224.png) depends only on *t*, and not on *r*. In our context, using squares centered at *z* and of side *r* for *B*(*z*, *r*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si221.png), would show lack of stationarity if *s* is small and you try different values of *t*, say *t* = 1/(2*λ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si225.png) and *t* = 1/*λ*![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si226.png).
*   •  Independence – this test (discussed in Section [16.1.3](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#s0025)) is used, for instance, to assess whether the point counts *N*(*B*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si19.png) in various nonoverlapping domains *B* are independent or not. In our context, this is not generally the case.
*   •  **Ergodicity** – for some statistics based on simulations (as opposed to a real-life data set), one can use a single realization of the process with many points or a large window of observations, to make inference. Or one can use many realizations, each with a few points or small window, to compute the same statistic and average the observed values across all the realizations. If the results are statistically the same in both cases, the statistic in question is ergodic, for the point process model in question. A good example is the **nearest neighbor distance**, between two neighbor points of the process.
*   •  Repulsion (or attraction) – an **attractive point process** is one where points tend to cluster together, leaving large areas empty, and some areas filled high point density. An example is a **cluster process**. The opposite is a repulsive process: points tend to stay as far away as possible from each other. The most extreme case is when the scaling factor *s* is zero, as in the left plot in [Fig. 16.6](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#f0040). Typically, the degree of attraction is determined by *s*. However, a cluster process can be both: for instance, if the unobserved cluster centers come from a parent point process with a very small *s*, such as in [Fig. 16.3](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#f0020).
*   •  Number of clusters – determining the number *m* of clusters in an *m*\-interlacing (superimposition of *m* Poisson–binomial point processes), or the number of components in a mixture of *m* processes, is not easy and usually not feasible if cluster overlap is substantial, at least not exactly. This is discussed in Section [5.3.2](#Chp005_83-102_B9780443218576000096.xhtml). A black-box version of the **elbow rule** (the traditional tool to estimate the number of clusters) is discussed in Section [18.6](#Chp018_361-386_B9780443218576000229.xhtml).
*   •  Shift vectors – the parameters *μ*[*i*], *μ*[*i*]^′![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si227.png) in formulas [(16.11)](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#deq15) and [(16.12)](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#deq16), or “centers” associated to *m***\-interlacings** (a superimposition of *m* Poisson–binomial processes). Each of the *m* individual processes has a shift vector attached to it: it determines the position of a cluster center modulo 1/*λ*![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si38.png). If these vectors are well separated and *s* is small, they can be retrieved. This is a clustering problem; see Section [5.3.2](#Chp005_83-102_B9780443218576000096.xhtml) and [Fig. 16.8](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#f0055) featuring 5 different shift vectors (*m* = 5![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si228.png)) and thus 5 clusters.
*   •  To decide whether you are dealing with a mixture rather than a superimposition of *m* point processes, one has to look at the point count distribution on a square *B*[*λ*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si229.png) of area 1/*λ*²![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si230.png). The theoretical expectation of the point count is *E*\[*N*(*B*[*λ*])\] = *m*![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si231.png) if the process is an *m*\-interlacing; in that case, the number of points in each *B*[*λ*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si229.png) is also very stable. The first thing to do is to estimate *λ*, then look at the empirical variance of *N*(*B*[*λ*])![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si232.png) computed on the observations. When *s* is small enough, *N*(*B*[*λ*])![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si232.png) is almost constant (equal to *m*) for an *m*\-interlacing; it almost has a **binomial distribution** for a **mixture**.
*   •  Size of **connected components** – an interesting problem is to identify the connected components in the **undirected graph** of nearest neighbors associated to a point process, see [Exercise 16.1](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#enun0010). These connected components are featured in [Fig. 16.6](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#f0040). Their size distribution is of particular interest: for instance, on the left plot in [Fig. 16.6](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#f0040), corresponding to *s* = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si10.png), there is only one connected component of infinite size; on the right plot, there are infinitely many small connected components (about 50% only have two points). It is still an open question as to whether or not this statistic can be used to discriminate between different types of point processes, or whether its theoretical distribution is exactly the same for a large class of point processes (that is, it is an **attractor distribution**) and thus of little practical value.

#### 16.3.2.3 Rayleigh test

The **Rayleigh test** is a generic statistical test to assess whether two data sets consisting of points in two dimensions arise from the same type of stochastic point process. It assumes that the underlying point process model is uniquely characterized by the distribution of nearest neighbor distances. The most popular use is when the assumed model is a stationary Poisson process: in that case, the statistic of the test has a **Rayleigh distribution**. It generalizes to higher dimensions; in that case the Rayleigh distribution becomes a **Weibull distribution**. In short, what the test actually does is comparing the empirical distributions of nearest neighbor distances computed on the two data sets, possibly after standardization, to assess if from a statistical point of view they are indistinguishable.

The test is performed as follows. Let us say you have two data sets consisting of points in two dimensions, observed through a window. You compute the empirical distribution of the nearest neighbor distances for both data sets, based on the observations, after taking care of **boundary effects**. Let *η*[1](*u*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si233.png) and *η*[2](*u*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si234.png) be the two distributions in question. The statistic of the test is

*V* = ∫[ − ∞]^∞|*η*[1](*u*) − *η*[2](*u*)|*d**u* = ∫[0]¹|*ν*[1](*u*) − *ν*[2](*u*)|*d**u*,

![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si235.png)(16.13) 

where *ν* is the empirical **quantile function**, that is, the inverse of the empirical distribution. An alternative test is based on *W* = sup[*u*]|*η*[1](*u*) − *η*[2](*u*)|![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si236.png), or on *W*^′ = sup[*u*]|*ν*[1](*u*) − *ν*[2](*u*)|![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si237.png). The test based on *W* is the traditional Kolmogorov–Smirnov test \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kolmogorov-Smirnov_test)\] with known tabulated values. In Excel, it is easier to use the empirical quantile function, readily available as the PERCENTILE Excel function. In practice, the integral in formula [(16.13)](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#deq18) is replaced by a sum computed over 100 equally spaced value of *u* ∈ \[0, 1\]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si238.png). The advantage of *W* is that it is known (asymptotically) not to depend on the underlying (possibly unknown) point process model that the data originates from.

I provide an illustration in [PB\_inference.xlsx](https://github.com/VincentGranville/Point-Processes/tree/main/Spreadsheets): see the “Rayleigh test” tab in the spreadsheet. I compare two data sets, one from a simulation of a two-dimensional Poisson–binomial process with *s* = 20![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si239.png), and one with *s* = 0.4![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si240.png). In both cases, *λ* is set to 1.5 in the simulator; its estimated value on the generated data set is close to 1.5. I then compare the **nearest neighbor distances** (their empirical quantile function) with the theoretical distribution of a two-dimensional stationary Poisson process of intensity *λ*²![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si1.png). The theoretical distribution is Rayleigh of expectation 1/(2*λ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si241.png). The data set with *s* = 20![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si239.png) is indistinguishable, at least using the Rayleigh test, from a realization of a stationary Poisson process. This was expected: as *s* → ∞![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si8.png), the Poisson–binomial process converges to a Poisson process, and the convergence is very fast. But the data set with *s* = 0.4![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si240.png) is markedly different from a Poisson point process realization, as seen by looking at the statistic *V* or *W*^′![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si211.png).

Tabulated values for the statistics *V* and *W*^′![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si211.png) can be obtained by simulations. For *W*, they have been known since at least 1948, since *W* is the Kolmogorov–Smirnov statistic [\[17\]](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#br0085). Here I simply used tabulated values of the Rayleigh distribution since I was comparing the simulated data with a realization of stationary Poisson process. **Confidence bands** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confidence_and_prediction_bands)\] for the empirical quantile function can be obtained using **resampling** methods \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resampling_\(statistics\))\] such as bootstrapping or **parametric bootstrap**. See also Section [18.3](#Chp018_361-386_B9780443218576000229.xhtml).

[Fig. 16.7](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#f0050) illustrates the result of my test, using the empirical quantile function of the nearest neighbor distances, and the statistic *V* for the test. No resampling or confidence bands were needed, the conclusion is obvious: *s* = 0.4![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si240.png) provides a simulated data set markedly different from a Poisson point process realization (the gray curve is way off) while *s* = 20![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si239.png) is indistinguishable from a Poisson point process (the red and blue curves, representing the empirical quantile function of the **nearest neighbor distances**, are almost identical). Interestingly, the scatterplot corresponding to *s* = 0.4![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si240.png) (rightmost in [Fig. 16.7](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#f0050)) seems more random than with *s* = 20![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si239.png) (middle plot), but actually, the opposite is true. The plot with *s* = 0.4![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si240.png) corresponds to a **repulsive process**, where points are more away from each other than pure chance would dictate; thus it exhibits fewer big empty spaces and less clustering, falsely giving the impression of increased randomness.

![Figure 16.7 Rayleigh test to assess if a point distribution matches that of a Poisson process.](images/B9780443218576000205/gr013.jpg)

Figure 16.7 Rayleigh test to assess if a point distribution matches that of a Poisson process.

#### 16.3.2.4 Exercises

The following exercises are a useful complement to the theory, and should be considered part of the core material. This section provides a simple introduction to **covering problems** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disk_covering_problem)\] and stochastic geometry.

Exercise 16.3

Distribution of nearest neighbor distances. In two dimensions, *T* = *T*(*λ*, *s*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si242.png) represents the distance between a point of the process and its **nearest neighbor**.

*   •  Prove that when *s* → ∞![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si8.png), the limiting distribution of *T* is **Rayleigh** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rayleigh_distribution)\] of mean $\\frac{1}{2\\lambda}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si243.png).
*   •  Show by simulations or logical arguments, that unlike in the one-dimensional case, *E*\[*T*\]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si244.png) depends on *s*.
*   •  Also, show that depending on *F*, the maximum **nearest neighbor distance**, computed over the infinitely many points of the process, can have a finite expectation. Is this true too when *s* → ∞![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si8.png), that is, for stationary Poisson point processes?
*   •  Finally, what is *T*'s distribution if *T* is replaced by the distance between an arbitrary location in ℝ²![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si166.png), and its closest neighbor among the points of the process?

**Solution**

In two dimensions, the fact that *E*\[*T*(*λ*, *s*)\]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si245.png) depends on *s*, is obvious: if *s* = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si10.png), it is equal to $\\frac{1}{\\lambda}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si246.png), and if *s* = ∞![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si106.png), it is equal to $\\frac{1}{2\\lambda}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si243.png). Between these two extremes, there is a continuum of values, of course depending on *s*. The maximum nearest neighbor distance (over all the infinitely many points) always has a finite expectation if *F* is uniform, regardless of *s* < ∞![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si247.png). To the contrary, for a Poisson point process, the maximum is infinite, see [here](https://mathoverflow.net/questions/412891/maximum-nearest-neighbor-distance-for-a-poisson-point-process/412895#412895).

Now let us prove that *T* has a Rayleigh distribution when *s* = ∞![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si106.png), corresponding to a Poisson process of intensity *λ*²![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si1.png). We have *P*(*T* > *y*) = *P*\[*N*(*B*) = 0\]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si249.png), where *B* is a disc of radius *y* centered at an arbitrary point of the process, and *N* is the **point count**, with an exponential distribution of mean *λ*²*μ*(*B*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si250.png) with *μ*(*B*) = *π**y*²![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si251.png) being the area of *B*. Thus *P*(*T* > *y*) = exp ( − *λ*²*π**y*²)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si252.png), that is, *P*(*T* < *y*) = 1 − exp ( − *λ*²*π**y*²)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si253.png). This is the CDF of a Rayleigh distribution of mean $\\frac{1}{2\\lambda}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si243.png).

Exercise 16.4

Cell networks: coverage problem. Points are randomly distributed on the plane, with an average of *λ* points per unit area. A circle of radius *R* is drawn around each point. What is the proportion of the plane covered by these (possibly overlapping) circles? What if *R* is a random variable, so that we are dealing with random circles? Such **stochastic covering problems** are part of **stochastic geometry** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stochastic_geometry)\] [\[14](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#br0070),[40\]](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#br0200). See also Hall's book on coverings [\[21\]](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#br0105). Applications include wireless networks \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stochastic_geometry_models_of_wireless_networks)\].

**Solution**

The points are distributed according to a Poisson point process of intensity *λ*. The probability that an arbitrary location *x* in the plane is not covered by any circle is the probability that there is zero point from the process, in a circle of radius *R* centered at *x*. This is equal to exp ( − *λ**π**R*²)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si254.png). Thus the proportion of the plane covered by the circles is 1 − exp ( − *λ**π**R*²)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si255.png). Now, let us say that we have two types of circles: one with radius *R*[1]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si256.png), and one with radius *R*[2]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si257.png), each type equally likely to be picked up. This is like having two independent, superimposed Poisson processes, each with intensity *λ*/2![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si258.png), one for each type of circle. Now the probability *p* that *x* is not covered by any circle is thus a product of two probabilities:
