$p = \\exp\\left( - \\frac{\\lambda}{2}\\pi R\_{1}^{2} \\right) \\times \\exp\\left( - \\frac{\\lambda}{2}\\pi R\_{1}^{2} \\right) = \\exp\\left( - \\lambda\\pi\\frac{R\_{1}^{2} + R\_{2}^{2}}{2} \\right).$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si259.png)

You can generalize to *m* types of circles, each type with a radius *R*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si260.png) and probability *p*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si261.png) to be picked up, with 1 ≤ *k* ≤ *m*![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si262.png). It leads to

$1 - p = 1 - \\exp\\left\\lbrack - \\lambda\\pi\\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{m}p\_{k}R\_{k}^{2} \\right\\rbrack,$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si263.png)(16.14) 

which is the proportion of the plane covered by at least one circle. If *R*, the radius of the circle, is a continuous random variable, the sum in formula [(16.14)](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#deq20) must be replaced by *E*\[*R*²\]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si264.png). A related topic is the smallest circle problem \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smallest-circle_problem)\]. See also [\[36\]](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#br0180).

## 16.4 Special topics

This section covers special topics of interest, that do not fit well in the previous sections. Minimum contrast estimation is a powerful, yet simple, inference technique applicable to many problems, especially when the true parameters are impossible to compute, buried into some hidden layer, or face identifiability problems. This topic is discussed in Chapter [18](#Chp018_361-386_B9780443218576000229.xhtml) (Section [18.3.5](#Chp018_361-386_B9780443218576000229.xhtml)). Here I focus on the specifics related to perturbed-lattice point processes. Identifiability issues and the hidden model (the lattice) are also discussed in this section.

### 16.4.1 Minimum contrast estimation and explainable AI

The idea behind **minimum contrast estimation** is to use proxy statistics as substitutes for the parameter estimators. It makes sense here as it is not clear what combination of variables represents *s*. The goal is to estimate (*λ*, *s*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si219.png) using proxy parameters (*p*, *q*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si265.png) to be defined shortly, then map (*p*, *q*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si265.png) back to (*λ*, *s*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si219.png) to get the estimates that we are interested in. In particular, (*λ*, *s*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si219.png) – the intensity and scaling factor – is easy to interpret while (*p*, *q*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si265.png) is rather obscure. Thus estimates of (*λ*, *s*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si219.png) lead to explainable AI, while (*p*, *q*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si265.png) do not.

For simplicity, I consider one-dimensional Poisson–binomial processes. The observations consist of 2*n* + 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si266.png) points *X*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si29.png) (*k* =  − *n*, …, *n*![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si267.png)), realization of a one-dimensional Poisson–binomial process of intensity *λ* and scaling factor *s*, obtained by simulation. I chose a logistic *F* in the simulation. Unless *F* has an unusually thick or thin tail, it has little impact on the point distribution. Let

$R = \\frac{1}{2n + 1}\\left\\lbrack \\max\\limits\_{|k| \\leqslant n}X\_{k} - \\min\\limits\_{|k| \\leqslant n}X\_{k} \\right\\rbrack,$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si268.png)(16.15) 

$B\_{k} = \\left\\lbrack \\frac{k}{R},\\frac{k + 1}{R}\\left\\lbrack ,\\quad k = - n,\\ldots,n - 1, \\right. \\right.$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si269.png)(16.16) 

and

$p = \\frac{1}{2n}\\sum\\limits\_{k = - n}^{n - 1}\\chi\\lbrack N(B\_{k}) = 0\\rbrack,\\quad q = \\frac{1}{2n}\\sum\\limits\_{k = - n}^{n - 1}\\chi\\lbrack N(B\_{k}) = 1\\rbrack,$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si270.png)(16.17) 

where *χ* is the indicator function \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indicator_function)\] and *N*(*B*[*k*])![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si271.png) is the number of points in *B*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si195.png). If there is a one-to-one mapping between (*λ*, *s*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si219.png) and (*p*, *q*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si265.png), then one can easily compute (*p*, *q*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si265.png) using formula [(16.17)](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#deq23) applied to the observed data, and then retrieve (*λ*, *s*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si219.png) via the inverse mapping. It is even possible to build 2D confidence regions for the bivariate parameter (*λ*, *s*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si219.png). The method is highly generic (not specific to point processes) and thus, all the details are found in Sections [18.3](#Chp018_361-386_B9780443218576000229.xhtml) (confidence regions) and [18.3.5](#Chp018_361-386_B9780443218576000229.xhtml) (minimum contrast estimation).

### 16.4.2 Model identifiability, hard-to-detect patterns

Poisson–binomial and related point processes such as *m***\-interlacings**, exhibit many hard-to-detect patterns. Some cannot even be detected with statistical tests. Depending on model parameters, many are not visible to the naked eye. In some cases, this is due to **identifiability**: two apparently different models, with different sets of parameters, are statistically identical and indistinguishable from each other. Most of the times though, the differences are real but subtle or imperceptible. To the contrary, on occasions, the naked eye perceives differences when there are none, akin to visual illusions. Examples of hard-to-detect differences include:

*   •  Discriminating between two different *F*'s (the distribution attached to the points), for instance, logistic versus Gaussian or Cauchy, unless *s* is very small.
*   •  If *s* is large, the process is hard to distinguish from a stationary Poisson process.
*   •  Point count statistics (expectation, variance and so on) are periodic, but amplitudes are extremely small.
*   •  The cluster structure in *m*\-interlacings may be invisible unless some transformation is applied: see the left plot in [Fig. 16.8](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#f0055). **Nearest neighbor distances** are generally better at detecting differences, compared to point counts.

![Figure 16.8 Realization of a 5-interlacing with s = 0.15 and λ = 1: original (left), modulo 2/λ (right).](images/B9780443218576000205/gr014.jpg)

Figure 16.8 Realization of a 5-interlacing with *s* = 0.15 and *λ* = 1: original (left), modulo 2/*λ* (right).

*   
*   •  Unless *s* is very small, it may be impossible to detect if the underlying lattice is square or hexagonal, or if we are dealing with an *m*\-interlacing or a mixture of Poisson–binomial processes.

To the contrary, in some cases, the naked eye perceives nonexistent differences, for instance, the fact that the right plot in [Fig. 16.6](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#f0040) has fewer points than the left, when in fact they both have the same number. In fact, the Poisson–binomial model is a good framework to test and benchmark statistical techniques in contexts that require a very high level of precision. For instance, those aimed at detecting exoplanets, early signs of cancer, or subtle patterns in the stock market.

#### 16.4.2.1 Stochastic residues

Each individual process of an *m*\-interlacing has its own shift vector, which determines the center of a cluster. By translation, the cluster is stochastically replicated around each lattice location. As a result, for statistical inference, it is customary to study the process (the observed data) modulo 2/*λ*![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si272.png) or 1/*λ*![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si38.png), where statistical patterns are magnified and easier to detect. By modulo 2/*λ*![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si272.png), I mean the following: instead of studying the original points (*X*, *Y*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si101.png), we focus on (*X* *m**o**d* 2/*λ*, *Y* *m**o**d* 2/*λ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si273.png). The transformed data, after the modulo operation, is called the residual data, or **stochastic residues**. The fact that there are *m* = 5![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si228.png) clusters (albeit with huge overlap) in [Fig. 16.8](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#f0055) is apparent on the right plot featuring the residues, but not on the left plot. Typically, in the context of unsupervised clustering, we do not known which individual process a point *m*\-interlacing belongs to.

Remark

The modulo operator is defined as *α* *m**o**d* *β* = *α* − *β* ⋅ ⌊*α*/*β*⌋![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si274.png), where the brackets represent the floor function (also called integer function \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Floor_and_ceiling_functions)\]). It is identical to that used in modular arithmetic \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modular_arithmetic)\], except that here *α*, *β*![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si275.png) are usually real numbers rather than integers.

### 16.4.3 Hidden model and random permutations

In one dimension, the unobserved index *k* attached to any point *X*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si29.png) of the Poisson–binomial point process gives rise to an interesting random process called the **hidden process** or index process. It can be used to generate infinite, locally random permutations (here in one dimension), using the following algorithm:

Algorithm

Generate a locally random permutation of order *m*.

*   Step 1: Generate a 1D realization of a Poisson–binomial process with 2*n* + 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si266.png) points *X*[ − *n*], …, *X*[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si276.png). 
    *   Let *L*(*X*[*k*]) = *k*![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si277.png), for  − *n* ≤ *k* ≤ *n*![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si278.png). The function *L* is stored as a **hash table** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hash_table)\] in your source code; the keys of your hash table are the *X*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si29.png)'s. In practice, no two *X*[*h*], *X*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si279.png) with *h* ≠ *k*![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si280.png) have the same value *X*[*h*] = *X*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si281.png), so this collision problem will not arise.
*   Step 2: Sort the 2*n* + 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si266.png) points *X*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si29.png), with  − *n* ≤ *k* ≤ *n*![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si278.png). 
    *   Denote as *X*[(*k*)]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si282.png) the *k*th point after ordering.
*   Step 3: Select *m* consecutive ordered points, say *X*[(1)], …, *X*[(*m*)]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si283.png) with *m* much smaller than *n*. 
    *   Retrieve their original indices: *σ*(*k*) = *L*(*X*[(*k*)])![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si284.png), *k* = 1, …, *m*![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si285.png).
    *   Set *τ*(*k*) = *L*(*X*[(*k* + 1)])![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si286.png), *k* = 1, …, *m*![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si285.png) (so *X*[*τ*(*k*)]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si287.png) is the closest point to *X*[*σ*(*k*)]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si288.png), to the right).

 Now *σ* is a **random permutation** on {1, …, *m*}![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si289.png) \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Random_permutation)\]. To produce the plots in [Fig. 16.9](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#f0060), I used *m* = 10³![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si290.png), *n* = 3 × 10⁴![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si291.png), and a Poisson-0binomial process with *λ* = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si49.png), *s* = 3![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si292.png), and a logistic distribution for *F*. Since the theory is designed to produce infinite rather than finite permutations, **boundary effects** can take place. To minimize them, take both *m* and *n* large. The boundary effects, if present (for instance when using a thick tail distribution for *F* such as Cauchy, or when using a large *s*) will be most noticeable for *σ*(*k*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si293.png) when *k* is close to 1 or close to *m*.

![Figure 16.9 Locally random permutation σ; τ(k) is the index of Xk's closest neighbor to the right.](images/B9780443218576000205/gr015.jpg)

Figure 16.9 Locally random permutation *σ*; *τ*(*k*) is the index of *X*[*k*]'s closest neighbor to the right.

These permutations can be used to model local reshuffling in a long series of events. Effects are mostly local, but tend to spread to longer distances on average, when *s* is large or *F* has a thick tail. For instance, in [Fig. 16.9](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#f0060), the biggest shift in absolute value is *σ*(*k*) − *k* = 35![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si294.png), occurring at *k* = 108![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si295.png) (see the peak on the left plot). However, peaks (or abysses) of arbitrary height will occur if *m* is large enough, unless you use a uniform distribution for *F*, or any distribution with a finite support domain.

The right plot in [Fig. 16.9](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#f0060) shows the joint empirical distribution (data-based as opposed to theoretical) of the discrepancies *σ*(*k*) − *k*![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si296.png) and *τ*(*k*) − *k*![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si297.png) in the index space ℤ × ℤ![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si298.png). Of course, since the index *τ*(*k*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si299.png) points to the closest neighbor of *X*[*σ*(*k*)]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si288.png) to the right, that is, to *X*[*τ*(*k*)]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si287.png), we have *τ*(*k*) ≥ 1 + *σ*(*k*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si300.png), which explains why the main diagonal is blank. Other than that, the plot shows independence, symmetry, and **anisotropy** (absence of directional trend in the scattering). It means that

*   •  Given a point *X*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si29.png), the index *τ*(*k*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si299.png) of its nearest neighbor to the right is randomly distributed around *k*, according to some radial distribution;
*   •  Given a point *X*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si29.png), its order *σ*(*k*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si293.png) once the points are ordered, is randomly distributed around *k*, according to the same radial distribution;
*   •  There is independence between the two.

Two metrics used to compare or describe these permutations are the average and maximum **index discrepancy**, measured as the average and maximum value of |*σ*(*k*) − *k*|![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si301.png) for 1 ≤ *k* ≤ *m*![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si262.png). It gets larger as *s* increases. Another metric of interest, related to the **entropy** of the permutation \[[Wiki](https://www.aptech.com/blog/permutation-entropy/)\] [\[43\]](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#br0215), is the correlation between the integer numbers *k* and *σ*(*k*) − *k*![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si296.png), computed over *k* = 1, …, *m*![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si285.png). While the example featured in [Fig. 16.9](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#f0060) exhibits essentially a zero correlation, some other cases not reported here, exhibit a strong correlation. See also [\[2\]](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#br0010). For an elementary introduction to permutations, see [\[7\]](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#br0035).

### 16.4.4 Retrieving the *F* distribution

For simplicity, let us assume that we are dealing with a one-dimensional Poisson–binomial process. It is difficult if not impossible to retrieve the common distribution *F* attached to each point *X*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si29.png). However, see Section [16.4.4.2](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#s0165). In many cases, two different *F*'s result in essentially the same model, causing **identifiability** issues. The situation if much easier if *s* is very small, small enough that $|X\_{k} - \\frac{k}{\\lambda}| < \\frac{1}{2\\lambda}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si302.png) for most *k* ∈ ℤ![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si30.png). Then the index attached to a point *X*, usually unknown, is now equal to

$\\left. L(X) = \\underset{k\\in\\mathbb{Z}}{\\arg⁡\\min} \\middle| X - \\frac{k}{\\lambda} \\middle| . \\right.$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si303.png)

That is, *X* = *X*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si304.png) with *k* = *L*(*X*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si305.png). See definition of arg min ![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si306.png) [here](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arg_max). This assumes that *λ* and *s* are known or estimated. In this particular situation, empirical distribution of *s**X* − *s**L*(*X*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si307.png) computed over many points *X*, converges to *F* as the number of observed points tends to infinity.

A more practical situation is when one has to decide which *F* provides the best fit to the data, given a few potential candidates for *F*. In that case, one may compute (using simulations) the theoretical expectation *η*(*r*, *λ*, *s*, *F*) = *E*\[*T*^(*r*)(*λ*, *s*)\]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si308.png) as a function of *r* > 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si169.png) for various *F*'s, and find which *F* provides the best fit to the estimated *E*\[*T*^(*r*)(*λ*, *s*)\]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si309.png), denoted as *η*[0](*r*, *λ*, *s*, *F*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si310.png) and computed on the data (the expectation being replaced by an average when computed on the data). By best fit, I mean finding *F* that minimizes (say)

*γ*(*F*) = ∫[0]²|*η*(*r*, *λ*, *s*, *F*) − *η*[0](*r*, *λ*, *s*, *F*)|*d**r*.

![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si311.png)(16.18) 

Again, *s* and *λ* should be estimated first. The statistic *T*(*λ*, *s*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si170.png) is the **interarrival time** or distance between a point and its closest neighbor the right (in one dimension). However, a simultaneous estimation of *λ*, *s*, *F*![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si312.png) is feasible and consists of finding the parameters *λ*, *s*, *F*![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si312.png) minimizing *γ*(*F*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si313.png), now denoted as *γ*(*λ*, *s*, *F*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si314.png). See Section [16.3.1](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#s0085) to estimate *λ* and *s* separately: this stepwise procedure is simpler and less prone to **overfitting** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overfitting)\].

The estimation technique introduced here, especially formula [(16.18)](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#deq25), is sometimes referred to as **minimum contrast estimation**. See slides 114–116 in the presentation entitled “Introduction to Spatial Point Processes and Simulation-Based Inference”, by Jesper Møller [\[31\]](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#br0155).

#### 16.4.4.1 Theoretical values obtained by simulations

This section highlights some simulation results obtained with [PB\_main.py](https://github.com/VincentGranville/Point-Processes/blob/main/Source%20Code/PB_main.py) to compute moments *E*\[*T*^(*r*)\]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si315.png) of the interarrival times *T* = *T*(*λ*, *s*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si242.png) for various *λ*, *s*![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si316.png), as well as statistics related to the point count (random variable) *N*(*B*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si19.png), where *B* = \[*a*, *b*\]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si317.png) is an interval. The goal is to:

*   •  Show that except if *F* has a finite support or *s* is very small, the choice of *F* has very little impact;
*   •  Show how fast the Poisson–binomial process converges to a stationary Poisson process as *s* increases; 
*   •  Show that any point of the process can be used to compute the *theoretical distribution* of *T*, thus choosing *X*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si318.png) or any *X*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si29.png), or averaging over many points, yields the same theoretical distribution;
*   •  Show that you can use one realization of the process with many points, or many realizations of the process, each with few points, to compute the theoretical distribution of *T*.

The last fact illustrates the **ergodicity** of *T*.

[Table 16.2](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#t0015) shows simulation results based on *λ* = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si49.png), *r* = 1/2![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si321.png) and *B* = \[*a*, *b*\]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si317.png) with *a* =  − 0.75![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si322.png) and *b* = 0.75![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si323.png). Three different *F* were tested: uniform, logistic, and Cauchy. The notation *μ*(*B*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si324.png) stands for *b* − *a*![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si325.png). In two dimensions, it represents the area of the set *B* (typically, a square or a circle). In one dimension, when *s* = ∞![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si106.png), *N*(*B*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si19.png) has a Poisson distribution of expectation *λ**μ*(*B*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si326.png), and *T* has an exponential distribution of expectation 1/*λ*![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si38.png). The limiting process is a stationary Poisson process of intensity *λ*. The exact formula for $E\\lbrack\\sqrt{T}\\rbrack$![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si319.png), when *s* = ∞![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si106.png), was obtained with the online version of Mathematica: you can check the computation, [here](https://bit.ly/30t354T). In general, convergence to the Poisson process, when *s* → ∞![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si8.png), is slower and more bumpy if *F* is uniform, compared to using a logistic or Cauchy distribution for *F*.

#### 16.4.4.2 Retrieving *F* from the interarrival times distribution

I assume here that *F* has a density *f*, and we are dealing with a one-dimensional Poisson–binomial process. The random variable *T*(*λ*, *s*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si170.png) measuring the distance between a point and the closest neighbor to the right on the X axis is called the interarrival time. Given the limit distribution of the standardized interarrival times, the purpose is to retrieve the distribution of *F*. If you are familiar with the concept of **characteristic function** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Characteristic_function_\(probability_theory\))\], this exercise is easy. If not, you should first get familiar with this concept. The theorems referred to are from my book “Stochastic Processes and Simulation: A Machine Learning Approach”.

The **standardized interarrival times** is defined as $\\frac{1}{s}\\lbrack T(\\lambda,s) - \\frac{1}{\\lambda}\\rbrack$![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si327.png) and has zero expectation by virtue of Theorem 4.3. By virtue of Theorem 4.2, it can be rewritten as $\\frac{1}{\\lambda s}\\lbrack T(1,\\lambda s) - 1\\rbrack$![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si328.png). Its limit, as *s* → 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si329.png), is denoted as *T*^(\*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si330.png). One of the simplest cases, besides Gaussian and Cauchy, is the following: If *T*^(\*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si330.png) has a standard **Laplace distribution** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laplace_distribution)\] (that is, symmetric centered at zero, and with variance *π*²/3![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si135.png)), show that *F* is a **modified Bessel distribution** of the second kind [\[35\]](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#br0175). Note that as a consequence of L'Hôpital's rule \[[Wiki](https://bit.ly/3sQXEbL)\], *T*^(\*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si330.png) is the derivative of *T*(*λ*, *s*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si170.png) with respect to *s*, evaluated at *s* = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si10.png).

By virtue of Theorem 4.4, we have

*P*(*T*^(\*) < *y*) = ∫[ − ∞]^∞*F*(*y* − *x*)*f*(*x*)*d**x*,

![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si331.png)

which is a **convolution** of *F* with itself. Thus *T*^(\*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si330.png) has the distribution of the sum of two independent random variables, say *Z*[1], *Z*[2]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si332.png), of distribution *F*. Its characteristic function is therefore

$E\\lbrack\\exp( - itT^{\\ast})\\rbrack = \\frac{1}{1 + t^{2}} = E\\lbrack\\exp( - itZ\_{1})\\rbrack \\times E\\lbrack\\exp( - itZ\_{2})\\rbrack = \\left( E\\lbrack\\exp( - itZ\_{1})\\rbrack \\right)^{2}.$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si333.png)

Thus *E*\[exp ( − *i**t**Z*[1])\] = (1 + *t*²)^( − 1/2)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si334.png). Taking the inverse **Fourier transform** to retrieve the density of *Z*[1]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si335.png), which is the density attached to *F*, one finds

$f(x) = \\frac{1}{2\\pi}\\int\_{- \\infty}^{\\infty}\\frac{\\cos(tx)}{\\sqrt{1 + t^{2}}}dt = \\frac{1}{\\pi}K\_{0}(x),$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si336.png)

where *K*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si337.png) is the modified **Bessel function** of the second kind \[[Wiki](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/ModifiedBesselFunctionoftheSecondKind.xhtml)\]. More about the Laplace distribution and its generalization can be found in [\[25\]](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#br0125). The cases when *T*^(\*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si330.png) is Gaussian or Cauchy are easy because these distributions belong to **stable families of distributions** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stable_distribution)\]: in that case, *F* is respectively Gaussian or Cauchy.

### 16.4.5 Record distances between an observed point and its vertex

[Fig. 16.10](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#f0065) shows the points (*X*[*h*], *Y*[*k*])![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si4.png) of a Poisson–binomial process with a logistic *F*, in blue. Their lattice vertices (*h*/*λ*, *k*/*λ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si96.png) are shown with little red crosses. The arrows connected both. Here, *λ* = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si49.png). This picture shows how far away a point can be from the **vertex** it is attached to. If *s* = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si10.png), both locations coincide, but when *s* is large, the distances can be arbitrarily large.

![Figure 16.10 Each arrow links a point (blue) to its vertex (red): s = 0.2 (left), s = 1 (right).](images/B9780443218576000205/gr016.jpg)

Figure 16.10 Each arrow links a point (blue) to its vertex (red): *s* = 0.2 (left), *s* = 1 (right).

Note that both plots (left and right in [Fig. 16.10](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#f0065)) have the same number of points. But points are clustered in some areas, and sparse in other areas on the right plot, giving the impression that there are fewer of them. Clearly, the empirical distribution of the distance between nearest neighbors (especially extreme distances), or the average area of the largest empty zone, can be used to estimate the **scaling factor** *s* once *λ* is known or estimated.

This brings me to my next discussion, namely **extreme values**, or **records**. This is part of a field know as **order statistics** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_statistic)\] or extreme value theory \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extreme_value_theory)\]. Extreme values are different from **outliers** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outlier)\]: they can be predictable, with known distribution. To the contrary, outliers are usually considered as errors, glitches, or data points obeying a different model. In any case, both have an impact on the window of observations, delimited by the “boundary”, and have the potential to introduce biases.

One question is how far a point can be from its vertex, and how frequently such “extremes” occur. Even more interesting is the reverse question, associated to the inverse or **hidden model**: can a point (*X*[*h*], *Y*[*k*])![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si4.png) close to the origin, well within the small window of observations, have its vertex very far away? Such a point will not be generated by the point process simulator. It will be unaccounted for, introducing a bias. This happens with increased frequency as *s* increases, requiring a larger and larger observation window.

Unless *F* has a finite support domain (for instance, if *F* is uniform), unobserved points in the small window of observations – even though their expected number is finite and rather small – can be attached to any arbitrary vertex, no matter how far away. In two dimensions, the probability *P*\[*R* > *r*\]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si338.png) that the distance *R* between a point and its lattice location is greater than *r* is

$P(R > r) = \\int\_{- \\infty}^{\\infty}\\int\_{- \\infty}^{\\infty}\\chi(x^{2} + y^{2} > r)F\\left( \\frac{x}{s} \\right)F\\left( \\frac{y}{s} \\right)dxdy,$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si339.png)

where *χ*(*A*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si340.png) is the indicator function, equal to one if *A* is true, and to zero otherwise.

The distance *R* corresponds to the length of the arrow, in [Fig. 16.10](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#f0065). If *F* is Gaussian, then *R* has a **Rayleigh distribution** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rayleigh_distribution)\]. In two dimensions, the distance between two nearest neighbor points, for a stationary Poisson point process, also has a Rayleigh distribution, see Section [16.3.2.3](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#s0120) and [Exercise 16.3](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#enun0025).

#### 16.4.5.1 Distribution of records

Now let *M*[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si341.png) be the maximum distance between a point and its vertex, measured over *n* points of the process, randomly selected. In other words *M*[*n*] = max (*R*[1], …, *R*[*n*])![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si342.png) where *R*[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si343.png) (*i* = 1, …, *n*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si344.png) is the distance between the *i*th point, and its vertex. Depending on *F*, the standardized distribution of *M*[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si341.png) is asymptotically **Weibull**, Gumbel, or Fréchet: these are the tree potential **attractor distributions** in the context of extreme value theory \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extreme_value_theory)\]. The Rayleigh distribution is a particular case of the Weibull distribution. Surprisingly, in *d* dimensions, the distribution of the **nearest neighbor distances**, for a stationary Poisson point process, is also Weibull, see Section [16.3.2](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#s0105).

[Fig. 16.11](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#f0070) shows (on the Y-axis) the distance *R* between a point (*X*[*h*], *Y*[*k*])![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si4.png) and its vertex (*h*/*λ*, *k*/*λ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si96.png). These are the same points as on the right plot in [Fig. 16.10](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#f0065); *R* represents the length of the arrows. The points are ordered by how close they are to the origin (0, 0)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si345.png), and the X-axis represents their distance to the origin, that is, their norm. By looking at [Fig. 16.11](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#f0070), it is easy to visualize the extreme values of *R*, and when they occur on the X-axis.

![Figure 16.11 Distance between a point and its vertex (λ = s = 1).](images/B9780443218576000205/gr017.jpg)

Figure 16.11 Distance between a point and its vertex (*λ* = *s* = 1).

#### 16.4.5.2 Distribution of arrival times for records

Now let us assume that *n* is infinite, and let us look at the arrival times of the successive records in the sequence *R*[1], *R*[2], *R*[3]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si346.png), and so on. The *i*th arrival time is denoted as *L*[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si347.png) with *L*[1] = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si348.png), and defined as follows: *L*[*i* + 1] = min {*j* : *R*[*j*] > *R*[*L*[*i*]]}![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si349.png). In other words, the *i*th record is *R*[*L*[*i*]]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si350.png). The random variable *L*[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si347.png) has the following properties:

*   •  The distribution of *L*[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si347.png) does not depend on *F*.
*   •  Let *η*[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si351.png) be the probability that *R*[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si343.png) is a record. The *η*[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si351.png)'s are independent Bernoulli random variables, and *P*(*η*[*i*] = 1) = 1/*i*![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si352.png).
*   •  *P*(*L*[*i*] ≥ *m*) = *P*(*η*[1] + *η*[2] + ⋯ + *η*[*m*] ≤ *i*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si353.png). We are again dealing with a **Poisson–binomial distribution** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poisson_binomial_distribution)\].
*   •  *E*\[*L*[*i*]\] = ∞![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si354.png) if *i* > 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si355.png). However, *E*\[log *L*[*i*]\] ∼ *i* − *γ*![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si356.png) as *i* → ∞![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si357.png), where *γ* = 0.5772…![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si358.png) is the Euler–Mascheroni constant \[[Wiki](https://bit.ly/35eVQQl)\].
*   •  *V**a**r*\[log *L*[*i*]\] ∼ *i* − *π*²/6![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si359.png) as *i* → ∞![Image](images/B9780443218576000205/si357.png).

These results, and many others, are found in Chapter 19 (*A Record of Records*) in Balakrishnan handbook entitled “Order Statistics: Theory & Methods” [\[5\]](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml#br0025); see pages 517–525.

# Chapter 17: Synthetizing multiplicative functions in number theory

## New perspective on the Riemann Hypothesis

## Abstract

Machine learning relies on mathematics to solve real-life problems. But what if you switched the roles and relied on machine learning to solve or at least explore pure mathematical problems? This is the subject of **experimental mathematics**. Over the years, I made considerable progress tackling famous conjectures using this approach. In addition, I leveraged mathematical objects such as functions or numbers, to build infinite **synthetic data sets** with an infinite number of features, to test and benchmark new machine learning techniques, and to produce new types of animated data videos. Here I share the culmination of this research, to address one of the most famous mathematical problems in number theory. Some of this material is used in Section [11.2.1](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml) to design a strong test of randomness. Also, the number-theoretic “synthetic data” discussed here is used in Section [4.2.3](#Chp004_61-82_B9780443218576000084.xhtml) to illustrate a simple, yet efficient, probabilistic clustering method in machine learning, to handle massive cluster overlap.

This chapter provides a solid introduction to the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis and related functions, including Dirichlet series, Euler products, noninteger primes (Beurling primes), Dirichlet characters, and Rademacher random multiplicative functions. The topic is usually explained in obscure jargon or inane generalities. To the contrary, this presentation will intrigue you with the beauty and power of this theory. The summary style is very compact, covering much more than traditionally taught in a first graduate course in analytic number theory. The choice of the topics is a little biased, with an emphasis on probabilistic models. My approach, discussing the “hole of the orbit” – called the eye of the Riemann zeta function in a previous article – is particularly intuitive.

The accompanying Python code covers a large class of interesting functions to allow you to perform as many different experiments as possible. If you are interested in knowing a lot more than the basics and possibly investigating this conjecture using machine learning techniques, this chapter is for you. The Python code also shows you how to produce beautiful videos of the various functions involved, in particular their orbits. This visual exploration shows that the Riemann zeta function (based on the trivial character *χ*), and a specific Dirichlet-*L* function (based on the nontrivial character *χ*[4]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si1.png)), behave very uniquely and similarly, explaining the connection between the Riemann and the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, in pictures and videos rather than words.

### Keywords

synthetic function; multiplicative number theory; multiplicative function; number theory; Riemann Hypothesis; orbit Dirichlet function

## 17.1 Introduction

Let *z* = *σ* + *i**t*![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si2.png) be a complex number: *σ* is the real part, and *t* is the imaginary part. Let *P* be a set of numbers, called primes: an element of *P* cannot be factored into a product of elements of *P*. In some sense, numbers are to molecules what primes are to atoms. Typically, but not always, *P* is the standard set of all prime numbers, or a subset of it, either finite or infinite. Finally, *p* represents an element of *P* and *χ*(*p*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si3.png) is any function taking on two possible values: +1 or −1 depending on *p*. The function *χ*( ⋅ )![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si4.png) is extended outside *P* using the formula *χ*(*a**b*) = *χ*(*a*)*χ*(*b*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si5.png), with *χ*(1) = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si6.png).

This chapter summarizes known properties and conjectures about various functions of *z* that can be represented by the following product, called Euler product:

$\\prod\\limits\_{p \\in P}\\frac{1}{1 - \\chi(p)p^{- z}}.$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si7.png)

The most well-known example is when the function *χ*( ⋅ )![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si4.png) is constant (thus equal to 1) and *P* is the full set of prime integers: this corresponds to the Riemann zeta function *ζ*(*z*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si8.png). When expanded into a series, the Euler product becomes what is called a Dirichlet series. The series and product may not convergence on the same domain; when the series is conditionally but not **absolutely convergent** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Absolute_convergence)\] the product can diverge. This typically happens if *σ* < 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si9.png). It is the source of considerable difficulties, and the reason why the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis (GRH) is unproven to this day. Also, this explains why all the action takes place when $\\frac{1}{2} \\leqslant \\sigma < 1$![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si10.png).

I will not discuss complex analysis in details here. It is sufficient to know that if *z* = *σ* + *i**t*![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si2.png), then *p*^( − *z*) = exp ( − *z*log *p*) = *p*^( − *σ*)cos (*t*log *p*) − *i**p*^( − *σ*)sin (*t*log *p*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si11.png). Also, the factors in the Euler product are ordered by increasing values of *p*. Without this specification, the product may be subject to multiple interpretations with different values, when convergence is conditional but not absolute. An introduction to the Riemann zeta and Dirichlet functions can be found in [\[4\]](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#br0020) and [\[18\]](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#br0090). Finally, I occasionally use the term conditionally or absolutely convergent product. This intuitive concept is defined [here](https://encyclopediaofmath.org/wiki/Infinite_product).

### 17.1.1 Key concepts and terminology

The complex plane is the standard two-dimensional space: the real axis is the horizontal or X-axis; the imaginary axis is the vertical or Y-axis. The Riemann Hypothesis (RH) states that the Riemann zeta function *ζ*(*z*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si8.png) defined earlier, has no root (that is, *ζ*(*z*) ≠ 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si12.png)) if $\\frac{1}{2} < \\sigma < z$![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si13.png). I use the notation *σ* = ℜ(*z*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si14.png) to indicate that *σ* is the real part of the complex number *z* = *σ* + *i**t*![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si2.png). Throughout this text, a positive number is a number ⩾0. A number >0 is called strictly positive.

The Generalized Riemann Hypothesis (GRH) makes the same statement as RH, for a larger class of well behaved functions, not just *ζ*(*z*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si8.png). In short, it applies to Dirichlet functions where *χ*( ⋅ )![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si4.png) is completely multiplicative and periodic; these are called Dirichlet-*L* functions. Here, we limit ourselves to *χ*(*p*) ∈ { − 1,  + 1}![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si15.png). However, we also consider *χ*( ⋅ )![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si4.png)'s that are not periodic. The classic nontrivial periodic *χ*( ⋅ )![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si4.png) is *χ* = *χ*[4]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si16.png), the nontrivial Dirichlet character modulo 4. It leads to an Euler product suspected to converge if $\\sigma > \\frac{1}{2}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si17.png). Proving the convergence, even only at *σ* = 0.99![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si18.png), would be a major milestone towards proving GRH. Of course, the product converges if *σ* > 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si19.png). If *χ*( ⋅ )![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si4.png) is allowed not to be periodic, there are known cases, discussed in this chapter, that meet the requirements of GRH. Typically, these functions are much less interesting and do not satisfy a Dirichlet-like functional equation.

### 17.1.2 Orbits and holes

An original concept, the hole of the orbit of a Dirichlet function, is introduced in this chapter for the first time. It is epitomized in [Fig. 17.1](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#f0010) dealing with finite Euler products, and in [Fig. 17.5](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#f0030) featuring the orbit of truncated Dirichlet series (the truncated expansion of an infinite product or, in other words, the partial sums). In the RH and GRH contexts, the hole is present if $\\frac{1}{2} < \\sigma < 1$![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si20.png) is fixed and 0 < *t* < *T*![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si21.png) is bounded. But as *T* → ∞![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si22.png), the hole shrinks to a singleton at the origin in the absence of roots ($\\frac{1}{2} < \\sigma < 1$![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si20.png)), or to an empty set if roots are present ($\\sigma = \\frac{1}{2}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si24.png)). Studying modified Dirichlet functions that always have a hole may be key to making progress towards RH and GRH. In particular, it is interesting to study the behavior at their limit as they approach standard Dirichlet functions, and the hole slowly evaporates. This is the topic of Sections [17.3.1](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#s0065) and [17.3.3](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#s0095).

![Figure 17.1 Three orbits (σ = 0.5,0.75,1.25) with finite Euler product: P = {2,3} (left) vs {2,3,5} (right).](images/B9780443218576000217/gr001.jpg)

Figure 17.1 Three orbits (*σ* = 0.5,0.75,1.25) with finite Euler product: *P* = {2,3} (left) vs {2,3,5} (right).

The hole is a circle of maximum radius, with center on the X-axis (due to symmetry), that the orbit never crosses. The center of the hole may not be at the origin (see Section [17.2.2.1](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#s0050) for examples), even when there is no root. The absence of root can be caused by a hole, or because the orbit never gets too close to the Y-axis. The orbit on a fixed domain 0 < *t* < *T*![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si21.png), for a fixed *σ*, is defined as the set of all possible values of the corresponding Dirichlet function in the complex plane, as *t* (called the “time”), varies continuously between *t* = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si25.png) and *t* = *T*![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si26.png). Here, *t* is the imaginary part of the argument *z* = *σ* + *i**t*![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si2.png). The full orbit corresponds to *T* = ∞![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si27.png). The size of the hole, as well as its presence/absence and location, depends on *σ*, and of course on *T*, *P*![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si28.png), and *χ*( ⋅ )![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si4.png).

Finally, the hole is called a repulsion basin in the context of dynamical systems. The orbit may be bounded if *σ* > 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si19.png) or unbounded otherwise (in that case, typically extending to the entire complex plane).

### 17.1.3 Industrial applications

While not discussed in this chapter, there are very interesting industrial applications of GRH. See Section [11.2.1.1](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml) on the prime test used to test and design better pseudorandom number generators for cryptography purposes, based on Rademacher random multiplicative function and the Dirichlet character modulo 4. See also Section [4.2.3](#Chp004_61-82_B9780443218576000084.xhtml) featuring synthetic data in machine learning applications, based on the orbits of Dirichlet functions and used to benchmark classification algorithms.

## 17.2 Euler products

I start with finite Euler products, where everything works fine: here the set *P* is a finite subset of the prime integers; there is no convergence issue, and orbits always have a hole. I first introduce the Dirichlet version *η*(*z*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si29.png) of the Riemann function *ζ*(*z*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si8.png), as we need it to extend the convergence domain from *σ* > 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si19.png) to *σ* > 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si30.png) in order to study the behavior (presence of a hole and/or roots) when 0 < *σ* < 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si177.png). For *ζ*(*z*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si8.png), the function *χ*( ⋅ )![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si4.png) is constant and equal to 1. I then move to arbitrary *χ*( ⋅ )![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si4.png)'s including Dirichlet characters modulo 4, and to infinite products. The function *χ* is extended to all integers via the formula *χ*(*a**b*) = *χ*(*a*)*χ*(*b*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si5.png): this extension leads to the fundamental formulas [(17.4)](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#deq5), [(17.5)](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#deq6), and [(17.6)](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#deq7), linking the Euler product to its Dirichlet series expansion whenever both converge. The Euler product establishes the connection between the analytic properties of Dirichlet functions, and the distribution of prime numbers.

### 17.2.1 Finite Euler products

Let *p*[1] = 2![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si32.png) and *P* = {*p*[1], *p*[2], …, *p*[*d*]}![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si33.png) be a set of primes, listed in increasing order. Let *Q* = {*q*[1], *q*[2], *q*[3], …}![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si34.png) be the set of all *p*[1]^(*a*[1])*p*[2]^(*a*[2])*p*[3]^(*a*[3])⋯![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si35.png) where the *a*[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si36.png)'s are positive integers (including zero). The elements *q*[1], *q*[2], …![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si37.png) are also listed in increasing order. Thus *q*[1] = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si38.png) and *q*[2] = 2![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si39.png).

The Dirichlet eta function *η*[*P*](*z*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si40.png) induced by *P* is then defined as

$\\eta\_{P}(z) = \\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{\\infty}\\delta\_{k}q\_{k}^{- z} = (1 - 2^{1 - z})\\prod\\limits\_{p \\in P}\\frac{1}{1 - p^{- z}},$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si41.png)(17.1) 

where *δ*[*k*] = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si42.png) if *q*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si43.png) is odd, and *δ*[*k*] =  − 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si44.png) otherwise. The **Euler product** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euler_product)\] in formula [(17.1)](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#deq2) is finite and has *d* factors, while the infinite series always converges. Indeed, it can be proved (see [Exercise 17.1](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#enun0015)) that

$q\_{k} \\sim \\exp\\left\\lbrack k^{1/d}\\left( d!\\prod\\limits\_{p \\in P}\\log p \\right)^{1/d} \\right\\rbrack\\quad\\text{as~}k\\rightarrow\\infty.$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si45.png)(17.2) 

If *P* is the set of all prime numbers, and thus *d* = ∞![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si46.png), then the product in formula [(17.1)](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#deq2) converges if *σ* > 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si19.png) while the **alternating series** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternating_series)\] converges if *σ* > 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si30.png). This can be proved using the **Dirichlet test** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet%27s_test)\], see [here](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/1042512/proof-of-convergence-of-dirichlets-eta-function). For this reason, the series is called the **analytic continuation** of the product \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analytic_continuation)\]. This is the reason why we are interested in the alternating series, where *δ*[*k*] ∈ { − 1,  + 1}![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si47.png), rather than in the series with *δ*[*k*] = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si42.png): the latter, equal to the infinite product, diverges if *σ* ≤ 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si48.png). This issue occurs only if *d* = ∞![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si46.png). See [Exercise 17.3](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#enun0025) for details. When the product diverges, the alternating series converges, but it is not **absolutely convergent** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Absolute_convergence)\].

Now let *τ*[*z*] = |1 − 2^(1 − *z*)|![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si49.png). Assuming *z* = *σ* + *i**t*![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si2.png), the distance between *η*[*P*](*z*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si40.png) and the origin is equal to

$|\\eta\_{P}(z)| = \\tau\_{z}\\prod\\limits\_{p \\in P}\\frac{1}{|1 - p^{- z}|} = \\tau\_{z}\\prod\\limits\_{p \\in P}\\frac{1}{|1 - 2p^{- \\sigma}\\cos(t\\log p) + p^{- 2\\sigma}|} > \\tau\_{z}\\prod\\limits\_{p \\in P}\\frac{1}{1 + p^{- \\sigma}}.$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si50.png)(17.3) 

Here | ⋅ |![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si51.png) stands for the distance to the origin, and referred to as the **modulus** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Absolute_value#Complex_numbers)\] in complex analysis. An immediate consequence of formula [(17.3)](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#deq4) is this: if *σ* ≠ 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si52.png) is fixed and strictly positive, and if *P* only has a finite number of primes, then there is always a zone around the origin, with a strictly positive area, that the orbit of *η*[*P*](*z*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si40.png) will never hit or cross. This is illustrated in [Fig. 17.1](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#f0010). The zone in question corresponds to a hole in the orbit, also called **repulsion basin** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attractor)\] in dynamical systems, for the red (*σ* = 0.5![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si53.png)) and blue orbit (*σ* = 0.75![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si252.png)). For the yellow orbit (*σ* = 1.25![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si55.png)), the origin is outside the boundary of the orbit. The origin in [Fig. 17.1](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#f0010) is the black dot in the white area. Note that the “center” of the hole, in all three cases, is not the origin, but further to the right on the X-axis. See [here](https://youtu.be/uMRp9FruOqE) the video corresponding to *P* = {2, 3, 5, 7}![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si56.png), and [here](https://youtu.be/MDBaJ8RsLA8) for *P* = {2, 3, 5}![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si57.png).

As you add more and more primes in *P*, the hole shrinks. In the end, when *d* = ∞![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si46.png), the hole shrinks to a single point (the origin) if we plot the whole orbit, rather the restricted orbit to *t* ∈ \[0, *T*\]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si58.png) with *T* = 1000![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si59.png), as in [Fig. 17.1](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#f0010). Also, the center of the hole moves to the left on the X-axis (real axis) as *σ* is decreased from (say) 1.25 to 0.55.

For a fixed *T*, the center of the hole is denoted as *z*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si60.png). It lies on the X-axis, and depends both on *T* and *σ*. It is tempting to scale the *η* function and replace it by $\\sqrt{t} \\cdot (\\eta\_{P}(z) - z\_{0})$![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si61.png), in the hope that when *P* is the full set of prime numbers and *T* → ∞![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si22.png), the hole does not shrink to a singleton or an empty set. However, no matter how fast growing the scaling factor is (as a function of *t*), the **universality property** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zeta_function_universality)\] of the Dirichlet eta function implies that this goal cannot be achieved. Generally speaking, working on finite Euler products and taking the limit *d* → ∞![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si62.png), while very tempting, does not seem to lead to a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, despite numerous attempts by many mathematicians including myself.

#### 17.2.1.1 Generalization using Dirichlet characters

Formula [(17.1)](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#deq2) can be generalized as follows:

$\\eta\_{P}(z,\\chi) = \\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{\\infty}{( - 1)}^{\\Omega(q\_{k})}q\_{k}^{- z} = (1 - 2^{1 - z})\\prod\\limits\_{p \\in P}\\frac{1}{1 - \\chi(p)p^{- z}},$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si63.png)(17.4) 

where *χ*(*p*) ∈ { − 1,  + 1}![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si15.png). The product and the series may have different domains of convergence. However, on the domain where both converge, they have the same roots (except when 2^(1 − *z*) = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si64.png), that is, when *σ* = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si65.png) and *t* = 2*m**π*/log 2![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si66.png) with *m* an integer).

The generalized **Omega function** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_omega_function)\] is defined as follows: if the prime factorization of *q*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si43.png) is *q*[*k*] = *p*[1]^(*a*[1])*p*[2]^(*a*[2])⋯*p*[*d*]^(*a*[*d*])![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si67.png), then *Ω*(*q*[*k*]) = *a*[1]*χ*(*p*[1]) + ⋯ + *a*[*d*]*χ*(*p*[*d*])![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si68.png). The function ( − 1)^(*Ω*(*q*[*k*]))![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si69.png) is denoted as *λ*(*q*[*k*])![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si70.png) and referred to as the generalized **Liouville function** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liouville_function)\]. The series in formula [(17.4)](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#deq5) is called a **Dirichlet-***L* **function** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet_L-function)\]. The function *χ* can be extended to all strictly positive integers as follows: *χ*(1) = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si6.png), *χ*(*p*) = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si71.png) if *p* ∉ *P*![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si72.png), and *χ*(*a**b*) = *χ*(*a*)*χ*(*b*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si5.png). Then *χ*(*q*[*k*]) = *λ*(*q*[*k*])![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si73.png) is a **completely multiplicative function** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiplicative_function)\].

From now on, all functions denoted as *χ*( ⋅ )![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si4.png) are assumed to be completely multiplicative, and thus uniquely characterized by the values they take on prime arguments. Now, let *L*[*P*](*z*, *χ*) = (1 − 2^(1 − *z*))^( − 1)*η*[*P*](*z*, *χ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si74.png). Then we have:

$L\_{P}(z,\\chi) = \\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{\\infty}\\chi(k)k^{- z},\\quad\\eta\_{P}(z,\\chi) = (1 - 2^{1 - z})L\_{P}(z,\\chi) = \\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{\\infty}{( - 1)}^{k + 1}\\chi(k)k^{- z},$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si75.png)(17.5) 

$L\_{P}(z,\\chi) = \\prod\\limits\_{p \\in P}\\frac{1}{1 - \\chi(p)p^{- z}},\\quad|L\_{P}(z,\\chi)| = \\prod\\limits\_{p \\in P}|1 - \\chi(p)p^{- z}|^{- 1} \\geqslant \\prod\\limits\_{p \\in P}\\frac{1}{1 + p^{- \\sigma}}.$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si76.png)(17.6) 

If for a fixed integer *m* > 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si77.png) we have *χ*(*p*) = *χ*(*q*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si78.png) whenever *p*, *q* ∈ *P*![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si79.png) are two primes with *p* ≡ *q* *m**o**d* *m*![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si80.png), and if in addition *χ*(*p*) = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si71.png) if *p* divides *m*, then *χ*( ⋅ )![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si4.png) is called a **Dirichlet character** modulo *m* \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet_character)\]. The standard Omega and Liouville functions correspond to the case where *χ* is constant and equal to +1, and *P* is the set of all prime numbers. The standard Liouville function also satisfies

$\\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{n}\\lambda(k)\\left\\lfloor \\frac{n}{k} \\right\\rfloor = \\lfloor\\sqrt{n}\\rfloor,\\quad L(n) = \\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{n}\\lambda(k) = \\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{n}\\mu(k)\\left\\lfloor \\sqrt{\\frac{n}{k}} \\right\\rfloor,$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si81.png)

where *μ*(*k*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si82.png) is Liouville's sister function, called the **Möbius function** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C3%B6bius_function)\]. See [here](https://mathoverflow.net/questions/393351/exact-formula-for-partial-sums-of-liouville-function-ln-oeis-sequence-a0028) for details. The brackets stand for the integer part function. The partial sums of the Liouville function are denoted as *L*(*n*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si83.png), while the partial sums of the Möbius function are the **Mertens function** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mertens_function)\], and denoted as *M*(*n*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si84.png). If *q* = *q*[*k*] = *p*[1]^(*a*[1])*p*[2]^(*a*[2])⋯*p*[*d*]^(*a*[*d*])![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si85.png), then *μ*(*q*[*k*]) = ( − 1)^(*w*(*q*[*k*]))![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si86.png), with *ω*(*q*[*k*]) = *χ*(*p*[1]) + ⋯ + *χ*(*p*[*d*])![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si87.png). The standard Möbius function corresponds to the case where *χ* is a constant function equal to 1, and *P* is the set of all prime numbers.

Finally, formula [(17.3)](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#deq4), providing a lower bound for the distance between the origin and any point on the orbit of *η*[*P*](*z*, *χ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si88.png), is still applicable and remains unchanged. In particular, if *P* is the set of all primes (or a big enough, infinite subset), the lower bound is zero due to divergence of the product. If that lower bound is indeed reached, even if asymptotically only, then the hope to find a hole bigger than a singleton evaporates.

### 17.2.2 Infinite Euler products

If *P* is the set of all prime numbers, the products in formula [(17.1)](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#deq2), [(17.3)](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#deq4), and [(17.4)](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#deq5) become infinite. As a result, if 0.5 ≤ *σ* < 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si89.png), the holes in the orbit in [Fig. 17.1](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#f0010) may shrink to an empty set (*σ* = 0.5![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si53.png)) or a single point – the origin – if 0.5 < *σ* < 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si90.png). Actually, it may well be an empty set too in the latter case; nobody knows. But the Riemann hypothesis states that it should be a single point. This is the situation if *χ* is a constant function equal to 1. This function is called **principal character** in this context. But what happens if *χ* is not a constant? In this latter case, depending on *χ*, the orbit may never get too close to the origin.

Let us consider the **completely multiplicative** function *χ* called nontrivial **Dirichlet character modulo** 4, and denoted as *χ*[4]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si1.png) or *χ*[4, 1]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si91.png). It is uniquely characterized by its values on prime numbers *p*, as follows: *χ*[4](*p*) =  + 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si92.png) if *p* *m**o**d* 4 = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si93.png), *χ*[4](*p*) =  − 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si94.png) if *p* *m**o**d* 4 = 3![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si95.png), and *χ*[4](2) = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si96.png). It satisfies *χ*[4](*k* + 4) = *χ*(*k*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si97.png) for all positive integers. Again, *P* is the set of all primes.

Primes satisfying *p* *m**o**d* 4 = 3![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si95.png) seem to be more numerous than the others, at least the smaller ones: they get a good head start. This is known as **Chebyshev's bias** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chebyshev%27s_bias)\]. If these two types of primes are not evenly distributed, the orbit could get arbitrarily close to the origin. However, thanks to **Dirichlet's theorem** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet%27s_theorem_on_arithmetic_progressions)\], we know that the distribution is even. Thus one would expect that the Euler product in formulas [(17.4)](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#deq5) and [(17.6)](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#deq7) would alternate nicely between *χ*[4](*p*) =  + 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si92.png) and *χ*[4](*p*) =  − 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si94.png) on average, thus converging for some *σ* = *σ*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si98.png) smaller than 1, and thus for all *σ* > *σ*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si99.png). This is in contrast to the product in formula [(17.1)](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#deq2), corresponding to the principal character *χ*(*p*) = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si100.png) for all *p*, denoted as *χ*[4, 0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si101.png) and converging only for *σ* > 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si19.png).

Having no root if *σ*[0] < *σ* < 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si102.png) due to the nonvanishing product in formula [(17.4)](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#deq5), one would conclude that the orbit of *L*[*P*](*z*, *χ*[4])![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si103.png) never crosses the X-axis if *σ*[0] < *σ* < 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si102.png). However, to this day, nobody knows if the smallest possible value of *σ*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si104.png), called the **abscissa of absolute convergence** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Dirichlet_series)\] is less than 1. It is conjectured to be as low as 0.5, or lower. This is part of the **Generalized Riemann Hypothesis** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generalized_Riemann_hypothesis)\], an active research topic in number theory. Yet, the associated series *L*[*P*](*z*, *χ*[4])![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si103.png) defined in formula [(17.5)](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#deq6) is **conditionally convergent** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conditional_convergence)\] if *σ* > 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si30.png), see Example 2.39, page 36, in [\[4\]](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#br0020).

For a reference focusing on completely multiple functions *χ* in the RH context, not just Dirichlet characters, see [\[1\]](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#br0005). Finally, I discuss *χ*[4]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si1.png) in more details in Section [17.3.2.3](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#s0085). In particular, I show the big contrast between *L*[*P*](*z*, *χ*[4, 1])![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si105.png) and the standard Riemann zeta function *ζ*(*z*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si8.png) corresponding to *L*[*P*](*z*, *χ*[4, 0])![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si106.png).

#### 17.2.2.1 Special products

Again, I investigate the infinite product *L*[*P*](*z*, *χ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si107.png) in formula [(17.6)](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#deq7), with *z* = *σ* + *i**t*![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si2.png). If for some 0 < *σ*[0] < 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si108.png), the set *P* contains infinitely many primes, but sufficiently spaced out so that

$\\rho = \\prod\\limits\_{p \\in P}\\frac{1}{1 + p^{- \\sigma\_{0}}} > 0,$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si109.png)

then the orbit of *L*[*P*](*z*, *χ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si107.png) corresponding to *σ* = *σ*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si98.png) will stay away from the origin, at a distance ⩾*ρ* at all times. This is true regardless of the function *χ*. In particular, it means that *L*[*P*](*z*, *χ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si107.png) has no root if *σ* = *σ*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si98.png).

Now, if *P* is the set of all primes, *χ*(*p*) = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si100.png) for all primes (the standard case) and *σ* = 0.5![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si53.png), then *η*[*P*](*z*, *χ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si88.png), defined in formula [(17.4)](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#deq5), has infinitely many roots. In addition, if its orbit gets too close to the origin, it gets attracted to it, otherwise it gets deflected: the origin seems to have an event horizon similar to that of a black hole. If you get too close, there is no way out, you will hit the origin very fast. See the blue curve in [Fig. 17.2](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#f0015), where the X-axis represents the time *t*, and the Y-axis the distance to the location (*c*, 0)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si110.png) in the complex plane. For the blue curve, *c* = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si111.png). Note that as long as 0.5 < *σ* < 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si90.png) and 0 < *t* < *T*![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si21.png) with *T* finite, the (finite) portion of the orbit exhibits a hole. But the hole shrinks very slowly to a single point, as *T* → ∞![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si22.png). If *σ* < 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si9.png), the hole encompasses the origin at all times. But its actual center is located further to the right on the X-axis. See Figs. [17.2](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#f0015), [17.3](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#f0020), and [17.4](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#f0025): each curve represents a distance to a specific location (*c*, 0)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si110.png). The center moves to the left as *T* increases, or as *σ* decreases and gets closer to 0.5, until it merges with the origin. If *σ* > 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si19.png), the hole may not contain the origin, but the orbit is bounded and the origin is outside the external boundary of the orbit: see the yellow orbit in [Fig. 17.1](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#f0010).

![Figure 17.2 Distance between orbit and location (c,0) depending on t on the X-axis.](images/B9780443218576000217/gr002.jpg)

Figure 17.2 Distance between orbit and location (*c*,0) depending on *t* on the X-axis.

![Figure 17.3 Distance between orbit and location (c,0) depending on t on the X-axis.](images/B9780443218576000217/gr003.jpg)

[Figure 17.3](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#cs0010_2) Distance between orbit and location (*c*,0) depending on *t* on the X-axis.

![Figure 17.4 Distance between orbit and location (c,0) depending on t on the X-axis.](images/B9780443218576000217/gr004.jpg)

[Figure 17.4](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#cs0010_3) Distance between orbit and location (*c*,0) depending on *t* on the X-axis.

Finally, another case worth investigating is as follows. Let *P* be the set of all primes, and *p*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si112.png) be the *k*th prime with *p*[1] = 2![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si32.png). Define *χ*(*p*[2*k* + 1]) =  + 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si113.png) and *χ*(*p*[2*k*]) =  − 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si114.png). Then the product in formula [(17.4)](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#deq5) converges if *σ* > 0.5![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si115.png) (prove it for *t* = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si25.png), using the fact that the product is alternating; see also [here](https://mathoverflow.net/questions/159534/does-this-alternating-euler-product-converge-for-all-res-0)). Thus the infinite product (which has no root) can be used to compute *η*[*P*](*z*, *χ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si88.png). But the convergence is not absolute. I expect that there is no root if 0.5 < *σ* < 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si90.png). But I also expect that the hole is reduced to a single point (the origin), as in the standard case.

#### 17.2.2.2 Probabilistic properties and conjectures

Here *P* is the set of all primes, and *χ*(*p*) = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si100.png) for all *p*. The Liouville function *λ*( ⋅ )![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si116.png) and Möbius function *μ*( ⋅ )![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si117.png), introduced in Section [17.2.1.1](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#s0040), have many interesting properties and open questions. Many are equivalent to or generalizing RH. Here I present here a brief summary; more can be found [here](https://mathoverflow.net/questions/391736/normal-numbers-liouville-function-and-the-riemann-hypothesis). Again, let *L*(*n*) = *λ*(1) + ⋯ + *λ*(*n*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si118.png).

*   •  The numbers *λ*(*k*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si119.png), for positive integers *k*, are equal to −1 or +1 in equal proportions, thus averaging to zero. But due to a good head start with negative values, it takes a long time for *L*(*n*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si83.png) to turn positive. In fact, the **Pólya conjecture** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%B3lya_conjecture)\] claims that *L*(*n*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si83.png) is always negative, but it was disproved in 1958. The smallest possible *n* satisfying *L*(*n*) > 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si120.png), namely ![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/fx001.jpg), was found in 1980. The sign changes in *λ*(*k*) =  ± 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si121.png) occur somewhat randomly, as in independent Bernoulli trials. If the +1 and −1 were truly randomly distributed with zero mean, they would satisfy the **law of the iterated logarithm** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_of_the_iterated_logarithm)\]:

$\\underset{n\\rightarrow\\infty}{\\lim⁡\\sup}\\frac{|L(n)|}{\\sqrt{n\\log\\log n}} = C,$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si122.png)(17.7) 

*   for some constant *C* with 0 < *C* < ∞![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si123.png). It is conjectured that this is not the case. In fact, the *λ*(*k*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si119.png)'s cannot possibly be independent, not even asymptotically, since the function is completely multiplicative. But to prove RH, all that is needed is a weaker statement, the fact $L(n)/\\sqrt{n^{1 + \\epsilon}}\\rightarrow 0$![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si124.png) as *n* → ∞![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si125.png), for any *ϵ* > 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si126.png). This is yet unproved. A similar conjecture exists for the Möbius function: the Mertens conjecture \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mertens_conjecture)\], also implying RH, and thus yet unproved. See [\[11\]](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#br0055) for a stochastic version, based on random multiplicative **Rademacher functions** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rademacher_distribution)\], used as a substitute to emulate the “randomness” of the Möbius function.
*   •  A stronger conjecture, yet not as strong as the law of the iterated logarithm, is this: the *λ*(*k*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si119.png)'s behave like the binary digits of a **normal number** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normal_number)\]. In short, the number $\\nu = \\sum\_{k = 1}^{\\infty}\\lambda(k)2^{- k}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si127.png) is normal. Of course, *ν* is irrational, otherwise *λ*( ⋅ )![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si116.png) would be a periodic function. It is not yet known if *ν* is transcendental, though some closely related numbers are [\[2\]](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#br0010). The normality (or equivalently, ergodicity) of the sequence {*λ*(*k*)}![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si128.png) would imply that the **Chowla conjecture**, itself stronger than RH, is true; see [\[6\]](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#br0030). But this is yet unproved.
*   •  The numbers *μ*(*k*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si82.png), for positive integers *k*, are equal to −1, 0, or +1. The proportion of those equal to zero is 1 − 6/*π*²![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si129.png). This is because *μ*(*k*) = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si130.png) if and only if *k* has a square factor. It is well known and easy to prove that the proportion of **square-free integers** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Square-free_integer)\] is 6/*π*²![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si131.png). The proportions of *μ*(*k*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si82.png)'s equal to −1 or −1 are identical, a consequence of **Dirichlet's theorem** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet%27s_theorem_on_arithmetic_progressions)\].

Finally, an application of **Kronecker's theorem** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kronecker%27s_theorem)\] leads to the following result: over time, for any fixed *σ*, the orbit of the Dirichlet *L*\-function defined by formula [(17.5)](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#deq6) (assuming convergence) eventually fills a dense area in the complex plane. This is true whether the orbit is bounded or not, and whether it is has a “visible” hole or not. In other words, the image domain of *η*[*P*](*z*, *χ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si88.png) or *L*[*P*](*z*, *χ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si107.png) is a **dense set** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dense_set)\]. I provide an elegant proof of this fact in [Exercise 17.5](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#enun0035), using arguments similar to those used to prove its **universality property** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zeta_function_universality)\]. This implies that if 0.5 < *σ* < 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si90.png), assuming *P* contains sufficiently many prime numbers, the Dirichlet eta function, regardless of *χ*, gets arbitrarily close to zero, even though it may never actually hit zero. In other words, in that case, the hole eventually shrinks to a single point.

## 17.3 Finite Dirichlet series and generalizations

This section covers a large class of functions, starting with truncated modified Dirichlet series to assess the status of the hole in the orbit. I then move back to infinite Euler products in Section [17.3.2](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#s0070), but this time not over the full set of primes as in Section [17.2.2](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#s0045), but instead on infinite subsets arising from additive number theory. Some of these functions have no root if *σ* > *σ*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si99.png), with (say) *σ*[0] = 5/6![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si132.png). They thus satisfy a weaker version of GRH, called quasi-GRH. Section [17.3.3](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#s0095) covers non-Dirichlet functions that do not have an Euler product, but behave like the Dirichlet eta function *η*(*z*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si29.png) with regard to the orbit and its hole. Here *P* is the set of all primes, but the sine and cosine attached to *p*^( − *z*) = *σ*^( − *z*)cos (*t*log *p*) − *i**σ*^( − *z*)sin (*t*log *p*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si133.png) are now replaced by wavelets. Section [17.3.4](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#s0100) deals with noninteger primes (even matrices) that mimic the behavior of prime integers, and called Beurling primes. They come with Euler products too, and the corresponding Dirichlet series is now called a Dedekind zeta (or eta) function. Section [17.3.5](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#s0105) deals with random Dirichlet functions: their interest lies in the fact that the corresponding (random) Euler products converge, albeit conditionally, when $\\frac{1}{2} < \\sigma \\leqslant 1$![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si134.png).
