Thus they satisfy a probabilistic version of GRH, in particular the absence of root if $\\sigma > \\frac{1}{2}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si17.png).

### 17.3.1 Finite Dirichlet series

Formula [(17.1)](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#deq2) features a finite (Euler) product. However, the corresponding series, on the left-hand side, is infinite. Here I discuss a different approach, using a finite version containing the first *n* terms of the full Dirichlet series when *P* is the set of all prime numbers. The new function is defined as

$\\eta(z,\\beta,n) = \\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{n}\\delta\_{k}\\lambda\_{k}p\_{k}^{- z},$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si135.png)(17.8) 

where *λ*[*k*] = 1/*k*![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si136.png) for all *k* except *k* = 2![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si137.png). The coefficient *λ*[2]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si138.png) is denoted as *β*. Here, *δ*[*k*] = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si42.png) if *k* is odd, otherwise *δ*[*k*] =  − 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si44.png). If *n* is infinite and *β* = 1/2![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si139.png), then *η*(*z*, *β*, *n*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si140.png) coincides with the standard Dirichlet eta function.

Despite the finite number of terms in the series, this approach is considerably more difficult. Unlike in Section [17.2.1](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#s0035), there is no simple product (finite or infinite), to represent the truncated *η* function. While the approach in Section [17.2.1](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#s0035) has a strong number theory flavor, here we are dealing with approximations and numerical analysis. Yet, the case *n* = 3![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si141.png) is trivial: the orbit fills a ring. The hole is a circle centered at (1, 0)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si142.png), not at the origin. Both the interior and exterior boundaries of the orbit are circles, with known radius. See [Exercise 17.4](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#enun0030) for a complete solution.

But the general case is much more complicated. Of course, the series corresponding to the finite Euler product results in an orbit with a solid hole of radius >0, always encompassing the origin, and not shrinking to a singleton when you display the full, infinite orbit. But that series always has an infinite number of terms. As you increase the number of terms in the truncated series, keeping the first *n* terms only and *β* = 1/2![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si139.png), the hole disappears when *n* ≥ 5![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si143.png) is small enough, only to reappear when *n* > 50![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si144.png). The hole then stays there all the way to *n* = ∞![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si145.png). As *n* increases, it eventually shifts to the left on the X-axis, to encompass the origin. For instance, at ![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/fx002.jpg), the origin is inside the hole. This is based on visually inspecting the orbit at *σ* = 0.90![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si146.png), with ![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/fx003.jpg); see [Fig. 17.6](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#f0035).

For small values of *n* with no hole, increasing *β* is one way to reintroduce the hole in the orbit, as pictured in [Fig. 17.5](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#f0030). This leads to a possible new path to explore RH: using a large *n*, with *β* > 1/2![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si147.png) (the larger *β*, the larger the hole), and let *β* → 1/2![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si148.png) as *n* → ∞![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si125.png). In [Exercise 17.4](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#enun0030), I discuss some conditions that guarantee the presence of a hole encompassing the origin, for small values of *n*.

![Figure 17.5 Four orbits where the “hole” (repulsion basin) is apparent.](images/B9780443218576000217/gr005.jpg)

Figure 17.5 Four orbits where the “hole” (repulsion basin) is apparent.

![Figure 17.6 Three orbits with “hole” closer to the origin, showing impact of \\beta > \\frac{1}{2}Image and larger n.](images/B9780443218576000217/gr006.jpg)

[Figure 17.6](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#cf0275) Three orbits with “hole” closer to the origin, showing impact of $\\beta > \\frac{1}{2}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si149.png) and larger *n*.

The Python code in Section [17.5.1](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#s0120) allows you to replicate my experiments. You need to set the parameter method to Eta, and the parameter Dirichlet to True. This allows you to work with a series that converges when $\\frac{1}{2} \\leqslant \\sigma < 1$![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si10.png), as opposed to *σ* > 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si19.png). Of course, for finite Euler products, the infinite Dirichlet series always converges regardless of *σ*, with or without Dirichlet set to True.

### 17.3.2 Nontrivial cases with infinitely many primes and a hole

Now, let us get back to Euler products. Thus the associated Dirichlet series (the expansion of the product) always contains infinitely many terms, even if the product is finite. For a given *σ*, in order to get a hole encompassing the origin, with the distance between the orbit and the origin always ⩾*ρ* at all times *t*, the following must be satisfied:

$\\rho = \\prod\\limits\_{p \\in P}\\frac{1}{1 + p^{- \\sigma}} > 0.$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si150.png)(17.9) 

This is briefly discussed at the beginning of Section [17.2.2.1](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#s0050). Note that this requirement is independent of the function *χ*. It is satisfied if the product is finite (that is, if the set *P* is finite), or if *σ* > 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si19.png), or if *σ* < 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si9.png) and *P* is infinite but sparse enough so that the product converges. This section discusses the latter.

Because of the generalized **universality property** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zeta_function_universality)\] discussed in [Exercise 17.5](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#enun0035), the inequality ⩾*ρ* becomes an equality: the largest circle encompassing the origin, not crossed by the orbit, has radius exactly equal to *ρ*.

We already know that if *P* is the full set of primes and *σ* < 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si9.png), there is no hole. According to the Riemann Hypothesis, the hole at the origin is reduced to a singleton if 0.5 < *σ* < 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si90.png), and to an empty set if *σ* = 0.5![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si53.png). The **Generalized Riemann Hypothesis** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generalized_Riemann_hypothesis)\] claims that this is true regardless of the **Dirichlet character** *χ*( ⋅ )![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si4.png) \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet_character)\]. But what if we use the set of **twin primes** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twin_prime)\] for *P*? Then the product in formula [(17.9)](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#deq12) converges if *σ* = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si65.png), thus there is a hole with *ρ* > 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si151.png) encompassing the origin, if *σ* = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si65.png). The convergence is a direct consequence of **Brun's theorem** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brun%27s_theorem)\]: the fact that the sum of the inverse of twin primes converges. I did not investigate the case *σ* < 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si9.png).

I now discuss two cases that are known to satisfy [(17.9)](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#deq12). Both illustrate methods of **additive number theory** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Additive_number_theory)\]. The idea is to look at two (or more) sets of integers *A* and *B*, and then check the density of integers in *A* + *B*![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si152.png). The most well-known example is **Goldbach's conjecture** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldbach%27s_conjecture)\]: it states that if *A* = *B*![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si153.png) is the set of all primes, then *A* + *B*![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si152.png), defined as the set of all integers *a* + *b*![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si154.png) with *a* ∈ *A*![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si155.png), *b* ∈ *B*![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si156.png), covers all positive even integers greater than 2. The second most well-known example is when *A* = *B*![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si153.png) is the set of square integers. The problem is referred to as **sums of squares** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss_circle_problem)\]. The resulting *A* + *B*![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si152.png) is too large to be of interest here. A more general version is the sum of higher powers, known as **Waring's problem** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waring%27s_problem)\]. If *A* = *B*![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si153.png) is the set of positive cubes, or *A* is the set of positive cubes and *B* the set of squares, then *A* + *B*![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si152.png) is small enough to lead to interesting results. Let us now investigate these popular cases.

#### 17.3.2.1 Sums of two cubes, or cuban primes

Let *P* be the set of primes, greater than 2, that are the sum of two cubes. They are called **cuban primes** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuban_prime)\], and featured in the OEIS list of integer sequences as entries [A334520](https://oeis.org/A334520) and [A002407](https://oeis.org/A002407). These primes are of the form 3*x*² + 3*x* + 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si157.png) where *x* is a positive integer. Because cuban primes are less numerous than square integers, we have ∏[*p* ∈ *P*](1 + *p*^( − *σ*))^( − 1) < ∞![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si158.png) if *σ* > 0.5![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si115.png). Thus, if *σ* > 0.5![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si115.png) and regardless of *χ*, the associated *L*[*P*](*z*, *χ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si107.png) orbit has a hole at the origin, with radius >0 (not a single point or an empty set). In short, *L*[*P*](*z*, *χ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si107.png) never gets too close to zero if *σ* > 0.5![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si115.png). This is in stark contrast to the standard Riemann zeta function *ζ*(*z*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si8.png), which has a hole of strictly positive radius only if *σ* > 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si19.png).

It is conjectured that there are infinitely many cuban primes. For primes of the form *x*³ + 2*y*³![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si159.png), a proof was published in 2001, see [\[12\]](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#br0060).

#### 17.3.2.2 Primes associated to elliptic curves

Now, let *P* = {*p*[1], *p*[2], …}![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si160.png) be the set of primes of the form *x*³ + *y*²![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si161.png), listed in increasing order. These primes are far less numerous than primes of the form *x*² + *y*²![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si162.png), but far more numerous than primes of the form *x*³ + *y*³![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si163.png) (the cuban primes). Here *x*, *y*![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si164.png) are positive integers. Note that if *p* ∈ *P*![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si165.png), then *y*² = *x*³ + *p*![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si166.png) for some integers *x* ≤ 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si167.png), *y* ≥ 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si168.png). This is the equation of an **elliptic curve** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elliptic_curve)\].

When *n* is large enough, the number of positive integers smaller than *n*, of the form *x*³ + *y*²![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si161.png), is less than *n*^(5/6)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si169.png). We do not know how many of them are prime numbers, but we know that it must be less than that. Thus *p*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si112.png) is asymptotically larger than *k*^(6/5)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si170.png). For details, see [Exercise 17.6](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#enun0040), based on a general summation formula posted [here](https://mathoverflow.net/questions/364559/general-asymptotic-result-in-additive-combinatorics-sums-of-sets). Then, using formula [(17.6)](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#deq7), we have

$\\rho = |L\_{P}(z,\\chi)| \\geqslant \\prod\\limits\_{k = 1}^{\\infty}\\frac{1}{1 + p\_{k}^{\\sigma}} \\geqslant \\prod\\limits\_{k = 1}^{\\infty}\\frac{1}{1 + k^{6\\sigma/5}}.$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si171.png)(17.10) 

Regardless of the function *χ*( ⋅ )![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si4.png), the rightmost product in formula [(17.10)](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#deq13) converges (absolutely) if 6*σ*/5 > 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si172.png), that is, if $\\sigma > \\frac{5}{6}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si173.png). So, not only *L*[*P*](*z*, *χ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si107.png) has no zero if $\\sigma > \\frac{5}{6}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si173.png), but there is a circle of radius *ρ* > 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si151.png) centered at the origin (a hole), that the orbit never crosses.

For other Dirichlet-*L* functions with known **abscissa of convergence** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet_series#Abscissa_of_convergence)\] *σ* < 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si9.png), see the article “Modular Elliptic Curves”, pages 14–18, in [\[16\]](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#br0080). Interestingly, (conditional) convergence is proved also for $\\sigma > \\frac{5}{6}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si173.png), by looking at the series rather than the product. Primes of the form *x*³ + *y*²![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si161.png) are listed in the [Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences](https://oeis.org/), as entry [A066649](https://oeis.org/A066649). Related entries include [A022549](https://oeis.org/A022549), [A055393](https://oeis.org/A055393), [A173795](https://oeis.org/A173795), and [A123364](https://oeis.org/A123364).

**Note.** The theory of elliptic curves is now a hot topic in number theory. They were used in the proof of **Fermat's last theorem** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat%27s_Last_Theorem)\]. The proof was published in 1995, more than 350 years after it was first conjectured. The theorem states that *x*^(*n*) + *y*^(*n*) = *z*^(*n*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si174.png) has no nontrivial solution in integer numbers if *n* > 2![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si175.png).

#### 17.3.2.3 Analytic continuation, convergence, and functional equation

If the Euler product converges only for *σ* > 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si19.png), you need to find and extension to *σ* > 0.5![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si115.png) to assess whether *L*[*P*](*z*, *χ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si107.png) has roots when 0.5 < *σ* < 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si90.png). One way to do it to get an **analytic continuation** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analytic_continuation)\], at least down to *σ* = 0.5![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si53.png). If *χ*( ⋅ )![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si4.png) is constant and equal to 1, try using the alternating Dirichlet series *η*[*P*](*z*, *χ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si88.png) defined by formula [(17.4)](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#deq5), rather than the Euler product, to compute *L*[*P*](*z*, *χ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si107.png). It may converge over a larger domain. If the analytic continuation satisfies a standard **Dirichlet functional equation** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Functional_equation_\(L-function\))\] and *z*[0] = *σ* + *i**t*![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si176.png) is a root with 0 < *σ* < 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si177.png), then 1 − *z*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si178.png) is also a root. Thus in that case, if there is no root with 0.5 < *σ* < 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si90.png), then any possible root with 0 < *σ* < 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si177.png) must have *σ* = 0.5![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si53.png). The functional equation, when it exists, can be derived using **exponential sums** such as $\\sum\_{k = 1}^{\\infty}\\exp( - \\pi k^{2}y)$![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si179.png). See Section 4.1 (page 71) in [\[4\]](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#br0020).

If for some *σ*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si104.png) the Dirichlet series converges, then it converges for all *z* with ℜ(*z*) = *σ* > *σ*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si180.png). The **abscissa of conditional convergence** for the *η*[*P*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si181.png) series defined in formula [(17.5)](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#deq6) is denoted as *σ*[*c*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si182.png). It is the minimum value satisfying

$\\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{\\infty}{( - 1)}^{k + 1}\\chi(k)k^{- \\sigma\_{c}} < \\infty.$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si183.png)(17.11) 

The **abscissa of absolute convergence**, denoted as *σ*[*a*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si184.png), is the minimum value satisfying

$\\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{\\infty}|\\chi(k)|k^{- \\sigma\_{a}} < \\infty.$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si185.png)

Note that *χ*(*k*) ∈ { − 1, 0,  + 1}![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si186.png). It is equal to 0 only if *k* cannot be expressed as a product of elements of *P*. This happens when *P* is not the full set of primes. Similar arguments can be used to obtain the abscissa of convergence for the *L*[*P*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si187.png) series, or to study the convergence of the product. For instance, for the product in formula [(17.4)](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#deq5), conditional convergence is equivalent to the convergence of the series ∑[*p* ∈ *P*]*χ*(*p*)*p*^( − *σ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si188.png). In particular, for *χ* = *χ*[4]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si16.png), the **Dirichlet character modulo 4** introduced at the beginning of Section [17.2.2](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#s0045), the series for *L*[*P*](*z*, *χ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si107.png) has *σ*[*c*] = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si189.png) because *χ*[4]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si1.png) is periodic, and thus the series in formula [(17.11)](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#deq14) is alternating.

#### 17.3.2.4 Hybrid Dirichlet–Taylor series

An interesting generalization of the **Euler product**, with *χ*(*p*) = *x*^(*ν*(*p*))![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si190.png), is as follows:

$L\_{P}(z,x,\\nu) = \\prod\\limits\_{p \\in P}\\frac{1}{1 - x^{\\nu(p)}p^{- z}} = \\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{\\infty}\\varphi(k)x^{\\Omega\_{\\nu}(k)}k^{- z},$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si191.png)

where *ν*(*p*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si192.png) is defined on the primes *p* ∈ *P*![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si165.png). If the unique factorization of *k*, using primes in *P*, is *k* = *p*[1]^(*a*[1])*p*[2]^(*a*[2])*p*[3]^(*a*[3])⋯![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si193.png), then *Ω*[*ν*](*k*) = *a*[1]*ν*(*p*[1]) + *a*[2]*ν*(*p*[2]) + ⋯![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si194.png), where the latter sum is actually finite. Here the *a*[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si36.png)'s are integers ⩾0. If *k* cannot be factored in *P*, for instance, if *P* does not contain all the prime integers, then *φ*(*k*) = *Ω*[*ν*](*k*) = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si195.png) otherwise *φ*(*k*) = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si196.png). Note that *Ω*[*ν*]( ⋅ )![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si197.png) is a function defined on *Q* = *Q*[*P*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si198.png), the multiplicative group generated by *P*, containing all product combinations of elements of *P* (including 1). In fact, *Ω*[*ν*]( ⋅ )![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si197.png) generalizes the **Omega function** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_omega_function)\]. If the elements of *Q*[*P*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si199.png) are denoted (in increasing order) as *q*[1], *q*[2]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si200.png), and so on, then the following notation is more flexible:

$L\_{P}(z,x,\\nu) = \\prod\\limits\_{p \\in P}\\frac{1}{1 - x^{\\nu(p)}p^{- z}} = \\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{\\infty}x^{\\Omega\_{\\nu}(q\_{k})}q\_{k}^{- z}.$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si201.png)(17.12) 

This notation works even if the *p*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si112.png)'s (and thus the *q*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si43.png)'s) are not integers, as in Section [17.3.4](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#s0100). We can also define *η*[*P*](*z*, *x*, *ν*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si202.png) using the same mechanism as in formula [(17.5)](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#deq6); it may provide an analytic continuation when *x* → 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si203.png).

Examples

Assuming *P* is the set of all prime integers, interesting examples include:

*   •  If *ν*(*p*) = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si204.png) and *x* = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si205.png), then *L*[*P*](*z*, *x*, *ν*) = *ζ*(*z*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si206.png), the **Riemann zeta function** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_zeta_function)\]. If *ν*(*p*) = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si204.png) and *x* =  − 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si207.png), then *L*[*P*](*z*, *x*, *ν*) = *ζ*(2*z*)/*ζ*(*z*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si208.png). If *ν*(*p*) = log *p*![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si209.png) and 0 < *x* ≤ 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si210.png), then *L*[*P*](*z*, *x*, *ν*) = *ζ*(*z* − log *x*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si211.png). If *ν*(*p*) = *p*![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si212.png) and  − 1 < *x* < 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si213.png), then we have absolute convergence when *σ* ≥ 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si214.png). In addition, the series in formula [(17.12)](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#deq17) is a Taylor series in *x*, and a Dirichlet series in *z*. This function has no roots, but it does have **poles** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zeros_and_poles)\]. Furthermore, lim[*x* → 1]*L*[*P*](*z*, *x*, *ν*) = *ζ*(*z*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si215.png).
*   •  Let *x* =  − 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si207.png) and *ν*(*p*) = 2*d*(*π*(*p*), *α*) − 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si216.png), where *π*( ⋅ )![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si217.png) is the **prime-counting function** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime-counting_function)\] and *d*(*k*, *α*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si218.png) is the *k*th binary digit of the real number 0 < *α* < 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si219.png). Choose *α* so that its binary digits are random enough, behaving like an infinite fair coin-tossing game. Then, by virtue of the **Glivenko–Cantelli theorem** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glivenko%E2%80%93Cantelli_theorem)\], the empirical distribution \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empirical_distribution_function)\] of the digits converge to the underlying theoretical distribution of the process described in Section [17.3.5](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#s0105). In particular, we have both convergence of the product and no root if *σ* > 0.5![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si115.png). Thus the **Generalized Riemann Hypothesis** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generalized_Riemann_hypothesis)\] (abbreviated as GRH) is verified in this case. You still need to find some *α* that works, for instance, some **normal number** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normal_number)\] that would fit the bill. Of course, $\\alpha = \\sqrt{2}/2$![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si220.png) is a great candidate, but no one knows if it is normal or not, despite the fact that it successfully passed all the statistical tests ever designed.
*   •  In the previous example, if *α* = 2/3![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si221.png), GRH is also satisfied, despite the lack of randomness: the digits alternate perfectly between 0 and 1. But *p*[2*k*]^( − *σ*) − *p*[2*k* + 1]^( − *σ*) → 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si222.png) fast enough as *k* → ∞![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si223.png) (see [here](https://mathoverflow.net/questions/159534/does-this-alternating-euler-product-converge-for-all-res-0)), thus we have convergence of the product if *σ* > 0.5![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si115.png) and therefore, no root. Now, let *α* be defined as follows: the first digit is zero; then *d*(*π*(*p*), *α*) = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si224.png) if *p* ≡ 1 *m**o**d* 4![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si225.png) and *d*(*π*(*p*), *α*) = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si226.png) if *p* ≡ 3 *m**o**d* 4![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si227.png). Then *L*[*P*](*z*, *x*, *ν*) = *L*(*z*, *χ*[4])![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si228.png) where *χ*[4]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si1.png) is the nontrivial **Dirichlet character modulo** 4. The digits have limited randomness; the proportion of zero/one is 50/50 thanks to **Dirichlet's theorem** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet%27s_theorem_on_arithmetic_progressions)\], and this **Dirichlet-***L* **function** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet_L-function)\] enjoys a number of interesting properties. If its product converges when *σ* > 0.5![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si115.png) (nobody knows), then *L*(*z*, *χ*[4])![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si229.png) would also satisfy GRH. The nonrandomness of the digits (this in itself does not rule out GRH) is caused by the fact that *χ*[4]( ⋅ )![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si230.png) is completely multiplicative and periodic. In particular, if *p* is a prime, then *χ*[4](*p*²) = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si231.png) and thus *d*(*π*(*p*²), *α*) = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si232.png).
*   •  Let *ν*(*p*) = 1/*p*![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si233.png) and 0 < *x* ≤ 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si210.png). When *ν*(*p*) = log *p*![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si209.png), you approach *ζ* (when *x* → 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si203.png)) in the exact same way as moving to the left on the real axis, from *σ* > 0.5![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si115.png) (no root if GRH is true) to *σ* = 0.5![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si53.png) (infinitely many roots). The case *ν*(*p*) = 1/*p*![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si233.png) offers a different perspective. Also *x*^(1/*p*) → 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si234.png) as *p* → ∞![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si235.png), regardless of 0 < *x* < 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si236.png). Thus *ν*(*p*) = 1/*p*![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si233.png) is appealing. For instance, when *x* = 0.99![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si237.png) and *σ* = 0.55![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si238.png), the orbit of *η*[*P*](*z*, *x*, *ν*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si202.png) has a small hole around the origin (if might shrink to a singleton if you display the full orbit for all *t* > 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si239.png), as it does if *x* = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si205.png)). The orbit regularly gets close to the origin before moving away again: this happens only when *t* is close to the imaginary part of a nontrivial root of *ζ*. For a fixed value of *σ* (say 0.5), increasing *x* from (say) 0.4 to 0.8 will move the hole to the left, closer to the origin as expected. Of course, lim[*x* → 1]*L*[*P*](*z*, *x*, *ν*) = *ζ*(*z*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si215.png). For instance, let $\\sigma = \\frac{1}{2}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si24.png). Then if *x* = 0.4![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si241.png), the orbit has a massive hole centered around (0, 1)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si242.png) on the X-axis. If *x* = 0.8![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si243.png), the orbit has a massive hole centered around $(0,\\frac{1}{2})$![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si244.png).

### 17.3.3 Riemann Hypothesis with cosines replaced by wavelets

The standard Dirichlet eta function *η*(*z*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si29.png), with *z* = *σ* + *i**t*![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si2.png), can be represented by two nonperiodic trigonometric series: one for the real part involving cosine terms, and one for the imaginary part (a phase shift of the first one) involving sine terms. If you modify even very slightly the coefficients in these series, you lose the interesting properties: **Dirichlet functional equation** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Functional_equation_\(L-function\))\], infinite number of roots when $\\sigma = \\frac{1}{2}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si24.png) (in other words, the orbit passing through the origin over and over), no root and hole in the orbit when $\\frac{1}{2} < \\sigma < 1$![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si20.png).

But what about a drastic change, replacing the sine and cosine functions by other periodic functions? Depending on the replacement, this actually works (except for the functional equation and therefore the roots when $\\sigma = \\frac{1}{2}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si24.png)), proving that there is nothing special about the sines and cosines when dealing with the Riemann Hypothesis, at least when $\\frac{1}{2} < \\sigma < 1$![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si20.png). I start by introducing the following real-valued function:

$\\varphi(z,\\theta) = \\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{\\infty}{( - 1)}^{k + 1}\\frac{W(\\theta + t\\log k)}{k^{\\sigma}},$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si245.png)(17.13) 

where *z* = *σ* + *i**t*![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si2.png), 0 ≤ *θ* < 2*π*![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si246.png), and *W* is a periodic function of period 2*π*, to be defined later. I also use the notation *φ*[1](*z*) = *φ*(*z*, 0)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si247.png) and *φ*[2](*z*) = *φ*(*z*, *π*/2)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si248.png). In particular, if *W*(*x*) = cos *x*![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si249.png), then *φ*[1](*z*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si250.png) is the real part of *η*(*z*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si29.png), and *φ*[2](*z*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si251.png) is the imaginary part. Also, here *P* is the full set of prime integers and *χ*( ⋅ )![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si4.png) is the constant function equal to 1.

The top part of [Fig. 17.7](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#f0040) shows the orbit of the modified *η*(*z*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si29.png) function for *σ* = 0.75![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si252.png) and 0 < *t* < 200![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si253.png), using the three functions *W* discussed in this section. The left plot corresponds to the cosine wave (in this case *η*(*z*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si29.png) is the standard Dirichlet function), the middle plot to the triangular wave, and the right plot to the alternating quadratic wave.

*   •  Triangular wave

$W(x) = \\begin{cases} {- 2x/\\pi,} & {\\text{if~}0 \\leqslant x \\leqslant \\pi/2,} \\\\ {- 2 + 2x/\\pi,} & {\\text{if~}\\pi/2 \\leqslant x \\leqslant 3\\pi/2,} \\\\ {4 - 2x/\\pi} & {\\text{if~}3\\pi/2 \\leqslant x \\leqslant 2\\pi;} \\\\ \\end{cases}$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si254.png)

*   
*   •  Alternating quadratic wave

$W(x) = \\begin{cases} {- 4x(x - \\pi)/\\pi^{2},} & {\\text{if~}0 \\leqslant x \\leqslant \\pi,} \\\\ {4(x - \\pi)(x - 2\\pi)/\\pi^{2}} & {\\text{if~}\\pi \\leqslant x \\leqslant 2\\pi;} \\\\ \\end{cases}$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si255.png)

*   
*   •  Cosine wave

*W*(*x*) = cos *x*.

![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si256.png)

*   

![Figure 17.7 Orbit of Dirichlet eta η(z) when cosines are replaced by other periodic functions.](images/B9780443218576000217/gr007.jpg)

[Figure 17.7](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#cf0390) Orbit of Dirichlet eta *η*(*z*) when cosines are replaced by other periodic functions.

I used the first ![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/fx004.jpg)terms in formula [(17.13)](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#deq18). In each case, the origin is inside the hole, clearly showing the absence of roots when 0 < *t* < 200![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si253.png). Other waves tested do not exhibit a hole. The bottom plots show the corresponding errors, magnified by a factor 20: they represent the difference between the approximate computations based on ![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/fx005.jpg)terms, and the more accurate results based on ![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/fx004.jpg)terms.

### 17.3.4 Riemann Hypothesis for Beurling primes

Beurling primes are real or complex numbers used to mimic and study distributions related to prime integers. A Beurling prime set *P* = {*p*[1], *p*[2], …}![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si160.png) is any set of real or complex numbers with the constraint that the product of elements of *P* cannot be an element of *P*. We then define *Q* = *Q*[*P*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si198.png) as the set of all product combinations *q* = *p*[1]^(*a*[1])*p*[2]^(*a*[2])⋯![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si257.png) where *a*[1], *a*[2], …![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si258.png) are integers ⩾0. It is also required that the factorization of *q* ∈ *Q*[*P*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si259.png), using Beurling primes from *P*, is unique.

A counterexample is the set of **Hilbert primes** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_number)\]: for instance, 1617 = 21 × 77 = 33 × 49![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si260.png) where 21, 33, 49, 77![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si261.png) are Hilbert primes (they cannot be factored as a product of Hilbert primes). A good example is when *Q* is the set of numbers that are sums of two square integers: if *q*, *q*^′ ∈ *Q*![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si262.png) then *q* ⋅ *q*^′ ∈ *Q*![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si263.png). In this case, *P* = {2, 5, 9, 13, …}![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si264.png), see [here](https://oeis.org/A055025). Note that 9, 49![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si265.png), and 121 are primes in *Q*. Related to this set is the set of **Gaussian primes** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaussian_integer)\], which are complex numbers.

The Python code in Section [17.5.1](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#s0120) handles Beurling primes. In the current implementation, *P* is the set of all prime integers except that 3 is replaced by 2 + log 3 ≈ 3.0986![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si266.png). When using the Beurling option, set the Dirichlet parameter to True, to get convergence when $\\frac{1}{2} \\leqslant \\sigma < 1$![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si10.png). The orbit of *η*[*P*](*z*, *χ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si88.png), assuming *χ*( ⋅ )![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si4.png) is constant and equal to 1, exhibits a hole that encompasses the origin if $\\frac{1}{2} < \\sigma < 1$![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si20.png). The hole shrinks to a point (the origin) if the full, infinite orbit is plotted, pointing to the absence of roots, just like for the standard Dirichlet eta function *η*(*z*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si29.png). Of course, this is part of the GRH conjecture, not a proven fact. Likewise, if $\\sigma = \\frac{1}{2}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si24.png), there are infinitely many roots. In the context of Beurling numbers, the associated Dirichlet function *L*[*P*](*z*, *χ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si107.png) is called a **Dedekind zeta function** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedekind_zeta_function)\], and Dedekind eta for the alternating series *η*[*P*](*z*, *χ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si88.png).

**Beurling primes** can be defined for objects other than numbers, like polynomials or matrices. For instance, let *A* be a square matrix, and define *p*[*k*] = exp (*μ*[*k*]*A*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si267.png), where the *μ*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si268.png)'s are distinct, strictly positive real numbers ordered by increasing values, and linearly independent over the set of positive integers, so that the factorization in *Q*[*P*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si199.png) is unique. For instance, *μ*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si268.png) is the logarithm of the *k*th prime integer. Any element (matrix) *q* ∈ *Q*[*P*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si259.png) can be written as

$q = p\_{1}^{a\_{1}}p\_{2}^{a\_{2}}\\cdots = \\exp(|q|A) = \\sum\\limits\_{k = 0}^{\\infty}|q|^{k}\\frac{A^{k}}{k!},\\quad\\text{~with~}|q| = \\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{\\infty}a\_{k}\\mu\_{k}.$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si269.png)

Here *a*[1], *a*[2], …![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si258.png) are integers ⩾0 and |*q*|![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si270.png) is called the norm. We can define an order on *Q* as follows: if *q*, *q*^′ ∈ *Q*![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si262.png), then *q* < *q*^′![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si271.png) if and only if |*q*| < |*q*^′|![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si272.png). Note that *q*, *q*^′![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si273.png), and the *p*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si112.png)'s are matrices. We can build Dirichlet series and Euler products for these primes, and study properties when $\\frac{1}{2} \\leqslant \\sigma < 1$![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si10.png), as we do for standard prime integers. For more on Beurling primes, see [\[5\]](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#br0025) and [\[13\]](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#br0065).

### 17.3.5 Stochastic Euler products

There are different ways to randomize functions related to Euler products. You may want to randomize *L*[*P*](*z*, *χ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si107.png) or *η*[*P*](*z*, *χ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si88.png) using **complex random variables** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_random_variable)\]. Or you may want to randomize the real or imaginary parts of these functions, or their norm. These random products have gained a lot of interest recently, at they provide insights about RH and its generalized version, GRH. For a recent reference on **random Euler products**, see [\[15\]](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#br0075). I briefly discussed randomized multiplicative functions such as random **Rademacher functions** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rademacher_distribution)\] in Section [17.2.2.2](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#s0055). More on this topic can be found in Chapter [11](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml) and in [\[9](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#br0045)–[11](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#br0055),[15\]](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#br0075). My recent book on stochastic processes [\[8\]](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#br0040) discusses tiny random perturbations applied to Dirichlet series: it shows that the hole at the origin, observed on any finite portion of the orbit if 0.5 < *σ* < 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si90.png), quickly vanishes if you slightly modify the series.

Here I focus on randomizing *L*[*P*](*z*, *χ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si107.png). Let *z* = *σ* + *i**t*![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si2.png) be fixed, 0.5 < *σ* < 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si90.png), and for each prime *p* ∈ *P*![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si165.png), *χ*(*p*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si3.png) be a random variable equal to +1 or −1 with probability 0.5. The *χ*(*p*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si3.png)'s are assumed to be independent. It follows immediately that

$\\text{E}\\lbrack L\_{P}(z,\\chi)\\rbrack = \\prod\\limits\_{p \\in P}\\text{E}\\left\\lbrack \\frac{1}{1 - \\chi(p)p^{- z}} \\right\\rbrack = \\prod\\limits\_{p \\in P}\\frac{1}{1 - p^{- 2z}} = L\_{P}(2z,\\chi\_{0}),$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si274.png)

where *χ*[0]( ⋅ )![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si275.png) is the constant function equal to one. Note that the product converges if *σ* > 0.5![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si115.png). So this type of randomization extents the abscissa of convergence from *σ* > 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si19.png) to *σ* > 0.5![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si115.png). Now let the random variable *ρ*²![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si276.png) be the square of the distance to the origin:

$\\rho^{2} = |L\_{P}(z,\\chi)|^{2} = \\prod\\limits\_{p \\in P}|1 - \\chi(p)p^{- z}|^{- 2} = \\prod\\limits\_{p \\in P}\\frac{1}{1 - 2p^{- \\sigma}\\chi(p)\\cos(t\\log p) + p^{- 2\\sigma}}.$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si277.png)(17.14) 

We have

$\\text{E}\\lbrack\\rho^{2}\\rbrack = \\prod\\limits\_{p \\in P}\\text{E}\\left\\lbrack |1 - \\chi(p)p^{- z}|^{- 2} \\right\\rbrack = \\prod\\limits\_{p \\in P}\\frac{1 + p^{- 2\\sigma}}{{(1 + p^{- 2\\sigma})}^{2} - 4p^{- 2\\sigma}\\cos^{2}(t\\log p)}.$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si278.png)

In particular,

$\\prod\\limits\_{p \\in P}\\frac{1}{1 + p^{- 2\\sigma}} = \\frac{L\_{P}(4\\sigma,\\chi\_{0})}{L\_{P}(2\\sigma,\\chi\_{0})} \\leqslant \\text{E}\\lbrack\\rho^{2}\\rbrack \\leqslant \\prod\\limits\_{p \\in P}\\frac{1 + p^{- 2\\sigma}}{{(1 - p^{- 2\\sigma})}^{2}} = \\frac{L\_{P}^{3}(2\\sigma,\\chi\_{0})}{L\_{P}(4\\sigma,\\chi\_{0})}.$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si279.png)(17.15) 

Again, *χ*[0]( ⋅ )![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si275.png) is the constant function equal to 1. The maximum is attained when *t* = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si25.png). If *P* is the full set of primes, formula [(17.15)](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#deq26) becomes *ζ*(4*σ*)/*ζ*(2*σ*) ≤ E\[*ρ*²\] ≤ *ζ*³(2*σ*)/*ζ*(4*σ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si280.png), where *ζ* is the **Riemann zeta function** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_zeta_function)\]. Similar bounds are available for E\[*ρ*\]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si281.png). It is interesting to note that by averaging over all potential *χ*( ⋅ )![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si4.png)'s, the orbit has a hole encompassing the origin, with a strictly positive radius. This is in contrast to the nonrandom case, where the hole is reduced to a point regardless of *χ* (assuming 0.5 < *σ* < 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si90.png)).

Let *P* = {*p*[1], *p*[2], …}![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si160.png) with the primes listed in increasing order. Now let us define the random variable $L\_{\\chi}(n) = \\sum\_{k = 1}^{n}\\chi(p\_{k})$![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si282.png). It satisfies the **law of the iterated logarithm** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_of_the_iterated_logarithm)\], stated in formula [(17.7)](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#deq10), and translating here to

$\\underset{n\\rightarrow\\infty}{\\lim⁡\\sup}\\frac{|L\_{\\chi}(n)|}{\\sqrt{n\\log\\log n}} = C,$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si283.png)

for some constant *C* with 0 < *C* < ∞![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si123.png). But the prime numbers are not perfectly random, and one would expect $\\sqrt{n\\log\\log n}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si284.png) to be replaced by (say) $\\sqrt{n^{1 + \\epsilon}}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si285.png) for any arbitrary small *ϵ* > 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si126.png). This may be the case in the deterministic example where *χ*(*p*) =  + 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si286.png) if *p* ≡ 1 *m**o**d* 4![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si225.png) and *χ*(*p*) =  − 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si287.png) if *p* ≡ 3 *m**o**d* 4![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si227.png). One way to make the random Euler product more realistic is to introduce weak dependencies among the *χ*(*p*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si3.png)'s. Then one can test whether the improved stochastic model (with weak dependencies) is a better fit to the observed data – the actual *χ*(*p*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si3.png)'s. The weak dependencies can be introduced as follows, when simulating *χ*(*p*[*n* + 1])![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si288.png) for *n* large enough:

*   •  If $|L\_{\\chi}(n)| < \\beta\\sqrt{n{(\\log\\log\\log n)}^{\\nu}}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si289.png), then $P\\lbrack\\chi(p\_{n + 1}) = 1\\rbrack = \\frac{1}{2} + \\mu n^{- \\alpha}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si290.png), $P\\lbrack\\chi(p\_{n + 1}) = - 1\\rbrack = \\frac{1}{2} - \\mu n^{- \\alpha}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si291.png).
*   •  Otherwise choose between +1 and −1 so that |*L*[*χ*](*n* + 1)| < |*L*[*χ*](*n*)|![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si292.png).

You may try with various values of *α*, *β*, *ν* > 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si293.png) and *μ* to see which ones provide the best fit for very large *n*, say *n* > 10^(15)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si294.png). You could also change the sign of *μ* every now and then. The choice of log log log *n*![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si295.png) is inspired by Gonek's conjecture; see [\[14\]](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#br0070) page 29.

Finally, another random Euler product also investigated in [\[15\]](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#br0075) is the following:

$\\rho^{2} = \\prod\\limits\_{p \\in P}\\frac{1}{1 - 2p^{- \\sigma}\\cos(\\Theta\_{p}) + p^{- 2\\sigma}}.$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si296.png)(17.16) 

Here the *Θ*[*p*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si297.png)'s are independent uniform deviates on \[0, 2*π*\]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si298.png). Compare this to formula [(17.14)](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#deq24). Since

$\\frac{1}{2\\pi}\\int\_{0}^{2\\pi}\\frac{1}{1 - 2p^{- \\sigma}\\cos\\theta + p^{- 2\\sigma}}d\\theta = \\frac{1}{1 - p^{- 2\\sigma}},$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si299.png)

we have

$\\text{E}\\lbrack\\rho^{2}\\rbrack = \\prod\\limits\_{p \\in P}\\text{E}\\left\\lbrack \\frac{1}{1 - 2p^{- \\sigma}\\cos(\\Theta\_{p}) + p^{- 2\\sigma}} \\right\\rbrack = \\prod\\limits\_{p \\in P}\\frac{1}{1 - p^{- 2\\sigma}} = L\_{P}(2\\sigma,\\chi\_{0}),$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si300.png)

where again, *χ*[0]( ⋅ )![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si275.png) is the constant function equal to 1. If *P* is the full set of primes, *L*[*P*](2*σ*, *χ*[0]) = *ζ*(2*σ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si301.png). The proof that the distribution attached to *ρ*²![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si276.png) exists and is not singular can be found in [\[15\]](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#br0075).

## 17.4 Exercises

The following exercises require out-of-the-box thinking. They complement the theory or provide a proof to some of the theoretical results discussed in this chapter.

Exercise 17.1

**– Asymptotic formula.** Prove the asymptotic formula [(17.2)](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#deq3).

**Solution**

By definition, we have *q*[*k*] = *p*[1]^(*a*[1])*p*[2]^(*a*[2])⋯*p*[*d*]^(*a*[*d*])![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si67.png) for some positive integers *a*[1], …, *a*[*d*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si302.png). In other words, *a*[1]log *p*[1] + … + *a*[*d*]log *p*[*d*] = log *q*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si303.png). This is the equation of a (*d* − 1)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si304.png)\-dimensional simplex with vertices (log *p*[1], 0, …, 0)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si305.png), (0, log *p*[2], …, 0), …, (0, 0, …, log *p*[*d*])![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si306.png). If you add the origin as a vertex, then the number of points *v*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si307.png) with integer coordinates, inside the newly created *d*\-dimensional simplex, is approximately equal to the volume *V*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si308.png) of that **simplex** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simplex#Volume)\]. Also, *v*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si307.png) is the number of positive integers less than or equal to *q*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si43.png), since each integer has a unique factorization in (ordered) prime numbers. So, *q*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si43.png) is the inverse of the function *v*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si307.png), which is asymptotically equal to the inverse of *V*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si308.png). To complete the proof, use the well known fact that

$V\_{k} = \\frac{1}{d!}\\left( \\log q\_{k} \\right)^{d}\\prod\\limits\_{p \\in P}\\frac{1}{\\log p} = \\frac{1}{d!}\\prod\\limits\_{p \\in P}\\log\_{p}q\_{k},$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si309.png)

where log[*p*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si310.png) stands for the logarithm in base *p*. The result is easy to verify if *d* = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si311.png).

Exercise 17.2

**– Equivalence between series and Euler product.** Prove formula [(17.1)](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#deq2).

**Solution**

Expanding the product in formula [(17.1)](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#deq2), one obtains

$\\prod\\limits\_{p \\in P}\\frac{1}{1 - p^{- z}} = \\prod\\limits\_{p \\in P}\\left( 1 + p^{- z} + p^{- 2z} + \\cdots \\right) = \\sum\\limits\_{a\_{1},a\_{2},\\ldots,a\_{d}}\\left( p\_{1}^{a\_{1}}p\_{2}^{a\_{2}}\\cdots p\_{d}^{a\_{d}} \\right)^{- z} = \\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{\\infty}q\_{k}^{- z}.$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si312.png)

Let us denote the rightmost series in the above equation as *ζ*[*P*](*z*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si313.png). To complete the proof, use the fact that

$\\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{\\infty}\\delta\_{k}q\_{k}^{- z} = \\zeta\_{P}(z) - 2\\sum\\limits\_{q\_{k}\\text{~even}}q\_{k}^{- z} = \\zeta\_{P}(z) - 2\\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{\\infty}{(2q\_{k})}^{- z} = (1 - 2^{1 - z})\\zeta\_{P}(z).$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si314.png)

Another interesting identity is the following:

$(1 - 2^{1 - z})\\prod\\limits\_{p \\in P}\\frac{1}{1 + p^{- z}} = (1 - 2^{1 - z})\\frac{\\zeta\_{P}(2z)}{\\zeta\_{p}(z)} = \\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{\\infty}\\delta\_{k}\\lambda(q\_{k})q\_{k}^{- z},$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si315.png)

where *λ*( ⋅ )![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si116.png) is the **Liouville function** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liouville_function)\].

Exercise 17.3

**– Convergence problem.** If *P* is the set of all primes and *δ*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si316.png) is replaced by +1, then the series in formula [(17.1)](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#deq2) will not converge if *σ* < 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si9.png). Here, *z* = *σ* + *i**t*![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si2.png). That is, *σ* is the real part of the complex number *z*. 

**Solution**

In this case *q*[*k*] = *k*![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si317.png). Note that *k*^( − *z*) = *k*^( − *σ*) ⋅ \[cos (*t*log *k*) + *i*sin (*t*log *k*)\]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si318.png). It suffices to prove that the series with *k*th term equal to *k*^( − *σ*)cos (*t*log *k*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si319.png) cannot converge, even though cos (*t*log *k*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si320.png) oscillates infinitely often between positive and negative values, as *k* increases. The reason is because log *k*![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si321.png) grows too slowly. When *k* is very close to a multiple of (say) 2*π*, too many consecutive terms are all positive, and *k*^(*σ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si322.png) does not grow fast enough (if *σ* < 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si9.png)) to keep the partial sums bounded and converging. To the contrary, if log *k*![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si321.png) is replaced by $\\sqrt{k}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si323.png) in the cosine function, and *σ* = 0.75![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si252.png), then the series converge: the corresponding integral between 0 and ∞ is equal to $\\sqrt{2\\pi/|t|}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si324.png).

Exercise 17.4

**– Truncated Dirichlet function.** Determine the area covered by the orbit, for a fixed value of *σ*, when *n* = 3![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si141.png) and *t* runs though all the positive real numbers in formula [(17.8)](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#deq11). Generalize to *n* = 4![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si325.png).

**Solution**

Let us assume that the center of the hole is (1, 0)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si142.png) in this case. Proving it is left to the reader. Then the square of the distance between a point on the orbit at time *t* and the origin is equal to

$d^{2}(t) = \\left\\lbrack \\beta^{\\sigma}\\cos(t\\log 2) - \\lambda\_{3}^{\\sigma}\\cos(t\\log 2) \\right\\rbrack^{2} + \\left\\lbrack \\beta^{\\sigma}\\sin(t\\log 2) - \\lambda\_{3}^{\\sigma}\\sin(t\\log 2) \\right\\rbrack^{2} = \\beta^{2\\sigma} + \\lambda\_{3}^{2\\sigma} - 2\\beta^{\\sigma}\\lambda\_{3}^{\\sigma}\\left\\lbrack \\cos(t\\log 2)\\cos(t\\log 3) + \\sin(t\\log 2)\\sin(t\\log 3) \\right\\rbrack = \\beta^{2\\sigma} + \\lambda\_{3}^{2\\sigma} - 2\\beta^{\\sigma}\\lambda\_{3}^{\\sigma}\\cos\\left( t\\log\\frac{2}{3} \\right).$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si326.png)

Since the cosine takes all values between −1 and +1, infinitely often with period 2*π*/(log 3 − log 2)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si327.png), the outer boundary of the orbit is a circle of radius *ρ*[1]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si328.png) centered at (1, 0)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si142.png), and the inner boundary (that is, the shape of the hole) is a circle of radius *ρ*[2]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si329.png) also centered at (1, 0)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si142.png). Here

$\\rho\_{1} = \\sqrt{\\beta^{2\\sigma} + \\lambda\_{3}^{2\\sigma} + 2\\beta^{\\sigma}\\lambda\_{3}^{\\sigma}} = |\\beta^{\\sigma} + \\lambda\_{3}^{\\sigma}|,\\quad\\rho\_{2} = \\sqrt{\\beta^{2\\sigma} + \\lambda\_{3}^{2\\sigma} - 2\\beta^{\\sigma}\\lambda\_{3}^{\\sigma}} = |\\beta^{\\sigma} - \\lambda\_{3}^{\\sigma}|.$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si330.png)

Thus the larger the *β*, the bigger the hole. I assumed that *β*, *λ*[3] ≥ 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si331.png).

The case *n* = 4![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si325.png) is considerably more complicated. The center is no longer (1, 0)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si142.png), but typically (*c*, 0)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si110.png) with *c* < 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si332.png). Also, the shapes may no longer be circles. There may or may not be a hole. However, if *β* is large enough, there will be a hole, big enough to encompass (1, 0)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si142.png). The square of the distance to (1, 0)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si142.png) is now

$d^{2}(t) = \\beta^{2\\sigma} + \\lambda\_{3}^{2\\sigma} + \\lambda\_{4}^{2\\sigma} - 2\\beta^{\\sigma}\\lambda\_{3}^{\\sigma}\\cos\\left( t\\log\\frac{2}{3} \\right) - 2\\beta^{\\sigma}\\lambda\_{4}^{\\sigma}\\cos\\left( t\\log\\frac{2}{4} \\right) - 2\\lambda\_{3}^{\\sigma}\\lambda\_{3}^{\\sigma}\\cos\\left( t\\log\\frac{3}{4} \\right).$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si333.png)

The minimum possible value for *d*²(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si334.png) is *d*[min] = *β*^(2*σ*) + *λ*[3]^(2*σ*) + *λ*[4]^(2*σ*) − 2*β*^(*σ*)*λ*[3]^(*σ*) − 2*β*^(*σ*)*λ*[4]^(*σ*) − 2*λ*[3]^(*σ*)*λ*[3]^(*σ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si335.png). If *d*[min] > 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si336.png), there is a hole big enough to encompass (1, 0)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si142.png).

Exercise 17.5

**– The orbit covers a dense area in the complex plane.** The purpose of this exercise is to prove a particular case: if *σ* < 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si9.png), then lim inf |*L*[*P*](*z*, *χ*)| = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si337.png) regardless of *χ*. The infimum \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limit_inferior_and_limit_superior)\] is over all complex numbers *z*. Here we assume that *P* is an infinite subset of primes (or the full set), and that the sum of *p*^( − *σ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si338.png) over all *p* ∈ *P*![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si165.png) diverges. This proves that the orbit is dense around the origin under certain conditions. It implies, under these conditions, that the hole shrinks to a singleton (the origin) if |*L*[*P*](*z*, *χ*)| > 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si339.png) for all *z*, and to an empty set if *L*[*P*](*z*, *χ*) = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si340.png) for some *z*.

**Solution**

Assume the Euler product is finite, and contains only the first *d* primes *p*[1], …, *p*[*d*] ∈ *P*![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si341.png). Let *z* = *σ* + *i**t*![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si2.png) as usual, with *t* large enough so that *t*log *p*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si342.png) gets extremely close to a multiple of *π*, say *m*[*k*]*π*![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si343.png), for all *k* = 1, …, *d*![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si344.png). This is possible thanks to **Kronecker's theorem** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kronecker%27s_theorem)\]. Then sin (*t*log *p*[*k*])![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si345.png) gets very close to 0, and cos (*t*log *p*[*k*])![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si346.png) gets very close to either −1 or +1 depending on whether *m*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si347.png) is odd or even. Thus, the imaginary part of *L*[*P*](*z*, *χ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si107.png), involving the sine terms only, gets very close to 0. The real part, involving the cosine terms only, gets very close to

$S(\\chi^{\\star}) = \\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{\\infty}\\chi^{\\star}(k)\\chi(k)k^{- \\sigma},$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si348.png)

where

*   •  The function *χ*^⋆![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si349.png) is a **completely multiplicative** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Completely_multiplicative_function)\] and thus entirely defined by its values on prime numbers,
*   •  *χ*^⋆(*p*[*k*]) ∈ {1,  + 1}![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si350.png) if *p*[*k*] ∈ *P*![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si351.png) and 1 ≤ *k* ≤ *d*![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si352.png), otherwise *χ*^⋆(*p*[*k*]) = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si353.png),
*   •  *χ*^⋆(*p*[*k*]) =  + 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si354.png) if *m*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si347.png) is even, otherwise *χ*^⋆(*p*[*k*]) =  − 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si355.png).

Also, *p*^( − *z*) = \[cos (*t*log *p*[*k*]) + *i*sin (*t*log *p*[*k*])\] ⋅ *p*^( − *σ*) → *χ*^⋆(*p*[*k*])*p*^( − *σ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si356.png) as *t* → ∞![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si357.png). Thus for the Euler product, with the special *t* discussed above (a function of *m*[1], …, *m*[*d*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si358.png)) and *z* = *σ* + *i**t*![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si2.png), we have

$L\_{P}(z,\\chi)\\rightarrow\\prod\\limits\_{k = 1}^{d}\\frac{1}{1 - \\chi^{\\star}(p\_{k})\\chi(p\_{k})p\_{k}^{- \\sigma}} \\in \\mathbb{R}\\quad\\text{as~}t\\rightarrow\\infty.$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si359.png)(17.17) 

If ∑[*p* ∈ *P*]*p*^( − *σ*) = ∞![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si360.png), then the product in formula [(17.17)](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#deq39) can approximate any positive value arbitrarily closely, as *d* → ∞![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si62.png). Indeed, *d*[*k*] = *χ*^⋆(*p*[*k*])![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si361.png) can be seen as the *k*th binary digit of the (real) number *L*[*P*](*z*, *χ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si107.png) in some special numeration system. And you can compute *d*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si362.png) using a technique similar to that used for standard binary digits in base 2, with a version of the **greedy algorithm** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greedy_algorithm)\]. To get arbitrarily close to zero, one way is to choose the function *χ*^⋆![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si349.png) so that *χ*^⋆*χ* =  − 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si363.png).

**Note.** In the computation of *S*(*χ*^⋆)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si364.png), I implicitly used the following facts. First, if *k* has the prime factorization *k* = *p*[1]^(*a*[1])⋯*p*[*d*]^(*a*[*d*])![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si365.png), then cos (*t*log *k*) = cos (*a*[1]*t*log *p*[1] + ⋯ + *a*[*d*]*t*log *p*[*d*])![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si366.png). Recursively using cos (*α* + *β*) = cos *α*cos *β* − sin *α*sin *β*![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si367.png), with the fact that all the sines are zero and cos (*a*[*i*]*t*log *p*[*i*]) → cos (*a*[*i*]*m*[*i*]*π*) = \[*χ*^⋆(*p*[*i*])\]^(*a*[*i*])![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si368.png) as *t* → ∞![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si357.png), one obtains cos (*t*log *k*) → \[*χ*^⋆(*p*[1])\]^(*a*[1])⋯\[*χ*^⋆(*p*[*d*])\]^(*a*[*d*]) = *χ*^⋆(*k*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si369.png).

Exercise 17.6

**– Density of integers of the form** **x**³ + **y**²![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si370.png)**.** Prove that the *k*th integer of the form *x*³ + *y*²![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si161.png) is asymptotically larger than *k*^(6/5)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si170.png).

**Solution**

Let *v*(*n*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si371.png) be the number of lattice points (*x*, *y*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si372.png), with *x*, *y*![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si164.png) positive integers, satisfying *x*³ + *y*² ≤ *n*![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si373.png). Estimating *v*[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si374.png) is a classic problem in **additive number theory** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Additive_number_theory)\], generalizing the **Gaussian circle problem** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss_circle_problem)\]. The solution to this class of problems is as follows. Let *S*[1], …, *S*[*m*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si375.png) be *m* infinite sets of positive integers, and *v*[*i*](*n*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si376.png) be the number of elements less than *n* in *S*[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si377.png). Let *v*(*n*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si371.png) be the number of lattice points (*x*[1], …, *x*[*m*])![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si378.png), with *x*[*i*] ∈ *S*[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si379.png), satisfying *x*[1] + ⋯ + *x*[*m*] ≤ *v*(*n*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si380.png). If *v*[*i*](*n*) ∼ *a*[*i*]*n*^(*b*[*i*])(log *n*)^( − *c*[*i*])![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si381.png) with 0 < *b*[*i*] ≤ 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si382.png), *c*[*i*] ≥ 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si383.png) and *a*[*i*] > 0  (*i* = 1, …, *m*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si384.png), then

$v(n) \\lesssim \\frac{\\prod\_{i = 1}^{m}a\_{i}\\Gamma(b\_{i} + 1)}{\\Gamma(1 + \\sum\_{i = 1}^{m}b\_{i})} \\cdot \\frac{n^{b\_{1} + \\cdots + b\_{m}}}{{(\\log n)}^{c\_{1} + \\cdots + c\_{m}}},$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si385.png)

where ≲ means “asymptotically smaller”, and Γ is the Gamma function. See [here](https://mathoverflow.net/questions/364559/general-asymptotic-result-in-additive-combinatorics-sums-of-sets) and [here](https://mathoverflow.net/questions/363055/goldbach-conjecture-and-other-problems-in-additive-combinatorics/) for details.

In our case, *m* = 2![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si386.png), *a*[1] = *a*[2] = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si387.png), *c*[1] = *c*[2] = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si388.png), *b*[1] = 1/3![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si389.png), *b*[2] = 1/2![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si390.png). Thus *v*(*n*) ≲ *n*^(5/6)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si391.png). Note that this method may result in double counting, for instance, 225 = 6³ + 3² = 5³ + 10² = 0³ + 15²![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si392.png). Thus the actual number *w*(*n*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si393.png) of positive integers of the form *x*³ + *y*²![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si161.png) is even smaller, thus definitely smaller than *n*^(5/6)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si169.png). It follows immediately, using the inverse of the function *w*(*n*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si393.png), that the *k*th element is asymptotically larger than *n*^(6/5)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si394.png).

Exercise 17.7

**– Strange factorization of the Dirichlet functions.** Show, based on the Euler product, that *L*[*P*](*z*, *χ*) = *L*[*P*](*z*/2, *ψ*)*L*[*P*](*z*/2,  − *ψ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si395.png) where *ψ*²(*p*) = *χ*(*p*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si396.png), thus *ψ*(*p*) ∈ {1,  − 1, *i*,  − *i*}![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si397.png). In particular, if *χ*(*p*) = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si100.png), one can choose *ψ*(*p*[2*k* + 1]) = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si398.png) and *ψ*(*p*[2*k*]) =  − 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si399.png) where *p*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si112.png) is the *k*th prime. In this case, *L*(*z*, *χ*) = *ζ*(*z*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si400.png), and the Euler products of *L*(*z*/2, *ψ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si401.png) and *L*(*z*/2,  − *ψ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si402.png) both converge if *σ* > 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si30.png). However, *L*[*P*](*z*/2, *ψ*)*L*[*P*](*z*/2,  − *ψ*) = *ζ*(*z*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si403.png) only if *σ* > 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si19.png). How can these formulas be generalized recursively?

**Solution**

Let *ψ*[0] = *χ*![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si404.png) and *ψ*[1] = *ψ*![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si405.png). Using the same logic, *L*(*z*/2,  − *ψ*[1]) = *L*[*P*](*z*/4, *ψ*[2])*L*[*P*](*z*/4,  − *ψ*[2])![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si406.png) where *ψ*[2]²(*p*) =  − *ψ*[1](*p*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si407.png). Applying this method recursively, one obtains

$L\_{P}(z,\\chi) = L(z/2^{n}, - \\psi\_{n})\\prod\\limits\_{k = 1}^{n}L\_{P}(z/2^{k},\\psi\_{k}),$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si408.png)

where *n* ≥ 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si409.png) and *ψ*[*k* + 1]² =  − *ψ*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si410.png) for *k* = 1, 2![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si411.png), and so on. For which values of *σ* is this formula valid? Based on the construction, all the associated Euler products must converge, suggesting *σ* > 2^(*n*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si412.png).

Exercise 17.8

**– Roots of the Riemann zeta function.** As usual, *z* = *σ* + *i**t*![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si2.png). Let *S*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si413.png) be any open interval containing exactly one value *t*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si414.png) such that $\\zeta(\\frac{1}{2} + it\_{0}) = 0$![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si415.png), and let *η*(*z*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si29.png) be the standard **Dirichlet eta function**. Discuss the existence (or not) of roots of *η*(*z*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si29.png) if *t* ∈ *S*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si416.png) and $\\frac{1}{2} < \\sigma < 1$![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si20.png). Show how it works when *S*[0] = \]199, 202\[![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si417.png). You can find a table of the first ![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/fx006.jpg)nontrivial roots of *ζ*(*z*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si8.png), [here](http://www.dtc.umn.edu/~odlyzko/zeta_tables/).

**Solution**

Assume *σ* is fixed. Let *μ*(*σ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si418.png) be the minimum of |*η*(*z*)|![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si419.png) if *t* ∈ *S*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si416.png), and let *τ*(*σ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si420.png) be the value achieving the minimum. That is,

$\\mu(\\sigma) = \\min\\limits\_{t \\in S\_{0}}|\\eta(\\sigma + it)|,\\quad\\tau(\\sigma) = \\underset{t\\in S\_{0}}{\\arg⁡\\min}|\\eta(\\sigma + it)|.$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si421.png)

If *S*[0] = \]199, 202\[![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si417.png) then *t*[0] ≈ 201.26![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si422.png). Let *t*[0]^′ = 44*π*/log 2 ≈ 199.42![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si423.png). We have 1 − 2^(1 − *z*) = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si424.png) where *z* = 1 + *i**t*[0]^′![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si425.png), and:

*   •  $\\mu(\\frac{1}{2}) = 0$![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si426.png) and $\\tau(\\frac{1}{2}) = t\_{0}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si427.png) since $\\eta(\\frac{1}{2} + it\_{0}) = 0$![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si428.png), 
*   •  *μ*(1) = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si429.png) and *τ*(1) = *t*[0]^′![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si430.png), since *η*(1 + *i**t*[0]^′) = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si431.png),
*   •  *μ*(*σ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si418.png) is strictly increasing and continuous if $\\frac{1}{2} \\leqslant \\sigma \\leqslant \\sigma\_{0}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si432.png) with *σ*[0] ≈ 0.75![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si433.png),
*   •  *μ*(*σ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si418.png) is strictly decreasing and continuous if *σ*[0] ≤ *σ* ≤ 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si434.png).

In other words, *μ*(*σ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si418.png) is convex. It seems to imply that there is no root if *t* ∈ *S*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si416.png) and $\\frac{1}{2} < \\sigma < 1$![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si20.png). However, proving that *μ*(*σ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si418.png) is increasing or decreasing, with only one change-point at some *σ*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si104.png) (depending on *S*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si413.png)), may be as hard as proving RH itself: it is based on empirical evidence only, and related to the (conjectured) absence of roots for the derivative of *ζ*(*z*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si8.png). Indeed, it is just a consequence of the Riemann Hypothesis, see [here](https://mathoverflow.net/questions/190802/zeros-of-the-derivative-of-riemanns-xi-function).

There is something particularly striking though, which could prove useful to make some progress: the function *τ*(*σ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si420.png) is almost flat, with a single discontinuity at *σ*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si104.png). Indeed, 201.26 ≤ *τ*(*σ*) ≤ 201.29![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si435.png) if $\\frac{1}{2} \\leqslant \\sigma < \\sigma\_{0}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si436.png), and 199.41 ≤ *τ*(*σ*) ≤ 199.42![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si437.png) if *σ*[0] < *σ* ≤ 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si438.png). These variations are so small that you wonder if they are real, or caused by numerical imprecision (implying the function *τ*(*σ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si420.png) could be perfectly flat with a single discontinuity, making it potentially easier to prove RH). If these variations really do exist, there might be a function other than *η*(*z*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si29.png) with the same roots, say a scaled version of *η*(*z*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si29.png) with a scaling factor free of roots, for which the variations are absent. Such a function may be easier to investigate.

More generally, the functions *μ*(*σ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si418.png) and *τ*(*σ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si420.png) have this same behavior whenever *S*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si413.png) contains a value *t*[0]^′![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si439.png) such that *z* = 1 + *i**t*[0]^′![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si425.png) is a root of 1 − 2^(1 − *z*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si440.png), and therefore a root of *η*(*z*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si29.png). Because these roots are evenly spaced by the increment 2*π*/log 2![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si441.png), and since the roots at $\\sigma = \\frac{1}{2}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si24.png) are closer and closer to each other as *t* → ∞![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si357.png) (see [\[3](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#br0015),[17\]](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#br0085)), there is either one *t*[0]^′![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si439.png) in *S*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si413.png), or none. There can't be more than one. When there is none, the situation is even easier and amounts to setting *σ*[0] = ∞![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si442.png), or at least *σ*[0] > 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si443.png).

Finally, if it was possible to prove the points discussed in this exercise, then, of course, RH would be proved. It suffices to consider the collection of all possible *S*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si413.png) to show that there would be no root anywhere, no matter how large *t* is, if $\\frac{1}{2} < \\sigma < 1$![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si20.png).

Exercise 17.9

**– Approximating the Dirichlet eta function.** The Dirichlet series for *η*(*z*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si29.png) converges very slowly and chaotically, especially if *σ* is small or *t* is large. One way to accelerate the convergence is to use **Euler's transform** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Series_acceleration)\]. See also Exercise 25 in [\[8\]](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#br0040). Other approximations exist, for instance, using Dirichlet polynomials [\[7\]](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#br0035). Here I investigate yet a different type of approximation. Let *z* = *σ* + *i**t*![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si2.png) as usual, with *σ* fixed, say *σ* = 0.8![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si444.png). Also assume that the values of *η*(*σ* + *i**k*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si445.png) are known and denoted as *η*[*k*](*σ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si446.png) if *k* is a positive integer. The approximation is as follows:

$\\eta(z) \\approx \\frac{\\sin\\pi t}{\\pi} \\cdot \\left\\lbrack \\frac{\\eta\_{0}(\\sigma)}{t} + 2t\\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{n}{( - 1)}^{k}\\frac{\\eta\_{k}(\\sigma)}{t^{2} - k^{2}} \\right\\rbrack.$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si447.png)

Show how good this approximation is. For the solution, see [Exercise 8.2](#Chp008_131-145_B9780443218576000126.xhtml) in Chapter [8](#Chp008_131-145_B9780443218576000126.xhtml).

## 17.5 Python code

The main code is in Section [17.5.1](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#s0120). The code in Section [17.5.2](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#s0125) is provided for convenience only: it does not further illustrate the theory, but instead focuses on producing beautiful videos of the orbits studied in this paper. Section [11.3.2](#Chp011_203-228_B9780443218576000151.xhtml) about the prime test for pseudorandom number generators, deeply related to the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, has more Python code directly relevant to the topics discussed here.

### 17.5.1 Computing the orbit of various Dirichlet series

The code below computes *η*[*P*](*z*, *χ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si88.png) if the Dirichlet variable is set to True; otherwise it computes *L*[*P*](*z*, *χ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si107.png). More specifically, it computes the value of the function in question for *z* = *σ* + *i**t*![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si2.png), with *σ* = ℜ(*z*) ≥ 0.5![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si448.png) fixed and determined by the variable sig, and for equally spaced values of *t* between minT and maxT. The spacing is determined by the variable increment, typically set to 0.01. It uses the Dirichlet series expansion, with the number of terms determined by nterms (typically set to 2000) to get at least 2 digits of accuracy in the worse case where *σ* = 0.5![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si53.png) or *t* is large. The function primes.check() from the primePy library tests if a number is a prime. The code actually handles the more general case where *χ*(*p*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si3.png) is replaced by *χ*(*p*) ⋅ *x*^(*ν*(*p*))![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si449.png), with *ν*(*p*) = 1/*p*![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si233.png) as in formula [(17.12)](#Chp017_329-360_B9780443218576000217.xhtml#deq17) and 0 < *x* ≤ 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si210.png). The standard case corresponds to *x* = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si205.png). The variable *x* is represented by x in the code.

The value of *η*[*P*](*z*, *χ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si88.png) or *L*[*P*](*z*, *χ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si107.png) is a complex number: its real and imaginary parts are respectively named etax and etay in the code. The function *χ*, and thus the set *P*, depends on the option selected in the code, determined by the variable method: Zeta (that is, *ζ*(*z*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si8.png) by default), Eta, Dirichlet4 (corresponding to *χ*[4]![Image](images/B9780443218576000217/si1.png)), Beurling, Alternating, or Random.
