## 18.3 Dual confidence regions

This tutorial explains how to build confidence regions (the 2D version of a confidence interval) using as little statistical theory as possible. I also avoid the traditional terminology and notation such as *α*, *Z*[1 − *α*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si7.png), critical value, confidence level, significance level, and so on. These can be confusing to beginners and professionals alike.

Instead, I use simulations and two keywords only, confidence region and confidence level. The purpose is to explain the concept using a framework that will appeal to machine learning professionals, software engineers and nonstatisticians. My hope is that you will gain a deep understanding of the technique, without headaches. I also introduce an alternative type of confidence region, called dual confidence region. It is asymptotically equivalent to the standard definition. In my opinion, it is more intuitive.

### 18.3.1 Case study

This example comes from a real-life application discussed in Section [16.4.1](#Chp016_293-327_B9780443218576000205.xhtml). Here I provide the minimum amount of material necessary to illustrate the methodology. The full problem is described Section [18.3.5](#Chp018_361-386_B9780443218576000229.xhtml#s0070), for the curious reader. In its simplest form, we are dealing with independent **bivariate Bernoulli trials**. The data set has *n* observations. Each observation consists of two measurements (*u*[*k*], *v*[*k*])![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si8.png), for *k* = 1, …, *n*![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si9.png). Here *u*[*k*] = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si10.png) if some interval *B*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si11.png) contains zero point (otherwise *u*[*k*] = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si12.png)). Likewise, *v*[*k*] = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si13.png) if the same interval contains one point (otherwise *v*[*k*] = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si14.png)).

The interval *B*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si11.png) can contain more than one point, but, of course, it cannot simultaneously contain one and two points. The probability that *B*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si11.png) contains zero point is *p*; the probability that it contains one point is *q*, with 0 < *p* + *q* < 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si15.png). The goal is to estimate *p* and *q*. The estimators (proportions computed on the observations) are denoted as *p*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si16.png) and *q*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si17.png).

Since we are dealing with Bernoulli variables, the standard deviations are $\\sigma\_{p} = \\sqrt{p(1 - p)}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si18.png) and $\\sigma\_{q} = \\sqrt{q(1 - q)}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si19.png). Also the correlation between the two components *u*[*k*], *v*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si20.png) of the observation vector is *ρ*[*p*, *q*] =  − *p**q*/*σ*[*p*]*σ*[*q*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si21.png). Indeed, the probability to observe (0, 0)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si22.png) is 1 − *p* − *q*![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si23.png), the probability to observe (1, 0)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si24.png) is *p*, the probability to observe (0, 1)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si25.png) is *q*, and the probability to observe (1, 1)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si26.png) is zero.

### 18.3.2 Standard confidence region

A confidence region of level *γ* is a domain of minimum area that contains a proportion *γ* of the potential values of your estimator (*p*[0], *q*[0])![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si27.png), based on your *n* observations. When *n* is large, (*p*[0], *q*[0])![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si27.png) approximately has a **bivariate normal distribution** (also called Gaussian), thanks to the **central limit theorem**. The **covariance matrix** of this normal distribution is specified by *σ*[*p*], *σ*[*q*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si28.png) and *ρ*[*p*, *q*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si29.png) measured at *p* = *p*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si30.png) and *q* = *q*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si31.png). For a fixed *γ*, the optimum shape – the one with minimum area – necessarily has a boundary that is a contour level of the distribution in question. In our case, that distribution is bivariate Gaussian, and thus contour levels are ellipses.

Let us define

$H\_{n}(x,y,p,q) = \\frac{2n}{1 - \\rho\_{p,q}^{2}}\\left\\lbrack \\left( \\frac{x - p}{\\sigma\_{p}} \\right)^{2} - 2\\rho\_{p,q}\\left( \\frac{x - p}{\\sigma\_{p}} \\right)\\left( \\frac{y - q}{\\sigma\_{q}} \\right) + \\left( \\frac{y - q}{\\sigma\_{q}} \\right)^{2} \\right\\rbrack,$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si32.png)(18.1) 

with

$\\sigma\_{p} = \\sqrt{p(1 - p)},\\quad\\sigma\_{q} = \\sqrt{q(1 - q)},\\quad\\rho\_{p,q} = - \\frac{pq}{\\sqrt{pq(1 - p)(1 - q)}}.$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si33.png)(18.2) 

This is the general elliptic form of the contour line. Essentially, it does not depend on *n*, *p*, *q*![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si34.png) when *n* is large. The standard confidence region is then the set of all (*x*, *y*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si2.png) satisfying *H*[*n*](*x*, *y*, *p*[0], *q*[0]) ≤ *G*[*γ*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si35.png). Here you choose *G*[*γ*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si36.png) to guarantee that the **confidence level** is *γ*. Replace ⩽ by = to get the boundary of that region.

In this case *G*[*γ*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si36.png) is a **quantile** of the **Hotelling distribution** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hotelling%27s_T-squared_distribution)\]. In Section [18.3.4](#Chp018_361-386_B9780443218576000229.xhtml#s0065), I show how to compute *G*[*γ*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si36.png). The simulations apply to any setting, whether *G*[*γ*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si36.png) is a Hotelling, Fisher, or any quantile. Or whether the limit distribution of your estimator (*p*[0], *q*[0])![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si27.png) is Gaussian or not, as *n* – the sample size – increases. These simulations provide a generic framework to compute confidence regions.

### 18.3.3 Dual confidence region

The **dual confidence region** is simply obtained by swapping the roles of (*x*, *y*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si2.png) and (*p*, *q*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si37.png) in *H*[*n*](*x*, *y*, *p*, *q*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si38.png). It is thus defined as the set of (*x*, *y*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si2.png) satisfying *H*[*n*](*p*, *q*, *x*, *y*) ≤ *H*[*γ*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si39.png). Again, you choose *H*[*γ*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si40.png) to guarantee that the confidence level is *γ*. Also, (*p*, *q*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si37.png) is replaced by (*p*[0], *q*[0])![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si27.png). This is no longer the equation of an ellipse. In practice, both confidence regions are very similar. Also, *H*[*γ*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si40.png) is almost identical to *G*[*γ*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si36.png). The interpretation is as follows. A point (*x*, *y*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si2.png) is in the dual confidence region of (*p*[0], *q*[0])![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si27.png) if and only if (*p*[0], *q*[0])![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si27.png) is in the standard confidence region of (*x*, *y*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si2.png). I use the same *n* and confidence level *γ* for both regions. You can use the same principle to define dual confidence intervals.

Dual confidence regions are based on the same principle as **credible regions** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Credible_interval)\] in Bayesian statistics. Other methods producing nonelliptic regions are described in [\[4\]](#Chp018_361-386_B9780443218576000229.xhtml#br0020).

### 18.3.4 Simulations

The simulations consist of generating *N* data sets, each with *n* observations. Use the joint Bernoulli model described in Section [18.3.1](#Chp018_361-386_B9780443218576000229.xhtml#s0050), for the simulations. The purpose is to create data sets that have the same statistical behavior as your observations: in other words, synthetic data. In particular, I simulate the bivariate Bernoulli model using some prespecified *p*[0], *q*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si41.png), the true but unknown values that we want to estimate. I now describe how to proceed.

For each simulated data set, compute the proportions, standard deviations, and correlations. They are denoted as *x*, *y*, *σ*[*x*], *σ*[*y*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si42.png), and *ρ*[*x*, *y*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si43.png) (one set of values per data set). Use the standard formulas, but this time with *x*, *y*![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si5.png) observed, and *p*[0], *q*[0]![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si41.png) the variables. That is,

$H\_{n}(p\_{0},q\_{0},x,y) = \\frac{2n}{1 - \\rho\_{x,y}^{2}}\\left\\lbrack \\left( \\frac{p\_{0} - x}{\\sigma\_{x}} \\right)^{2} - 2\\rho\_{x,y}\\left( \\frac{p\_{0} - x}{\\sigma\_{x}} \\right)\\left( \\frac{q\_{0} - y}{\\sigma\_{y}} \\right) + \\left( \\frac{q\_{0} - y}{\\sigma\_{y}} \\right)^{2} \\right\\rbrack,\\sigma\_{x} = \\sqrt{x(1 - x)},\\quad\\sigma\_{y} = \\sqrt{y(1 - y)},\\quad\\rho\_{x,y} = - \\frac{xy}{\\sqrt{xy(1 - x)(1 - y)}}.$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si44.png)

Also compute *G*(*x*, *y*) = *H*[*n*](*x*, *y*, *p*[0], *q*[0])![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si45.png) and *H*(*x*, *y*) = *H*[*n*](*p*[0], *q*[0], *x*, *y*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si46.png) for each data set. Put the results in a table with *N* rows and 7 columns. Proceed as follows.

*   •  **Standard confidence region** – sort the table by *G*(*x*, *y*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si47.png).
*   •  **Dual confidence region** – sort the table by *H*(*x*, *y*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si48.png).

The first ⌊*γ**N*⌋![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si49.png) rows in your sorted table determine your confidence region of level *γ*. All the (*x*, *y*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si2.png) in those rows belong to your confidence region. Here ⌊ ⋅ ⌋![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si50.png) represents the integer part function. In the first ⌊*γ**N*⌋![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si49.png) rows, the last value of *H*(*x*, *y*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si48.png) – if sorted by *H*(*x*, *y*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si48.png) – is *H*[*γ*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si40.png). Likewise, if sorted by *G*(*x*, *y*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si47.png), the last value of *G*(*x*, *y*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si47.png) is *G*[*γ*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si36.png). See example in [Fig. 18.4](#Chp018_361-386_B9780443218576000229.xhtml#f0035), with ![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/fx004.jpg)and ![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/fx005.jpg). As *N* increases, your simulations yield regions closer and closer to the theoretical ones. The spreadsheet with these simulations is available on my GitHub repository, [here](https://github.com/VincentGranville/Point-Processes/tree/main/Spreadsheets).

![Figure 18.4 Example of 90% dual confidence region for (p,q).](images/B9780443218576000229/gr004.jpg)

[Figure 18.4](#Chp018_361-386_B9780443218576000229.xhtml#cf0055) Example of 90% dual confidence region for (*p*,*q*).

### 18.3.5 Original problem with minimum contrast estimators

The original problem introduced in Section [18.3.1](#Chp018_361-386_B9780443218576000229.xhtml#s0050) consisted of estimating the two parameters *λ*, *s*![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si51.png) of a perturbed-lattice point process, namely the intensity and scale. These stochastic processes have applications in sensor locations and cell network optimization. Rather than a direct estimation which is not possible in this case (these parameters are attached to a hidden lattice process), I used proxy statistics *p*, *q*![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si52.png) instead. This method, called **minimum contrast estimation**, requires a one-to-one mapping between the original parameter space, and the proxy space. Minimum contrast estimation is a general technique encompassing **maximum likelihood estimation** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximum_likelihood_estimation)\]. It is used in the context of point processes by Tilman Davies [\[2\]](#Chp018_361-386_B9780443218576000229.xhtml#br0010) and Jesper Møller [\[5\]](#Chp018_361-386_B9780443218576000229.xhtml#br0025). See also slides 114–116 [here](https://cimpatogo2018.sciencesconf.org/data/pages/Handout_Moller_CIMPA_Togo_2018.pdf) or [here](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1y5TZXvAL8fP9G5UkmV3npKgoVB0YWtXk/view?usp=sharing).

The point count statistic discussed in Section [18.3.1](#Chp018_361-386_B9780443218576000229.xhtml#s0050) measures the number of points of this process that are in a specific interval *B*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si11.png). I used *n* nonoverlapping intervals *B*[1], …, *B*[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si53.png), each yielding one observation vector (*u*[*k*], *v*[*k*])![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si8.png) for *k* = 1, …, *n*![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si9.png). The observation vectors are almost identically and independently distributed across the intervals. However, the first and second components of the vectors are negatively correlated. This explains the choice of the bivariate Bernoulli distribution for the model.

More specifically, the situation is almost identical (and asymptotically identical) to the following: we observe a bivariate Bernoulli sequence of independently and identically distributed (*U*[*k*], *V*[*k*])![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si54.png) but for each *k*, *U*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si55.png) and *V*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si56.png) are negatively correlated with the same correlation as in formula [(18.2)](#Chp018_361-386_B9780443218576000229.xhtml#deq2). The random variables have the following joint distribution:

*P*(*U*[*k*] = 0, *V*[*k*] = 0) = 1 − *p* − *q*, *P*(*U*[*k*] = 1, *V*[*k*] = 0) = *p*, *P*(*U*[*k*] = 0, *V*[*k*] = 1) = *q*, *P*(*U*[*k*] = 1, *V*[*k*] = 1) = 0.

![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si57.png)

The following must be satisfied: 0 < *p*, *q* < 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si58.png) and *p* + *q* < 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si59.png).

The scatterplot in [Fig. 18.5](#Chp018_361-386_B9780443218576000229.xhtml#f0040) illustrates the estimation procedure, using minimum contrast estimators. The X-axis represents *p*, and the Y-axis represents *q*. There are two main features:

*   •  **Observed data.** The three purple dots correspond to estimated values of (*p*, *q*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si37.png) derived from three sets of observations, each with ![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/fx006.jpg).
*   •  **Theoretical model.** The four overlapping clusters show, based on simulations, the distribution of (*p*, *q*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si37.png) for four different theoretical values of (*λ*, *s*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si60.png). Each cluster – identified by its color – has 100 points corresponding to 100 simulations. Each simulation within a same cluster uses the same hand-picked (*λ*, *s*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si60.png). The purpose of these simulations is to find the inverse mapping (*p*, *q*) ↦ (*λ*, *s*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si61.png) via numerical approximations, to retrieve the hidden parameter (*λ*, *s*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si60.png) when (*p*, *q*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si37.png) is observed. Four colors is just a small beginning. In [Table 18.1](#Chp018_361-386_B9780443218576000229.xhtml#t0010), each cluster is summarized by two statistics: its computed center in the (*p*, *q*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si37.png)\-space, associated to the hand-picked parameter vector (*λ*, *s*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si60.png).

Table 18.1

Extract of the mapping table used to recover (*λ*,*s*) from (*p*,*q*).

 
| Cluster || (*λ*,*s*) || (*p*,*q*) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Orange || (1.4,0.6) || (0.3275,0.4113) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Gray || (1.4,0.5) || (0.3186,0.4216) |
| Yellow || (1.6,0.7) || (0.3321,0.3995) |
| Blue || (1.8,0.6) || (0.3371,0.4007) |

*   

Now let us focus on the rightmost purple dot in [Fig. 18.5](#Chp018_361-386_B9780443218576000229.xhtml#f0040), corresponding to one of the three observation sets. Its coordinates vector is denoted as (*p*[0], *q*[0])![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si27.png). The (*p*, *q*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si37.png)\-space is called the **proxy space**. In this case, it is a subset of \[0, 1\] × \[0, 1\]![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si62.png). If the proxy spaced contained only the four points (*p*, *q*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si37.png) listed in [Table 18.1](#Chp018_361-386_B9780443218576000229.xhtml#t0010), the estimated value (*λ*[0], *s*[0])![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si63.png) of (*λ*, *s*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si60.png) would be the center of the orange cluster. That is, (*λ*[0], *s*[0]) = (1.4, 0.6)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si64.png) because (0.3275, 0.4113)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si65.png) is the closest cluster center to the purple dot (*p*[0], *q*[0])![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si27.png) in the proxy space.

![Figure 18.5 Minimum contrast estimation for (λ,s) using (p,q) as proxy stats.](images/B9780443218576000229/gr005.jpg)

Figure 18.5 Minimum contrast estimation for (*λ*,*s*) using (*p*,*q*) as proxy stats.

But let us imagine that I hand-picked 10⁵ vectors (*λ*, *s*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si60.png) instead of 4, thus generating 10⁵ cluster centers and a very large [Table 18.1](#Chp018_361-386_B9780443218576000229.xhtml#t0010) with 10⁵ entries. Then again, the best estimator of (*λ*, *s*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si60.png) would still be that obtained by minimizing the distance between the purple dot (*p*[0], *q*[0])![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si27.png) computed on the observations and the 10⁵ cluster centers. In practice, the hand-picking is automated (computerized) and leads to a black-box implementation of the estimation procedure.

Finally, the glow effect in [Fig. 18.5](#Chp018_361-386_B9780443218576000229.xhtml#f0040) may be used for classification or clustering purposes. It generates cluster boundaries given observed points, in a way similar to the method described in Chapter [5](#Chp005_83-102_B9780443218576000096.xhtml).

### 18.3.6 General shape of confidence regions

Before establishing the fundamental result, I briefly discus how to plot confidence regions in 3D. [Fig. 18.6](#Chp018_361-386_B9780443218576000229.xhtml#f0050) shows an atypical nonelliptic example, arising from a **mixture model**. The **contour levels** correspond to **confidence levels**. This type of chart is called **contour plot**. However, in the literature, most contour plots are 2D. And those that are 3D usually feature vertical rather than horizontal contours, as the horizontal ones are more difficult to produce. In this case, I produced it with **Mathematica** \[[Wiki](https://www.wolframalpha.com/)\]. See the code below.

![Figure 18.6 Nonelliptic confidence regions with various confidence levels.](images/B9780443218576000229/gr006.jpg)

[Figure 18.6](#Chp018_361-386_B9780443218576000229.xhtml#cf0115) Nonelliptic confidence regions with various confidence levels.

![](images/B9780443218576000229/fx007.jpg)

Now let us get to the core of the subject. In our particular case, the standard confidence region is asymptotically elliptic because the underlying distribution of the statistic (*p*, *q*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si37.png) – itself a random vector depending on the *n* observations – approaches a multivariate Gaussian law as *n* → ∞![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si66.png). See Exercise 27 in my book on stochastic processes [\[3\]](#Chp018_361-386_B9780443218576000229.xhtml#br0015) for details. Since contour levels of Gaussian distributions are ellipses, the result follows immediately.

More generally, the confidence region of level *γ* is the minimum set covering a proportion *γ* of a the mass of the distribution attached to the estimated parameters. Let *S*[*γ*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si67.png) be the set in question, and *f*(*x*, *y*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si68.png) be the density attached to the distribution. I assume that the density has one maximum only, and that it is continuous everywhere on ℝ²![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si69.png). Thus the problem consists of finding the set *S*[*γ*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si67.png) of minimum area such that

∫∫[*S*[*γ*]]*f*(*x*, *y*)*d**x**d**y* = *γ*.

![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si70.png)(18.3) 

It is easy to see that the boundary of *S*[*γ*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si67.png) is a contour line of *f*(*x*, *y*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si68.png). To build *S*[*γ*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si67.png), you start at the maximum of the density, and to keep the area minimum, the set must progressively be expanded, strictly following contour lines, until [(18.3)](#Chp018_361-386_B9780443218576000229.xhtml#deq5) is satisfied. So

*S*[*γ*] = {(*x*, *y*) ∈ ℝ² such that *f*(*x*, *y*) ≤ *G*[*γ*]},

![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si71.png)

where *G*[*γ*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si36.png) must be chosen so that [(18.3)](#Chp018_361-386_B9780443218576000229.xhtml#deq5) is satisfied. Assuming max *f*(*x*, *y*) = *M*![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si72.png), the volume covered by *S*[*γ*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si67.png) is

*γ* = *z*[*γ*] ⋅ |*S*[*γ*]| + ∫[*z*[*γ*]]^(*M*)|*R*(*z*)|*d**z*,

![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si73.png)(18.4) 

where *R*(*z*) = {(*x*, *y*) ∈ ℝ² such that *f*(*x*, *y*) = *z*}![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si74.png), and | ⋅ |![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si75.png) denotes the area of a 2D domain. Clearly, |*S*[*γ*]| = |*R*(*z*[*γ*])|![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si76.png). So there is only one unknown in Eq. [(18.4)](#Chp018_361-386_B9780443218576000229.xhtml#deq7), namely *z*[*γ*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si77.png). Finally, *G*[*γ*] = *z*[*γ*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si78.png), and thus the value of *G*[*γ*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si36.png) is found by solving [(18.4)](#Chp018_361-386_B9780443218576000229.xhtml#deq7). The area of *S*[*γ*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si67.png) is thus |*S*[*γ*]| = |*R*(*G*[*γ*])|![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si79.png).

## 18.4 Fast feature selection based on predictive power

In all machine learning problems, deciding which metrics to use is one of the core problems. This section addresses this topic. I propose a simple metric to measure predictive power. It is used for combinatorial feature selection, when a large number of feature combinations need to be ranked automatically and very fast, for instance, in the context of transaction scoring, in order to optimize predictive models. You can easily implement it with a **parallel architecture** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parallel_computing)\], such as **Map-Reduce** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MapReduce)\]. I used this methodology for credit card fraud detection, keyword scoring (assessing the commercial value of keyword for keyword bidding purposes), and Internet traffic quality scoring.

Feature selection is used to detect the best subset of features, out of dozens or hundreds of features (also called independent variables). By “best”, I mean with highest predictive power as defined in Section [18.4.2](#Chp018_361-386_B9780443218576000229.xhtml#s0090). In short, you want to remove duplicate features, correlations between features, and features lacking predictive power, or features (sometimes called rules) that are rarely triggered – except if they are excellent predictors of rare but costly fraud, for instance.

The problem is combinatorial in nature. You want a manageable, small set of features (say 20 features) selected from (say) a set of 500 features, to run machine learning algorithms in a way that is statistically robust. But there are 2.7 × 10^(35)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si80.png) combinations of 20 features out of 500, and you need to compute all of them to find the feature set with maximum predictive power. This problem is computationally intractable, and you need to find an alternate solution. The good thing is that you do not need to find the absolute maximum; you just need to find a subset of 20 features that is good enough.

One way to proceed is to compute the predictive power of each feature. Then, add one feature at a time to the subset (starting with zero feature) until either you reach 20 features (your limit), or adding a new feature does not significantly improve the overall predictive power of the feature subset (in short, convergence has been attained). At each iteration, choose the feature to be added, among the two remaining features with the highest predictive power: you will choose (among these two features) the one that increases the overall predictive power (of the subset under construction) most. Now you have reduced your computations from 2.7 × 10^(35)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si80.png) to 40 = 2 × 20![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si81.png). A possible improvement consists in removing one feature at a time from the subset, and replace it with a feature randomly selected from the remaining features. If this new feature boosts the overall predictive power of the feature subset, keep it, and otherwise switch back to old subset. Repeat this step ![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/fx008.jpg)times or until no more gain is achieved (whichever comes first).

Finally, you can add two or three features at a time, rather than one. Sometimes, combined features have better predictive power than isolated features. For instance, if feature *A* is the country, with values in {USA, UK}![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si82.png) and feature *B* is the hour of the day, with values in {“Day - Pacific Time”, “Night - Pacific Time”}![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si83.png), both features separately have little predictive power. But when you combine both of them, you have a much more powerful feature: “UK/Night” is good, “USA/Night” is bad, “UK/Day” is bad, and “USA/Day” is good, if your response (what you are predicting) is Internet traffic quality in the US. Using these two features together also reduces the risk of false positives and false negatives.

Also, in order to avoid highly granular features, use feature binning. So instead of having country as feature *A* (with 200 potential country values) use country group, with 3 list of countries (high risk, low risk, neutral). These groups can change over time. And instead of (say) “IP address” as feature *B* (with billions of potential values), use type of IP address instead, with 6 or 7 types, one being for instance “IP address is in some whitelist”.

### 18.4.1 How cross-validation works

I illustrate the concept of predictive power on a subset of two features. Let us say that you have two binary features A and B taking two possible values 0 or 1. Also, in the context of fraud detection, one would assume that each observation in the training set is either Good (no fraud) or Bad (fraud). The fraud status (G or B) is called the response or dependent variable in statistics. The features *A* and *B* are also called rules or independent variables.

Cross-validation works as follows. First, split your **training set** (the data where the response B or G is known) into two parts: validation set and training data. Make sure that both parts are data-rich: if the validation set is big (millions of observations) but contains only one or two clients out of 200, it is data-poor and your statistical inference will be negatively impacted (low robustness) when dealing with data outside the training set. It is a good idea to use two different time periods for training and validation. You are going to compute the predictive power (including rule selection) on the training data. When you have decided on a final, optimum subset of features, you then compute the predictive power on the validation set. If the drop in predictive power is significant in the validation set (compared with training data), something is wrong with your analysis: detect the problem, fix it, start over. You can use multiple validation and training sets: this will give you an idea of how the predictive power varies from one validation set to another one. Too much variance is an issue that should be addressed.

### 18.4.2 Measuring the predictive power of a feature

Standard methods are based on classic goodness-of-fit metrics \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goodness_of_fit)\], such as various ratios computed on the **confusion matrix** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confusion_matrix)\]. Examples are discussed in this Wikipedia article, and include false positive and false negative rates. Here I describe an original approach to compute the **predictive power**. Using our above example with two binary features *A*, *B*![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si84.png) taking on two values 0, 1, we can break the observations from the control data set into 8 bins. Let us denote as *n*[1], *n*[2], …, *n*[8]![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si85.png) the number of observations in each of these 8 bins shown in [Table 18.2](#Chp018_361-386_B9780443218576000229.xhtml#t0015).

[Table 18.2](#Chp018_361-386_B9780443218576000229.xhtml#cf0150)

Eight bins: 2 features (*A*,*B*) times 2 outcomes (Good/Bad).

 
| Bin || Feature *A* || Feature *B* || Response |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 || 0 || 0 || G |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2 || 0 || 1 || G |
| 3 || 1 || 0 || G |
| 4 || 1 || 1 || G |
| 5 || 0 || 0 || B |
| 6 || 0 || 1 || B |
| 7 || 1 || 0 || B |
| 8 || 1 || 1 || B |

![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/t0015.png)

Now let us introduce the following quantities:

$P\_{00} = \\frac{n\_{5}}{n\_{1} + n\_{5}},\\quad P\_{01} = \\frac{n\_{6}}{n\_{2} + n\_{6}},\\quad P\_{10} = \\frac{n\_{7}}{n\_{3} + n\_{7}},\\quad P\_{11} = \\frac{n\_{8}}{n\_{4} + n\_{8}},\\quad p = \\frac{n\_{5} + n\_{6} + n\_{7} + n\_{8}}{n\_{1} + n\_{2} + \\cdots + n\_{8}}.$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si86.png)

Let us assume that *p*, measuring the overall proportion of fraud, is less than 50% (that is, *p* < 0.5![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si87.png), otherwise we can swap between fraud and nonfraud). For any 0 < *r* < 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si88.png), define the *W* function (shaped like a W), based on a parameter 0 < *a* < 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si89.png) (typically *a* = 0.5 − *p*![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si90.png)) as follows:

$W(r) = \\begin{cases} {1 - r/p,} & {\\quad\\text{if~}\\text{~~}0 < r < p,} \\\\ {a(r - p)/(0.5 - p),} & {\\quad\\text{if~}\\text{~~}p < r < 0.5,} \\\\ {a(r - 1 + p)/(p - 0.5),} & {\\quad\\text{if~}\\text{~~}0.5 < r < 1 - p,} \\\\ {(r - 1 + p)/p,} & {\\quad\\text{if~}\\text{~~}1 - p < r < 1.} \\\\ \\end{cases}$

![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si91.png)

Typically, *r* = *P*[00], *P*[01], *P*[10]![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si92.png), or *P*[11]![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si93.png). The function *W* has the following properties:

*   •  It is minimum and equal to 0 when *r* = *p*![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si94.png) or *r* = 1 − *p*![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si95.png), that is, when *r* does not provide any information about fraud / nonfraud, 
*   •  It is maximum and equal to 1 when *r* = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si96.png) or *r* = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si97.png), that is, when we have perfect discrimination between fraud and nonfraud, in a given bin.
*   •  It is symmetric: *W*(*r*) = *W*(1 − *r*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si98.png) if 0 < *r* < 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si88.png). So if you swap Good and Bad (G and B), it still provides the same predictive power.

Now let us define the **predictive power** as

*H* = *P*[00]*W*(*P*[00]) + *P*[01]*W*(*P*[01]) + *P*[10]*W*(*P*[10]) + *P*[11]*W*(*P*[11]).

![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si99.png)

The function *H* is the predictive power for the feature subset {*A*, *B*}![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si100.png) with four bins “00”, “01”, “10”, “11” corresponding to (*A* = 0, *B* = 0)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si101.png), (*A* = 0, *B* = 1)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si102.png), (*A* = 1, *B* = 0)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si103.png), (*A* = 1, *B* = 1)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si104.png). Although *H* is remotely related to the **entropy metric**, it has specific properties of its own. Unlike entropy, *H* is not based on physical concepts or models; it is actually a **synthetic metric**.

The weights *P*[00], *P*[01], *P*[1, 0], *P*[11]![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si105.png) guarantee that bins with low count have low impact on *H*. Set *W*(*r*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si106.png) to 0 for any bin that has less than 20 observations. For instance, the frequency of bin “00” is (*n*[1] + *n*[5])/(*n*[1] + ⋯ + *n*[8])![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si107.png), its size or bin count is *n*[1] + *n*[5]![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si108.png), and *r* = *P*[00] = *n*[5]/(*n*[1] + *n*[5])![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si109.png) for this bin. If *n*[1] + *n*[5] = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si110.png), set *P*[00]![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si111.png) to 0 and *W*(*P*[00])![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si112.png) to 0. I actually recommend doing this not just if *n*[1] + *n*[5] = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si110.png), but also whenever *n*[1] + *n*[5] < 20![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si113.png), especially if *p* is low. If *p* is very low, say *p* < 0.01![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si114.png), you need to oversample bad transactions when building your training set, and adjust the counts accordingly. Of course, the same rules applies to *P*[01], *P*[10]![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si115.png), and *P*[11]![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si93.png).

Also, you should avoid feature subsets resulting in a large proportion of observations spread across a large number of almost empty bins, as well as feature subsets that produce a large number of empty bins: observations outside the training set are likely to belong to an empty or almost empty bin, and it leads to high-variance predictions. To avoid this drawback, stick to binary features and use fewer than 20 features if possible. Finally, *P*[*i**j*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si116.png) is the estimator of the probability *P*(*A* = *i*, *B* = *j*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si117.png) for *i*, *j* = 0, 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si118.png) in **naive Bayes classification** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naive_Bayes_classifier)\].

The technique easily generalizes to more than two features, and the predictive power *H* has interesting properties: 0 ≤ *H* ≤ 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si119.png), with *H* = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si120.png) if the feature subset has no predictive power, and *H* = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si121.png) if it has maximum predictive power. If *p* = 0.5![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si122.png), then the function *W* is shaped like a V rather than a W. You may try *p* = 0.5![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si122.png) and check whether it provides good enough predictions.

### 18.4.3 Efficient implementation

Given a subset of 20 binary features, you can precompute all the bin counts in any extended **flag vector**, and store them in a hash table Hash – also called “associative array” or “dictionary” in Python. Such an extended vector has 21 components: 20 for the features, with value 0 or 1, and one for the response, with value G or B.

In Python, an entry in this **hash table** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hash_table)\] would look like Hash\[(v,y)\]=56 where (say) *y* = “G”![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si123.png) and *v* = “01101001010110100100![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si124.png)”. The hash table is made of **key–value pairs**. In this example, the value is 56 and the key is (*v*, *y*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si125.png). It means that the flag vector *v* has 56 observations with response G. More precisely, a flag vector is a binary string showing which rules are triggered. Here a rule is a feature, and “triggered” means that the value of the feature in question is equal to one. Nonbinary flag vectors or responses are not discussed here, but they are also widely used. This framework is sometimes referred to as **association rule learning** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_rule_learning)\].

The hash table is produced by parsing your training set one time, sequentially: for each observation, compute the flag vector *v*, check if the response is Good (G) or Bad (B), and update the associated key–value pairs accordingly, with the following instruction: Hash\[(v,G)\]++ if the response is Good, or Hash\[(v,B)\]++ if the response is Bad.

Then whenever you need to measure the predictive power of a subset of these 20 features, you do not need to parse your big data set again (potentially billion of observations), but instead, just access this small hash table: this table contains all you need to build your flag vectors and compute predictive scores, for any combination of features that is a subset of the top 20. You can do even better than top 20, maybe top 30. While this would create a hash table with 2 billion keys, most of these keys would correspond to empty bins and thus would not be in the hash table. Your hash table might contain only 200 million keys, maybe too big to fit in memory, but easily manageable with a distributed architecture such as Map-Reduce.

Even better: build this hash table for the top 40 features. However now, your hash table could have up to 2 trillion keys. But if your data set has only 100 billion observations, then, of course, your hash table cannot have more than 100 billion keys. In this case, you create a training set with 20 million observations, so that your hash table will have at most 20 million keys (and probably less than 5 million due to empty bins). Thus, it can fit in memory, because you are working with a **sparse hash table**.

You can now estimate the predictive power of many different feature subsets. To do it, parse the hash table obtained in the previous step. For each key (*v*, *y*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si125.png) in this input hash table, loop over the desired feature subsets to create new bin counts: these counts are stored / updated in an output hash table. The key in the newly created output hash table has two components: the “subset ID” (a number representing the feature subset)) and the key (*v*, *y*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si125.png) of the input hash table. When the output hash table is created, you then loop over its keys to compute the predictive power for each feature subset.

## 18.5 NLP: taxonomy creation and text generation

This section is about structuring unstructured data. I used the techniques described in this section to automatically enhance online directories such as Wikipedia, Yelp, Amazon, or DMOZ \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DMOZ)\]. It involves extensive web crawling. One of the noteworthy results obtained by analyzing online user queries was a better breakdown of the “restaurant” category into more meaningful subcategories: romantic restaurant, dinner, wine pub, downtown or nearby restaurant, restaurant with a view or by the river, cheap, ethnic, casual or upscale restaurant, restaurant chefs, recipes, jobs, and furniture. The classic breakdown is by type of cuisine, but it does not fit as well with what users are looking for.

The technique allows you to find related keywords or synonyms, and can be combined with using a table of synonyms, to generate text in the context of **natural language generation** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_language_generation)\]. It is one of the core components of many **large language models** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Language_model)\] such as **ChatGPT** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ChatGPT)\]. Here I do not cover basic steps such as cleaning the data using **stop words** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stop_word)\], **n-gram** permutations \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/N-gram)\], using a dictionary of synonyms, fixing typos, handling special characters, **text normalization** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Text_normalization)\] using **regular expressions** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regular_expression)\], and so on. This can be found in any elementary introduction on natural language processing.

### 18.5.1 Designing a keyword taxonomy

Here I discuss an algorithm to perform fast clustering on big data sets, as well as the graphical representation of such complex clustering structures. By fast, I mean a **computational complexity** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computational_complexity)\] of order *O*(*n*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si126.png). This is much faster than **hierarchical agglomerative clustering** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hierarchical_clustering)\] which are typically *O*(*n*²log *n*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si127.png). By big data, I mean several millions, possibly billions of observations.

The application in mind is the creation of a keyword, product or document taxonomy. In particular, I want to create a keyword taxonomy from scratch, based on crawling billions of webpages to extract and cluster keywords into categories. This is a typical unsupervised natural language processing (NLP) problem. The proposed algorithm is as follows:

**Step 1: Preprocessing**

You gather billions of keywords over the Internet by crawling (say) Wikipedia or Google results, clean the results, and compute the frequencies for each keyword and for each “keyword pair”. A “keyword pair” is two keywords found on the same webpage, or close to each other on the same web page. Also by keyword, I mean an entity like “California insurance”, so a keyword usually contains more than one token, but rarely more than three. You then can create a keyword table, where each entry is a pair of keywords followed by three counts, such as A=“California insurance”, B=“home insurance”, *x* = 543![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si128.png), *y* = 998![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si129.png), *z* = 11![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si130.png) where

*   •  *x* is the number of occurrences of keyword A in all the web pages crawled,
*   •  *y* is the number of occurrences of keyword B in all the web pages crawled,
*   •  *z* is the number of occurrences where A and B form a pair (e.g., they are found on a same page).

You can build the keyword table using a distributed architecture. The vast majority of keywords A and B do not form a “keyword pair”. In other words, *z* = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si131.png) most of the time. So by ignoring these null entries, your final keyword table can be stored in memory as a **hash table** (see Section [18.4.3](#Chp018_361-386_B9780443218576000229.xhtml#s0095)) where the key is (A, B)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si132.png) and the value attached to a key is (*x*, *y*, *z*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si133.png). Let us name this table Keyword.

**Step 2: Clustering**

To create a taxonomy, you want to group the keywords into similar clusters. The **cosine distance** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosine_similarity)\] measuring the distance between two keywords or web pages, is popular in this context. To perform keyword clustering, I use the following **dissimilarity metric** *d*(A, B)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si134.png) to compare two keywords A, B: $d(\\text{A},\\text{B}) = z/\\sqrt{xy}$![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si135.png), although other choices are possible. This metric is known as the **Otsuka–Ochiai coefficient**. Note that the denominator prevents extremely popular keywords (for instance, “free”) from being close to all the keywords, and from dominating the entire keyword relationship structure: indeed, it favors better keyword bonds, such as “lemon” with “law” or “pie”, rather than “lemon” with “free”. The larger the *d*(*A*, *B*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si136.png), the closer the keywords A and B. I describe the clustering part in Section [18.5.2](#Chp018_361-386_B9780443218576000229.xhtml#s0110).

### 18.5.2 Fast clustering algorithm for keyword data

Here I have *n* = 10⁷![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si137.png) unique keywords and *m* = 10⁸![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si138.png) keyword pairs {A, B}![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si139.png) where *d*(*A*, *B*) > 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si140.png). That is, an average of *r* = 10![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si141.png) related keywords attached to each keyword. These keyword pairs are stored in the hash table Keyword created in the preprocessing step in Section [18.5.1](#Chp018_361-386_B9780443218576000229.xhtml#s0105). The algorithm builds the new hash tables Hash (the category table) and Weight. It proceeds incrementally as follows:

**Initialization** – The small data (or seeding) step. Select ![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/fx008.jpg)seed keywords, create (say) 100 categories, and create a hash table Hash where the key is one of the ![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/fx008.jpg)seed keywords, and the value is a list of categories the keyword is assigned to. For instance,  Hash\['cheap car insurance'\]={'automotive','finance'} The choice of the initial ![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/fx008.jpg)seed keywords is very important. I suggest to pick up the top ![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/fx008.jpg)keywords, in terms of number of associations: that is, keywords A with many B's where *d*(A, B) > 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si142.png). This will speed up the convergence of the algorithm.

**The big data step.** Browse the hash table Keyword from the beginning to the end. We now build the tables Hash and Weight. Let (A, B)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si132.png) be the current keyword pair in Keyword.

If Hash\[A\] exists and Hash\[B\] does not, do:

Hash\[B\]=Hash\[A\]

Weight\[B\]=d(A,B)

Else If Hash\[A\] does not exist and Hash\[B\] exists, do:

Hash\[A\]=Hash\[B\]

Weight\[A\]=d(A,B)

Else If Hash\[A\] and Hash\[B\] exist, recategorize:

If d(A,B)>Weight\[B\] do:

Hash\[B\]=Hash\[A\]

Weight\[B\]=d(A,B)

Else If d(A,B)>Weight\[A\] do:

Hash\[A\]=Hash\[B\]

Weight\[A\]=d(A,B)

You could replace Hash\[A\]=Hash\[B\] by Hash\[A\]=Concatenate(Hash\[A\],Hash\[B\]), and the other way around. This will increase the number of categories a keyword is assigned to. I did not test that option.

**The loop.** Repeat the “big data step” 6 or 7 times: Hash and Weight are kept in memory and keep growing at each subsequent iteration of the loop.

#### 18.5.2.1 Computational complexity

The computational complexity is asymptotically (*N* + 1)*m* = *O*(*n*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si143.png), where *N* is the number of iterations in the loop. This is very fast. However, accessing the hash tables slows it down a bit as Hash and Weight grow bigger at each new iteration.

Presorting the Keyword hash table by the *d*(A, B)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si134.png) values allows you to reduce the number of hash table accesses, by making all the recategorizations not needed anymore. You can also improve the computational complexity by keeping the most important keys – based on count and *d*(A, B)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si134.png)) – and deleting the others. In practice, deleting 65% of the Keyword hash table (the long keyword tail) has little impact on the performance: you will have a large bucket of uncategorized keywords, but in terms of volume, these keywords might represent less than 0.1% of the Internet traffic.

Finally, one could use **Tarjan's algorithm** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tarjan%27s_strongly_connected_components_algorithm)\] to perform the clustering, based on strongly **connected components** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Component_\(graph_theory\))\]. To proceed, you first bin the distances: *d*(A, B)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si134.png) is set to 1 if it is above some prespecified threshold, and to 0 otherwise. This is a graph theory algorithm: each keyword represents a node, each pair of keywords where *d*(A, B) = 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si144.png), represents an edge. The computational complexity of the algorithm is *O*(*n* + *m*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si145.png), where *n* is the number of keywords and *m* is the number of keyword pairs (edges). To take advantage of this algorithm, you might want to store the Keyword hash table in a **graph database** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graph_database)\]. For those interested in graphical representations of the cluster structure, see the **Fruchterman and Rheingold algorithm** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Force-directed_graph_drawing)\]. However, its computational complexity is *O*(*n*³)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si146.png).

#### 18.5.2.2 Smart crawling of the whole Internet and a bit of graph theory

Crawling the web must be done in parallel. You need a to create a log file, updated in real time, to store all the pages that you already visited along with the status (successful crawl or not, number of bytes downloaded, domain/subdomain, and time spent to access the page). That way, if your computer crashes, you can resume from where it stopped without losing any data. You may limit the amount of data extracted by page to 16 kilobytes, and limit the number of web pages visited per website to (say) ![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/fx009.jpg). Pages that were not successfully crawled may be recrawled later at least one more time. Identify duplicate URLs such as web.com, web.com/ and web.com/?source=Facebook so you crawl only one of them.

You also need to avoid getting stuck in an infinite loop, crawling the same pages again and again. Keep a hash table of all the pages already crawled: a copy of the log file, in memory. If done well, in a few months you can crawl billions of web pages, covering (in traffic volume) most of the Internet pages ever browsed by human beings.

At level 1, you start with a list of (say) ![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/fx008.jpg)web pages obtained by extracting data from online directories such as Wikipedia or Dmoz, or search result pages from Google, based on a list of thousands of top search keywords. All links gathered at level 1 (links found on the web pages you visited) are stored in a list used for level 2 crawling. From that list, remove links already visited at level 1. Likewise, all links found at level 2 constitute the target URLs to crawl at level 3. Again, remove from that list pages already crawled at level 1 or 2. Move on to level 4, 5, and 6 using the same principles. A practical application of this methodology is tested in my training sessions. [Table 18.3](#Chp018_361-386_B9780443218576000229.xhtml#t0020) shows the amount of data (in megabytes) collected at each level. This distribution is typical.

[Table 18.3](#Chp018_361-386_B9780443218576000229.xhtml#cf0170)

Amount of data collected at each level, when crawling the Internet.

 
| Level || Data (GB) |
| --- | --- |
| 1 || 0.002877 |
| --- | --- |
| 2 || 0.456084 |
| 3 || 8.722723 |
| 4 || 26.942508 |
| 5 || 39.443366 |
| 6 || 42.429041 |
| 7 || 13.175749 |

It is interesting to note the connection to the **six degrees of separation** problem in graph theory \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Six_degrees_of_separation)\]. Most web pages with some traffic are connected to any other one by a path involving at most 6 or 7 intermediate links (called “levels” here). The **Watts and Strogatz model** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watts%E2%80%93Strogatz_model)\] shows that the average path length between two nodes in a random network is equal to log *N*/log *K*![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si147.png), where *N* is the number of nodes (a web page here) and *K* the number of acquaintances per node (that is, the number of links on any given web page).

In the case of friend connections, if *N* = 3 × 10⁸![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si148.png) (the US population) and *K* = 30![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si149.png) (the number of friends per individual), then the number of degrees of separation between any two people is 5.7. Now if *N* = 6 × 10⁹![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si150.png), it is equal to 6.6. The Python code below perform the simulations to study these distributions.

The algorithm below is rudimentary and can be used for simulation purposes by any programmer: It does not even use tree or graph structures. Applied to a population of 2,000,000 people, each having 20 friends, we show that there is a path involving 6 levels or intermediaries between you and anyone else. Note that the shortest path typically involves fewer levels, as some people have far more than 20 connections. Starting with you, at level one, you have twenty friends or connections. These connections in turn have 20 friends, so at level two, you are connected to 400 people. At level 3, you are connected to 7985 people, which is a little less than 20 × 400![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si151.png), since some level-3 connections were already level-2 or level-1. And so on.

![](images/B9780443218576000229/fx010.jpg)

A previous version of this program used a faulty random generator that could not produce 2 million distinct integers. Thus I could never achieve full connectivity no matter how many levels I used. Watch out for issues like that when doing this type of simulations. You could actually use this code to test pseudorandom number generators.

## 18.6 Automated detection of outliers and number of clusters

In the context of unsupervised clustering, one of the most popular recipes to identify the number of clusters, is the **elbow rule** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elbow_method_\(clustering\))\]. It is usually performed manually. Here, I show how it can be automated and applied to other problems, such as outlier detection. The idea is a follows: a clustering algorithm (say K-means \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K-means_clustering)\]) can identify a cluster structure with any number of clusters on a given data set; typically, a function *v*(*m*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si152.png) provides a statistical summary of the best cluster structure consisting of *m* clusters, for *m* = 1, 2, 3![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si153.png), and so on. For instance, *v*(*m*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si152.png) is the sum of the squares of the distances from any observed point to its assigned cluster center. The function *v*(*m*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si152.png) is decreasing, sharply initially for small values of *m*, then much more slowly for larger values of *m*, creating an elbow in its graph. The value of *m* corresponding to the elbow is deemed to be the optimal number of clusters. See [Fig. 18.7](#Chp018_361-386_B9780443218576000229.xhtml#f0060). Instead of *v*(*m*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si152.png), I use the standardized version *v*^′(*m*) = *v*(*m*)/*v*(1)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si154.png).

![Figure 18.7 Elbow rule (right) finds m = 3 clusters in Brownian motion (left).](images/B9780443218576000229/gr007.jpg)

Figure 18.7 Elbow rule (right) finds *m* = 3 clusters in Brownian motion (left).

I illustrate how to use the elbow rule to detect **outliers** in Section [18.6.1](#Chp018_361-386_B9780443218576000229.xhtml#s0130). The same methodology applies to detect the number of clusters. The data consists of a realization of a 2D Brownian motion. I am interested in the increments *R*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si155.png), measuring the distance between a point of the process, and the next one. For practical purposes, the simulated realization can be interpreted as a 2D random walk, and *R*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si155.png) is the length of the segment joining two successive points in [Fig. 18.7](#Chp018_361-386_B9780443218576000229.xhtml#f0060). These segments are visible if you zoom in on the picture. The model used to produce this synthetic data is described in Section [12.2.1](#Chp012_229-241_B9780443218576000163.xhtml).

### 18.6.1 Black-box elbow rule to detect outliers

[Fig. 18.7](#Chp018_361-386_B9780443218576000229.xhtml#f0060) shows a realization of a **Brownian motion** with 10⁴ points, using *γ* = 2![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si156.png) and *λ* = *Γ*(1 + *γ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si157.png) in formula [(12.6)](#Chp012_229-241_B9780443218576000163.xhtml). The goal is to detect the number of values, among the top *R*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si155.png)'s, that significantly outshine all the others. Here, they are not technically outliers in the sense that they are still deviates of the same distribution; rather, they are called extremes. The first step is to rank these values. The ordered values (in reverse order) are denoted as *R*[(1)], *R*[(2)]![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si158.png), and so on, with *R*[(1)]![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si159.png) being the largest one. I used *v*(*m*) = *R*[(*m*)]![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si160.png) as the criterion for the elbow rule, that is, after standardization, *v*^′(*m*) = *v*(*m*)/*v*(1)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si154.png).

On the right plot in [Fig. 18.7](#Chp018_361-386_B9780443218576000229.xhtml#f0060), the Y axis on the left represents *v*^′(*m*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si161.png), the X axis represents *m*, and the *Y* axis on the right represents the strength of the elbow signal (the height of the red bar; I discuss later how it is computed). The top 10 values of *v*^′(*m*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si161.png) (*m* = 1, …, 10![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si162.png)) are

1.00, 0.92, 0.77, 0.76, 0.71, 0.69, 0.63, 0.61, 0.60, 0.56, 0.55, 0.55.

![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si163.png)

Clearly, the third value 0.77 is pivotal, as the next ones stop dropping sharply, after an initial big drop at the beginning of the sequence. So the “elbow signal” is strongest at *m* = 3![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si164.png), and the conclusion is that the first two values (2 = *m* − 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si165.png)) outshine all the others. The purpose of the black-box elbow rule algorithm is to automate the decision process: in this case deciding that the optimum is *m* = 3![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si164.png).

Note that in some instances, it is not obvious to detect an elbow, and there may be none. In my example, the elbow signal is very strong, because I chose a rather large value *γ* = 2![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si156.png) in formula [(12.6)](#Chp012_229-241_B9780443218576000163.xhtml), causing the Brownian process to exhibit an unusually strong cluster structure, and large disparities among the top *v*(*m*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si152.png)'s. A larger *γ* would generate even stronger disparities. A negative value of *γ*, say *γ* =  − 0.75![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si166.png), also causes strong disparities, well separated clusters, and an easy-to-detect elbow. The resulting process is not even Brownian anymore if *γ* =  − 0.75![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si166.png), since in that case, *V**a**r*\[*R*[*k*]\] = ∞![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si167.png). The standard Brownian motion corresponds to *γ* = 0![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si168.png) and can still exhibit clusters depending on the realization. Finally, in our case, *m* = 3![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si164.png) also corresponds to the number of clusters on the left plot in [Fig. 18.7](#Chp018_361-386_B9780443218576000229.xhtml#f0060). This is a coincidence, one that happens very frequently, because the top *v*(*m*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si152.png)'s (left to the elbow) correspond to unusually large values of *R*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si155.png). Each of these very large values typically gives rise to the building of a new cluster, in the simulations.

The elbow rule can be used recursively, first to detect the number of “main” clusters in the data set, then to detect the number of subclusters within each cluster. The strength of the signal (the height of the red bar) is typically very low if the *v*^′(*m*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si161.png)'s have a low variance. In that case, there is no set of values outshining all the others, that is, no true elbow. For an application of this methodology to detect the number of clusters, see a recent article of Chikumbo [\[1\]](#Chp018_361-386_B9780443218576000229.xhtml#br0005). An alternative to the elbow rule, to detect the number of clusters, is the silhouette method \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silhouette_\(clustering\))\].

I now explain how the strength of the elbow signal (the height of the red bars in [Fig. 18.7](#Chp018_361-386_B9780443218576000229.xhtml#f0060)) is computed. First, compute the first- and second-order differences of the function *v*^′(*m*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si161.png): *δ*[1](*m*) = *v*^′(*m* − 1) − *v*^′(*m*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si169.png) for *m* > 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si170.png), and *δ*[2](*m*) = *δ*[1](*m* − 1) − *δ*[1](*m*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si171.png) for *m* > 2![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si172.png). The strength of the elbow signal, at position *m* > 1![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si170.png), is *ρ*[1](*m*) = max \[0, *δ*[2](*m* + 1) − *δ*[1](*m* + 1)\]![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si173.png). I used a dampened version of *ρ*[1](*m*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si174.png), namely *ρ*[2](*m*) = *ρ*[1](*m*)/*m*![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si175.png), to favor cluster structures with few large clusters, over many smaller clusters. Larger clusters can always be broken down into multiple clusters, using the same clustering algorithm. The data, including formulas, charts, and simulation of the Brownian motion is in the spreadsheet PB\_inference.xls on my GitHub repository, [here](https://github.com/VincentGranville/Point-Processes/tree/main/Spreadsheets). See the Elbow\_Brownian tab. You can modify the parameters highlighted in orange in the spreadsheet: in this case, *γ* in cell B16. Note that *λ* is set to *Γ*(1 + *γ*)![Image](images/B9780443218576000229/si176.png) in cell B17.

## 18.7 Advice to beginners

In this section, I provide guidance to machine learning beginners. After finishing the reading and the accompanying classes (including successfully completing the student projects), you should have a strong exposure to the most important topics, many covered in detail in this book. At this point, you should be able to pursue the learning on your own – a never ending process even for top experts – in particular, with the advice provided in Section [18.7.1](#Chp018_361-386_B9780443218576000229.xhtml#s0140).

### 18.7.1 Getting started and learning how to learn

The first step is to install Python on your laptop. While it is possible to use Jupyter notebooks instead \[[Wiki](https://jupyter.org/)\], this option is limited and will not give you the full experience of writing and testing serious code as in a professional, business environment. Once Python is installed, you can install Notebooks from within Python, on the command prompt with the instruction python -m pip install jupyter, see [here](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/how-to-install-jupyter-notebook-in-windows/). You may want to have it installed on a virtual machine on your laptop: see VMware virtual machine installation [here](https://www.vmware.com/products/workstation-player.xhtml). Or you can access Notebooks remotely via Google Collab, see [here](https://colab.research.google.com/notebooks/) and [here](https://colab.research.google.com/).

Installing Python depends on your system. See the official Python.org website [here](https://www.python.org/downloads/) to get started and download Python. On my Windows laptop, I first installed the Cygwin environment (see [here](https://www.cygwin.com/) how to install it) to emulate a Unix environment. That way, I can use Cygwin windows instead of the Windows command prompt \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cmd.exe)\]. The benefits is that it recognizes Unix commands. An alternative to Cygwin is [Ubuntu](https://ubuntu.com/download). You could also use the [Anaconda](https://www.anaconda.com/products/distribution) environment.

Either way, you want to save your first Python program as a text file, say test.py. To run it, type in Python test.py in the command window. You need to be familiar with basic file management systems, to create folders and subfolders as needed. Shortly, you will need to install Python libraries on your machine. Some of the most common ones are pandas, scipy, seaborn, numpy, random, and matplotlib. You can create your own too, as illustrated in Section [5.4.3](#Chp005_83-102_B9780443218576000096.xhtml). In your Python script, only use the needed libraries. Typically, they are listed at the beginning of your code, as in the following example:

![](images/B9780443218576000229/fx011.jpg)

To install (say) the numpy library, type in pip install numpy in the Windows command prompt.

#### 18.7.1.1 Getting help

One of the easiest ways to learn more and solve new problems using Python or any programming language is to use the Internet. For instance, when I designed my sound generation algorithm in Python (see Section [18.1](#Chp018_361-386_B9780443218576000229.xhtml#s0010)), I googled keywords such as “Python sound processing”. I quickly discovered a number of libraries and tutorials, ranging from simple to advanced. Over time, you discover websites that consistently offer solutions suited to your needs, and you tend to stick with them, until you “graduate” to the next level of expertise and use new resources.

It is important to look at the qualifications of people posting their code online, and how recent these posts are. You have to discriminate between multiple sources, and identify those that are not good or outdated. Usually, the best advice comes from little comments posted in discussion forums, as a response to solutions offered by some users. Of course, you can also post your own questions. Two valuable sources here to stay are GitHub and StackExchange. There are also numerous Python groups on LinkedIn and Reddit. In the end, after spending some time searching for sound libraries in Python, I have found solutions that do not require any special library: numpy can process sound files. It took me a few hours to discover all I needed on the Internet.

Finally, the official documentation that comes with Python libraries can be useful, especially if you want to use special parameters and understand the inner workings (and limitations) rather than using them as black-boxes with the default settings. For instance, when looking at model-free parameter estimation for time series (using optimization techniques), I quickly discovered the curve\_fit function from the Scipy library. It did not work well on my unusual data sets (see Section [1.3.3.2](#Chp001_1-34_B9780443218576000059.xhtml)). I discovered, in the official online documentation, several settings to improve the performance. Still unsatisfied with the results (due to numerical instability in my case), I searched for alternatives and discovered that the swarm optimization technique (an alternative to curve\_fit) is available in the Pyswarms library. In the end, testing these libraries on rich synthetic data allows you to find what works best for your data.

I also offer classes related to this book, see [here](https://mltechniques.com/2022/09/29/course-intuitive-machine-learning/). This is another option to learn more and get answers to your questions. See also how I solve a new problem step by step and find the relevant code, in Section [14.4.3](#Chp014_259-276_B9780443218576000187.xhtml).

#### 18.7.1.2 Beyond python

Python has become the standard language for machine learning. Getting familiar with the R programming language will make you more competitive on the job market. Section [18.2](#Chp018_361-386_B9780443218576000229.xhtml#s0030) shows you how to create videos and better-looking charts in R. Finally, machine learning professionals should know at least the basics of SQL, since many jobs still involve working with traditional databases.

In particular, in one of the companies I was working for, I wrote a script that would accept SQL code as input (in text file format) to run queries against the Oracle databases, and trained analysts on how to use it in place of the dashboard they were familiar with. They were still using the dashboard (Toad in this case) to generate the SQL code, but run the actual queries with my script. The queries were now running 10 times faster: the productivity gain was tremendous.

To summarize, Python is the language of choice for machine learning, R is the language of statisticians, and SQL is the language of business and data analysts.

### 18.7.2 Automated data cleaning and exploratory analysis

It is said that data scientists spend 80% of their time on data cleaning and **exploratory analysis** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exploratory_data_analysis)\]. This should not be the case. To the beginner, it looks like each new data set comes with a new set of challenges. Over time, you realize that there are only so many potential issues. Automating the data cleaning step can save you a lot of time, and eliminate boring, repetitive tasks. A good Python script allows you to automatically take care of most problems. Here, I review the most common ones.

First, you need to create a summary table for all features taken separately: the type (numerical, categorical data, text, or mixed). For each feature, get the top 5 values, with their frequencies. It could reveal a wrong or unassigned zip-code such as 99999. Look for other special values such as NaN (not a number), N/A, an incorrect date format, missing values (blank), or special characters. For instance, accented characters, commas, dollar, percentage signs, and so on, can cause issues with text parsing and **regular expression** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regular_expression)\]. Compute the minimum, maximum, median, and other percentiles for numerical features. Check for values that are out-of-range: if possible, get the expected range from your client before starting your analysis. Use **checksums** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checksum)\] if possible, with encrypted fields such as credit card numbers or ID fields.

A few Python libraries can take care of this, in particular, Pandas-Profiling, Sweetviz, and D-Tale. See [here](https://medium.com/@karteekmenda93/exploratory-data-analysis-tools-83ef538c879f) for details.

The next step is to look at interactions between features. Compute all cross-correlations, and check for redundant or duplicate features that can be ignored. Look for IDs or keys that are duplicate or almost identical. Also two different IDs might have the same individual attached to them. This could reveal typos in your data. Working with a table of common typos can help. Also, collect data using prepopulated fields in web forms whenever possible, as opposed to users manually typing in their information such as state, city, zip-code, or date. Finally, check for misaligned fields. This happens frequently in NLP problems, where data such as URLs are parsed and stored in CSV files before being uploaded in databases. Now you can standardize your data.

Sometimes, the data has issues beyond your control. When I was working at Wells Fargo, internet session IDs generated by the Tealeaf software were broken down into multiple small sessions, resulting in wrong userIDs and very short Internet sessions. Manually simulating such sessions and looking how they were tracked in the database, helped solve this mystery, leading to correct analyses. Sometimes, the largest population segment is entirely missing in the database. For instance, in Covid data, people never tested who recovered on their own (the vast majority of the population in the early days) did not show up in any database, giving a lethality rate of 6% rather than the more correct 1%, with costly public policy implications. Use common sense and out-of-the-box thinking to detect such issues, and let stakeholders known about it. Alternate data sources should always be used whenever possible. In this case, sewage data – a proxy data set – provides the answer.

### 18.7.3 Example of simple analysis: marketing attribution

Sometimes, a simple solution that requires a few days of work as opposed to several weeks, easy to understand as in explainable AI, is good enough and makes everyone happy. When working for NBC, I was asked to perform some **marketing attribution** analysis. The project, also referred to as marketing mix modeling \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marketing_mix_modeling)\] consisted of assessing the individual impact of 20 different channels – in this case specific TV shows – on Internet traffic growth.

Each week, about 12 TV shows were used to boost traffic to the target website. Collected data included the GRP (gross rating point, measuring the size of the TV audience attached to a particular TV show) and the number of unique and new users on the website. The selected TV shows were booked well in advance based on inventory availability, and could not be tested separately: in short, it was not possible to use **experimental design** techniques \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Design_of_experiments)\] such as **A/B testing** \[[Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A/B_testing)\].

I created a **flag vector** for each week, with 20 components: one for each potential TV show. The component associated to a specific TV show was set to 1 if it was used during the week in question, and to 0 otherwise. I then compared weeks that were in a similar time period (to avoid seasonality effects) after excluding weeks with major holidays. My summary table included pairs of weeks, say weeks A and B, as well as the increase or decrease in Internet traffic between A and B. Also, I selected pairs {A, B} with the same mix of TV shows except for one that was either absent in A but not in B, or the other way around.

It was then possible, for a given TV show, to see if using it in a specific week was associated with traffic growth more frequently than traffic decline. This led to the identification of the best and worst performing TV shows. Eventually “Law & Order” was found to be the winner, and used more frequently whenever possible.
